Place of publication: Devakōṭṭai;
Country of publication: India. Tattvaprakāśaḥ.
Accompanied by the *Tātparyadīpikā* composed by Śrī Kumāra and the commentary (*vṛtti*) authored by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya:
[He is] the single mass of consciousness, all-pervading, eternal, perpetually manifest, the Lord, and peaceful.
Victorious is Śambhu, the sole seed of the world and the benefactor of all. || 1 ||
The *Tātparyadīpikā*: Salutations to the god Śarva, the cause of the three causes;
to Śambhu, who is stainless and whose nature is eternal bliss and consciousness.
Having bowed to Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśa, and the goddess Sarasvatī,
this *Tattvaprakāśatātparyadīpikā* is composed by me.

He performs a hymn of praise to his chosen deity for the sake of the unimpeded completion and widespread propagation of this treatise he intends to begin—beginning with the words "Ciddhana" (the Mass of Consciousness).
Now, one might ask: how can the hymn of praise and prostration to a chosen deity be the cause for the completion and propagation of a treatise?

How is this understood? We reply: it is understood from scripture inferred from the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). At the commencement of a treatise, the performance by the learned of such acts as the praise and salutation of their chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) would not be possible without its being the cause for the desired completion and so forth of that work. Therefore, its status as that cause is known precisely from scripture, and not from anything else.

Because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible here [for its direct perception], its understanding arises from the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "For those engaged in the practice of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), no misfortune occurs. Likewise, since the completion [of a work] is an occasional occurrence, it must depend upon a cause;

and since no other [cause] is possible, it is postulated that this is a specific merit (*dharmaviśeṣa*) produced by acts such as salutation. How, then, does that [merit] serve as the cause for that [completion]?

To this it is replied: Prostration and so forth—whether physical, verbal, or mental—by accomplishing a specific dharma (merit), they eliminate the non-dharma that serves as a cause for obstacles and thus attain the status of being causes for completion and so on; for such [prostration] is desired, and because dharma is the cause of what is desired. If it is asked, "How is it then that in some cases, even when prostration has been performed, there is no completion? [the answer follows].

We say it is due to a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in that [cause]. Just as in the case of the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and others, when the means for achieving rain and so forth have been performed, the absence of rain and so forth leads to the postulation of a deficiency in that [performance] or the postulation of an abundance of obstructing demerit (*adharma*), so it is here as well; thus there is no contradiction. If it is asked: "How then is there completion in some cases despite the absence of salutation and so forth, given that an effect cannot arise in the absence of its cause? [the answer follows:]

It is not so; for even in the absence of a verbal salutation there, a physical or mental one can be inferred, since otherwise the completion [of the work] would be impossible. If it is argued, "In that case, let that very [mental or physical salutation] suffice here as well; what is the use of a verbal one that merely results in the bulkiness of the text?", we say: no, for the verbal one is adopted because it serves other purposes.

For instance, even one who proceeds to listen while forgetting the praise and salutation to the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) has nonetheless performed that salutation by the mere recitation of the first three verses; thus, since another purpose is possible, there is no contradiction in its inclusion.

Now, regarding the meaning of the words: "a mass of consciousness" (*cidghana*) means one who is a solid mass of sentience (*caitanya*), whose essence is sentience, that is to say, pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). This is established by such scriptural passages as, "This very [Self] is supreme bliss, without interior or exterior, a solid mass of knowledge" (*vijñānaghana*), and by such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as, "The auspicious [Lord], devoid of beginning and end, pure, consisting of consciousness and bliss. Thus, the nature of the Lord Śambhu as being of the form of consciousness is proven. Likewise—

By the auspicious author of the Sūtras—through the first aphorism, "The Self is consciousness" (1.1)—the nature of the Self as being of the form of consciousness has been described; thus, it is established that He is "a mass of consciousness" (*cidghana*).
"One" (*eka*) means "without a second" (*advitīya*). As it is said: "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and "I am one."
"I existed in the first month, and I shall exist; there is nothing whatsoever other than me" (*Atharva Upaniṣad* 1);

according to such scriptural passages. Likewise, in the *Śvetāśvatara*: "Rudra is one; he does not stand for a second" (3.2). In the *Traisambaka* chapter of the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā*: "Rudra is indeed one; he does not stand for a second" (1.8.6.1). And in the *Nīlarudra*: "All is Rudra; to him..."

Since the non-duality of Śiva is established by such passages as "Salutation be to Rudra" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.16.1), the oneness of Śiva is logically consistent. Nor should it be argued that the non-duality of Śiva is untenable because various objects appear through means of valid cognition such as perception; for it is possible for even a single entity to appear in manifold ways due to differences in its states. Just as [the same person appears differently]—

Just as a lump of clay appears in many ways through its various states of existence— such as a jar, a bowl, a pot, a wall, or a drum— and just as a single lump of gold appears through its various states of existence— such as a ring, an earring, a bracelet, or a crown— so too, although Rudra is one and existent, he is said to be "the jar exists," "the cloth exists," "the granary exists," "it exists," and so forth.

Since manifestation in manifold ways occurs through the distinction of states— both by direct perception as a totality and by such scriptural passages as "That which is one, the wise call many" (Ṛgveda 1.164.46) and "Being one,

they conceive it as many" (Ṛgveda 10.114.5)— there is no possibility of contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, especially given that the Veda is of non-human origin and thus free from the possibility of error.

Because the non-duality of Śiva is established by the powerful mass of the Vedas, which are intrinsically valid, and because the plurality established by weak means such as perception— which is contrary to that [Vedic teaching]— is necessarily sublated; for thus, the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of Vedic sentences is demonstrated, and by that, the causes of invalidity—

Since knowledge, passion, hatred, and the like are impossible within the Vedic sentences, there is no possibility of their lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). For a defect does not arise inherently (*svataḥ*) in a word, because it is possible to establish a rule regarding the authority and non-authority of the statements of both trustworthy and untrustworthy persons. Indeed, [the determination of truth] cannot occur through inherent defects or excellences without following the presence or absence of defects residing in the speaker.

The determination of validity and invalidity is possible only if one accepts [the possibility of] both; for being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*) or an unreliable person (*anāpta*) is not the cause of that [determination]. Since the eternal collection of the Vedas cannot be the work of an unreliable person, invalidity is impossible. Given its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), the non-duality of Śiva established by it is proven by powerful means of knowledge; therefore, no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge is possible. Nor is it the case that...
It should not be argued that because of the absence of an author, there is an absence of excellence (*guṇa*), and consequently an absence of validity (*prāmāṇya*);
for we observe that in one who has mastered words and their meanings, the cognition of an object arises as soon as they hear that sentence.
Furthermore, the presence of excellence is not the cause of validity, since its purpose is merely the avoidance of defects (*doṣa*) which are the cause of invalidity.

Likewise, because it is established by the Veda which is devoted to that [truth], the purport (*tātparya*) of the statement propounding the non-duality of Śiva is understood from the presence of the sixfold marks (*liṅga*). As it has been stated by those who know the Nyāya:
"The beginning, middle, and end; repetition; novelty; the fruit; explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); and logical consistency—these are the marks."
Regarding the determination of the intended meaning (*tātparya-nirṇaya*): these indicative marks (*liṅga*) indeed exist within the Śruti passages that establish the non-duality of Rudra.
For instance: "Śarva is indeed Rudra" (*Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* 10.11); "Puruṣa is indeed Rudra" (*Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* 10.11);
"For all this is Rudra" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.16.1). These constitute the group known as the connection with the beginning, middle, and end.

The indicative mark of purport (*tātparyaliṅga*) is perceived. Likewise, because of the repeated instruction in such passages as "All this, indeed, is Rudra" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.16.1) and "For all this is Rudra" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.16.1), the indicative mark of purport characterized by repetition (*abhyāsa*) is established.
Similarly: "The universe, the being, the world, the manifold, that which has been born and is being born in many ways" (*Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad*).

Furthermore, the indicative mark of the purport (*tātparyaliṅga*) is established by the nature of the meaning of such scriptural passages as "For all this is indeed Rudra" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 10.16.1). Likewise:
"One who knows him thus becomes immortal here" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 3.1.3); "By knowledge one finds immortality" (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 2.4); "The Self is to be known;
the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 7.1.3); and "He does not return again" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* [8.15.1]).

Furthermore, because the fruits of the knowledge of the identity of Śiva and the Self are heard in such passages as "And again, at the end, there is the cessation of all illusion" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.10), "He who is indeed the one [Lord] in both emergence and existence" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.1), and "Those who know this become immortal" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.1), the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of those scriptures is established as being directed toward that [identity]. In that state, what delusion, what sorrow? (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.18).

The fact that there exists an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for praise, such as "for one who perceives oneness" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 7), establishes that the scriptural statement regarding oneness has its purport (*tātparya*) in oneness.

Likewise, its establishment is also due to the existence of explanatory passages for censure, such as "He who makes even a slight distinction within this [Self] has cause for fear; indeed, he who lacks knowledge has cause for fear" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.7). Similarly, "All is indeed... [and so forth].

The fact that Rudra is the self of all, as established by such statements as "Rudra" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.16.1), would otherwise be contradicted by another statement, namely, "Puruṣa alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.15; Ṛg Veda 8.4.17). In this regard, the lack of contradiction is demonstrated by the passage, "Puruṣa indeed is Rudra" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 10.11); thus, there exists the indicative mark of purport known as "logical consistency" (*upapatti*).

It is established. Furthermore, the statement "Rudra is Being" (*Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* 13.2) serves as a supporting authority, resolving the contradiction with other scriptural passages that establish the non-duality of Being, such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1). Likewise, [it is supported] by such texts as "I know this great Puruṣa" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 3.7).

By means of the Vedic statement ending with "There is no other path for going" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.7), which establishes the non-duality of the Great Person, the text [the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad] provides the supporting argument that resolves the contradiction regarding Rudra being the "Great One" (mahas) in the passage "Being Rudra, he is the Great One" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 13.2). By this, the intention of this scripture is all the more clearly established as being the non-duality of Rudra.
Therefore, this non-duality of Śiva, established through restatement (anuvāda), must be accepted; otherwise, it would be purposeless.
As it has been said by Ārya [Nāgārjuna]:
"An unknown object is fruitful when repeatedly corroborated by examples."
"How can that which is heard as following a sequence of prior and posterior [states] be said to be otherwise?

Thus, there is no room for sublation by weaker means such as perception (*pratyakṣa*). Or, as it is said regarding the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*): "O Rudra! There is nothing more powerful than you" (*Ṛgveda* 2.33.10; *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 4.5.7); "Out of fear of him the wind blows, out of fear the sun rises."

From the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, beginning with "Out of fear of him, fire and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run away" (2.7–8), and from the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad], the supreme preeminence of the Blessed Lord Maheśvara Rudra is understood. For instance: "He who alone, possessing the net, rules by his ruling powers, rules all worlds by his ruling powers" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.1), and so forth.

"Those who do not declare the Pinākin to be superior to all, but remember him as common [to all], enter into you along with your wife. Thus it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*. Therefore, his preeminence is to be believed.
He is called *vyāpī* because he possesses pervasiveness (*vyāpti*), meaning he is omnipresent; that is, without moving, he possesses conjunction with all material forms.

It is all-pervading and yet non-moving, because it exists everywhere like space; for there are scriptural texts such as, "Like the ether, it is all-pervading and eternal," and so forth. And there are traditional texts (smṛti) such as: "He alone, the one of great prowess, dwells within all beings—both the stationary and the moving—endowed with manifold forms. Nor should it be said that, like space, this [Self] is insentient.

Because it would contradict the scriptural texts that establish the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*). Alternatively, "pervasiveness" (*vyāpitva*)—meaning the state of being the essential nature of all things—is stated as the reason for [the Self's] oneness.
And that [is expressed thus]:
"He is indeed the light; he was the sacrificer; he is Mātariśvan; he rises as the sun; he is the moon; he is the earth."
"He, the all-pervading space, has entered all beings"—thus it is established by the scriptural statement of the *liṅga-sūkta* which sets forth the eightfold form (*mūrty-aṣṭaka*).

"Eternal" (*nitya*) means indestructible (*avināśin*), according to the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "The perishable is the primary matter (*pradhāna*); the immortal and imperishable is Hara" (1.10). Alternatively, eternity may mean pervading the three periods of time, or being devoid of that [temporal limitation] in all things.

The realization of this [Self] follows from such scriptural passages as "whose self is continuous throughout the times," and from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad passage beginning with "He is seen as beyond the three times, indeed partless" (6.5).
Regarding the term "constantly risen" (*satatodita*): he is so called because his rising—that is, his manifestation—occurs constantly, at all times.

"His light neither rises nor sets" means that he is self-luminous. This is understood from the Vedic scripture, "In this regard, this person is self-luminous" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9), and from the Smṛti of the *Īśvaragītā*, "The Supreme Person is all-pervading" (2.2.17). Regarding the term "Lord" (*prabhu*):
lordship consists in the possession of unimpeded sovereignty, characterized by the capacity to bring about all factors of action, such as the agent, the object, and the instrument. And that—

This is established by the Śruti: "Just as a spider emits [its web], even so does He emit" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7), and by Smṛti such as: "He is the cause of saṃsāra when transmigrating, and the cause of liberation when at peace; He is born, He generates, and He is born again and again. Furthermore, His capacity to produce all effects without instruments and the like is demonstrated by the text: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking."
"He thought, 'Shall I now create the worlds? He created these worlds" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1)—thus it is understood from such scriptural passages.

Or rather, [it refers to] the agency of one who is actionless (*niṣkriyakartṛtva*). As it is said by the wise: "Just as a magnet is an auxiliary cause through its mere proximity, so too is Śiva for this [creation], even though he is motionless. Just as fragrance [is perceived] by its mere presence...
It arises for the sake of agitation; because it does not benefit the mind, he is therefore the Supreme Lord.

His sovereignty is understood from such Purāṇas and Āgamas as these, because [in his case] fatigue and the like are impossible. Furthermore, the state of being an agent engaged in activity constitutes a lack of sovereignty due to the presence of fatigue and so forth.
He states the reason for this: "He is peaceful" (*śānta*). Since Śiva is devoid of all activity, he is therefore the Sovereign (*prabhu*).

Alternatively, the possibility that the Blessed One might be subject to transmigratory existence— due to his connection with activities such as the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, which would entail the possession of a body and so forth under the influence of karma— is refuted by the word "peaceful" (*śānta*). For the Supreme Lord, who is omniscient and whose nature is indifferent due to being devoid of all activity, there is no [transmigration] through the activity belonging to another.

Regarding the phrase "the origin of saṃsāra": this is because that [Self] is understood from such scriptural passages as, "That which is partless, actionless, tranquil, devoid of qualities, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19). Likewise, it is stated in the *Īśvaragītā* Smṛti: "Liberated sages perceive their own Self according to ultimate reality—the immutable Self, free from modification, devoid of suffering, and full of bliss" (2.2.13). Or, [it may refer to] the liberated one (*mukta*).

Its realization comes from such scriptural passages as, "That one is unborn, unmanifest, eternally vanished, yet its vision is never lost," and from such traditional texts as, "I am the immutable Brahman— peaceful, stainless, actionless, undecaying, solitary, the Blessed One, liberated, absolute, and the Supreme Lord" (Īśvaragītā 2.8.2).

"Victorious" (*jayati*) means that He exists with supreme excellence. This is understood from such scriptural passages as, "There is nothing whatsoever higher than Him" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 3.9) and "Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great" (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 2.20). The wise say that the mind is superior to all the senses; the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is superior even to the mind, and the Great One (*mahat*) is superior to the ego. Greater than the Great One... [is He].
Beyond the supreme unmanifest is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa; beyond the Puruṣa is the Blessed Prāṇa, whose this entire world is.

This is also supported by such Smṛti passages as: "Space is higher than the vital breath; Agni, the Lord, is beyond space; there is nothing higher than the Lord" (Īśvara-gītā 2.3.18–20). Furthermore, the meaning of the root *ji* (to conquer) here is either "overpowering" because he overpowers knowledge and the like when his own worshippers attain the vision of the ultimate reality through hearing and other means, or "existing," as he exists having brought everything under his own control.

Or it is "subjugation" (*vaśīkāra*). Likewise, it is "acceptance" (*svīkāra*), meaning that at the time of dissolution and emergence, the entire web of effects is withdrawn into one's own self and remains there.

Regarding the phrase "the sole seed of the world": it is the one primary seed, the cause, the root cause of the world—that is, of the collection of effects such as time and so forth. Alternatively, it is the "sole seed of the worlds," being both the single agent (*kartā*) and the seed as the material cause (*upādāna*).

That is to say, it is the cause of the objective basis (*nimitta-upādāna*). For it is stated in scripture: "That from which these beings are born, that into which they enter when they depart" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.1);

and "Rudra is one, death is one, the unmanifest is the single seed; the God is one, he alone is the universe" (*Īśvara Gītā* 2.8.16); and from the *Īśvara Gītā* tradition: "For from this everything is born, and into this very thing it dissolves" (2.2.6).
The Supreme Lord's status as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world is understood from such scriptural passages as: "The one God, generating heaven and earth" (Ṛgveda 10.81.3);

"With these songs, [we praise] the Father of the world" (Ṛgveda 6.49.10); and "He is the maker of all, the knower of all, whose source is the Self" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.16). Furthermore, His status as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) is understood from such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as: "At the time of creation, He brings about the creation."

Since the Supreme Lord, whose body is *māyā*, can be both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe, there is no consequence of His being subject to modification (*vikāritva*) and so forth; He is the benefactor of all. He is so described because He bestows grace—namely liberation and the like—upon all sentient and insentient beings. And the author will state later: "Liberation for the individual souls" (Śloka 35). Now, if...

If [God] acts for the sake of bestowing grace for His own purpose, then His state of being all-blissful would be lost, because the happiness to be accomplished by that act did not exist prior to its production. On the other hand, if there were no purpose for Himself, activity would be impossible. As it has been said by those learned in Nyāya: "Not even a fool acts without aiming at a purpose; if the aim of a purpose were abandoned, then [God] would be of the nature of bliss [only]."

This is not so, because activity [on the part of the Lord] is possible through compassion or by his very nature. Now, if he acts for the sake of favoring others out of compassion, then he should create only liberation; he should not create the world consisting of *saṃsāra*, because that would be unjust. For instance, those who act out of compassion preceded by the perception of suffering do so solely for the purpose of eliminating that suffering.

Activity is appropriate, but not for the sake of producing that suffering; therefore, the creation of a world consisting of suffering is not logical. This is not so, because the creation of the world is justified by the fact that liberation—which consists in the cessation of ignorance—depends upon knowledge and its causes.
For instance, direct (non-conceptual) knowledge is indeed the cause of liberation, and this directness...

When the latent impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃskāra*) are dispelled through profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*), [the knowledge of the Self] arises. And profound meditation is possible once the knowledge of the Self as Śiva has been produced through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*). These two, in turn, arise from the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*). That purification comes about through the performance of obligatory and occasional duties (*nitya-naimittika-karma*) while avoiding optional and prohibited actions (*kāmya-pratiṣiddha-karma*).

The performance of those [Vedic rites] is preceded by the protection of cattle, crops, and the king; therefore, all of this is subsidiary to liberation (*mokṣa-śeṣa*), and thus the creation of the world is not purposeless. Furthermore, the scriptural injunctions regarding desires that yield worldly fruits—such as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā* [offering]" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.4.6.1)—were introduced in order to engage on the Vedic path those Brahmins whose minds were intent upon worldly results.

And for those who are eager for the fruit of heaven, [the scriptures provide] the injunctions for rites such as the Śyena and Āghāra intended to destroy enemies, in order to set them upon the Vedic path. Then, when mental purity has been achieved through the sequence of performing prescribed acts such as ritual bathing, the destruction of sin, the anvādhāna, and the agnihotra, and when desire has ceased—

Through the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nityanaimittika-karma*), when the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*) in the form of the desire to know the Self (*ātmavividiṣā*) arises,

and when the knowledge of Śiva as the Self is produced by means of hearing and reflection (*śravaṇa-manana*), then, following the removal of ignorance and its latent impressions (*avidyā-tat-saṃskāra*) through the practice of meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), liberation (*mokṣa*) occurs upon the direct realization (*aparokṣya*) of Śiva as the Self. Thus it has been said:

In the *Mokṣadharma* and other sections [of the Mahābhārata], it is said: "Dharma is prescribed everywhere; heaven is the fruit that arises from truth. For dharma, which has many doors, there is no action here that is fruitless" (*Mahābhārata* 12.174.2). In this regard, those who engage in ritual actions—whether Vedic (*śrauta*) or traditional (*smārta*)—as enjoined by Maheśvara, are liberated; whereas those who do not so engage continue to transmigrate.

This has been stated at the beginning of the *Aitareya Upaniṣad* and elsewhere: "This is the path, this is the action; therefore, one should not be negligent, nor should one overstep it, for those of old who overstepped perished" (1.1.1), and so forth. Alternatively, its activity [proceeds] because its very nature is benevolence (*anugraha*).
In that case, since it depends upon other causes, there is no contingency of the entire world attaining liberation simultaneously.
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Vāyavīya*: "If Śiva were of the nature of mere grace, he would not liberate everyone;
for the very nature of things is the cause of what is to come. Indeed, a creator cannot bring about an object that is non-existent by its own nature.
Just as the sun causes the lotuses to bloom with its rays, yet they do not all bloom at the same time."
"According to their own respective natures; thus Śiva liberates only those whose impurities are matured, not others," and so forth (*Śivavimarśinī* 1.31.55–57).
Regarding the term *śambhu*: *śam* means happiness; he in whom that [happiness] exists is *śambhu*, meaning that his very nature is bliss (*ānanda*).

The realization of that [Brahman] follows from such scriptural passages as, "Consciousness, Bliss is Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28), and from such Smṛti texts as the *Īśvaragītā*, which state, "It is declared to be blissful, unborn, unmanifest, and partless. Now, an objection may be raised: if Śiva consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), then because he would take the form of the quality of *sattva*—which is of the nature of affection—he would possess attributes (*saguṇatva*). Consequently, defects such as transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth would necessarily follow. For instance:

The Sāṃkhya teachers have stated: "The *guṇas* consist of pleasure (*prīti*), pain (*aprīti*), and dejection (*viṣāda*); they serve the purposes of illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and restraint (*niyama*);

and their functions consist of mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 12). This is not so, because the words "pleasure" (*prīti*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*) have different meanings. To explain: [the former refers to] impermanent, surpassable happiness produced by the contact of the senses with objects.

Some maintain that there is no room for the aforementioned objection, because the word *prīti* denotes the bliss whose essential nature is eternal, unsurpassed, and of a single constant form, which is what is expressed by the word *ānanda*. Others, however, hold that when the pure quality of *sattva* has been transformed through contact with sense objects caused by merit, the eternal bliss itself is reflected therein and taught by the word *prīti*; and all other beings [partake] of this very *ānanda*.
Based on the Vedic scripture, "They subsist upon the measure" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32), it is held that the quality of *sattva* does not consist of happiness itself;
rather, it is designated as being of the nature of happiness because it serves as the substratum for the reflection of happiness. || 1 ||
Having bowed to Śiva, who transcends the thirty-six principles and is accompanied by his Śakti,
I shall compose a clear and concise commentary on the *Tattvaprakāśa*.

Since this has been explained otherwise by others who are permeated by the latent impressions of non-duality (advaita) but are devoid of knowledge of our established tenets (siddhānta), therefore we have made this effort.

In this regard, first of all, the Teacher, for the sake of the unimpeded completion of the treatise he intends to compose, praises with the first verse the Supreme Śiva— who transcends all categories of reality, who is partless, and who is the cause for the emergence of the established scriptures— describing him as "the mass of consciousness."

By the word *cit*, knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) are here intended. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Consciousness (*caitanya*) consists of the nature of knowledge and action" (Vi. 2.5). He whose body is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*) is thus called *cidghana*. However, he is not insentient like the [entities] of those who propound God as the cause of karma and time; for that which is unconscious cannot function without being presided over by a conscious principle. Not...

Furthermore, it is not logical for Him to undergo a body consisting of the *bindu* (the point of origin) and so forth, because that would entail the consequence of His being non-sovereign (*anīśvara*). Moreover, if He were to require another agent—whether that agent were Himself or someone else—it would result in the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He is "one" (*eka*), meaning without a second.
Nor is the position of multiple gods (*anekeśvara*) tenable, for even in the case of chariots and other such things created by many agents, there is a conformity to a single will.

Because [the effect] does not arise without [a cause]. As it has been said: "Where there are many leaders, all of whom consider themselves wise, and they all desire greatness, the undertaking clearly comes to ruin. By this, the position of the *pravāheśvara* (the Lord as the continuous flow) is also refuted, because since sovereignty consists in the attainment of the manifestation of one's own nature, its destruction is impossible. It is all-pervading and omnipresent, but not...

It is not limited by the body like that of the Jainas (Kṣapaṇakas) and others, nor does it possess the property of contraction and expansion, because such a [soul] would entail defects such as insentience and impermanence. It is eternal, devoid of beginning and end; it is not momentary like that of the Buddhists and others, for one who perishes at the very moment of birth cannot possibly be the creator of the universe. Now, [an objection]:

Even those whose selves are liberated are likewise [dependent on another], and therefore he says: "Ever-arisen" (*satatodita*), meaning eternally liberated. He is not like those liberated souls who are freed by the grace of another Lord, for that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). "The Lord" (*prabhu*) means one whose nature is to be sovereign;
the sense is that he is not impelled by another Lord, for the very reason previously stated.

Nor is He a non-agent, for He is established precisely as the creator of the universe. He is "peaceful" (*śānta*), meaning free from passion, hatred, and the like. As it is said: "Delusion, pride, passion, despondency, emaciation, diversity, and joy—these seven are the innate impurities" (*Mālinīvijayottara-tantra*, VI.103–104). This is because the causes of those [impurities], such as *mala* and so forth, are impossible in His case. What [more could be said]?
If it is asked what the proof for the existence of such an Īśvara is, he says: "The sole seed of the world.

This means He is the efficient cause (*nimittakartā*) of the world. The intended meaning is as follows: having understood that the world is an effect because it possesses structure and so forth, one infers its efficient cause, known as Īśvara, by means of the reason that it is an effect. Whatever is composed of parts is [an effect].

[The universe is] an effect; for according to the logical principle (*nyāya*) that "whatever is an effect is produced by an agent," it is stated: "The universe, which is the subject of dispute, is preceded by an omniscient creator, because it is an effect—just as jars and other such effects are established as being effects for both of us. (One may infer from this [citation] that this is a verse from the *Pauṣkarāgama*, as indicated by the reference: *lu0 saṃ0*, *bhā0 2*, p. 120).
In the venerable *Mataṅga* as well, it is said: "The Lord, however, is the efficient cause" (*Viṣṇu-Ṣaṭka*, 6.99).

This doctrine of Īśvara has been explained by us in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*; it should be understood from that very source. He is the bestower of grace upon all. And here, "grace" (*anugraha*) is a term used figuratively to include creation and the other [cosmic functions] as well. Therefore:

The meaning is that He bestows both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) upon all souls through five functions known as creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace. Furthermore, His omniscience is established precisely because He is the agent of all things;

for it is impossible for that which is unknown to be a cause. And it has been said: "He is omniscient because He is the agent of all things, together with the means, the auxiliaries, and the results."

"What one knows, that alone one does"—this is well-established (*Mṛgendra-vṛtti* 5.13). Thus, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, is victorious; he exists in a state of supreme excellence for the very reasons already stated. || 1 ||
Victorious is that Śāmbhava fire, whose nature is knowledge and action, which neither arises nor perishes, and which neither extinguishes nor bestows extinction.

Since this first verse constitutes a summary of the entire meaning of the treatise, the *Tātparyadīpikā* explains the praise of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) indicated therein by means of the following verse; or alternatively, [it reveals] the partless [reality] under the guise of praising the chosen deity.

Having declared the reality of Śiva (śivatattva) as that which is to be attained, he now praises the light (tejas) which serves as the means for attaining it—light that consists of both the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala), and which abides in forms such as the jyotirliṅga—with the verse beginning "nodayati.
This is the meaning: that light neither rises nor manifests like the sun and other luminaries; nor does it perish or set.

He does not extinguish, nor is he liberated. Because of the absence of ignorance, its root—attachment and aversion—the activities prompted by them, merit and demerit, and the body, senses, and so forth that are subject to them, there is an absence of saṃsāra. And the absence of ignorance is due to omniscience. Alternatively, *nirvāṇa* is the negation of destruction characterized by decay; or rather, *nirvāṇa* is the absolute cessation (*ni-vāna*) of decay, which is deficiency.

That does not exist, because it is eternally of a single nature; and that [nature] exists because of its permanence. It bestows liberation (*nirvṛti*); "liberation" means release, and it bestows—that is, grants—that to its own worshippers. Its nature is knowledge and action, its nature is that of the knower and the agent;
that is the Śāmbhava splendor, belonging to Śambhu. It is superior to all other masses of splendor for the reasons already stated.

Alternatively, [the term] *sakala* refers to the form consisting of the *mantra*, which is of the nature of *śāmbhava-tejas*—that is to say, that which serves as the means for attaining that [state]. "It triumphs" (*jayati*) means that it exists above all else. Why? Because this form, unlike subsequent forms, lacks origination, destruction, and so forth; and that is because it consists of the Veda, and the Veda is eternal. || 2 ||

The commentary: Having thus introduced Śiva as the nature of the substrate (dharmin), [the author] now demonstrates, under the guise of praise, the state of dissolution of the nature of His attributes (dharma) and their functional power (sāmarthya)— beginning with the words "He does not cause to arise."

By the phrase "empty of arising and destruction," he demonstrates the distinction between that Śiva-tejas—which possesses consciousness as its essence—and the Buddhist cognition of the yogi. If this is so, one might ask: given the scriptural authority of the *Mṛgendrāgama* (which is cited here as "śruti"), namely the statement, "Consciousness, consisting of vision and action, belongs to him [Śiva] in his own self at all times" (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā* 2.5), what is the specific difference between the capacity of the Self and the capacity of Śiva?

To this he says: "It is extinguished, yet it does not grant extinction. This specific distinction of his from the power of the fettered (paśu) has been shown; namely, that which cannot be liberated by anyone else is here made manifest through this release from bonds. What follows from that? To this he says: "That Śāmbhava light, whose nature is knowledge and action, is victorious. Because it is the very attribute of consciousness, this too—
The meaning is that it consists of consciousness (*cidātmaka*). As it is heard [in scripture]: "Power is not insentient; it is of the nature of consciousness" (*Mṛgendratantravṛtti* 3.4). || 2 ||

I bow down with my whole being to that one, primordial, and conscious-natured [Prakṛti], by whom Śambhu is empowered to effect both the enjoyment and liberation of this multitude of bound souls (paśu). || 3 ||

Having thus praised Maheśvara, the *Tātparyadīpikā* [praises] Maheśvarī, the beloved of Mahādeva and mother of all worlds, who is eternally united with him: "This is your portion, O Rudra, together with your sister Ambikā; enjoy it" (*Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā* 3.57; *Taittirīya Saṃhitā*).

He praises [the Goddess] for the sake of attaining the fruit and to demonstrate the accompaniment of worship, praise, and so forth, as established by such scriptural passages as (Saṃhitā 1.8.6.12): "He is capable"—this is the meaning:

"I bow to that Śakti by which the Blessed Lord Maheśvara becomes capable and empowered to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon this host of bound souls (paśu). Thus, the necessity of performing the praise of Maheśvarī is established.

Because without her, it would be impossible for the Blessed One to be a bestower of grace. For instance, since it is impossible for Śiva—who is omnipresent, solitary, inactive, and of indifferent nature—to grant enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) to the multitude of bound souls (*paśu*), it is only through his possession of power (*śaktimat*) that such granting is logically possible. Therefore, he can only be a bestower of grace when accompanied by Power. "One" (*ekām*) means "without a second. Now, [an objection]:
If it is asked, "Since it was previously established that Śiva alone is everything—that is, the non-duality of Śiva—how is the expression of non-duality used here?
we reply: because every object exists as being essentially composed of both the Goddess and the God, the statement of their mutual non-duality is logically consistent.
To explain: liberation, characterized by abiding in the absolute Self, possesses the nature of the Goddess and the God by virtue of its form being consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*).

It exists. For if liberation lacked the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) would be lost, since pleasure alone is the primary human goal. Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of the nature of bliss in liberation, its status as a human goal is possible through the mere absence of contact with suffering, because the absence of suffering [is not itself the goal].

Because it is sought by persons only as something conducive to pleasure, it lacks the status of being the primary human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, since happiness alone is the primary human goal, liberation (*apavarga*) must be accepted as having the nature of bliss (*ānanda*). Furthermore, since that [bliss] does not possess the status of a human goal if it is not experienced, its experience must also be accepted; thus, for him, liberation consists of the identity of bliss and consciousness (*sukha-cid-ātmaka*).

The establishment of the identity of the Goddess and the God: therein, the Goddess is the consciousness of supreme bliss (*paramānanda-saṃvit*), and the God is the bliss of consciousness (*saṃvidānanda*). This is understood from the Purāṇas and Āgamas, which state: "I am indeed this Vidyā, the object of knowledge. Likewise, it is said in the *Devīmantrakalpa*: "Ādinātha is the Seer (*ṛṣi*); the Goddess Gāyatrī is declared to be the Metre (*chandas*); and the deity taught here is the consciousness of supreme bliss."
Thus it is said. And in the *Bhuvaneśvarīkalpa*: "The teachers have declared that *saṃvit* (consciousness), which denotes the very nature of awakening, is the deity.
Likewise, its realization comes from such Vedic scriptures as: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.28).
I bow to her who is experience—unborn, immeasurable, infinite, whose form is the bliss of the Self, and who is the canvas upon which the world of Mahat and the rest is painted by Māyā.

And from the words of the learned, this is understood. Nor should it be said that consciousness (*saṃvit*) and bliss (*sukha*) are mutually distinct from the Self and are of the nature of attributes of the Self; for such a claim contradicts scriptural passages such as "Śiva consists of consciousness and bliss," and because if their difference were admitted, it would follow that they could not possibly be its attributes. [Objection: But if consciousness and bliss are non-different, then it would be impossible for one to experience the other.

Does it not follow that, because [the Self] is self-luminous, there would be no distinction between liberation and worldly existence? Not so; for in the state of worldly existence, since the Self is as if non-existent—like a self-luminous crystal when not in proximity to a hibiscus flower—it is impossible to experience bliss, and thus there is no contradiction.
This is expressed in the passage: "Bliss is the nature of Brahman, and in that [bliss] one is established in liberation."

The statement of an authoritative source is seen in the *Yoginīhṛdayadīpikā* (3.108). This same statement also occurs in the *Kulārṇava* (5.80): "That form of Brahman is manifested in liberation," as established by the Śruti.
Now, let it be granted that the pure principle (*śuddhatattva*) has the nature of Goddess and God; but how can this be so for the causal principle (*kāraṇatattva*), which is mixed with Māyā?

If it is argued that [the Goddess] is the self-nature of the God, we reply that it is because she exists as both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*). As it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"Of this Śarva, the auspicious one who possesses eight forms and is a householder, Prakṛti is the divine wife, and the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest are the offspring.

For this very reason, the reality of the effect possesses the nature of both the Goddess and the God, by virtue of being composed of consciousness (*cit*) and non-consciousness (*acit*). And thus, regarding all beings...

The nature of being both Goddess and God arises from the two-fold form of the fourteen types of beings as body and embodied soul. Now, one might ask: how can living beings possess the nature of Goddess and God? We reply: because they are their manifestations (*vibhūti*). Thus says the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: "He was alone and did not find delight.
He desired a second. He became as large as this [universe]. He brought forth masculinity and femininity. Because he fell (*patana*) [into these forms], he is called the Lord (*pati*)."

"And his wife. She became a cow; the other became a bull. From those two, cattle were produced. She became a mare; the other became a stallion. From those two, horses were produced (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.3–4). Through such passages, because the appearance of the God and Goddess—the causes of the universe—who exist as the self of all living beings, is manifested, it is established that everything is their manifestation (*vibhūti*). And in the *Mānava* [Śrautasūtra]:...
"Dividing his own body into two parts, the Lord became a man with one half and a woman with the other; and upon her, the Lord generated Virāj. (Manusmṛti 1.32).
"The God [is] all that is masculine, and the Supreme Goddess is that which is feminine."
And from this statement in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*, its establishment [is known].

Because there is no difference between Maheśvarī and Maheśvara, they are described as both being non-dual. For instance, the single reality of Śiva is designated by words in the masculine, feminine, and neuter genders, since all entities are observed to possess these three genders.

Because, if it were to exist as any one [gender] by virtue of its ontological reality (*bhāvatayā*), there would be no possibility of a regulating factor (*niyāmaka*) for that. To explain: since the Śiva-principle lacks both femininity and neuter-ness, it is designated by the masculine term *Maheśvara*, just as a jar is designated by the word "jar. Nor should it be argued that the jar is designated by the word "jar" because of the presence of masculinity [in the jar].

Because masculinity is absolutely not perceived here [in the word *śivā*], even so, if one were to admit its existence, it would follow that even things such as a hare’s horn must exist. Likewise, because both masculinity and neuter-ness are absent, there is the conventional usage of the feminine word *śivā*.
Nor should it be argued that this is due to the actual presence of femininity in it; for words such as *śālā* (house) and *mālā* (garland) lack that [femininity] yet apply to their own referents.

Because it would follow that there is an absence of any linguistic function [for gender]. Nor should it be argued that this would entail the application of feminine words even to objects such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), for we accept that, like the word *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), such application occurs only in specific instances. Likewise, because both masculinity and femininity are absent in the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), it is designated by the neuter term *brahman*; yet this is not due to the actual existence of neuterness.

For otherwise, words such as *kuṇḍa* (pot) and *mitra* (friend) would result in the impossibility of functioning in their own primary meanings due to the absence of those [qualities]. Likewise, it should be understood that words such as *puruṣa* (man) function on the basis of a cause consisting in the non-existence of other forms; this is because of the presence of parsimony (*lāghava*) and because of the actual occurrence of their application to the Self (*ātman*), which is devoid of masculinity (*puṃstva*).
Therefore, because there is no difference between Maheśvarī and Maheśvara, the statement that both are non-dual is logically established. As it is said in the *Bṛṃhaṇī*:
"The Lord is Śiva, the Goddess is Śivā, and the Light is Śiva; thus [Śiva] is threefold."
"That reality which is indeed without gender is described through the differentiation of genders. Thus [it is said].
The Blessed Lord Śrī Bādarāyaṇa has also stated in the Sanatsujāta-parvan: "That is the foundation; that is the immortal; those are the worlds;
that is Brahman; that is glory. From that all beings were born, and into that they go at the time of dissolution" (Mahābhārata 5.44.30).
Furthermore, regarding the absence of gender and so forth: "This is neither female, nor male, nor indeed is this neuter" (5.10).

This is established by such Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad passages as well as by the venerable Vāyavīya Āgama, which states: "Neither female, nor male, nor even neuter" (Śivapurāṇa-Vāyavīya Saṃhitā 1.5.48). If it is asked, "In that case, how can there be a salutation through differentiation?", we reply:
because the distinction is logically possible between the Power characterized by Śiva and the Śiva characterized by Power.

The establishment of non-duality follows from the non-distinction between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*). Nor should it be argued that their non-distinction is impossible due to the relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*); for if one were to admit only their difference, the designation "this is the attribute of that" would be untenable. Nor should it be argued that this designation is possible because of the existence of a relation [between them].

Furthermore, if one were to admit yet another relation for the relation itself, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If no such relation is admitted, then because the relation would be common to all things, there could be no designation such as "this belongs to this. Therefore, the non-difference (*abheda*) between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) must be accepted. Nevertheless, since some degree of difference (*bheda*) also exists, the conventional usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) is maintained.

"It is like the conventional usage of distinctions such as mouth, belly, and so forth. He states the reason for the non-difference between Śiva and Śakti: "She whose nature is consciousness" (*cidrūpām*). Śiva is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), and she is "of the nature of consciousness," having the very form of consciousness (*citsvarūpā*) and being nothing but consciousness (*cinmātrā*); thus, there is no difference between them. This meaning is also stated in the *Śaivarahasya*:
"Like fire and its heat, Śakti and Śiva possess non-duality, yet they somehow maintain a mutual duality; [nevertheless], they are one in essence."
"Because it is logical, like the radiance of a gem. Regarding the phrase "the first": the meaning is that she is the first to arise because she is the cause of all things.

And he will say: "For the sake of favoring both the conscious and the unconscious" (verse 27). And it is stated in the *Siddhāntahṛdaya*: "The first unfolding of the one desiring to emit [the universe], which consists in the equilibrium of his powers—that limiting adjunct of Śiva is designated as the *Śaktitattva*. I am [this] in my entirety.
"Prostrate" means that one has surrendered through mind, speech, and action. || 3 ||
The commentary now states that even in the state of [His] office (*adhikārāvasthā*), Śiva’s power alone is the cause: "He is capable" (*śakta*).
By means of the instrument which is His very nature as power (*śaktyātman*), Śiva acts for the accomplishment of the enjoyment and liberation of souls in the performance of His fivefold duties.

It is capable and competent, not by means of any other instrument distinct from that [power]. If it is objected: "But agency is never seen in one who is devoid of body and senses," we say no; for even in the absence of those, the Self's capacity is observed through its mere power in such acts as the movement of its own body. And it has been said: "The cause, however, is nothing other than power" (Mṛgendravidyāpāda 3.4). By the word "one" (*ekām*), the distinctions of will (*icchā*) and so forth [within this power] are indicated.

He shows that the distinction between the left-hand path (*vāmā*) and so forth is merely figurative, based on the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the objects of knowledge and their effects, but not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), according to the scripture:

"The single Śiva-power attains multiplicity through limiting adjuncts. By the phrase "whose nature is consciousness" (*cidrūpām*), he shows that even though there is a differentiation of effects, there is no transformation (*pariṇāma*) of her, as in the case of *māyā* and other [principles], because transformation is a property of insentient things (*jaḍadharma*). [She is] the primordial...

"Being the primary [cause], she is inherent. By this, he indicates that although its nature consists of the *bindu* and *māyā*, it also possesses two external powers (*śakti*) consisting of the capacity for grasping (*parigraha*), because the production of the universe is impossible without a material cause (*upādāna*). And he will state here: "Without an agent..."
"The effect is not [produced] in that manner by means of its material cause and its instrument" (Śloka 37). || 3 ||
For the sake of favoring the world, with a mind overflowing with the essence of compassion,
we shall provide this exposition of reality in brief.

In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, the author of the treatise— having dispelled all obstacles through the praise of his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and other such acts— proclaims his intention to compose the scripture, which possesses a subject matter, a connection, and a purpose, as follows: "For the sake of favoring the world."

The favoring of the world and its creatures is liberation; "for that purpose" is the statement of the objective. For if that were not stated, there would be no grasping of the scripture. As it was said by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda: "For of every scripture, or indeed of any action whatsoever, as long as the purpose has not been stated, by whom will it be grasped? (Ślokavārttika 1.12).

Thus [he says]. And he will state: "This is indeed for the sake of favoring consciousness" (Śloka 36). Since it is said that "this *Tattvaprakāśa* is for the purpose of favoring the world," the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between the treatise and its purpose is established; otherwise, such a purpose would be impossible. That treatise by which the principles (*tattvāni*) are illuminated—that is, revealed—is the *Tattvaprakāśa*.

By this, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this treatise has been established, because the principles (*tattva*) are its subject matter insofar as they are being expounded herein. Now, one might object: "Knowledge concerning the principles to be expounded arises from the treatise;

therefore, how can the treatise itself be the means to liberation (*apavarga*"? To this it is replied: [the treatise is the means] by virtue of the knowledge of the principles being its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).
Because it is logically established as the means to that [liberation]. To explain: from hearing the scripture, knowledge of reality arises concerning the subject matter of the scripture.

When that [knowledge] exists, there is the cessation of ignorance and false knowledge. From that, there is the absence of passion and other afflictions rooted in them. From that, activity, which is their effect, ceases. From that, there is the non-production of merit and demerit. As for those previously produced and accumulated, they are [destroyed] by the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Destruction: For those two whose effects have not yet begun, there is destruction through experience alone, because they have been employed like an arrow that has already been discharged.

Then, due to the absence of limiting adjuncts such as the body, the individual self (*jīvātman*), which is by nature Śiva—just as the space within a jar [merges] into the supreme space when its limiting adjunct, the jar, is destroyed—undergoes dissolution into the Supreme Lord Śiva; this is what is called liberation (*apavarga*). This has been stated in the *Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa*:
(This statement is not found in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* as printed by Kāśīrāja in the *Ślokārdhasūcī*:
"May my individual soul (*jīva*) dissolve into the Supreme Self called Śiva, like the space within a jar into [great] space, or like river water into the ocean.
And in the *Śivadharmottara*: "From the awakening to the reality of the world, ignorance (*ajñāna*) ceases; and upon the cessation of ignorance, passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions]..."

"Name does not arise. Through the subsiding of passion and the like, there is the complete exhaustion of merit and demerit for men; and through that exhaustion, one is no longer joined with a body. Being bodiless, one is not afflicted by any defilements whatsoever. One who is freed from defilements and whose self is serene is called 'liberated'. And so forth. Therefore, from this scripture, liberation [is attained] by means of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Thus it is established that [the treatise] exists.

Now, an objection: if the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) occurs from this very treatise, then it follows that the author of the treatise lacks the knowledge of reality, because prior to the treatise, it did not exist. Nor can it be said that [the knowledge arises] after the composition of the treatise...

It must be said that his knowledge of reality arises from hearing that [scripture], because without such knowledge, it would be impossible for him to be the author of a treatise that expounds reality; for the employment of words regarding an object not known is not possible.
This is not so, because the principles (tattvas) have already been expounded in works such as the *Kiraṇa* and the *Māparameśvara*, and thus his [knowledge] comes from hearing them.

Because the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is possible [through this treatise]. Nor should it be argued that this scripture is unnecessary because the knowledge of reality is likewise possible for people like us; for since people like us lack such intellectual capacity, it is impossible for them to acquire knowledge regarding the subject matter of reality—which is presented in a scattered and extensive manner—without [the aid of this work]. Now, [if one asks]: [The text continues: ...because the knowledge of reality is possible. Nor should it be said that this treatise is not to be commenced because the knowledge of reality is possible even for those such as ourselves; for since those such as ourselves lack the power of such wisdom, it is impossible to achieve knowledge concerning the objects of reality as they are taught in a dispersed and detailed fashion. Now...

If the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) were the means to liberation (*apavarga*), then those who have produced that knowledge would be liberated immediately thereafter; consequently, the composition and explanation of scriptures would be impossible, and thus the knowledge of reality would be unattainable for people such as ourselves. If it is argued that the author of the scripture remains for that very purpose, then the knowledge of reality is not the means to liberation.
"Even when that knowledge exists, there is an absence of liberation"— this is not a fault,

because it is accepted that the direct (aparokṣa) realization of the Self as Śiva is what produces liberation. For instance, even when the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) derived from scripture has arisen, liberation does not occur until there is the directness of knowledge (jñānāparokṣya) made possible through meditative contemplation (nididhyāsana).

Because it is non-existent at that time. For when the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) derived from the sacred scriptures (*śruti*) has arisen, there occurs—dependent upon reflection (*manana*)—a direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) whose object is the identity of Śiva and the Self;
this [realization], consisting in the removal of the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that has become directly manifest regarding the body and so forth, brings about liberation (*apavarga*). And that...

This is because the cessation of an indirect (parokṣa) error is impossible through indirect knowledge; furthermore, it is observed that an indirect error regarding direction—such as [mistaking] "the sun has risen in the north"—is not seen to cease through an inference of the east being preceded by the sun's rising;
and finally, because cessation is observed when indirect knowledge arises through the power of repeated practice.

For indeed, the scriptural texts residing at the crest of the Vedas establish one and the same meaning. Thus, in the passage, "O, the Self is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), the vision of the auspicious Self alone is prescribed as the means for liberation without qualification. As a means to that [vision], hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption are enjoined: "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon."
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5). Therefore, it is understood that the knowledge produced by mere hearing (*śravaṇa*) alone is not the means to liberation;

rather, it is the vision of the Self as Śiva (*śivātma-darśana*) arising from meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*). These [means], beginning with hearing, serve as auxiliaries toward the vision of the Self, both through the "gate of existence" (*sadvāra*) and the "gateless way" (*nirdvāra*); for it is said: "One should hear from the words of the scriptures and reflect through logical reasoning."

And it is established that "having known [the truth], one should constantly meditate upon it," for these are the causes of realization. Therefore, there is no impossibility of composing or explaining the scriptures, because it is accepted that those who possess knowledge of reality remain in that state until direct perception (*aparokṣya*) is attained. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that this scripture—which yields the fruits of heaven and liberation—is unworthy of being commenced because there is no qualified person for it due to the non-existence of a self distinct from the body and so forth; for the existence of an eternal individual soul (jīvātman) distinct from the body and so forth will be established hereafter. Nor [is it the case that] liberation and its means...

It should not be argued that this treatise is unnecessary because other foundational scriptures exist, for those other scriptures do not expound the Śiva-tattva, as stated in the Āraṇa [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad]: "When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, then, without knowing Śiva, there will be an end to suffering. (ŚveU 6.20).

Because the *Śvetāśvatara* [Upaniṣad] rejects that [knowledge of Śiva] is the cause of liberation, the status of being a cause of liberation is rejected for those statements that establish Śiva by means of defining Him through the exclusion of other principles (*itara-tattva-vyāvṛtti*). For instance, in both Śruti and Smṛti, it is stated that knowledge of Śiva is here twofold as the cause of liberation: by way of the exclusion of others and by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*). Thus: [The text continues with citations from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.]

Because of the injunction [to know]: "The Self is to be known; It is to be distinguished from primordial nature (prakṛti)," and such scriptural passages as, "It is indeed other than the known, and likewise other than the unknown" (Kena Upaniṣad 1.4), which establish knowledge by means of the exclusion of other things; and [passages] such as, "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), "Bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6), and "Brahman is Consciousness" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 5.3), which establish knowledge even by way of Its own essential nature (svarūpa).

This is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor ether; it is not the vital breath, nor the mind, nor the unmanifest, nor sound, nor even touch; it is not form, taste, or smell; it is not the agent of "I-making," nor speech; it is not the hands, the feet, the anus, or the generative organ, O best of the twice-born; it is neither the doer nor the enjoyer, nor is it primordial nature (prakṛti) or the individual soul (puruṣa). Nor...

"Neither Māyā nor Prāṇa is consciousness from the perspective of ultimate reality" (Īśvaragītā 2.3.7–9). Such Smṛti passages distinguish [the Self] from others, stating: "This Self alone is absolute, pure, peaceful, subtle, and eternal; it exists as the inner witness of all, consisting of pure consciousness, beyond darkness."

(Īśvaragītā 2.2–4), and so forth, establish that the knowledge of Śiva as one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is to be understood in both ways; therefore, it is established that this scripture, which is the means for attaining such knowledge, must be commenced. Regarding the phrase "with a mind overflowing with the essence of compassion" (*karuṇārasanirbhareṇa cetasā*): the "essence of compassion" (*karuṇārasa*) is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) produced from compassion.

The desire to favor [others]. Or rather, it is both compassion (*karuṇā*) and aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); thus, "filled with the flavor of compassion" means intensely and unrestrainedly so, by that [flavor]. "With the mind" means with the heart. The composition of this treatise is not for the sake of fame, gain, or honor;
rather, the meaning is that it is being composed by us whose minds are solely uplifted by compassion. Regarding oneself and toward the gurus...

The plural designation "by us" (*asmābhiḥ*) is employed because of the rule governing the plural number. "In brief" (*samāsena*) means by way of condensing or summarizing those principles (*tattva*) which have been taught in detail and scattered throughout the Śaiva Āgamas, for the sake of favoring those of dull intellect. || 4 ||

The commentary now declares the subject matter to be expounded in this treatise with the words "loka... and so forth. It is the illumination of the principles (tattvas) beginning from earth and ending with Śiva, of their creator Śiva, and of the selves (ātman) who are benefited by them.
The meaning is "it is performed. || 4 ||

In the Śaiva Āgamas, the primary triad is, in order: Pati, Paśu, and Pāśa. Among these, Pati is said to be Śiva; the Paśus are indeed the individual souls (aṇus); and the five categories of objects constitute the Pāśa.

It has been stated that the *Tattvaprakāśa*, which is an elucidation of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), is being composed. In this regard, the following objection is raised: "What are those principles (*tattva*), and how many are they?
For various teachers have described the principles in many ways, ranging from one up to thirty-six.
Since [this] has already been established, a doubt arises. To dispel that doubt, he says: "Śaiva.

The intended meaning is as follows: among all the specific categories of principles (*tattva-pakṣa-viśeṣa*) ranging from one up to thirty-six, because it is the most fundamental and because the fault of logical inconsistency would otherwise follow, the threefold nature consisting of the Lord (*pati*), the bound soul (*paśu*), and the bond (*pāśa*) must be accepted.
For instance, if the transmigrating soul (*paśu*) were not admitted,
then saṃsāra— characterized by merit and demerit, birth and death, and the experience of pleasure and pain—
and its cessation would both be non-existent due to the absence of a substratum; this would likewise apply to the Vedas, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, which set forth those [matters].

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of invalidity due to the absence of an object [of cognition]. Likewise, in the absence of the bonds known as *mala*, *karman*, and *māyā*—which are the causes of transmigratory existence—and in the absence of the body and so forth, there would follow the non-existence of going to heaven or hell, birth, death, and so on; for all these are impossible for the actionless Self (*ātman*).

Likewise, in the absence of a Lord who is the Supreme Master, the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, as well as the investigation into dharma and adharma, bondage and liberation, and so forth, would be impossible;
for these cannot occur among individual souls who are non-omniscient and devoid of bodies. Therefore, the threefold nature of reality exists in all systems.
"It must be accepted in specific cases. [Objection:
But surely, we reply, the recourse to those [two] positions—one of unity and one of duality—is due to the existence of distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
For instance, just as the single reality of water, through the power of limiting adjuncts, appears as waves, foam, and bubbles without ever deviating from its own essential nature; so too...

Just as [the universe] is understood through its threefold division, so too this Śiva, whose own essential nature is never lost, experiences a threefold state consisting of the Lord (pati), the individual soul (paśu), and the fetter (pāśa). As it is stated in the *Śaivarahasya*: "Indeed, Śiva himself experiences the state of the bound soul (paśu) when his own qualities are concealed by the *aṇava* [impurity]. And that impurity is whatever fragment of power belonging to Śarva [that remains unmanifested] in every respect."

While there is a twofold division consisting of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, a threefold division is possible by way of *prakṛti*, that which is conditioned by it (*tadupahita*), and that which is unconditioned by it (*anupahita*). This threefold nature is established because the other principles (*tattvas*) are included within these very categories among the fourfold groupings ending with the thirty-sixth principle. To explain: the pure principles (*śuddhatattvas*) are included within the Lord (*pati*), while the effects of *māyā* [are included within *prakṛti*].

The pure and impure [entities] are included within the *pāśas* (bonds). That which consists of everything from the unmanifest (*avyakta*) down to the earth (*pṛthivī*), being exclusively impure, is called a *pāśa*. As it is stated in the *Śaivarahasya*: "All things, whose nature is Śiva, manifest in their entirety within the Lord; yet some of them are contained without remainder within the *pāśas* and the *paśus*. Therefore...
Thus, these three possess primacy because all others are included within them. Alternatively, their primacy is according to their sequence.
To the question, "How is this understood?", he says: "In the Śaiva Āgamas. And they are as follows: Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, Kāraṇa, Ajita, Parama, Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, and Suprabhedaka.
Furthermore, there are the *Vijaya*, the *Niḥśvāsa*, and after that the *Svāyambhuva*; the *Vīra*, the *Raurava*, as well as the *Mukuṭa* and the *Vimala*;
the *Candrajñāna*, the *Bimba*, the *Prodgīta*, and likewise the *Lalita*;
the *Siddha*, the *Santāna*, the *Sarvokta*, and the *Pārameśvara*; the *Kiraṇa*, and the *Vātula*—these are the twenty-eight *Saṃhitās*.
"It is known as the primary division, with innumerable sub-divisions. This is because it has been stated in these [texts]. For instance, in the *Pārameśvara*:
"The bound, the binder, and the bonds—this triad is established" (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā* 6.2). And in the *Kiraṇa*:
"The great tantra named *Kiraṇa*, which establishes the knowledge concerning the analysis of the bound, the bonds, and the Lord" (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā* 1.13), and so forth.

And in the *Śrīvāyavīya*: "The non-inert, the inert, and the controller of both—these three are called, in order, the bound soul (*paśu*), the fetter (*pāśa*), and the Lord (*pati*)" (*Śivapurāṇa*, Vāyavīyasaṃhitā 1.5.12).
By the qualifying term "Śaiva"—meaning "proclaimed by Śiva"—the authority of the scriptures (*āgamas*) is indicated. For instance, [the authority] of Śiva’s...

Because of omniscience, there is an absence of ignorance, false knowledge, passion, hatred, and other such causes for the composition of unauthoritative statements; therefore, the authority of the scriptures composed by him is indeed established. For it cannot be said that the composition of unauthoritative statements arises from ignorance, since ignorance is impossible for an omniscient being—precisely because of the absence of ignorance.

Because of the absence of passion, hatred, and the like which are rooted in that [ignorance], there is no possibility of composing unauthoritative statements based upon them. Therefore, since the status of being authoritative exists for those works composed by Maheśvara, who is an *āpta* (trustworthy person) due to his having exhausted all defects, the reality of the objects of knowledge taught therein must be accepted. This has been stated in the *Śivadharmottara* and other texts: "This Śaiva injunction..."
The teaching concerning the nature of Śiva is not a mere figurative statement; for how could He who acts for the benefit of the world speak that which is false?

Since he is fully perfected in omniscience, for what other reason would Śiva—the peaceful one, free from all defects—speak otherwise? Whatever object exists as it truly is by its own nature, with its qualities and defects, and whatever fruit or merit it entails, the Omniscient One speaks of that exactly so. Because they are seized by defects such as passion and ignorance, those [others] might speak untruthfully.

If these [defects] do not exist in Īśvara, how could he speak otherwise? That stainless word which was composed by Śiva—who has cast off all defects and is omniscient—is authoritative; there is no doubt about it. Therefore, the words of Īśvara are to be trusted by the wise regarding merit and demerit as they truly are; one who lacks faith in them goes downward. Thus it is said.

Now, from what is it known that the scriptures were composed by God? If you say it is from those very scriptures themselves, then there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*). Alternatively, if one requires a trustworthy author for the scripture as a means of valid knowledge, then since no other person capable of perceiving supersensuous objects can possibly be its author, [the author must be] the Lord, the creator of all.

If it is argued that the authorship of the scripture by an omniscient being is thus determined, it is not so; for such a construction is untenable precisely because the authority of the scripture has not been established. Furthermore, since there is no evidence that it was composed by anyone other than a trustworthy person, and because there is no contradiction in an all-seeing being being its author, the qualification "composed by Śiva" lacks purpose. This is not the case, because of the scripture...
Because validity is established through a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the efficacy of practice.

To explain: scripture (*āgama*) is indeed twofold—namely, that which has a perceptible object and that which has an imperceptible object. Among these, in the case of those scriptures with perceptible objects—such as statements enjoining the *citrayāga* sacrifice—the occurrence of the results described therein is observed through the performance of the actions prescribed by them.

Having inferred the authority [of a scripture], once the author of that work is ascertained to be a supreme authority by virtue of being a perceiver of supersensible objects, then the authority of other [scriptures] concerning unseen matters is also inferred— on the grounds of their being composed by that same author— to be like the authority of those statements concerning seen matters. Nor can the author of the scripture perceive through direct observation the fact that specific ritual acts, such as worship and recitation, are the means for achieving their respective specific results.
He would not be omniscient, for one who perceives this [limited object] lacks the perception of other things that are unperceived.

Nor should it be argued that he composes the sentences after apprehending this matter through inference and so forth, because the grasping of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the inferential mark (*liṅga*), and so on, are impossible. For inference occurs only when the pervasion between the mark and the possessor of the mark has been grasped through direct perception.

He states that the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) arises from the mere perception of the mark (*liṅga*). For instance, it is observed that after the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between smoke and fire—the mark and the possessor of the mark—has been grasped through direct perception in a kitchen or similar place, the inference of fire proceeds upon seeing smoke on another mountain or location. This is the case here regarding the fruit and the action.

Since the relationship of probandum and probans between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is not perceptible, and because it is impossible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) due to the non-perception of the mark, inference is not possible; thus, scriptures do not have inference as their foundation.
Nor do they have another scripture as their foundation, for that too...

If it were admitted that [the scriptures] have another scripture as their source because they are of human origin, there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress. Furthermore, we do not perceive any sentence other than the Veda that is of non-human origin, by which [such a source] might be postulated.
Therefore, the scriptures do not have another scripture as their source. Nor...
It must be stated that the authors of the scriptures (*āgama*) are yogins who perceive objects beyond the reach of the senses;

for it has already been established that because their omniscience depends upon the grace of Maheśvara, the existence of those scriptures—which reveal the means thereto, such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and worship—must necessarily be accepted. This is because the postulation of anyone other than Śiva, the creator of the world, as the author of the scriptures is untenable.
Furthermore, because of the respect [accorded to them], he alone is postulated as the author of the scriptures as well.
