Nor should it be argued that since it is impossible for scriptures teaching mutually contradictory properties to have a single authoritative author, this would entail the necessity of accepting multiple authoritative authors; for [the scriptures differ] by virtue of the distinction between those qualified [to follow them], such as the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).

Furthermore, since it is possible for the one object of knowledge, Śiva—the storehouse of compassion—to teach contradictory doctrines, there is no fault such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Nor should it be argued that mutual dependence would arise in the case of worldly consensus (*lokaparigraha*), because that [consensus] does not have the recognition of its own validity as its root. For instance, having first composed the scriptures (*āgamas*):

Maheśvara caused his own son Brahmā to grasp [the scriptures]; then Brahmā [caused] his own sons, and they in turn [caused] their own sons. Thus, since the acceptance of the Āgamas is established in the same manner as the acceptance of the Vedas, there is no room for the aforementioned objection.
Now, it was previously described that the authority of the Āgamas is due to their being composed by Śiva. Currently...

If it is argued that there is a contradiction between the earlier and later statements because of the capacity for practice (*pratipatti-sāmarthya*), we say no; for both are consistent when considered in relation to origination (*utpatti*) and manifestation (*jñapti*). To explain: the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the scriptures, which has already arisen from their being composed by Śiva, is understood through the capacity for their practice; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Alternatively, the authority of the scriptures is due to their being rooted in the Veda. Even in that case, [they remain] composed by Śiva.

Thus, it establishes the authority of scripture (*āgama*) on the basis of its consistency with reality (*tattva*), because the meaning of the Vedas as perceived through Śiva’s vision is uncontradicted.

That scripture is twofold: that which is rooted in directly perceived revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*) and that which is rooted in inferable revelation (*anumeyaśruti*). Among these, the authority of those scriptures rooted in directly perceived revelation is like that of the directly perceived revelation itself; and the authority of those rooted in inferable revelation is like that of the *Aṣṭakā* and other such Vedic injunctions. Thus it stands regarding the scriptures.

The fact that the Agamas are rooted in the Vedas is understood from the observation that the matters they expound are found within the Śrutis. For instance, from the Vedic statement "Rudra must necessarily be worshipped," the necessity of performing the sacrifice to Rudra is revealed. In that regard, the instruments and other details, which are understood from the mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas), are set forth by the Agamas; thus, the Agamas have their root in the Vedas. To illustrate: "Praise him... [and so on].

In the verse *yaḥ sviṣuḥ sudhanvā yaḥ* (Ṛgveda 5.42.11), it is understood that acts such as worship, praise, and prostration directed toward Rudra are the cause for liberation (*apavarga*) known as "Great Bliss" (*mahatsaukhya*). In the verse *antaricchanti* (Ṛgveda 8.72.3), it is understood that meditation (*dhyāna*) and recitation (*japa*) should be performed with Rudra as their object. In the verse *yajñaṃ rudrāya mīḍhuṣe* (Ṛgveda 1.122.1)...
It is understood thus: "Bring the drink called Soma, the food of the blind one, as an oblation for Rudra.

In this manner, the existence of the meanings propounded by the Āgamas in such texts as the Śatarudrīya, the Nīlarudra-sūkta, the Śvetāśvatara, the Īśāvāsya, the Atharvaśiras, the Tācchikhā, the Raudra-sūkta, and the Araṇa, should be recognized.
Thus [it is said].

Herein are the formal arguments (*prayoga*): The subject of dispute, the Tantric scripture (*tantraśāstra*), is authoritative (*pramāṇa*), because it is true to reality, like a sentence universally accepted as such. Likewise, the Tantric scripture is authoritative, because it was spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), whatever has been spoken by a reliable person [is authoritative].

That is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such as the Purāṇas and so forth; likewise, this [text] was spoken by an authoritative person (*āpta*), therefore it is a valid means of knowledge. Similarly, the Āgamas were composed by Śiva, because they are effects not produced by anyone other than him. Whatever is an effect not produced by anyone other than him was composed by Śiva, just like the manifest world (*prapañca*); and these [Āgamas] are likewise; therefore, they were composed by Śiva.

The Tantra scripture must be accepted as authoritative because it is a statement other than the Vedas; for whatever statement is distinct from the Vedas is seen to be produced by a human author, such as the *Mahābhārata* and similar works. Nor should it be argued that the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*) because the fact that the universe was composed by Śiva is unestablished, for that will be demonstrated later. Likewise, the Tantra scripture is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Because it is rooted in the Veda, like the Smṛtis of Manu and others. And that [text] is rooted in the Veda because it sets forth the matters taught therein, just like the Smṛtis of Manu and others. If it is argued that this scripture is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it was composed by an unreliable person (*anāpta*), leading to the fallacy of being sublated by a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*) as in the case of a commonly accepted [false work], we say: not so, because such an alternative is untenable. For instance:

What is the meaning of the phrase "because it was not made by an authoritative person" (*anāptakṛtatvāt*)? Does it mean that it was not made by an authoritative person (*āpta*), or rather that it was made by one who is not authoritative (*anāpta*)? If it is the first position, then there is a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the Vedic statements; for although they are indeed authoritative, the reason—that they were not made by an authoritative person—is absent from them. Furthermore, this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has already been proven that [the Vedas] were made by an authoritative person. If, on the other hand, it is the latter position, then...

Nor can it be argued that [the Shaiva scriptures] are unestablished (asiddha) precisely because they were composed by an unreliable person, for it is possible to prove that the scriptures are not composed by an unreliable person because they do not contradict the Veda, unlike the Buddhist and other scriptures. This is because those scriptures which are rooted in the Veda—since they expound the meaning of the Veda—cannot themselves be established as being in contradiction with the Veda. Therefore, regarding the Shaiva scriptures...
The threefold classification and so forth mentioned here are to be respected because they have been accepted by all learned people (*śiṣṭa*), such as Mārkaṇḍeya, Agastya, Rāma, Dadhīca, and others.
Regarding the phrase "the Lord, the bound souls, and the fetters": they are so called because they are the Lord (*pati*), the bound souls (*paśu*), and the fetters (*pāśa*). Who are these?

In response to this inquiry, he says: "Among those, the Lord (pati) is said to be Śiva; the individual souls (paśus) are the atoms (aṇavas); and the fivefold objects are the bond (pāśa). Among them, Śiva is designated by the word "Lord" because he protects (pālayati) the individual souls. The individual souls are indeed atoms, meaning they are characterized by their connection with impurities (mala) and other factors that produce atomicity. Living beings whose true nature is Śiva are the "individual souls" (paśus), and not merely four-legged animals.

Furthermore, because bipeds are heard of as being among the "beasts" (*paśu*). For instance, from such scriptural passages as: "These indeed are the beasts: the bipeds and the quadrupeds; whatever [is yours], O Indra and Varuṇa, among the biped beasts, or whatever among the quadruped beasts" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.3.13.1). Because He is the Lord (*īśvara*) of these, the Blessed Śiva is the "Lord of Beasts" (*Paśupati*), over whom Paśupati rules.
According to the Śruti: "Of animals, both four-footed and two-footed" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.1.4.1). And in the upper portion of the Liṅga Purāṇa:

"From Brahmā down to the immobile beings, all are proclaimed as 'paśus' (bound souls) belonging to the wise God of gods, subject to the power of saṃsāra. Because he is their Lord (pati), the Blessed Rudra is remembered as Paśupati. (Liṅga Purāṇa 2.9.11–12).

12) Thus [it is said]. Now, if it is asked by what cause the individual souls (*jīvātman*), whose true nature is Śiva, possess a connection with the bonds (*pāśa*) such as impurity (*mala*), it is replied: from the connection with the bond of impurity arises the connection with the bond of karma;
from that connection arises the connection with the bond of *māyā*. Since this connection with the bond of impurity is beginningless (*anādi*), it does not depend upon a further cause.

Thus it is said in the *Kiraṇa*: "Due to the connection with beginningless impurity (*mala*), the state of being sullied resides in the individual soul (*aṇu*); due to being freed from beginningless impurity, the state of being stainless resides in Śiva. When their possession of a beginning is established, then that which is called the 'efficient cause' (*nimitta*) is remembered by those two as being pure and impure according to reality. Therefore, the crystal is pure, whereas copper is [impure]."

"Simultaneous; just as there would be no such cause in this case, so too there would be none for Śiva and the Self" (Vīop 3.3–5). If it is objected that, in that case, it would follow that bound souls (*paśu*) lack the nature of Śiva, we say: not so. For it will be stated later that there exists scriptural and other evidence proving their essential nature (*svabhāva*) to be Śiva. Precisely because they are bound by fetters (*pāśa*), they are called "bound souls. By that [bondage],...
Their atomicity (*aṇutva*) consists in a certain degree of agency and so forth, not because they abide like atoms due to being non-pervasive, for that is impossible.
"The five objects are the bond" means that the objects— namely *mala*, karma, and the subtle and gross *māyā*— [are the bond].
The pentad of objects consists of the fivefold group of Śiva’s powers that govern the bonds; this is the principle (tattva) known as "bond" (pāśa). As it has been said:
"Impurity (mala), karma, Māyā, the entire world arising from Māyā, and the power that effects concealment—this is called the pentad of objects."

Thus [it is said]. Now, an objection: here it has been established that the pentad of objects (*arthapañcaka*) constitutes the bond (*pāśa*), whereas in another scripture, a threefold nature of bonds is taught; thus there is a contradiction. For instance, in the *Śaivarahasya*:
"Inherent and beginningless impurity (*mala*) is the most predominant among all three types of bonds; and both action (*karma*) and illusion (*māyā*) exist only when impurity is present."
"They function as fetters (pāśa). And in the *Prayogamañjarī*: "The three fetters bind. This is not so;

for the Lord's power is designated as a "fetter" precisely because it favors the fetters, and because the fetter of Māyā is said to have fivefold divisions through its twofold nature as gross and subtle.

Some read "the fivefold path is the bond" (*adhvapañcakaṃ pāśaḥ*). In that case, the "fivefold path" refers to the pentad of the six paths—namely, the principles (*tattva*), phonemes (*varṇa*), mantras, worlds (*bhuvana*), words (*pada*), and kalās—which constitute the bond. This has been stated in the *Siddhāntahṛdaya*:
Śiva is declared to be the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati), while the individual souls (aṇus) are considered to be the beasts (paśus).
Bound by fetters, they are beasts; the fetter (pāśa) consists of the five paths (adhvapañcaka).
The paths consist of the principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), limited powers (kalā), phonemes (varṇa), words (pada), and mantras;
bound by these, men transmigrate from one state of existence to another.

"The six paths, beginning with the *tattvas*, arise from impurity (*mala*) and so forth, and they are fivefold according to the divisions of *nivṛtti* and the rest; thus is the fivefold path described.
And in the *Gurudevapaddhati*:
Now, the pervasion of these paths in their proper sequence is correctly described:
the earth principle (pṛthvītattva), the letter *kṣa*, and the two mantras, Hṛdaya and Sadyojāta.
Kālāgni, Kuṣmāṇḍa, and Hāṭaka, as well as the realms of Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
and that of Rudra— these six worlds exist within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Outside the egg, one hundred Rudras are stationed in the ten directions:
Kapālīśa, Aja, Buddha, Vajradeha, and Pramardana.
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākin, and Tridaśādhipa are in the eastern direction.
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Khādaka, and Hara are [also there].
Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmānta, and Kṣayātmaka.
In the southeastern direction:
Yama, Mṛtyu, Hara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and another, as well as Kartṛ, Saṃyoktṛ, Niyojaka, and Dharma himself.
In that same way, the Lord of Dharma stands there as the tenth on the right;
he is Nirṛti, the slayer and destroyer, with a cruel gaze and terrifying appearance,
with hair standing erect, deformed eyes, and smoke-colored, reddish fangs.
In the southwest are Bala and Atibala, who hold nooses and possess great strength;
then Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghahasta, and Balāntaka.
In the western quarter, Meghanāda and Sunāda are proclaimed;
[and there are] Śīghra, Vāyu, Vāyuvega, Sūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, and Kṣayāntaka.
Pañcāntaka, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, and Meghavāhana [are in the] northwestern [direction].
Nidhīśa, Rūpavān, Dhanya, Saumyadeha, and Jaṭādhara [are in the] northwestern [direction].
Lakṣmīdhara, Ratnadhara, Śrīdhara, Prasādhana,
and Prakāma as the tenth— these are situated in the northern direction.
Lord of the sciences, omniscient, enjoyer of knowledge, one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas;
lord of the gods, eldest of all, protector of beings, and lover of offerings.
In the northeast:
Viṣa, Viṣadhara, Ananta, Krodhana, Mārutāśana, Nyagrodha, Udumbarīśa, Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭrin.
In the lower part:
Śambhu, Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Triyakṣa, Tridaśeśvara,
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Nabholipsu, and Trilocana.
Above those Rudras stands Vīrabhadra;
such is the world of Bhadrakālī, consisting of one hundred and eight [worlds].
The worlds of the Rudras, as described in the sequence, are listed individually by their own names,
beginning from the station at the end of the mantra up to the station of Mahādeva.
The words, numbering twenty-eight, should be in reverse order;
thus the fivefold path is conjoined with the sixth, the *nivṛtti-kalā*.
The sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan) should be contemplated as pervading [all things] through its divisions:
water, fire, wind, space, smell, and taste and form.
Touch and sound, speech and hands, feet, anus, and genitals,
as well as the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose— these are the sense organs.
The triad of internal organs consists of the mind (manas), ego (ahaṅkāra), and intellect (buddhi);
furthermore, for all of these, the supreme cause is Prakṛti, which is composed of the three guṇas.
The twenty-three principles (tattvas) are [assigned] in reverse order by number;
consequently, there are twenty-three letters beginning with 'ha' and ending with 'ṭa'.
The head [is presided over] by the mantra named Vāmadeva; likewise, there are fifty-six cities in sequence, known by the names beginning with Amareśa.
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Aṣāḍhī,
Ḍiṇḍi, Muṇḍi, and Bhārabhūti— these are the eight [shrines] in the water-element (ambutattva).
Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Jalpīśa, Āmrātakeśvara, Madhyameśa, Mahākāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava.
This group of eight worlds is established within the element of fire (tejas-tattva):
Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Naula, and likewise Kanakhala.
Vimaleśa, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and Bhīmakeśvara—
these eight worlds belong to the Vāyu-tattva.
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu as well.
The group of eight worlds is situated within the principle known as Ākāśa:
Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mārka, and Gomaṇḍaleśvara.
Beginning from Kālañjara, Dāruvana, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Sthaleśvara,
along the path extending from the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra) up to the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra).
These eight worlds are situated in their proper order:
the realms of the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Indra, Soma, and Ka.
The eight divine wombs (devayoni) reside in the intellect: Prājeśa and Brāhma, as well as Akṛta and Kṛta; and Bhairava resides in both the Brāhma and Vaiṣṇava wombs.
The eight wombs are known as Kaumāra, Auma, and Śrīkaṇṭha;
this Bhauvana [world] is stable within the principle of Guṇaprakṛti.
Thus, by means of seven groups of eight, fifty-six worlds are situated in their respective order; likewise, there are twenty-one *padas*.
Beginning from the one called Maheśvara and extending up to the plane of Arūpin,
the fivefold path (adhvan) thus exists together with the level of Pratiṣṭhā.
Having contemplated that which is pervaded by the sixth [tattva], such is the sixfold pervasion of the paths (adhvan). Now, within the kalās of Vidyā, there are indeed the Puruṣa and Rāga.
Impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā), limited agency (kalā), necessity (niyati), time (kāla),
and illusion (māyā)— these are the seven principles (tattvas) conjoined with the group of seven phonemes.
The mantras beginning with *ña* and ending with *gha* are the Śikhā and Ghorā;
the worlds, beginning with Vāma, are twenty-seven in number.
Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Bhava, Īśāna,
and Ekavīrapuruṣa— these six are the lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśvaras).
Pracaṇḍa, Umāpati, Aja, Ananta, and Ekarudraka—
this pentad of worlds is situated within the principle of Rāga (Passion).
Krodhacaṇḍa and Aśuddha are established in Vidyā;
then, in Niyati, are Jyotis and Saṃvarta, followed by the one known as Sūkara.
Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, Śiva, and Kalāgata; Mahādeva, Vāmadeva, Udbhava, and Ekapiṅgala.
Ekanetra, Īśāna, and thereafter Bhuvaneśa;
and Aṅguṣṭhamātra—these eight are the Sthaleśvaras.
And within the principle of Time (kālatattva) and Māyā, there are twenty-seven Bhauvanīs,
beginning from Vyāpin and ending with Dhyānāhāra.
There are twenty words here; one should contemplate that everything is pervaded by the *vidyā-kalā*. Such is the arrangement of the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidhādhvan*).
Now, within the Śāntikalā, there are the principles (tattvas) beginning from Śuddhavidyā up to Īśvara, and Sadāśiva; indeed, three principles reside therein.
The three phonemes *ga*, *kha*, and *ka* are the mantras for the armor (*kavaca*) and the person (*puruṣa*).
Here, there are exactly eighteen worlds, designated by the names Vāmā and so forth.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikariṇī,
Balavikaraṇī, and likewise Balapramathinī.
The one called Sarvabhūtadamanī, the ninth, is Manonmanī;
they are situated in this sequence within the principle (tattva) known as Śuddhavidyā.
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, and then Śivottama;
Ekanetra, Ekarudra, and likewise another, Trimūrti.
Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin are the worlds called Īśvara;
the world named Sadāśiva is situated in the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva.
In this very [mantra], there are eleven words beginning with *nityayogin* and ending with *vyomavyāpin*; thus, they are established in five groups.
The wise should understand that the pervasion consisting of the sixfold path occurs sequentially, being pervaded by the sixth, the Śāntikalā.
In the same way, the Śiva-tattva is established within the Śāntyatītā [kalā].
There are sixteen vowels, beginning with *sarga* (ṛ), which are [to be arranged] in reverse order.
Indeed, the root-mantras and the mantras consist of Aṣṭa and Īśāna;
here, there are exactly fifteen worlds, beginning with Nivṛtti.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise Śāntyatītā—these indeed are the Kalās; for within the Bindu reside the worlds.
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocis, Mocikā, and likewise Ūrdhvagā—these are the five worlds; they are indeed the kalās of Nāda.
The pervasive, the ether-like, the infinite, the lordless,
and the unsupported— these are the kalās, and they are also capable of being worlds.
That which is the *praṇava* at the beginning of the mantra is the end when reversed; thus it becomes a single word. In this way, this path is declared to be fivefold.
"Pervaded by the kalā beyond tranquility (śāntyatīta), one should know [it] through the sequence of the paths;
thus, the sixfold pervasion has been declared according to the determination of the Śaiva Āgamas."

One who possesses knowledge of the six paths is liberated and can liberate others from the ocean of existence. The paths are of six kinds, yet they are one; there are eleven mantras and eighty-one words.
Furthermore, there are thirty-six principles here, fifty phonemes, and five groups.
Now, the extraction of the words:
the first word is the *praṇava* (Oṃ), which consists of a single syllable and has Śiva as its essence;
the second word is "vyomavyāpin," ending in the dative case, and consists of five syllables.
The third [syllable] is for Vyomarūpa;
likewise, another five-syllable [name] ending in the dative case is "Sarvavyāpine," and then the fifth is "Śivāya."
One should know the three syllables and the five limbs of Śiva;
"Anantāya" is the four-syllable designator of Ananta.
"Anāthāya" is the four-syllabled word for the Subtle One;
"anāśritāya," however, is the five-syllabled word for the Most Auspicious One.
The three-syllable word *dhruvāya* is proclaimed as belonging to Ekanetra;
the four-syllable word *śāśvatāya* belongs to Ekarudra.
To the one established on the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), the eight-syllable mantra of Trimūrti;
and the five-syllable word for Śrīkaṇṭha, the eternally united one.
This five-syllabled mantra of Śikhin, "dhyānāhārāya," is for the sustenance of meditation;
and the six-syllabled mantra "namaḥ śivāya" is preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ).
In the sequence of words, "Sarvaprabhu" ending in the dative case is a five-syllable word;
furthermore, there is another word, "Śivāya," which ends in the dative case and consists of three syllables.
O best of sages, the six-syllable mantra "Padam īśānamūrdhāya" should be understood as belonging to Īśāna, while the seven-syllable mantra belongs to Puruṣa.
It should be for the one whose mouth is Tatpuruṣa and whose heart is Aghora;
likewise, the seven-syllable mantra of Bahurūpa and that of Vāma are proclaimed.
It may be for Vāmadeva-Guhya; then that which belongs to Sadyojāta is also described: "To the form of Sadyojāta" is declared as the seven-syllable mantra.
The Praṇava (Oṃ) and so forth should be employed, as well as the five-syllabled "namo namaḥ";
then the six-syllabled phrase "guhyātiguhyāya," and finally the supreme two-syllabled [mantra].

The *goptre-pada* consists of four syllables; it is for the purpose of destruction when applied to the *mātaṅga*. Preceded by the letter *a*, this five-syllable mantra is proclaimed in the *Candrajñāna*.
The phrase "to the Lord of all Vidyās" consists of seven syllables;
whereas the phrase "to him who has gone before all Yogas" consists of eight syllables.
This most beautiful five-syllabled word is *jyotīrūpāya*;
preceded by *parameśvara*, it is followed by *parāya*, which consists of eight syllables.
They know "acetanācetanā" to be a word of seven syllables;
likewise, "vyominvyomin" is a word of four syllables, as is the word "vyāpinvyāpin."
Having repeated the formless [seed-syllable] twice, the six-syllabled word is thus declared;
likewise, the first [word] is repeated twice, and the other six-syllabled [word] is similarly [repeated].
"Tejas tena" is declared to be the four-syllabled word of the Lord;
likewise, "Jyotis jyotis" should be understood as a four-syllabled word.
The three-syllabled word called Arūpa, and likewise the auspicious word Anagna;
the three-syllabled word called Adhūma, and likewise the word Abhasman.

In the *anādi* [vyāhṛti], three syllables are taught; likewise, in *nā* there are three syllables and in *dhū* there are three. *Oṃ bhūḥ* should be known as having two syllables, and *oṃ bhuvaḥ* has three syllables.
Oṃ; *svo* consists of two syllables and is called *anidhana*;
*nidhana* consists of three syllables, while that which arises from *nidhana* consists of five syllables.
The state of Śiva consists of two syllables; the state of the all-pervading Śarva consists of two phonemes;
likewise, the state of Paramātman consists of four syllables, as does the state of Maheśvara.
O best of sages, that which is indeed the state of Mahādeva is declared to consist of four syllables;
however, the one known as Sadbhāveśvara consists of five syllables.
The four-syllable word "mahāteja" has been proclaimed;
the five-syllable word designated as "yogādhipati" is thus indicated.
Release, release! The four-syllable and six-syllable mantra, whose nature is that of the Pramathas, and the word *śarva-śarva*—the four-syllabled [mantra] should be understood here.
Likewise, there is a pair of *bhava* syllables, and again the word *bhavodbhava*;
another eight-syllable word bestows happiness upon all beings.
Preceded by the presence of all [deities], ending with the hand, consisting of seven syllables,
and having an eight-syllable word, it represents the succession of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
A word consisting of eight syllables that is repeated twice without being honored is called an *asaṃskṛta-pada* (unrefined word); likewise is a word that remains in its original position.
In the *sākṣin* [meter], there are likewise four syllables per foot due to the doubling;
in the *pataṅga* [meter], there are six syllables, and in the one named *piṅga*, there are four.
In the same way, the state of knowledge (jñānapada) consists of four syllables known as Śabda and Sūkṣma;
likewise, the state of Śiva (śivapada) and the state of the All-pervading Lord Śarva (śarvapada) consist of two syllables each.
The three-syllable mantra that removes all obstacles begins with the *praṇava* and ends with *namaḥ*.
The five-syllable mantra for Śiva is declared to consist of three syllables [when combined].
"The pair of salutations, five-colored, with the stars, is the supreme word. Thus [ends verse 5].
The commentary indicates those very [scriptures] that illuminate [the subject], stating "in the Śaiva Āgamas.
The word "of the categories" (*padārthānām*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. As it has been said in the *Tantralakṣaṇa*: "It consists of three categories and four feet."

"Mahātantra" (Mṛgendratantra-vṛtti 2.2). And for this reason, he demonstrates by means of a definition that other entities are included within those very [categories], starting with: "Among these, the Lord. Among those three categories, the category of the Lord (*pati*) is said to be Śiva. Here, by the word "Śiva," used in the singular to denote the genus, [it refers to] those endowed with the nature of Śiva—namely, the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, Mantramahēśvaras, and...

The category of the Lord (*pati*) is described here as including, along with its designations, the group of means—such as initiation (*dīkṣā*)—which serve as the instruments for attaining the state of Śiva by those who possess the powers of knowledge and action. Furthermore, the individual selves (*aṇu-ātman*) are the objects to be impelled; by this [category], those bound in the state of the fettered (*paśu*), who are divided into the various classes such as the *vijñānakala* and so forth, are also included.

The state of being an object of bondage for those whose souls are bound is expressed [by this]. By the term "fivefold object" (*arthapañcaka*), impurity (*mala*), obstruction (*rodha*), power (*śakti*), karma, *māyā*, and the *bindu* are denoted. Consequently, these five are subsumed within the category of the objects of bondage (*pāśapadārtha*) along with the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), elements (*bhūta*), and entities (*bhāva*) that arise from the *bindu* and *māyā*, which possess both pure and impure forms. Now, one might ask:
How can it be said that the single Śiva-power (śivaśakti) is subsumed within both the category of the Lord (pati-padārtha) and the category of the fetter (pāśa-padārtha)? It is true;

from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), the power is indeed included within the category of the Lord alone. However, its status as a fetter is merely figurative (upacāra), based on its conformity with the attributes of a fetter. As it is stated in the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra: "Of those [powers], the power of Maheśvara..."

"The auspicious one who bestows grace upon all; it is only because she conforms to the *dharma* that she is metaphorically designated as 'bond' (*pāśa*). (Vijñānabhairava 7.11). Thus [ends the fifth verse].
Although these [other] auspicious ones are liberated souls, they are liberated by His grace;
He alone, whose body consists of the five mantras, should be known as eternally liberated from the beginningless past.

In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the objection that since bound souls (*paśu*) possess the nature of Śiva, their separation from the Lord (*pati*) is impossible, and thus how there could be the contingency of a twofold division, he says: "The liberated... (*mukta*).

This is the intended meaning: liberation is indeed the very nature of Śiva for liberated souls; however, even for them, there is no state of being Śiva prior to liberation. This is because, before liberation, they are bound souls (*paśu*) whose Śiva-nature is concealed by the bonds (*pāśa*)—such as impurities (*mala*) that are like the blackness obscuring the golden nature of copper and other metals. For this very reason, they...

By His grace, they are liberated. He is Śiva, who is liberated from beginningless time (*anādimukta*). "The One" means that He alone is eternally liberated, because He is devoid of any connection with impurities (*mala*) and the like throughout the three periods of time. As it is said in the venerable *Vāyavīya*: "By nature, due to the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of any contact with beginningless impurity..."
"Because he is the absolutely pure Self, he is called Śiva. (Śivavimarśinī 1.32.29).
"Having the five mantras as his body" means that his entire body consists of all mantras, comprising the fivefold nature of *nāda*, *bindu*, *pada*, *varṇa*, and *vākya*.

This is the meaning. Or, [it means] "having the nature of mantra. From such scriptural passages as, "His hair is the *uṣṇih*, his skin the *gāyatrī*, his flesh the *triṣṭubh*, his sinews the *anuṣṭubh*, his bone the *jagatī*, his marrow the *paṅkti*, and his vital breath the *bṛhatī*" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.6.1), which demonstrate that Vedic and other mantras are composed of the bodily elements (*dhātu*), one understands that Śiva has mantra as His body. Alternatively, [He exists] in the form of the *praṇava* and the four Vedas.

"He whose body consists of the fivefold mantras. This is stated in the *Laiṅga* Purāṇa and other texts: "The unborn, all-pervading Lord has the form of the syllable Oṃ; the Ṛgveda is his face, he is endowed with the Sāmaveda as his tongue, the Yajurveda is his great neck, and the Atharvaveda is his lip" (1.1.30–31).

Alternatively, his body is the *praṇava* consisting of five aspects—namely, seed (*bīja*), point (*bindu*), resonance (*nāda*), power (*śakti*), and peace (*śānta*)—according to such scriptural passages as "Om is Brahman" and "Om, that which yonder shines. Or, his body consists of five syllables; or, his body consists of the five principles (*tattva*) beginning with *nivṛtti*;
or, his body consists of the five Brahmans. As it is said in the *Liṅgodbhava*:
Now, [the first two verses are seen in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* (1.17.89–90):
Having beheld him whose form consists of the *kalās*, syllables, and the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas— the Lord (*Īśāna*),
the Sovereign (*Īśa*), crowned with a diadem, ancient, and designated as the Puruṣa—
The Aghora-heart, the heart-pleasing Vāma-secret,
Sadāśiva, Sadyojāta-foot, Mahādeva, adorned by the great lords of yogins.
The Great Lord, who is both partless, subtle, and unmanifest, as well as manifest,
assumes the form of the *liṅga* for the sake of the play of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
"The primary [principle] is declared to be the *liṅga*, and the possessor of the *liṅga* (*liṅgin*) is the Supreme Lord," and so forth.
And in the *Pārameśvara*:
"The illustrious *sakala* [deity], whose body consists of the five mantras, is recited..."
The Lord is the master of yoga-yogins, independent, and the destroyer of the bonds of the bound souls (paśus).
The Lord Maheśvara has Īśāna as his head, Puṃs as his face, Aghora as his heart, Vāma as his secret organ, and Sadyojāta as his form. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.18, 19)
"Thus, these are the five mantras by which the body is bound as auspicious," and so forth.
(Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.14–15, 30).
Therefore, it should be understood in this way: Śiva is to be known specifically through his distinction from the bound souls (*paśu*). And not...

It should not be argued that because there exists a real difference between the Supreme Lord—the signifier—and the Vedic mantra and so forth—the signified, the mantra lacks the nature of being the Vedas; for if there were such a difference, it would follow that the fixed relationship between signifier and signified could not exist. Nor can that fixed relationship be established through a connection (*sambandha*), since it has already been stated that a connection requires another connection, leading to defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, the power of signification (*vācakatva-śakti*) is not...
Or rather, it should be called "the restrictor" (*yāmika*), for if there were a real difference between that [power] and the denotable object, it would not be restrictive, just like any other power.

Furthermore, since the exclusivity of a power to its denotable object cannot possibly exist apart from non-difference, one must admit the non-difference of the denoted and the denoter themselves; what is the use of this postulation of a power? Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that because the relationship between the signified and the signifier resides in different loci, their non-difference is impossible; for here, difference also exists, just as there is difference between a quality and its possessor. Nor can it be claimed that difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one place due to contradiction—since one is affirmative and the other negative—because this is established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the fact that the relationship of signifier and signified would otherwise be inexplicable. Thus, "This is a jar... [and so forth].

Because there is an appearance of the object conjoined with its designator in such cases as "this is a cloth" or "this is a sound," and because there is an appearance of the sound unjoined [with the object] in such cases as "this is the word 'jar,'" one must accept the identity of word and meaning.
For this very reason, through the placement of mantras that designate principles (tattva) and so forth, there occurs the presence of those principles; thus, everything is clear.

[Objection: Let it be that liberation consists in the state of Śiva due to the absence of contact with bonds (pāśa). But how can there be an absence of the state of a bound soul (paśutva) for the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara) and others, even though they possess a body consisting of bindu? To this, he says: "the liberated self" (muktātman).

Those whose souls are liberated have attained equality with Śiva. By the force of the word "also" (api), the Vidyeśvaras and others are likewise Śivas, because they are devoid of the impurity known as *paśutva* (the state of being a bound soul). For it is the possession of that [impurity] which constitutes *paśutva*, according to the scriptural statement: "A *paśu* [is so called] because of its conjunction with *paśutva*.

Therefore, because these [liberated ones] are endowed with the nature of Śiva—such as omniscience and other attributes—they possess nothing but the state of Śiva. As for their connection with a *baindava* (emanated from the Bindu) body:

Because a portion of the impurity of office (*adhikāra-mala*) remains, they are indeed bound by that office. For this very reason, due to having transcended *māyā* and being free from impurity, their attainment of the status of *Vidyā* and *Vidyeśvara* constitutes "lower liberation" (*apara-mukti*). But how can the *Mantraiśvaras* possess the nature of Śiva (*śivatva*) even while in conjunction with *kalā* and the other categories?
It is because they are directly graced by Śiva, because they possess omniscience and other such qualities, and because they are free from impurity. As for their conjunction with *kalā* and the rest:
Because they possess a remnant of the impurity pertaining to the office (*adhikāra*) within the womb of *māyā*, they are bound by that office, and because such a state is necessary for them.
As it has been said: "Even when in union with *kalā*, they are not subject to the *kalās* like a multitude of bound souls (*paśu*s)" (Mokṣakārikā 82). If this is so, one might ask:
although their state of Śiva-nature is equal [to others], what is the distinction of this Supreme Lord from liberated souls and the like? To this, he says: "But these..."
"By His grace they are liberated. These refer to the aforementioned Vidyeśvaras and others; "by His grace" means by the grace of that Supreme Lord.

"He is liberated from the beginningless" (anādimukta) means that He is endowed with the powers of knowledge and action, which are eternally pure, unsurpassed, and established by His very nature from the beginningless past.
Now, one might object: even for the Lord, the scriptures state through such passages as "five-faced" and "fifteen-eyed" that there is a connection with a body and sense organs.

Since it is heard [in scripture], he says: "His body consists of five mantras. The intention here is as follows: the form of the Lord with five faces and so forth is heard of solely for the purpose of meditation, because meditation, worship, and the like are impossible in the case of the formless. As they say: "You possess form; therefore, You are necessarily an object of worship, for the intellect cannot reach a reality that is formless. Also, in the venerable Pauṣkara:

"However, for the sake of the practitioner's goal, his form has been described [as follows]. Also, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Because no physical body exists [for him], whatever task he performs, in each instance his body is a reflection of the body of the agent of that action" (*Mṛgendrakriyāpāda* 3.41). Therefore, the [five faces] beginning with Īśāna consist of the five mantras and are employed for the fivefold acts.

It is the powers (*śakti*) themselves, performing the functions of the body, that are metaphorically called the "body" (*tanu*). As it has been said: "That body [is constituted] by the five mantras, which are employed for the fivefold acts; through Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha, [the body's parts] beginning with the head [are formed]. (Mṛgendrāgama-vṛtti 3.8–9) || 6 ||
Its fivefold function consists of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and likewise the bestowing of grace; this is declared to be the activity of that which is eternally manifest.

The *Tātparyadīpikā* [raises this objection]: "But surely, since there is no evidence for the existence of a Lord (*pati*), the threefoldness of the principles (*tattva*) is impossible. Anticipating this doubt, it says: "Five," etc.

The meaning is as follows: [the Lord acts] in a fivefold manner, consisting of five types, namely through creation (*sarga*), maintenance (*sthiti*), withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), concealment (*tirobhāva*), and grace (*anugraha*).

That "task" (tatkṛtya) is the work of Maheśvara; it is the authority in that regard because He alone is capable of performing it. Neither another soul (jīva) nor Māyā is able to perform the creation of the universe and so forth, because the bound soul (paśu) lacks knowledge of the sequence for the application of materials and instruments, and because Māyā, being insentient, lacks that capacity. That creation is fivefold.

This is because that which is to be created—consisting of dispositions (*bhāva*), principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), beings (*bhūta*), and causal conditions (*pratyaya*)—is fivefold. As it is stated in the *Śaivarahasya*: "The Lord, the ocean of compassion, creates dispositions, principles, worlds, beings, and also causal conditions, in order to bring karma to fruition through experience."
This will be established in detail further below. *Sthiti* (maintenance) means preservation. *Saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) means destruction;

that is to say, the dissolution of an effect into its own respective uncommon causes, which is to say, its subsistence in a subtle form. *Tirobhāva* (concealment) is the covering of the selves by bonds (*pāśas*). *Anugrahakaraṇa* (the act of grace) consists of liberation and so forth. Now, is it not contradictory to state this?

If it is argued that [the Lord] causes worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) by means of the fetters (*pāśa*) through the door of concealing the Self, and bestows liberation (*apavarga*) by removing the fetters such as the impurities (*mala*) that conceal the Self—this is not so;

for there is no contradiction between these two functions due to the distinction of their respective objects. [The Lord] exercises grace toward those who possess the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*).

For those who lack that [knowledge], it serves as the cause of *saṃsāra*. This is what was stated regarding this [Lord] who is eternally manifest (*satatodita*). Since the production of an effect is impossible without an agent, and since no other agent is possible, this Maheśvara—who is eternally manifest, consisting solely of self-luminous consciousness, perfectly full, devoid of activity, indifferent, and yet the witness—[is the cause].
The agency of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) in creation and other such acts has been declared; that is to say, it has been stated. As it has been said:
"Just as fire, though itself unchanging, effects the transformation of water and rice, so does Śambhu, remaining indifferent, effect the transformations of Māyā and the rest. (7)
The commentary says "fivefold" for this very reason:
these five functions, regarding the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), are performed directly by Śiva, whereas regarding the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*)...

It has been stated [that this occurs] by way of Ananta and the others. Likewise, in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*: "In the pure path, Śiva is declared to be the agent; in the impure, Ananta is the lord" (*Viśeṣādhikāra* 3.27). In that context, the direct creation of Śiva proceeds from the material cause consisting of the *bindu*, preceded by the production of the pure principles, worlds, and so forth, for the sake of those inhabitants of those worlds.

[The Lord performs] the conjunction of the Vidyās and the Vidyeśvaras with a body consisting of the *bindu*, as well as the production of the Vidyās through the sequence beginning with the *nāda*. However, by means of Ananta and others, following the taking up of *māyā* and other [causes], preceded by the production of the impure categories (*tattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*), He effects the conjunction of the multitudes of bound souls (*paśu*) with a subtle, essential body and with a cosmic body (*bhauvana*) corresponding to their own karma; and likewise for the Mantreśvaras—

And [it includes] the production of the body as the basis for authority. Maintenance (*sthiti*) is the establishment of the entire universe—which has been restrained by its own power—within its own domain. Withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) is the reabsorption of the two classes of effects, the pure and the impure, namely *bindu* and *māyā*. And concealment (*tirobhāva*) is [the act] of souls through the grasping of fetters (*pāśa*).

[The Lord's activity consists of] providing enjoyments according to [the soul's] fitness, and grace (*anugraha*), which is the bestowing of the lower and higher liberation upon souls by means of the concealment of their bonds (*pāśa*).

Now, one might object: since the venerable *Raurava* and other scriptures state that "He performs creation, preservation, withdrawal, obscuration, and grace" (1.15), and since even the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras possess authority over these five functions, how can it be said that these belong to Him alone who is eternally manifest?

What is the restrictive rule (*niyama*)? It is said: since even they possess the agency for the fivefold cosmic acts solely through the impulsion of Śiva, it is stated thus; therefore, there is no contradiction. The bound souls (*paśu*) are to be known as threefold: the *vijñānakevala*, the *pralayakevala*, and the *sakala*.
Among these, the first is joined with impurity (*mala*); the second would be joined with impurity and karma (*karman*). (7–8)

Having thus established the definition and examination of the category of *pati* according to the order of enumeration, the *Tātparyadīpikā* states "the bound souls" (*paśavaḥ*) and so forth, in order to determine the immediately following category of *paśu*.

The *pāśas* (bonds) are so called; those who are bound by them are *paśus* (bound souls). Now, if it is argued that this definition of a *paśu* is unestablished because there is no evidence for the existence of a transmigrating soul (*saṃsāryātman*) distinct from the body and so forth that wanders between this world and the next, we reply: not so, for [there is such a soul] distinct from the body.

Because the existence of an eternal self (*ātman*) is understood through means of valid cognition such as the recollection of past births; for instance, in another birth, one is found to take possession of a treasure or similar object deposited in a previous birth, thinking, "This was previously deposited here by me.
Therefore, there exists a single, eternal, embodied being who is the depositor of the treasure; otherwise, [this would not be possible].

Because its appropriation is impossible. Nor should it be said that what is deposited by one is appropriated by another, for since memory is impossible for one person regarding what was experienced by another, the appropriation preceded by such memory is impossible. Nor should it be said that this [memory] is rooted in error, because there is no subverting evidence; rather, its validity is established through correspondence, as it is perceived directly by perception. Thus:

Furthermore, from scriptural passages such as, "Some enter a womb" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.7), and because we observe the attainment of another body through the relinquishment of a previous body, the existence of a self distinct from the body is established. Nor is the vital breath (prāṇa) the self, because it is of the nature of air, like external air.

Furthermore, because a distinction is perceived between the self and the vital breaths—as in the case of "my vital breaths" or "my garment"—the view of certain Ārhata sectarians that the senses constitute the self is refuted; for even when a particular sense organ has perished, one observes the recollection of objects experienced by that very sense organ, since it is impossible for one person to remember what was experienced by another. Likewise:

Because it is impossible for the self to be the cognizer of indefinite objects while the sense organs grasp only fixed objects; and that [selfhood] is established through the synthesis of recognition: "I who experienced a form with the eye, I now experience a sound with the ear. Nor is the mind the self, because it is an instrument, like an axe, and likewise because it is limited and an effect.

Like a jar or other objects; thus, since the self is established as distinct, and since the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions regarding multiple sense-objects establishes the existence of the mind (*manas*), the self is not the mind. Likewise, the Buddhist conception that the self is the intellect (*buddhi*) in the form of the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) must be refuted on the grounds that it would result in the impossibility of memory. For instance, in the case of an object previously experienced by the intellect—

Because there is no experience of another cognition as being distinct [from itself], recollection is impossible. Furthermore, recollection of an object not previously experienced is not possible, as it is never observed. Nor can it be argued that the cognition persists [until the time of recollection], for the momentary destruction of cognitions is accepted by all schools of thought. [If this is so, how is recollection explained? It is explained by the continuity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through the unity of the single mental stream (*santāna*).

If it is argued that this is not so, [we reply] no; for even in the case of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the continuum (*saṃtāna*), the previously mentioned faults would arise due to their momentariness. Furthermore, since those two are non-different from cognition, the same refutation applies.
If they were non-momentary or distinct [from cognition], there would be a contradiction with your own tenets. As it has been said by the experts in logic:
"Even if [it were] eternal and ultimately real..."
"You have approached a state called 'continuity. Arise, O Bhikṣu! Your hopes have borne fruit;
this doctrine of momentary flux is now concluded. Thus [it is said].

Some maintain that the Self is the bliss derived from sense objects, because it serves no other purpose and is the object of the notion of being extremely dear. However, even that [bliss], which arises through the connection between the sense objects, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the Self, is merely a mental construction (buddhikalpa) and must therefore be disregarded.

Consequently, it is established that the Self is distinct from the intellect, the senses, and the body, and is called a "bound soul" (paśu) because it is bound by fetters (pāśa). As it has been said in the venerable Vāyavīya[-Saṃhitā]:
The soul is indeed distinct from the vital breaths, the sense organs, and the body; it is all-pervading and eternal.
Yet, the reason for asserting that such a conceptualized self exists is extremely difficult to establish.

"By the wise, the nature of self is not admitted for the intellect, the senses, or the body, because of memory, because of the lack of certainty in cognition, and because of the experience of bodily pain," and so forth.
(Śivapurāṇa, Vāyavīyasaṃhitā 1.5.43–44)

Thus, he states the classification of the bound souls (*paśu*) who have been explained in this way: "They are to be known as threefold. This means they should be understood as being of three types. To the question "In what way?", he says: "The *vijñānākala*s, the *pralayākala*s, and the *sakala*s. He states their respective characteristics in order: "Endowed with impurity" means bound by the fetter of impurity (*mala*). Among them, the first...

The second [category] consists of those whose time is determined by their consciousness (vijñānakala), who are joined with impurity and karma—that is, bound by the two fetters consisting of impurity and karma. || 8 ||

The commentary: Having thus stated the divisions of the category of the Lord (*pati*), it now states the divisions of the category of the bound soul (*paśu*) with the words "the bound souls" (*paśavaḥ*).
Among them (*tatra*), the first group is called the "isolated ones through knowledge" (*vijñānakevala*).

"Through the application of discernment (*vijñāna*), renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), or from the exhaustion of karma through experience" (Paśupatimokṣakārikā 55)—thus, due to the exhaustion of karma, since even the bondage of *kalā* and so forth, which exists for the purpose of experiencing karma, ceases to exist, one remains endowed with nothing but *mala* alone.

The second group, however, known as the *pralayakevala*, becomes possessed of both *mala* and *karman* because of the withdrawal of *kalā* and the other categories during cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). (8)
Among them, the Sakala is endowed with impurity (mala), māyā, and karma;
he is of two kinds, the first of which has completed his impurity and the second has not completed his impurity. || 9 ||

In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, following the definition of the *sakala* (the bound), he states the division of the *vijñānakala* with the words "beginning with *mala*": "Mala, Māyā, and Karma constitute *malamāyākarmāṇi*; one who is joined with—that is, connected to—these is the *sakala*."
Among those three, the first, the *vijñānakala*, is of two kinds: one whose impurity is exhausted (*samāptakaluṣa*) and one whose impurity is not exhausted (*asamāptakaluṣa*).
Of these, the first is the primary one, because it is the first among the *aṇus*. "One whose impurity is exhausted" means that impurity is the power of *mala*;
he in whom that has been exhausted—that is, destroyed—is *samāptakaluṣa*. The second is *asamāptakaluṣa*. By that [distinction], this...
The power of knowledge and action becomes concealed. || 9 ||

The *sakala* (the embodied soul), however, is conjoined with the three bonds (*bandha*). Since *māyā* has no direct connection [with the soul] therein, the term *māyā* refers to its effects, such as *kalā* and the rest. It is precisely because of being conjoined with these that it is called *sakala*.

Therefore, even when karma is exhausted through the destruction of consciousness and so forth, the persistence of the body for some time by the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) is possible; thus, it is heard in the scriptures that even when impurity (*mala*) and *māyā* have ceased, the state of being "with all" (*sakala-bheda*) still persists. And it has been said by the Sāṃkhyas:
"Upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, dharma and the other [factors] reach a state of non-causality."
"By the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), he remains holding his body like the whirling of a potter's wheel" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 67).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "among them": the first, the *vijñānakevalin*, is further divided into two types. To the question "What are those two divisions?", it says: "The first. Since impurity (*mala*) is a substance, its "cooking" (*pāka*) is possible because it is insentient, just as the cooking of cataracts and the like occurs in the eye. This is the first.
The meaning is that the *vijñānakevalin* is of two kinds, according to the distinction between one whose impurities are matured and one whose impurities are not yet matured. || 9 ||
Having first favored eight [beings], Śiva appoints them to the status of Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas);
he also creates other mantras, which are said to number seventy million.
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states: "Now, since both types of *vijñānakala* possess a connection with the fetters of impurity (*mala-pāśa*),

there can be neither union with Śiva— which consists in the cessation of that [connection]— nor abiding in the various states among gods and others within the intermediate realms of heaven and hell, through initiation (*dīkṣā*)."

When karma has been destroyed, the notion of self in what is not-self—which was produced by ignorance—is removed through hearing [the scriptures] and other means, because of the absence of connection with the illusion created by ignorance. Anticipating the question, "Where then does this [individual soul] abide?", he says: "The primordial ones" (ādyān).
Having extracted the primordial ones—the *vijñānakalas* whose impurities are exhausted—through initiation...
Having first bestowed grace in the form of providing indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) through the prior stages of hearing and reflection (*śravaṇa* and *manana*),

[the Lord bestows grace] not in the form of providing direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), because that [direct knowledge] cannot arise amidst the practice of contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) due to the occurrence of obstacles such as the exhaustion of karma. This occurs in the state of a Vidyeśa— that is, in the rank of a Vidyeśvara— which is equivalent to liberation.
The Lord Śiva appoints the eight portions of consciousness [as the Vidyeśvaras] and makes the other mantras into the forms of the mantra-deities.
As it is said in the *Siddhāntahṛdaya*:
"The Lord makes the eight Vidyeśvaras and the others into the deities of the mantras."
In response to the inquiry as to how many mantras there are, he says: "And they are said to be seven crores. This means that those great mantras are numbered at seven crores. || 10 ||
As for the commentary on those two [verses], it says "the first": having favored the first ones— those whose impurities have reached maturity— according to the gradations of their maturation,
making them fit for authority by removing their impurities and endowing them with omniscience and other qualities, as well as uniting them with the *bindu*-body.

Among them, he appoints eight who possess the ripening of distinguished *mala* to the state of *Vidyeśas*. The meaning is that he makes them the presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) over the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), residents of the *Īśvara-tattva*, and the authorities over the five cosmic functions (*pañcakṛtya*), bearing the names Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin. As for the others, numbering seventy million—

The meaning is that he makes the mantras the instruments for the act of grace and causes them to dwell in the principle of *vidyā*. Among those, one half remains as the instrument for the act of grace performed by Śiva—who has the guru as his substratum—with respect to the domain of the *sakala* (embodied souls); at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), it attains liberation. The other half, however, belongs to Śiva who is without a substratum (*niradhikaraṇa*), with respect to the domain of the *vijñānakalas* and others, [as the instrument] of the Lord of Mantras (*mantreśvara*).

And regarding the subject who possesses authority within the womb of *māyā*, having attained the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*), he becomes withdrawn immediately after the act of emission due to detachment from that authority. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"That [instrumentality] depends on the body of the agent throughout the entire path; it lasts for half [the duration]."
Having fulfilled his office at the end of the cosmic duration, he enters Śiva, who is accompanied by the Lord (Iśvara).

"Without an office (*adhikaraṇa*), another [soul], having performed the desired office below the primary transformation, attains [the state] during the withdrawal of its own paths" (ViP 4.78). However, those who have here reached the ultimate ripening of their impurities (*malapāka*) and are independent of offices, he unites them in the supreme station (*pare pade*). Those...
Their impurities are unripened; it is stated in the venerable Raurava and other scriptures that their state as *vijñānākala* lasts until the end of the ripening of those impurities. || 10 ||

Among the *pralayākala*s, those whose impurities (*mala*) and karma have ripened depart for all types of wombs, joined with a body consisting of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*), under the influence of their karma. (11)

The inner organ, consisting of the eightfold city—the instruments of cognition and action—Maheśvara bestows upon certain individuals after having extracted them [from their bodies], granting them the status of lords of the worlds. (Note: In the commentary by Śrī Kumāra, the order of the first and second halves of this verse is seen to be reversed. || 12 ||
At the time of dawn, all the remaining [deities] become complete through their conjunction with the *kalās* and other [factors];
he himself appoints one hundred and eighteen of them as lords of mantras (*mantreśas*).
The *Tātparyadīpikā* now states three verses for the purpose of determining the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the *pralayākala* and the *sakala*: "In the case of the *pralayākalas*," etc.
The intended meaning is as follows: [the body] consisting of the principles from *kalā* down to *dharā* has undergone a profound dissolution (*prakarṣeṇa layam gataṃ*).

Those [souls] are the *pralayākalas*. That is to say, they are souls who, in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), are bound only by the fetters of impurity (*mala*) and karma. Among them, for those whose impurity and karma (*malakarmaṇī*) have ripened—that is, reached full maturity through association with the fire of knowledge—Maheśvara [bestows grace].
It bestows the status of a Lord of Beings (*bhuvanapati*). "To them" means it grants or gives [this].

Among those [beings], having favored some whose karma has ripened, it makes them Lords of the Gaṇas (*gaṇeśa*); and having favored others whose impurities have ripened, it makes them Lords of Mantras and Tantras (*mantratantra-īśvara*) by way of being perceivers (*draṣṭṛtva*). In response to the inquiry as to how many Lords of Mantras there are, [the answer is] "one hundred and eighteen. "By itself" [is the meaning].

"Without depending on any other assistant such as Brahmā and the like. This has been stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "He created a thousand times a thousand [beings] who were neither superior nor inferior to himself, equal to his mind-born sons, clad in animal skins," and so forth.

Other than these, those remaining who have exhausted their impure karma (*pakvamalakarmāṇaḥ*) are the "perfected ones" (*śiṣṭāḥ*); they are "possessed of all parts" (*sakalāḥ*) because of their connection with the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā*.
Regarding the phrase "at the dawn of day, [it is] time": at the time of creation, the Blessed Lord Maheśvara brings about all this.
Endowed with the body of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), they alone proceed—that is, they move—through all wombs, such as those of gods, humans, animals, and so forth.

Anticipating the objection—namely, that since the selves (*ātman*) are all-pervasive and formless, how is the movement to and from all wombs possible?—the author says: "endowed with the body of the *puryaṣṭaka*. Because the subtle body known as the *puryaṣṭaka* exists as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), the coming and going of the bound soul (*paśu*), who is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), is indeed possible in accordance with that [subtle body]. Just as...

Just as the space within a jar undergoes coming and going through the coming and going of its limiting adjunct—the jar—so too, it is entirely logical that the attributes of the adjuncts, such as coming and so forth, can occur in the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) which is conditioned by them.
"By the power of karma" means in accordance with one's karma. Now, [one might ask], what is this *puryaṣṭaka* that serves as the adjunct of the individual soul (*jīva*)?

Anticipating the question "What is it?", he says: "The *puryaṣṭaka* is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), consisting of the instruments of cognition and action. That which exists within the city—the gross body—is the *puryaṣṭaka*. To the question "What is that?", he replies: "The internal organ consists of the instruments of cognition and action. The intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*) constitute the internal organ; the activity or operation of the intellect is its engagement with objects.

Ascertainment is the function of the intellect (*dhī*); some maintain that its instruments—the causes thereof, namely sound and the rest—constitute the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*). As it has been said:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
mind, intellect, and ego—this is declared to be the eightfold city. (Kārikāvalī 17.4–5)

The teachers, however, say that the intellect (*dhī*), its functions (*karman*), and the instruments (*karaṇa*) constitute the "intellect-function-instruments" (*dhī-karma-karaṇa*). In that regard, their eightfold nature arises from the division into [the five] objects—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—the [five] organs of cognition, the [five] organs of action, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and the self (*ātman*). Others [assert it consists of] the fourfold [set of] organs of action, cognition, and the internal organ; the pentad of vital breaths (*prāṇa*); the pentad of subtle elements (*tanmātra*);...
They say that the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*) consists of desire, action, ignorance, and the self. Thus it has been said:
"Indeed, there are five organs of action, and likewise five other organs of cognition, as well as the fourfold group beginning with the mind."
"Furthermore, the pentad beginning with prāṇa, the pentad beginning with ether, desire, action, and darkness—this is the eighth city. (11–13)

The commentary [explains]: among the *pralayākalas*, those whose impurity (*mala*) has become ripe— by virtue of that very ripening, all their karma also becomes ripe— and they "go," meaning they attain liberation (this is the ellipsis), because the ripening of impurity is the cause of liberation by means of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"Upon the cessation of the dominion of the power of darkness (*tamaśśakti*) and its subsequent removal, Śiva bestows upon the individual soul (*aṇu*), who is otherwise a bond for the world, the infinity of vision and action" (*Viṣamapada* 5.1).
Also in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "When that [impurity] has been exhausted, she [the intellect] shall, through wisdom, lead toward the supreme *niḥśreyasa* (final beatitude)" (32.17).
Others, however, whose impurities are unripened, being joined with the body of the *puryaṣṭaka*, wander through all wombs by the power of karma for the sake of experiencing that [result].

The phrase "they go" (*vrajanti*) from the preceding action must be supplied here as well, [meaning] "they go into those [wombs] consisting of bodies born of the world. Regarding the reading "these" (*ete*), some explain it as "those joined with the body of the *puryaṣṭaka* go into the wombs.

For them, there is the aforementioned contradiction with the Śruti, and the further fault that since even those whose impurities have been ripened would again be subject to transmigratory existence, the consequence would be the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*). || 11 ||
Now, as to what that "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka) is, he says: "It may be... and so forth.

In this context, the city of eight is the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha), which consists of thirty principles beginning with earth and ending with kalā; it is specific to each individual, remains constant from the beginning of creation until the end of the kalpa or until liberation, and possesses a unique form.
As it is heard [in the scriptures]:
"This [body], which extends from the user [the self] to the earth's limit, accomplishes subtle purposes;
it is restricted to each individual soul... (Mṛgendra-vṛtti 12.32–33).
Also in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
"This group of principles, beginning with Earth and ending with Kalā, is determined for each individual;
and it wanders, by the power of karma, through all the bodies born within the worlds" (verses 24–25).

Therefore, this is the meaning: by the term *antaḥkaraṇa* (internal organ), which denotes the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*), there are also indicated the other seven principles (*tattva*)—namely, *kalā*, *kāla*, *niyati*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *prakṛti*, and the *guṇas*—which are internal to the person’s activity of experience. By the term *dhīkarma* (the action of the intellect), those objects are to be understood which are grasped through the intellect’s process of determination (*adhyavasāya*).
The five elements beginning with earth and ending with space, along with their causes—the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such as sound and the rest—are thus described.
By the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*), he indicates the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*). Now, [it is said]:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth..."
"Intellect, mind, and ego—this is declared to be the *puryaṣṭaka*.

Thus it is heard in the venerable *Kālottara*. This is true; for this very reason, that aphorism was explained by the revered Rāmakaṇṭha as referring to the thirty principles (*tattvas*). But how, then, does this [group] possess the nature of an "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*)?

There is no contradiction [in this], because [the body] is composed of five groups— namely, the elements (*bhūta*), subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— as well as their cause, the *guṇa*, its fulfiller, the *pradhāna*, and the group consisting of the five sheaths beginning with *kalā*.
Now, among those [beings] joined with the *puryaṣṭaka*, Maheśvara— that is to say, the Mantra-Maheśvara— graces some.

This is because it is heard in scripture that the lords of the worlds (bhuvanapatī), such as those of the Guhya, Atiguha, Guhyatara, Pavitra, Sthāṇu, Pañcāṣṭaka, and others, are indeed appointed by Ananta; and because they possess "ointment" (añjana). Regarding the word *anugṛhya* (having favored): the meaning is that he has made certain individuals of distinguished merit into yogins who have manifested knowledge and action, along with powers such as *aṇimā*, up until the end of their own respective offices. || 12 ||

Furthermore, those who remain among those bound to *saṃsāra*—who, although their impurities (*mala*) have matured, do so only sluggishly due to the state of their impurities not being fully ripened—are called "residual" (*śeṣa*). Because at the commencement of creation they are joined with *kalā* and the other [categories] by virtue of their connection to their respective offices (*adhikāra*), they are "possessing all" (*sakala*). Even while joined with these, they are said to be "residual" because they are free from impurity (*mala*). How many are they?

To the question "By whom are they appointed?", he says: "One hundred and eighteen. Indeed, Śiva himself, having removed their impurities (*mala*), appoints those one hundred and eighteen to the rank of Mantreśas. The meaning is that they are not appointed by Ananta. However, their connection with *kalā* and the other *tattvas* is performed solely by Ananta, because it has been stated: "Ananta is the lord over the dark [state]" (*Kiraṇavṛtti* 3.27). || 13 ||
Therein, there are eight Maṇḍalins beginning with the Krodhas, as well as Vīreśa, Śrīkaṇṭha, and the hundred Śatarudras; thus, [the total] is one hundred and eighteen.
It has been stated that there are one hundred and eighteen Mantreśvaras. To address the inquiry as to who they are, [the author] says: "Among them, eight...
Among those Mantreśvaras, eight are the Maṇḍalins; [and] the Krodhas and others are equal to them.
The meaning is "eight. The remaining ones are Vīreśa and the others. This has been stated in the *Siddhāntahṛdaya*:
"They are of three kinds: the *vijñānakalas*, the *pralayākalas*, and the *sakalas*.
Among them, the first [the *vijñānakalas*] are endowed with only impurity (*mala*); the others..."

Those joined with impurity and karma, and those joined with the impurity of illusion and karma, are the "sakala" (conditioned) souls; among them, the first type is of two kinds, those whose defilements have been ripened.

And regarding the phrase "those whose impurities are unripened": here, the Lord, having first favored the former group, makes them the eight Vidyeśvaras, while he makes the others the deities of the Mantras.
The Pralayākalas are of four kinds: those who are twice-ripe and once-ripe, and those who are both ripe and twice-ripe.
Among them, the masters of the cities (purādhīśas) are those who are both ripe, while the lords of the hosts (gaṇeśas) are those whose karma has reached maturity.
There are eighteen hundred other Rudras with matured impurities;
the Sakala [deity] is eightfold, consisting of those with three, two, one, and none matured [impurities].
"The Lord [Brahmā] created Hiraṇyagarbha, Sanaka and the other yogis, as well as the teachers (ācāryas) and the gods, in due order among them," and so forth. Also, in the *Śaivarahasya*:
This person (puruṣa) is of three kinds— known as *vijñānākala*, *pralayākala*, and *sakala*— due to being bound by one, two, or all three types of fetters respectively.

Having bestowed grace upon the eight Vidyeśvaras— those who have brought the notions of consciousness and the jar to an end— and also upon the Mantras divided into seventy million classes, Śiva [establishes them].
And some *pralayākalas*, who are lords of worlds (*bhuvaneśas*) whose impure karma has been ripened, wander through all wombs (*yoni*),
remaining [in saṃsāra] by the power of their residual karma.
Due to their connection with all the *kalās* and so forth, they are specified as such during the state of emanation (*sṛṣṭidaśā*).
Among them, there shall be one hundred and eighteen lords of the mantras (*mantra*).
The hundred Rudras, Krodha and the others, and even the eight [deities] beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra, exist as Mantreśas, namely Vīreśa and Śrīkaṇṭha; and so forth. (14)
The commentary analyzes those very [categories] with the words "therein, eight.
Here, the eight *maṇḍalins* are the residents of the summit of Mount Kalāma, beginning with Gahaneśa, as well as the *krodhas* and others.

There are exactly eight [deities] stationed at the summit of the Guṇas. Vīreśa is Vīrabhadra, the presiding lord of the hundred Rudras. Śrīkaṇṭha resides in the principle of Guṇa (guṇatattva) and is the creator of the worlds situated below; the hundred Rudras, however, are the sustainers of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 14 ||

Abiding in the form of the Teacher, he unites those whose impurities are fully ripened with the Supreme Reality by means of initiation, which has the power to cause their eradication through the descent of grace. 15.
In the *Tātparyadīpikā*,
having raised the objection that "if this were so, then there would be no entry onto the path of liberation for bound souls (*paśu*) wandering in saṃsāra," it says:
"those whose impurities are fully ripened."

For the power of the Supreme Lord is twofold: that which binds and that which liberates. Of these two, the former has been active from time immemorial, binding individual souls (paśus) with the nets of fetters (pāśas). When, by the force of time, there arises a conflict due to the equilibrium of karma, this liberating power ceases its activity; remaining within Maheśvara, it seeks the moment for their descent [into the world].

It falls upon those fetters (*paśu*). Then, once it has fallen upon that power which is the cause for the destruction of *saṃsāra*, the Blessed One assumes the form of the Teacher (*ācārya*), performs initiation (*dīkṣā*), effects the ripening of impurities (*mala*) and so forth, and unites [the soul] with the principle of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratattva*);
thus, entry onto the path of liberation is not something that cannot be accomplished. As it has been said:
When that same karma has arisen again by the power of the lapse of time, [the result follows].
When one is initiated by a Guru through the descent of intense power (tīvra-śakti-nipāta),
he becomes omniscient like Śiva himself, entirely devoid of limited knowledge.
"At that time, the transmigrating soul is no longer [merely] a possessor of the manifestation of Śiva-nature," and so forth (*Kiṭikāviveka* 1.20–22).
Furthermore, the two powers were stated by the venerable Avadhūtapāda:
No power whatsoever, even though its own potency is unimpaired, can bind the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) with your irresistible nets of snares;
for he cuts away all qualities without exception by means of the sword of knowledge.
"None other [than this] leads a person who is intent upon action toward liberation. || 15 ||
(Bhāskara’s Stotra 17) Commentary: Now, among all those bound by the three fetters, that Śiva [is superior] everywhere, on all sides, and pre-eminently.

Having taken recourse to a Guru, he unites all those whose impurities are fully ripened—having been touched by the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*) through the withdrawal of the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) and the subsequent binding of their fetters—to the supreme state, which consists in identity with Śiva. However, those whose impurities are only slightly ripened, he unites to the level of Vidyeśvara and others by means of a very mild descent of power (*śaktipāta*). As it is heard in scripture:

"Those who possess the state of Īśāna, the Lord of the Rudra-mantras, become [liberated] while remaining [in this world], provided they rely upon a Guru who bestows grace upon those endowed with consciousness. (Mṛgendravidyāpāda 5.3).
"Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular realm, he is directed to that very place."

"One attains success through the power of mantra" (*siddhibhāṅ mantrasāmarthyāt*)—this [verse] is cited in its entirety in the commentary on the *Sārdhatriśatikālottara* (1.5), and also in the *Svacchanda-tantra* (39.2).

For this very reason, it is established that the grace of Śiva toward those who have attained the state of consciousness-only (*vijñāna-kevalin*) and the state of dissolution-only (*pralayakevalin*) is indeed without a substratum. For this very reason...

The meaning is that because impurity is a substance, its cessation occurs through the activity of the Lord known as initiation (dīkṣā)—just as a cataract or other defect of the eye is removed—rather than through knowledge alone. || 15 ||
He assigns all remaining bound souls without exception to enjoyment and liberation according to the persistence of their past karma; thus are the "bound souls" (paśus) described.
The *Tātparyadīpikā* concludes the preceding discussion on the application [of mantras] with the words "baddhān" (those who are bound):
"And for the sake of the liberation from experience of the remaining *sakala* souls, who are bound by the subtle body known as the *puryaṣṭaka*..."
The meaning is that for the sake of experiencing sense objects, it employs [the soul] by joining it with the gross body in the abodes of gods and other beings. || 16 ||
The commentary [explains] "those whose impurities are unripened" as "the bound ones.
This is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. Now, he concludes the topic of the category of the bound soul (paśu): "In this way, the bound souls have been described."
Thus [ends the section]. 16.
There are four kinds of bonds (pāśas) for the person (puṃs): the first two are considered to arise from impurity (mala) and karma;
the other two arise from the power of Śiva that conceals Māyā.
