The *Tātparyadīpikā* now states, beginning with "The fetters," for the purpose of defining and examining those [categories] that have reached their turn:
"The fetters (*pāśas*) are the binders of the bound souls (*paśus*). And they are of four kinds; they are of four types for the person (*puṃsaḥ*)."
Of the person who is like a sacrificial animal (*paśu*). Among those [fetters], the first two are the initial ones, known as *mala* and *karman*.

Even there, *mala* is the primary bond (*pāśa*), because *karman* and the others are preceded by it. Some say that it is the prior non-existence of knowledge (*jñāna-prāgabhāva*). Others hold that it is insentient in nature, resembling darkness (*timira*), consisting of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), and removable by knowledge. The Teachers (*guravaḥ*), however, maintain that its essence consists of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus they say. Regarding this, the author of the *Śivasūtravārttika* stated: "The knowledge that 'I am' and 'this is mine,' which consists of the manifestation of duality, is bondage" (1.2).
The cause of impurity belonging to the realm of Māyā arises from the interpenetration of sound (*śabdānuvedha*).
And in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Impurity is ignorance, the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), and the darkness that causes obscuration."
"Indeed, ignorance (*avidyā*), form (*ākṛti*), and fainting (*mūrchā*) are synonyms that denote it. (Vi. 2.20–21).

The second bond is called *karman*. The third is that which pertains to *māyā* (*māyīya*), produced by *māyā*, consisting of the subtle and gross bodies and so forth. The fourth is that which arises from the power of Śiva that effects concealment (*tirodhāyaka-śiva-śakti-samudbhava*) and has that as its nature.

Since bondage—characterized by birth, death, and so forth, which constitutes transmigratory existence—is impossible in the absence of that which binds, the existence of the *pāśa* (the fetter) is established.

Furthermore, bondage is established through authoritative means such as the Vedas (*śruti*). Now, one might object: since impurity (*mala*) and karma are effects of *māyā*, [they must reside] within *māyā*.

If it is argued that there is the fallacy of mutual dependence—since the emergence of those two occurs when they have already begun to function, and the activity of *māyā* occurs upon the emergence of those two which were previously existent—the answer is no; for this is avoided by the fact that the process is beginningless (*anādi*), like the relationship between a seed and a sprout. || 17 ||
Commentary: Now, he states the divisions of the category of *pāśa* (bonds), beginning with the words "The bonds (*pāśāḥ*).

[An objection is raised: "But was it not previously stated that the five categories of objects constitute the *pāśa*? Is not the statement here that they are fourfold contradictory? [The author replies: No.

Although the Bindu, being of the nature of Mahāmāyā, is considered a bond (*pāśa*) from the perspective of supreme liberation (*paramukti*), it is not included here as a bond because its conjunction [with the soul] is the cause for attaining the status of a Vidyeśvara and so forth, which constitutes lower liberation (*aparamukti*). Thus, there is no contradiction.
For this very reason, he says "of the person" (*puṃsaḥ*); that is, of the *sakala* (the individual soul) who is conjoined with the impurity of limited agency (*puṃstva-mala*). Therefore...
For those residing on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), such as Ananta and others, there exists a pair of bonds (*pāśa*) consisting precisely of the power that obstructs *mahāmāyā*.

And this [pair of bonds] is not delusive like *māyā* and the rest; rather, it is purely enlightening. Thus, everything is well-established. Now, an objection: since the scripture states, "That supreme seed called Nāda, which resides within all beings" (*Sāṃkhyakārikā* 1.5), does not every soul (*sakala*) possess a connection with the effect of the Bindu?

True; it was stated in this way because he has no connection with the *bindu*-body (*baindava-śarīra*) and so forth, which are invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with omniscience and other such qualities. To the question "Which are those?", he says: "The first two are considered to be born of impurity (*mala*) and karma. Here, the terms "born of impurity and karma" refer to that which consists of impurity and karma itself, by means of a metaphorical identification of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇayor abhedopacārāt*), since their definitions will be stated in the immediately following sūtra.

Furthermore, because those respective causes and effects—namely, concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and the enjoyment of experience (*bhoga-bhojana*)—are well-known as bonds (*pāśa*) by virtue of being the nature of the fruit. This should also be understood in the context of the statement: "Thus, [the powers] born from the Śiva-power that conceals belong to Māyā. Regarding the establishment of the beginningless descent (*anādi-avanādi*): therein, impurity (*mala*) is beginningless for the individual soul (*puṃs*) and is the obstructor of knowledge and action; karma is also beginningless by way of a continuous flow (*pravāha-anādi*), according to the logic of the seed and the sprout.
Since the continuum of the body born of karma is established as being beginningless, the fetter consisting of *kalā* and so forth—which is illusory (*māyeya*)—is adventitious;
for it exists only when karma exists, and even in the absence of karma, it persists in the case of the *pralayakevalin* due to the conjunction of impurity (*mala*) and karma.
As for the power of Śiva, its status as a fetter is stated figuratively because it conceals the Self by presiding over the fetters.
And we shall explain [this] further. || 17 ||
For the impurity (mala) that obscures the vision and action of individual souls is indeed one, yet possesses manifold powers;
it is to be understood as being like the husk and the chaff [of grain], or like the blackness adhering to copper. (18)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states the definition of *mala*, which was mentioned first, with the words "one" (*eka*).
"One, possessing manifold powers" is the definition of *mala*. Because the *kārmika* and *māyīya* [impurities] are manifold, the word "one" is stated in order to exclude them.

[Objection: Since the power of concealment (*tirodhāyaka-śakti*) is also a bond (*pāśa*), it follows that because it is one, it would result in being a single impurity (*mala*). To avoid this [consequence], the term "multiple powers" (*aneka-śakti*) is used. [Objection: But if impurity consists of the form of ignorance (*avidyā*) and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), then because it is manifold, it is incorrect to say "impurity is one. [Reply: This is not so;

for some maintain that just as the waters of infinite rivers submerged in the ocean become one through their conjunction, so too these infinite [powers] attain oneness through their union. Others, however, [hold a different view].

They say that the statement regarding oneness is made with respect to the genus (*jāti*); because of the existence of multiple intermediate sub-genuses, there is multiplicity in *māyā* and *karman*, whereas due to the absence of such [sub-genuses], there is oneness in *vāsanā*. Likewise, even when [nescience] consists in the absence of knowledge (*jñāna*), the statement regarding oneness is made precisely with respect to the genus; otherwise, if some knowledge were to arise, the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of that knowledge would be terminated.
Because it would entail the liberation of the entire world.

If [the soul] were of the nature of existence (*bhāvātmaka*), the statement regarding its unity would be primary. Even when knowledge arises in one [soul], the persistence or cessation [of impurity] is possible—just as in the case of darkness—and because impurity possesses manifold powers, [impurity remains] only with respect to that [one soul] even when knowledge has arisen for it.
Due to the destruction of the power of concealment (*pracchādana-śakti*), the absence of liberation for the others is indeed possible.
Therefore, *mala* is a single [entity] possessing multiple powers. As it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "The destruction of that power of this all-pervading *mala* is brought about."
By means of skillful methods, the suppression of power is brought about within a certain impurity.
Likewise, the knowledge of Śiva acts as a restrainer of his power,
just as the burning power of fire is quickly suppressed by a mantra.
"Similarly, there is the suppression of that power" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.28–30), and so forth.

"The impurity (*mala*) which veils vision and action in souls should be known as being like the husk and the chaff. Just as the husk and the chaff, when united with the grain, are the cause for the emergence of the root, the sprout, and so on, so too is the impurity in relation to bound souls (*paśu*).

By concealing the knowledge and action that constitute its own nature (*svarūpa*), it remains as one with the Self (*ātman*), acting as the cause for the production of the primary sprouts of *mala*, *māyā*, and so forth. As it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "Innate *mala* is the concealer of consciousness; purity and the state of Śiva are inherent. It is like the blackness residing in copper; just as the blackness inherent in copper is innate to it.

Just as [an alloy] remains by concealing its true nature as gold and manifesting its copperiness, so too does impurity (mala) remain by concealing the self’s essential nature consisting of knowledge and action and manifesting the state of being a bound soul (paśutva). If it is objected that if impurity were innate, then upon its destruction, the possessor of that impurity would also necessarily perish—the answer is: not so.

Just as the blackness inherent in copper is not destroyed when that [blackness] is removed without the destruction of its own nature, so too, even upon the destruction of innate impurity, the destruction of the self's true nature is logically untenable. As it has been said:
"The innate blackness exists in copper; yet with its removal, there is no destruction of the copper itself."
Just as there may be a depletion of copper, so too is there a depletion of the impurities of the person;
yet, just as when the husk of the rice is destroyed, that [grain] itself is not destroyed, and so forth. (18)
(Ki0 Vi0 2.31-32) Regarding that, the commentary states the definition of impurity: "One," etc.
Impurity (*mala*) is indeed one; for if it were multiple while being insentient (*jaḍa*) and eternal, it would follow that it is impermanent like multiple insentient things such as jars.

If this were so, then because impurity is one, the cessation of that [impurity] for the sake of the liberation of one person would entail the liberation of everyone. Therefore, he says: "possessing manifold powers" (*anekaśakti*). It is endowed with manifold powers that conceal the manifold selves; thus, through the ripening and subsequent obscuration of one particular power, [the liberation of one occurs].

Then liberation belongs only to the Obstructed One (*āvārya*). It is "like the husk and the bran": just as the husk and so forth, or the blackness [of copper], which are innate coverings of the rice grain or the copper and have existed from beginningless time, are later removed by the power of the essence through cooking; in the same way, impurity (*mala*), though an innate covering of the Self from beginningless time, is removed by initiation (*dīkṣā*) through the process of maturation (*pāka*). Or else, just as...

Just as the husk and so forth are the cause for the production of a sprout from rice and other grains, so too is the impurity (*mala*) of the self the cause for the production of the body and so forth. Or, just as the blackness of copper is removed by the power of mercury, so too is the impurity removed by the power of Śiva; this much is the analogy for the self, but not in terms of complete identity. || 18 ||
Karma is said to be beginningless, consisting of merit and demerit, and manifold;
and Māyā, which is of the nature of a real entity, is the eternal root of the universe. (19)

Immediately after the *Tātparyadīpikā*, he explains the two bonds (*pāśa*) consisting of karma and māyā through the first and second halves of the following verse, beginning with "karmānādi" (karma is beginningless).

Karma exists in the form of a beginningless stream, and not through the perpetual persistence of a single act of karma alone; for if that were the case, since karma, being a positive entity, would be beginningless like the self (*ātman*), the consequence would be the impossibility of liberation due to its eternity. Indeed, as long as karma is not destroyed, the cessation of *saṃsāra* is not possible. Thus it has been declared by those who know reality: "consisting of merit and demerit" (*dharmādharmātmaka*).

"It is twofold in the form of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). "And manifold" means that it is manifold because it is the cause of various fruits. To explain: some say that merit is the unique cause of happiness, while demerit is the unique cause of suffering. Others, however, state that merit is an object characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), and demerit is an object characterized by that same [injunction] which is disadvantageous. Still others [say that] merit...

The quality of the person (*puruṣaguṇa*) is the cause of what is pleasant, beneficial, and liberation for the agent; its opposite is *adharma*. Some maintain that *dharma* is characterized by non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).
The Buddhists hold that *dharma* is characterized by such acts as the veneration of shrines (*caityavandana*). Others maintain that *dharma* is characterized by altruism (*paropakāra*).
Among these, the latter three are untenable due to a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the scriptures of the Buddhists and others are not valid means of knowledge.

Because these [scriptures] are of human origin, they lack authority due to the absence of a foundational means of valid cognition (*mūlapramāṇa*). Furthermore, no such foundational means of valid cognition is perceived for them, since it has already been stated that perception and the other [means of knowledge] cannot possibly possess authority regarding *dharma*.
Nor can that which is characterized by benefit be considered *dharma*, because even acts such as the killing of Brahmins and others constitute a benefit to one's enemies and so forth.

[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence that [all action] would be of the nature of *dharma*. Nor can violence (*hiṃsā*) be considered *adharma*, for then there would be the undesirable consequence that the threshing of rice, the suppression of criminals, and the slaughter of animals in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice would also be *adharma*.
That *dharma* is threefold, because it is divided into the categories of obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). Among these:

The obligatory rites (*nitya*) are those prescribed as mandatory injunctions by such statements as: "One should offer the *agnihotra* for as long as one lives," "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* for as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma* for as long as one lives. The occasional rites (*naimittika*) are those arising from a specific occasion (*nimitta*). For example: "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.2.5.3).

The *jāteṣṭi* and other rites are those prescribed by injunctions such as "the *aṣṭakā* should be performed. The *kāmya* rites are those preceded by desire, prescribed by such scriptural statements as: "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*" (*Maitrī Upaniṣad* 6.36), "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 10.2.1), and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 10.2.1). These are of two kinds—

[They are] "with knowledge" (*savidya*) and "without knowledge" (*kevala*). "With knowledge" means preceded by the remembrance of the Lord (*īśvara*); the others are devoid of that. Dharma, characterized in this way, is twofold: "sacrificial" (*iṣṭa*) and "charitable" (*pūrta*). Among these, the sacrificial is Vedic, while the charitable is Tantric. Adharma is that which is prohibited. For example: "A Brahmin must not be killed," "One must not drink liquor," and "One must not drink water from a conch shell."

Acts such as the injury of Brahmins are prohibited by such scriptural statements as these. Others, however, say that unrighteousness (*adharma*) is threefold: the non-performance of obligatory duties (*nitya*), the non-performance of occasional duties (*naimittika*), and the performance of prohibited acts. Through the performance of obligatory and occasional duties, one avoids transgression (*pratyavāya*); through optional rites (*kāmya*), one attains heaven and so forth; and from unrighteousness, one goes to hell and other such realms. This is what has been stated.
In the *Siddhāntahṛdaya*: "The subtle form of action is indeed called karma, and it is of two kinds: *iṣṭa* and *pūrta*. Among these, *iṣṭa* is both Vedic and Tantric."

That which is called *pūrta* by the virtuous is further considered to be of three kinds: merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and the variegated (*citram*). Of these, merit is the domain of injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, that [action] is threefold, consisting of the optional (kāmya), the obligatory (nitya), and the occasional (naimittika).
Prohibited action is demerit (adharma); other than these, action is manifold. Optional action, moreover, is of two kinds.
It is both accompanied by knowledge and independent; "knowledge" here refers to meditation upon the Lord.
It may either destroy adverse results or bring about the exhaustion of previously accumulated demerit.
Through constant and occasional [non-performance of duty], one goes to the state of hell due to unrighteousness;
it extends from the human realm down to the level of stone, being exceedingly difficult to cross.
From desire arises the attainment of heaven; from that, the higher [attainment] culminating in Brahman;
and with knowledge, by the path of the gods, one is exempt from returning again.
The journey by the path of the ancestors alone consists of worldly transmigration;
when there is an equilibrium between that which is called dharma and adharma, a person attains human birth.
The two types of karma lead to results that are both manifold and uniform;
this great noose called karma is difficult to untie, and by it all living beings are bound.
"Just as animals are dragged here and there and led away," and so forth.

Thus, under the influence of impurity (*mala*) and karma, and by the will of Maheśvara, *māyā* transforms again and again into the form of bodies, senses, and objects—beginning with those of the gods—in the three states, for the sake of experiencing the fruits of merit and demerit. As it has been said:
From impurity (mala) come agency and enjoyership; from agency comes action, and from action comes experience.
By virtue of that [experience], there is the projection [of the world]; from that arises the bondage of māyā, and from that, the body.
The locus of enjoyment, the objects of enjoyment, and the instruments—
the sense organs— arise from that impurity for the sake of accomplishing experience.
"And consisting of desire, like the seed, sprout, fruit, and so forth;
this beginningless web of bonds binds the individual souls (aṇu) within the wheel of existence," and so on.
By the word "variegated" (vicitra), the proof for the existence of karma is also stated. For instance:

The manifold world, divided by distinctions such as the wealthy and the poor, cannot exist without a manifold cause; and since no such [visible] cause is perceived, there is the postulation of an unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa*), and thus its establishment. As it is said in the *Mātaṅga*:
"The two well-known factors of the world are the two karmas, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)."
"By those two, the person has always been perfumed since beginningless time" (Vijñānabhairava 8.98), and so forth.

He states the definition of that *māyā*: "the root of the universe. This means that *māyā* is the root—that is, the material cause (*upādāna*)—of the manifest world, such as *kalā* and the other categories. As it has been said: "The non-discrimination of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā*..."

Regarding the term *māyā* (*Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras* 3.3.14): by the very word "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), the proof for its existence is also stated. To explain: the entire world is produced from a single material cause, because it possesses a uniform nature; whatever possesses a uniform nature is produced from a single material cause, just as jars, pots, clay drums, bowls, walls, anthills, and so forth—which possess a uniform nature—are produced from the single material cause of clay; and this [world] is likewise.

Because it possesses a single form such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) and so forth, it is produced from a single material cause (*upādāna*). That which serves here as the material cause—consisting of the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) of the entire collection of principles (*tattva*) beginning with *sakala* and ending with the earth—is *māyā*; thus is its establishment. We shall demonstrate this in detail further on.
Lest there arise a suspicion that it is not ultimately real (*aparamārtha*) because it is denoted by the word *māyā*, he says [the following] to dispel that doubt:

"Having the nature of a real entity": that illusion (*māyā*) has the nature of a real entity and is ultimately real because it is the root of the universe, like Īśvara. And that illusion is eternal, precisely because it is the root of the universe, like Īśvara. For if it were impermanent, one would have to admit another root for it.

Because it lacks the status of being the root of the universe. Nor should it be argued that Māyā lacks the status of being the root of the universe because she is the root only of those things distinct from the Māyā of the Great Lord (Maheśvara); for there is no contradiction in the absence of being a root—given that only what is produced requires a root—if one is unproduced. Furthermore, it is not the case that there is a lack of evidence for the Supreme Lord being the root of the universe.

It should not be said that the illustration is devoid of proof, for its status as the root of the universe is heard [in scripture]. For instance, the status of the Supreme Lord as the root of the world is understood from Vedic statements such as: "From which indeed these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), "He created these worlds" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.2), and "From the Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). Therefore...

"The example is not deficient in its means of proof. Likewise, it was described by the supreme seer Vedavyāsa, the author of the Sūtras, through two aphorisms as the Supreme Lord’s being the root of the universe: "Because [the origin, etc.,] of this [world] proceed from Him" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2) and "Because He is the source of the scripture" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.3). Now, one might object: "In that case, Māyā is not the root of the universe; rather, it is the Supreme Lord alone."

If it is argued that [Māyā alone] is the root of the universe, it is not so; for both Māyā and Maheśvara, being mutually dependent in their creative activity, are established as the root of the universe, and thus both are logically justified in that role.
To explain: Māyā, being insentient, cannot serve as the material cause of the world unless presided over by the Supreme Lord.

And although Maheśvara is conscious, he does not attain the status of being the root of the universe without Māyā, because he is merely inactive and indifferent; therefore, it is only when these two are conjoined that they constitute the root of the world, like the iron ball and the fire in the case of cause and effect. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "Māyā and," the reality-status (*vasturūpatva*) of the universe, which is the effect of Māyā, is described.

Nor should it be said that this [position] is untenable because of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), for there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*) for that. If it is argued that the falsity of the phenomenal world is established through the following inference—"The subject of dispute is false, because it is visible; whatever is visible is false, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; and this too is visible; therefore, it is false"—it is not so.

This is because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a non-ultimate silver—which is distinct from the mother-of-pearl and is the object of the error "this is silver. Now, one might argue that the existence of silver in that mother-of-pearl is established by the following inference: "The subject under dispute, the cognition of silver, has silver as its object, because it is a cognition of silver, like a correct cognition of silver. [To this we reply: That [silver] is not real, because at that time...

Because it is impossible for it to possess both the nature of being erroneous and the nature of being sublated—just like real silver—it is not non-existent either, for if it were, there would follow the impossibility of its appearance and its subsequent sublation, as in the case of a rabbit’s horn. Nor is it both existent and non-existent, because of their mutual contradiction. Thus, it is established that its nature is distinct from both existence and non-existence. That very state of having an unascertainable form is what constitutes its falsity (*mithyātva*). As it has been said:
"In the case of existence, there can be neither error nor sublation; in the case of non-existence, there can be neither appearance nor sublation.
Therefore, ignorance—which is indefinable as either existent or non-existent—along with its objects, constitutes the delusion.
This is without substance, because therein a transcendent silver, which is ultimately real, appears. For it is thus:

For silver is of two kinds: worldly and non-worldly. Of these, the worldly is capable of functions such as making bracelets and the like, whereas the non-worldly, which appears here [in the illusion], is incapable of them. Because that [non-worldly silver] possesses equality with respect to properties such as duality and so forth, it is not false by virtue of its ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Nor is there a sublation (*bādha*) of this [silver] by the cognition "this is not silver," because [the latter lacks] the expected worldly silver—

This is because it does not sublate [the object], since its function is to produce the cognition of discrimination (*viveka*). Now, if it is argued that there would be the undesirable consequence of a person seeking ordinary silver failing to act toward [the shell] when there is a cognition of extraordinary silver, we say no; for action is possible even toward the extraordinary, provided there is a non-apprehension of its difference from the ordinary.
Or rather, one acts toward it by conceiving the extraordinary as being ordinary. The same applies to the cognition of indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) silver.

Since activity would otherwise be impossible, you must indeed follow the path I have set forth. Therefore, because there is no such thing as an ultimately real silver that is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) cannot be established due to the lack of an illustrative example.

Now, if it is argued that the non-apprehension of difference is what motivates action, then the postulation of an extraordinary silver is not tenable; for [action occurs] between the mother-of-pearl and the silver themselves.

Because the failure to perceive the difference between what is being perceived and what is being remembered accounts for the activity of one seeking silver there, it would entail the fault of unnecessary conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
To explain: in the cognition "this is silver," "this" is the perception whose object is the mother-of-pearl lying in front; however, "silver" is...
Memory is that which arises from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) awakened by the perception of a similar object, and has as its content silver located in another place.

In this case, because there is simply a non-apprehension of the difference between the mother-of-pearl being perceived and the silver being remembered, the activity of one desiring silver toward the mother-of-pearl in front of him is logically accounted for; thus, the postulation of an "extraordinary" (*alaukika*) silver is not tenable. Furthermore, in that context, it is not something false.

[Objection: "The inference that the world of manifestation (*prapañca*) is false lacks validity because it lacks a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), since [in the case of the silver illusion] something exists. [Reply: This is not so; for, because the cognition of silver is devoid of the verbal expression of that [word "silver"], it is impossible for it to be of the nature of memory (*smṛti*). Therefore, in this case, an extraordinary (*alaukika*) silver appears. [Objection: This is not so, because the apprehension of extraordinary silver cannot logically function as the motivator (*pravartaka*) for action. It is not [the case that it cannot motivate].
It must be stated that one acts by conceiving the non-worldly as worldly; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*).

Nor does action arise from the non-apprehension of a difference from the worldly, for there would be the undesirable consequence of a person desiring gold acting toward [an object] due to the non-apprehension of its difference from gold.

Nor is it the case that the non-apprehension of a difference between two things being apprehended is the motivator of action, because [otherwise], a person desiring gold would act toward [an object] due to the non-apprehension of gold.

It cannot be said that there is an absence of activity [toward the object], because even ordinary silver is not being perceived, and thus activity by one desiring it would be impossible there. Nor can it be said that this cognition of silver apprehends that [ordinary silver] as well, because, existing in another location, it cannot fall within the range of the senses. Nor is this [cognition] of the nature of both memory and direct experience.

It must be said that there are two distinct cognitions, each having as its object silver located in two different places—the one in front and the other elsewhere—because the cognition of silver arises from sensory contact and because it lacks the verbal designation [of "remembered"], which precludes its being a memory. Therefore, the silver appearing here is non-existent; thus, for the Śūnyavādins, falsity consists in having a non-existent object, based on the inference of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

[The opponent claims: "Even the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is non-existent. [The author replies: This is not so; for if one perceives non-existent silver, it would be impossible for a person seeking silver to act toward that object.

If it is argued that action is possible because of the non-apprehension of the difference between the non-existent silver and existent silver, or because of the apprehension of their non-difference, we say: no, for action is possible only through the non-apprehension of the difference between the silver and the mother-of-pearl, or through the apprehension of their non-difference.

Because it is impossible to conceive of silver that is non-existent and distinct from that [cognition], the proponents of *ātmakhyāti* (the theory of self-manifestation) maintain that the cognition of silver here manifests its own internal form of silver externally upon the surface of the mother-of-pearl; for the manifestation of the non-existent is untenable, and the existent silver is located in another place.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for silver to be the object of the cognition [of silver], the appearance of the form of silver residing in the cognition as something external is an error. The proponent of the non-duality of cognition (jñānādvaitavādī) maintains that waking cognitions are devoid of any object distinct from their own forms, because they are cognitions, like dream-cognitions; thus, through this inference, one understands that everything is mere cognition and that anything other than that does not exist.

It is not so, because this inference would be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the cognitions that apprehend its thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and so forth—which possess objects distinct from themselves. Furthermore, even if those [cognitions] were ungraspable, there would follow for this inference the faults of the non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), the non-establishment of its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), the non-establishment of the property-bearer (*dharmyasiddhi*), and the lack of an example (*adṛṣṭāntatva*). Nor [is it the case] regarding dream-cognitions...

The claim that [cognition] grasps its own form is untenable, because there is no proof for the existence of forms within cognitions. Nor can it be established that those cognitions possess forms such as blue or yellow on the grounds that the determination of each respective object—such as "this is the cognition of blue" or "this is the cognition of yellow"—would otherwise be inexplicable;
for blue, yellow, and so forth are established as valid by virtue of being the objective factors (*karmakāraka*) of that cognition. Therefore, one's own form does not exist as an external entity.
The claim that "errors manifest [themselves]" is untenable as a theory of self-manifestation (*ātmakhyāti*). What, then, is the erroneous nature of erroneous cognitions?

We say it is their shifting toward another object by abandoning their own object, as understood through the linguistic conventions of elders since beginningless time. And the proof for this is the subverting cognition that follows—such as "this is not silver, but rather mother-of-pearl"—wherein one perceives: "This is a fragment of mother-of-pearl."
"An uncontradicted perception consisting of recognition is apprehended in the form: 'This has been perceived by me as silver.

Therefore, the proofs put forward by those who advocate for theories such as the theory of the indefinable (anirvacanīya-khyāti), the theory of the non-worldly (alaukika-khyāti), the theory of the non-existent (asat-khyāti), or the theory of self-apprehension (ātma-khyāti) are invalid—just like the inference of "producedness" used to prove that fire is not hot. As it has been said:
The experts in logic have stated: "Some have asserted that all cognitions are in accordance with reality;
that is incorrect, for erroneous cognition (anyathākhyāti) is apprehended by the instrumental intellect."

Likewise, from inference as well, misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) is understood here. For instance: the disputed activity of those seeking silver toward a piece of mother-of-pearl lying before them is preceded by a cognition of silver regarding that which is its own object, because it is an activity dependent on a desire for silver, like an activity directed toward real silver. Or, the piece of mother-of-pearl is the object of the cognition of silver, because it is [the locus of] activity dependent on a desire for silver.

Because it is an object [of cognition], like real silver. Likewise, the subverting cognition—"This is not silver, but rather mother-of-pearl"—is not possible in other positions, because there is no attainment of the form of silver in the mother-of-pearl. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of a subverting cognition in another manner: "This is not real silver, but rather unreal silver. It is not the case that real silver exists here; rather...

Or else, "elsewhere" refers to the theory of the indefinable manifestation (*anirvacanīya-khyāti*): "There is no silver here capable of making a bracelet, but there is elsewhere," or "This is not silver capable of making a bracelet, but it is an extraordinary [silver]," according to the position of certain Mīmāṃsaka followers of Prabhākara. Or: "This is not real silver, but rather unreal silver," or "not here."

On the theory of *asatkhyāti* (the apprehension of the non-existent), it would be: "The real silver exists, but elsewhere. On the theory of *ātmakhyāti* (the apprehension of the self), it would be: "The silver does not exist here, but it is internal [to the mind]. On the theory of the apprehension of difference (*bhedagrahaṇapakṣa*), it would be: "This piece of mother-of-pearl is distinct from the silver.

Therefore, theories of erroneous cognition other than *anyathākhyāti* (the apprehension of something as otherwise) are impossible. Furthermore, they are untenable because the activity of one seeking silver would be impossible [under those theories].

There is no possibility of another cognition [of difference]. Since there exists a non-apprehension of the distinction between infinite objects, it would follow that those desiring a particular object would act toward whatever is present before them. Furthermore, action does not arise from a non-apprehension of the difference between two things being perceived;

for if it did, then since there is at that time an absence of apprehending the difference between a jar and a cloth when they are both being perceived, it would follow that one desiring a jar would act toward the cloth.

Furthermore, at the time of perceiving the locus (*dharmī*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the perception of their non-difference is not possible, because the occurrence of the notion of difference is preceded by the perception of both. If it is argued that since difference is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of things, difference is also grasped through the perception of that nature,
and thus there is no non-perception of difference leading to the absence of activity— then, in that case, one seeking silver would not act toward a piece of mother-of-pearl lying before them.

For it is impossible for there to be a non-apprehension of difference between the two cognitions— the perception "this" and the recollection "silver"— which are self-luminous, nor between the perceived shell and the remembered silver, due to the non-apprehension of their own forms. Furthermore,
if the non-apprehension of difference were the cause of activity, it would follow that the apprehension of the relationship between a word and its meaning would be impossible.

For instance, immediately upon hearing the prompter's sentence "Bring the cow," a child, observing the activity of the prompted elder, understands as follows: "An effort has arisen in him which is the cause of the act of going," because he perceives within himself that acts such as going are preceded by effort. He [further] perceives desire as the cause of that effort.

He infers [the intention] by means of the effort inferred from the act of going; and he understands that the speech of the authoritative elder (prayojaka-vṛddha) existing prior to the time of that [child's] cognition has as its cause the knowledge that [the action] is a means to a desired end, because of the desire [to act] and because there is no other entity that could be its cause.
Then, perceiving the object being brought toward him, he realizes: "This collection of objects was understood by this [child] from this collection of words."

Subsequently, through the process of inclusion and exclusion (*āvāpodvāpa*), one determines specifically: "this particular word is the denoter of this particular meaning," or "this particular meaning is the denoted by this particular word. In this regard, since non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*) consists in the prior absence of knowledge (*jñānaprāgabhāva*), it is not produced by words; therefore, there is no occasion for postulating a word-potency (*śabdaśakti*).

Because a word functions as an instigator [of action] by generating desire and effort through the medium of cognition, there is no possibility of perceiving difference in cases such as the illusions of a double moon or a yellow conch. Therefore, we maintain that activity does not arise from the non-apprehension of difference, but rather from apprehending something otherwise. But how is it known that the Śaivas accept *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) in their scripture?
Because it is stated in the *Bhūtaśuddhitantra*:
"For instance, the teaching of Śiva, like the Sāṃkhya, relies upon the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*);
whereas that which is 'indescribable' (*anirvacanīyā*) is according to the Siddhānta doctrine."

"The Vaiṣṇava doctrine is based on the perspective of the Vedāntins. By "Sāṃkhya" here, the *Seśvara-sāṃkhya* (Theistic Sāṃkhya) is intended, because the other [form of Sāṃkhya] is a proponent of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*). Thus it has been stated by the Sāṃkhya teachers: "Error is false knowledge, which is not established in the true nature of the object" (Yoga Sūtra 1.8).

Because the *sūtra* establishes *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension), there is no such thing as a false silver that arises from the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl, is based upon mother-of-pearl, is distinct from mother-of-pearl, and is removable by the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate; therefore, the inference of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is invalid due to the defect of the example lacking a locus (*dharmyasiddhi*).

[The opponent claims that] one attains the perfection of validity [of knowledge]. However, there is a fallacy of the reason (*hetu*) because the Self (*ātman*), though self-established, is also seen through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, just as the world (*prapañca*), which is the subject (*dharmin*), is established by the reason of "being visible" (*dṛśyatva*), if the falsity (*mithyātva*) of that very reason—namely, "being visible"—were likewise established by this same inference as the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), [then the reason would be false].

In that case, because the reason (hetu) would exist as only a part of the subject (pakṣa), it would not subsist in the entire subject; thus, being unascertained in its subsistence within the subject, it would be "unestablished" (asiddha).

Furthermore, since the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva) is not established elsewhere than in the subject itself—just like the phenomenal world—it would follow that the reason is "unestablished in part of its locus" (āśrayaikadeśāsiddha). If those two [the reason and the subject] were not established as false, then the property of "being visible" (dṛśyatva), which exists therein, would be "inconclusive" (vyabhicāra).

If its falsity is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then because the falsity of that [other means] has not been established, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) between the two in that case. If the falsity of that [second means] is also established, then because the falsity of the final [means] has not been established, there is a deviation between the two in that case. If even that [final means] does not have its falsity established... [the falsity of the first remains unestablished].

In that case, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason due to its being present [in the subject]. Furthermore, if falsity (*mithyātva*) were non-existence (*asattva*), then there would be a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) such as "the pot exists" or "the cloth exists. Moreover, since the substratum (*dharmin*)—the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—the property (*dharma*)—falsity—the reason (*hetu*)—visibility (*dṛśyatva*)—and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—nacre-silver—are all like the horns of a hare, they lack a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

There is the consequence of faults such as the non-establishment [of the reason]. If those [faults] exist, there is an inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason. Thus, in either case, the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) have no standing in debate. As it has been said:
"The proponent of emptiness has no standing in debate because of the lack of a means" (*Ślokavārttika*, Nirālambanavāda 129).

If it were to be sublated by knowledge, then there would be a contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition; for since perception and the like observe that things are sublated by the stroke of a hammer and so forth, it is impossible for them to possess the capacity to be sublated by a knowledge that is merely inferred from its effects. Furthermore, it is not the case that objects existing for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas perish only through some other cause and do not perish due to ignorance.

Regarding the word "struggles" (*ghaṭate*): even if falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being distinct from both existence and non-existence, there would still be a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, since objects are apprehended by perception and so forth as being either existent or non-existent. Furthermore, because it is contradictory, it is not possible for a single object to be distinct from both existence and non-existence simultaneously, just as it cannot be both existent and non-existent at once. However, [this distinction] applies to objects according to differences in space and time.

The existence of both being and non-being is untenable; however, their distinction from both [being and non-being] is not established in any way whatsoever. If it is argued that [the object] is "sublatable" (*bādhyatva*), let it be so.

If sublatibility means perishability, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in one part, and sublation by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādhā*) in another part, regarding the principles from Time (*kāla*) down to the Earth (*avanī*), as well as their effects.

Because perishability is established [for all things], and because the eternity of Māyā is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends it, the existence of Māyā is proven as the root cause when there is a requirement for a cause for the entire aggregate of universal effects. Therefore, she is eternal; since she is the cause of the universe of effects, she cannot be non-eternal as she is not herself an effect, and there is no need to postulate another cause for her.

Furthermore, because it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), one must accept the eternity (*nityatva*) of something. To avoid the burden of such conceptual proliferation (*kalpanā-gaurava*), this eternity is accepted as belonging to *māyā* itself, which exists from the very beginning. Thus, although that eternity is established by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the substratum (*dharmin*), there is no contradiction with that cognition of the substratum. Nor does this [cognition] contradict its...

The possibility of sublation [is not established], because if that [sublation] were absent, since it is the root of this [proof], the existence of *māyā* would be proven; consequently, there would be the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Alternatively, if "being sublated" means being the object of a cognition consisting of sublation, then that [quality] exists even in the case of the cognition of silver or a snake arising with respect to mother-of-pearl or a rope; thus, the example is not devoid of the property to be proved (*sādhyahīna*).

For instance, because the cognitions of silver and so forth abandon their own objects established from beginningless time and move toward another object such as mother-of-pearl, they are observed to be the objects of a sublation-cognition in the form:

"This cognition of mine regarding silver and so forth has arisen falsely. By the force of that example, the world-process (*prapañca*) likewise becomes the object of a sublation-cognition in the form of a [correct] cognition.

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the world] is being established [as Rudra], this is not so, because it would entail the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For instance, according to such scriptural passages as "All indeed is Rudra" (*Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* 10.11), when investigated, this entire world of moving and non-moving things is indeed Rudra.

Furthermore, because of such Smṛti passages, it is understood that everything exists in the form of the body and its possessor (the embodied), and thus possesses Rudra as its essence. Therefore, the appearance of all objects as being anything other than Rudra is merely an illusion. Consequently, this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not of a non-auspicious nature, but is indeed of the nature of Rudra; for it is established that [this world] is the object of a subverting cognition (*bādhātmakabodha*).

Regarding the objection that this leads to the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*): if it is argued that the falsity—meaning the nature of being a misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*)—of those cognitions which have as their object the non-auspicious self (*aśivātmatā*) and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is what is being proven, then we have already achieved our desired goal, since this does not contradict the reality of the phenomenal world. For the reality of the rope is not contradicted by the arising of the cognition of a snake in relation to that rope. Therefore...

It has been rightly stated that "illusion (māyā) is of the nature of a real entity," because it is impossible for an ultimate reality to arise from what is not ultimately real. Others, however, have explained this statement—"and illusion is of the nature of a real entity"—in another way. For instance: illusion is of the nature of a real entity, namely, the nature of Śiva; and its effect, the world, is also of the nature of Śiva, since nothing whatsoever exists apart from Śiva.

For instance: this very Self, Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, manifests as the nature of *māyā* and its effects; therefore, He alone is both of those. Nor should it be said that, if this were so, Śiva would be subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), because we rely upon the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*). Illusory manifestation is the appearance of a thing otherwise than its own nature without that thing ever losing its own essence, just as the appearance of a snake in a rope. Indeed, in the rope...

Since transformation and so forth are observed at the time of the state of being a serpent, it follows that even for Maheśvara, in his nature as the world, transformation and so forth are impossible in that same way; thus, Śiva alone manifests in the form of Māyā and its effects.
As it is said in the *Īśvaragītā*:

"He alone is the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), the primary matter (*pradhāna*), and the Person (*puruṣa*); he is also the transformations (*vikāra*) such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth—the eternal God of gods. (7.31).
For this [is not the case], since an error is observed regarding silver and the like when they exist elsewhere [but are perceived] in mother-of-pearl and so forth.

It should not be argued that because conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) cannot exist elsewhere, it is impossible for it to be of the nature of an error; for the mere prior perception, as the cause of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of error, is the operative factor, and its existence elsewhere does not render it non-operative. Therefore, since there is the possibility of error regarding what was experienced on preceding days, in previous births, or in prior kalpas, with respect to succeeding days, births, or kalpas, [the objection does not hold].
There is no fault here. As it was said by the author of the *Śataka*:
"In that Supreme Reality—which is devoid of all conceptual constructions, pure, tranquil, and free from arising and passing away—the universe consisting of thirty-six principles shines forth."

Just as a variegated array of cities, villages, and so forth appears within the surface of a mirror— appearing as distinct from one another and also distinct from the mirror itself— though it is actually indivisible.

"From that most pure and supreme Śāmbhava awakening, although it is devoid of division, the form of Śiva appears both as mutually distinct from one another and yet as undivided from that [awakening] itself. (19)

(VP 3.6.11–13) It has been stated that the beginninglessness of activity (*vṛtti*) is due to its beginninglessness as a continuous stream (*pravāha*). Furthermore, its diversity arises from the difference in the means (*sādhana*).

The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) consists of specific factors such as the agent and so forth, because one observes results consisting of various distinct types of enjoyment. Furthermore, *māyā* is of the nature of a real entity (*vastu-rūpā*), and not of an unreal nature as held by the Vedāntins. It is threefold: common to all, such as the *kalās* and other categories;
uncommon, such as the worlds (*bhuvana*) and their like; and of both natures, such as the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*).

She is the root and material cause (*upādāna*) of the entire impure universe, including the bodies and souls born of the world, because an effect cannot arise without a material cause. Furthermore, she is eternal, because she is the supreme cause; for if she were non-eternal, it would lead to the logical fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For this very reason, she is to be known as one. This same reasoning applies equally to the *bindu*, which serves as the material cause of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).

If it is argued that there is a contradiction because in that *uddeśasūtra* "māyeya" was listed as a fetter (*pāśa*), whereas here the definition of *māyā* itself is stated, [the response is: true. Since *māyā* does not possess the quality of being a binder (*bandhaka*) in its own right, its effect was listed there;
however, since here [the bondage] is dependent upon its cause, the definition of the cause is stated. As for the effect, because it is extensive, its definition will be given later.
There is no contradiction, because [the author] will explain this later. || 19 ||
Because it binds with fetters, the power of the All-pervasive Lord which conceals the Person is designated as "fetters" (pāśa);
and these fetters are of four kinds. || 20 ||

The *Tātparyadīpikā* now defines the group of powers (*śaktigaṇa*), beginning with the word "pāśa": since the bonds (*pāśas*)— which are the effects of impurity (*mala*), karma, and *māyā*— are insentient, they cannot exist without the penetration of the Supreme Lord’s power (*parameśvara-śaktyāveśa*).

Because she lacks the capacity to bind the *paśu* (the bound soul), yet through her own penetration (*svāveśa*) she effects the favoring of the fetters (*pāśa*) by setting them in motion toward their own function, she is called the "power that conceals the Person" (*puruṣācchādikā*), the power of the all-pervading Supreme Lord that obscures the Person; thus she is described as a fetter by the knowers of reality (*tattvavid*). He concludes that the fetters are indeed fourfold with the words "and the fetters are of four kinds, thus. The meaning is that in the manner described, the fetters are fourfold.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction between the beginning, which states "the five objects are the bond," and the conclusion, which states "the bonds are fourfold," we say:
not so. This is because the fourfold nature is mentioned with the intention of expressing the unity of Māyā, which has been described through its division into gross and subtle forms.
Furthermore, by the word "ca" (and) in the concluding sentence, "And the bonds are thus fourfold," the summary of the meaning of the scripture is indicated.
Thus illuminated: "In this way, reality is threefold. (20)
Thus ends the first chapter, the investigation into the nature of the Lord (pati), the bound soul (paśu), and the fetter (pāśa), in the Tattvaprakāśatātparyadīpikā.

The commentary (*vṛtti*) concludes the stated subject matter by showing that, having thus directly described the three bonds (*pāśa*), the state of being a bond is attributed to *śakti* only figuratively: "The bonds... (verse 20).
The five pure principles (tattvas) are remembered as being among them:
the Śiva-tattva, the Śakti-tattva and Sadāśiva-tattva, and the two principles known as Īśvara and Vidyā. || 21 ||
For the sake of the individual soul's status as a knower and an agent, there arise from Māyā five principles:
Time (kāla), Necessity (niyati), as well as Limited Agency (kalā), Knowledge (vidyā), and Attachment (rāga). || 22 ||
From Māyā arises the unmanifest (avyakta); following that, the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva), then intellect (buddhi) and ego (ahaṅkāra);
then mind (cetas), the organs of perception and action (dhī-karmendriya), the subtle elements (tanmātrā), and finally the five gross elements (pañcabhūta).
The *Tātparyadīpikā*: Now begins the second chapter.

Next, he teaches the detailed exposition of the Lord (*pati*), the bound soul (*paśu*), and the fetter (*pāśa*), which were previously mentioned only in brief—beginning with the words "the pure" (*śuddhāni*).

Here, the first pentad is pure because it is of the nature of Śiva; the middle heptad is both pure and impure because it has the form of the bound soul (paśu). To the question "How is there a heptad here?", he says: from Māyā, for the sake of the knowerhood and agency of the person (puṃs), the pentad of principles arises. That is, for the sake of the knowledge and agency of the Puruṣa, [the pentad] proceeds from Māyā.

The pentad of principles arises. By that, Māyā is the cause and the pentad is the effect; the Puruṣa, as conditioned by that, is the seventh—thus there is a state of being sevenfold. As it is said in the *Śaivarahasya*:
"Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, Vidyā, Abhilāṣakṛt, and Puruṣa."
"Thus, the principles (tattvas) are arranged in seven ways as pure-impure.

The remainder—beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta) and ending with the Earth—is exclusively impure. The emergence of the Unmanifest is from Māyā; from the Unmanifest comes the principle of the Guṇas; from the principle of the Guṇas comes Intellect (buddhi); from the principle of Intellect comes Ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); from Ego-sense..."

The emergence of the mind, the intellect, the sense organs, the organs of action, and the subtle elements; and from the subtle elements, the emergence of the elements beginning with space and ending with earth.

The commentary (*vṛtti*) states: Having thus described the three bonds (*pāśatraya*) which have all [the worlds] as their object, and the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) which has both as its object,
[the author] now declares the bond that has the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) as its object— that is, the nature of the pure path— as "the pure ones" (*śuddhāni*).

The pure principles (*śuddhatattva*) are pure. Are they eternal or non-eternal? If they were eternal, there would be a contradiction with the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*); if they were non-eternal, what would be their material cause (*upādāna*)? To this, he says: among them, the ancient teachers maintain that the first and primary material cause is the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*), which consists of the *bindu*. And precisely because it is the supreme material cause, unlike Māyā—

It has been stated that eternality is established; therefore, the other four [principles] are its effects—this is the intended meaning. As it has been said: "Above Māyā is Mahāmāyā" (Raurava Saṃhitā 4.28). The underlying intention here is as follows: since the principles beginning with Vidyā are heard of in scripture as possessing various arrangements such as worlds and so forth, they invariably possess the nature of being effects; and furthermore, regarding those who dwell within those respective principles...

Because of its connection with bodies and so forth, it is established that its cause consists of Mahāmāyā. As it has been said: "The material cause of the bodies of those who are Vidyās, Vidyeśvaras, and Ātman-s [is Mahāmāyā]. Furthermore, its status as the producer of Mantras, Tantras, and so forth through the gateway of Nāda and the rest is also heard: "From Śakti arises Nāda, then Bindu, then the Imperishable (Akṣara), and from that, Mātṛkā" (Mṛgendrakriyāpāda 1.2).
And so forth. Having thus established the Śiva-tattva as consisting of the *bindu*, he asks what the names of its four effects are, and therefore says: "Śakti, Sadāśiva," and so on. (21)
Having thus stated the pure principles by way of enumeration and name, he now likewise enumerates the impure ones as well, beginning with "puṃsaḥ" (of the person):
for the sake of establishing the ignorance and agency of the bound soul (puṃsaḥ), that is, for the sake of proving its state of being ignorant and an agent, [the principles arise] directly from Māyā.

And through this succession, there arises the pentad of principles beginning with Time (kāla). It will be stated that because this [Self], joined with the fivefold sheath, possesses the state of being an enjoyer, it acquires the nature of a male and is designated as the principle of Puruṣa. || 22 ||
Furthermore—regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*):

"the intellect and the organs of action" means the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*). We shall explain later that the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), beginning with the unmanifest, have arisen from *māyā* through a successive lineage. Here, by way of stating their definitions, [we shall discuss] these as well. 23.
For the sake of the Puruṣa’s experience, there are twenty-three principles arising from Pradhāna;
for, in reality, there is no absolute difference between the qualities (guṇas) of Prakṛti. (24)
Anticipating the question, "For what purpose was the production of these [elements] brought about by the Blessed Lord Maheśvara?", the author says: "Of the person (puruṣa).
The production of these is for the sake of the bound soul (paśu) experiencing pleasure and pain, which constitute the fruits of his own performed merit and demerit.

Experience, however, does not occur without the body—which is the locus of experience and composed of the elements—the sense organs—which are the instruments of experience—and the objects of experience, such as sound and so forth; thus it is established that their birth is for the sake of experience. Furthermore, because there is no absolute difference between the Unmanifest (avyakta) and the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva), there is no increase in the number of principles. This has been stated in the Śaivarahasya:

The unmanifest, intellect, ego, and mind—these four; the five subtle elements beginning with sound; the five sense organs beginning with the ear; the five organs of action beginning with speech; and the five gross elements beginning with ether, each distinct.
The twenty-four principles are exclusively impure by virtue of their nature as consisting of the three qualities. Thus [ends the verse]. (4)

What is the function of all these, and where is each of them employed? Furthermore, which [evolutes] are born directly from the Pradhāna, and which are born through the intervention of other principles? We shall demonstrate all of this. Now, as for the Unmanifest (avyakta), it arises from Māyā.

(Verse 23) Since twenty-four principles below *prakṛti* have been stated by [the preceding verses] beginning with this, how can twenty-three be mentioned here? To this he says: "Because of the qualities of *prakṛti*.
Since the Sāṃkhyas accept the qualities (*guṇa*) themselves as being *prakṛti*, in order to refute that, [it is said that] because they are insentient and manifold, like jars and other such things...

We assert that the establishment of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) follows from the necessity that there must be another cause; therefore, since this was stated with the intention of expressing the non-difference between cause and effect, there is no contradiction. || 24 ||
The teachers have declared that the Śiva-principle is all-pervading, unitary, eternal, the cause of the entire collection of realities, and has the nature of both knowledge and action. (25)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* defines the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), which was mentioned first, stating: "Pervasive" (*vyāpaka*).
This means it is all-pervading and omnipresent; it is one, without a second, and universal.

The meaning is that it exists in its true nature as a being (*bhūta*). It is eternal (*nitya*), meaning imperishable. It is the cause—that is, the producer—of the entire collection of principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kāla* and ending with earth. Regarding the phrase "having knowledge and action as its inherent nature" (*jñāna-kriyā-svabhāva*): that principle whose very nature (*svabhāva*) consists of pure knowledge (*jñāna-mātra*), action (*kriyā*) as its activity (*vyāpāra*), and witnesshood (*sākṣitva*), is the Śiva-principle (*śiva-tattva*); such is its definition. "They declared" (*jagaduḥ*) means the teachers (*ācāryas*) who are knowers of the scriptures (*āgama*).
Alternatively, it is called "all-pervading" (*vyāpaka*) because, if there exists anything distinct from itself, it pervades all of that.

It possesses "oneness" (*ekatva*) because of the absence of any other person—whether similar or dissimilar—to itself. Since both pervasiveness and oneness also belong to space (*ākāśa*), the term "eternal" (*nitya*) is employed to exclude that. Furthermore, since pervasiveness, eternality, and oneness also exist in the case of the bound soul (*paśu*), [the term "Lord"] is used to exclude that as well.

The term "the cause of the entire collection of principles" [is used] because Māyā possesses pervasiveness, eternity, unity, and the state of being the cause of all; therefore, to exclude her, it is stated that [the Supreme Reality] has the nature of knowledge and action. Consequently, that which is pervasive, one, eternal, the cause of all principles, and whose nature is knowledge and action—that is the Śiva-principle. This is stated in the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad]:
"He has all faces, heads, and necks; he dwells in the secret cave of all beings;
that Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent" (3.11).
And in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"The Lord is free from beginning, middle, and end; he is pure by nature, omniscient, and perfectly complete; Śiva is to be known thus in the Śivāgama.
And in the *Siddhāntahṛdaya*:
Brahman is immutably fixed, immortal, true, one, and changeless;
it is consciousness and bliss, free from opposition, eternally satisfied, and its vision is never lost.
It is the supreme ether beyond time, all-pervading and free from affliction;
subtler than the subtle, unborn, eternally liberated, and greater than the great.
It is beyond reasoning, formless and so forth, incomparable, and without defining characteristics;
it is of the nature of existence, self-luminous, and beyond the reach of speech and mind.
That which is known by the wise through the path of negating that [object],
and which is both an agent like a turner and an indicator like a lamp.
The wise declare that Śiva-tattva has Māyā as its companion. Thus [ends verse 5].
Regarding the commentary: among the principles (tattvas) as they have been enumerated, he first defines the principle of Śiva, which was mentioned first, with the word "pervasive" (vyāpakam).
That principle of Śiva, which was previously established as being of the nature of the Bindu and serving as the material cause (upādāna) for the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan), is pervasive.

The meaning is that [the Lord] pervades the universe through the *kalās*—such as *nivṛtti* and the rest—which are the forms of His own transformations (*nijapariṇati*) of the world consisting of pure and impure selves. As they say: "The *tattvas* exist in the state of *kalās*, and the multitude of worlds resides within the *tattvas*" (*Mṛgendrakriyāpāda* 8.71), and so forth. And that [Supreme Cause] is one, because it is the ultimate cause. For it has been stated that if there were multiplicity, then, being insentient, it would be an effect like a jar or similar objects due to its multiplicity. Therefore...

It must be eternal; for if it were impermanent, it would lack the status of being the ultimate cause, and because if that [cause] too required another material cause (*upādāna*), it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress. Furthermore, it is the cause—that is, the material cause—of the entire class of pure principles (*tattva*); it is not the cause of an impure principle, since the latter has been stated to be produced from *māyā*. And of this [pure cause],...

Because it is impossible for that which is pure to be the cause of the impure. Furthermore, it is "of the nature of knowledge and action" (*jñānakriyāsvabhāva*) because it brings about knowledge and action within itself for the sake of the selves (*ātman*). This is the meaning: through the propitiation of the respective lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*) or by means of initiation (*dīkṣā*), it manifests knowledge and action for those who have attained the worlds of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*), which is their own effect. As it has been said:
In the venerable *Mataṅga*:

"The supreme reality beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*) is indestructible and of an immutable nature; by which [reality] the powers of bound souls (*paśu*) are unfolded, so that they attain the state of Śiva. (This is the reading of the printed edition.)
"Pure! They have gone to the state of the living. (Vi. 3.32–33).

For this very reason, it possesses the capacity to awaken [consciousness]. Now, it has been stated that *māyā* also illuminates knowledge and action through the medium of *kalā* and the rest; this is true, because the knowledge and so forth produced by *māyā* have limited objects and serve as the cause for the notion of "self" and so on with respect to what is not the self.

That [other type] is delusive; however, this [present one] is called "awakening" (*bodhaka*) because it illuminates the knowledge of all objects and so forth by means of the materials established in the scriptures, and because it makes known pure realities such as Śiva—thus there is no contradiction. Alternatively, it is of the nature of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-svabhāva*), because it brings about—that is, manifests—the "own-wealth" (*sva-dhana*) consisting of knowledge and action belonging to the selves. Or else, knowledge and action do not belong to it...
The term *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) should be explained as having an insentient form due to the elision of the negative particle (*nañ*), and not as having the nature of consciousness;
for, like clay and other materials, it is insentient by virtue of being the material cause (*upādāna*), and that which has the nature of consciousness cannot function as a material cause.
As it is stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "For those [entities], the Lord is the efficient cause (*nimitta*), while that Sovereign Bindu is the material cause. It is also stated elsewhere:

(This is a statement from the Pauṣkara Āgama: "And that Kuṇḍalinī is the power (śakti) of Śambhu, pure yet insentient by nature. Thus, the teachers have declared that the Śiva-tattva, which serves as the material cause (upādāna-rūpa), is known as Mahāmāyā. However, this [verse] does not concern Paramaśiva, nor does it concern his power.

[This] must be explained [as follows], because in the context of defining the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, those two [Śakti and Sadāśiva], which transcend the principles, are not the subject at hand.

Furthermore, if it were accepted that those two alone constitute the nature of the Śiva-principle and serve as the material cause (upādāna) of the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan), there would follow the faults of being subject to transformation (pariṇāmitva) and insentience (acetanatva), among others. Nor is the acceptance of them as a phenomenal manifestation (vivarta) of consciousness tenable, since [the Pure Path] is established by all means of valid cognition (sarvapramāṇasiddhatvena).

Because the world lacks unreality, and because the nature of a vivarta (illusory manifestation) is admitted to be unreal; and because the Śiva-tattva, known as the Bindu and consisting of Kuṇḍalinī, is heard of in scripture as the power of grasping due to its non-separation from consciousness (citsamavāya), the aforementioned explanation alone is appropriate. As it has been said:

It is understood from the observation [of the *Luṅgīsaṃhitā*, Part 2, p. 121] that these verses belong to the *Pauṣkarāgama*: "Power (*śakti*) is the material cause (*upādāna*), because it has the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), just as Śiva does;
transformation (*pariṇāma*) is declared to belong to the non-conscious, but it is not possible for the conscious."
If it were so, consciousness would be said to be a mere illusory manifestation (vivarta), and in that case, there would be an absence of causal efficiency;
how then could the world, which is established by all means of valid cognition, be a manifestation of consciousness?
Even *māyā* is not the material cause here, because it causes delusion by its own power;
and that [power] is the pure, yet insentient, energy (*śakti*) of Śambhu known as Kuṇḍalinī.
She does not abide through identity, but rather through being present within the grasping;
this Kuṇḍalinī does not abide through identity with Śiva, the agent.
"From this cause, however, the material cause [is the Self], just as clay is for a potter.

Thus, even according to the position of the proponents of Śabdabrahman (the Word-Brahman), it is stated in the *Nādakārikās* that it is not logical for the Self alone to exist in manifold ways through the sequence beginning with *nāda*: [The relevant verse from the *Nādakārikās* follows:]... [omitted] ...it is not logical.

"The Self is said here to be unchangeable, and its power likewise; therefore, those two are not capable of existing in many ways if they were devoid of consciousness, because they would be subject to modification. (19) And so forth.
Thus, Mahāmāyā is established as the material cause (*upādāna*) of sound, and so on.
This has been shown by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*; therefore, it should be understood from that work. || 25 ||
All the powers, beginning with Will (icchā), having merged into this [consciousness], perform their respective functions;
therefore, they say that this [consciousness] is the benefactor of all.
In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the objection—namely, how the Śiva-principle, which is devoid of action (*niṣkriya*), can be the cause of all principles—he says: "In this [principle].
Within this supreme Lord-principle, the powers such as Will (*icchā*) and the rest are dissolved; that is, they remain supported by that respective principle.

They perform their respective functions, not independently, because they are of the nature of Śiva’s power (*śivasāmarthya*). Therefore, this Śiva is the cause of all the *tattvas*, and for that very reason, he is the bestower of grace upon all. The pervasion of this Śiva-tattva across the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is as follows:
the sixteen vowels are the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*); the nine beginning with *Tārā* (the syllable *Oṃ*) constitute the path of words (*padādhvan*).
The two mantras consist of six and five syllables; therein, the reality is of the nature of Śiva.
Salutation to the one who leads [the soul] beyond the five worlds beginning with Nivṛtti, as well as the three and five worlds; here also reside the five kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā.
The word "namaḥ" should be joined at the end of each [mantra]: "Obeisance to the one whose self is the six paths."

The commentary [states]: "For this very reason—'in this'. The powers of Śiva, such as will (*icchā*) and the rest, first become latent in this material cause (*upādāna*), and through its presiding over it...
They perform their own function, characterized by the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, as well as the creation and so forth that constitute its remainder.
Therefore, they say that this [nature] is also "the benefactor of all" through a succession of causes, because it is the benefactor of all;
however, this is not due to independence from the need for the presiding of Śakti, for that which is insentient cannot exist without the presiding of a sentient being.
Because it is impossible for an effect to arise [from that]. || 26 ||
The first unfolding of this [Lord], who desires to create for the sake of bestowing grace upon both the conscious and the unconscious,
is declared to be His Śakti-tattva, which has attained a state of non-differentiation from Him alone.
The *Tātparyadīpikā* now explains the principle of Power (*śaktitattva*), beginning with the word "cid" (consciousness).
The meaning is as follows: it is the first unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the Supreme Lord who desires to emanate for the sake of bestowing grace upon bound souls (*paśu*) and their fetters (*pāśa*).

The state of being awake—that is, vision—is called the *śakti-tattva* (the principle of power), and it is non-different from the *śiva-tattva* (the principle of Śiva), because a distinction between power and its possessor is impossible. Now, one might ask: how is the existence of power known? We reply: by the impossibility of the effect otherwise. For the creation of the universe and so forth by the inactive Śiva would not be possible in the absence of power; thus, its existence is established.

For instance—just as in the case of fire, even when contact with a finger exists, because the effect of burning does not arise during a state where an obstacle such as a jewel is present, a burning power distinct from the contact of the fire and the finger is postulated; so too here, the existence of power is established by the fact that the fivefold effects would otherwise be inexplicable. Nor is it the case that the contact of the fire and the finger alone [is sufficient].

It must be stated that [the capacity] is the cause of the manifestation (sphoṭa); for otherwise, since there would be no distinction between the states of being obstructed and unobstructed due to its continued existence, one would have to face the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the manifestation of the effect of the sphoṭa occurring at all times. Nor can it be argued that the non-arising of the effect at that time is due to the absence of the cause consisting of the absence of an obstructor, rather than due to the absence of the capacity;
for the absence of an obstructor is not a cause. [This is so] because of the past things...
