Even when there is the existence of the absence of future or present obstructors, the non-arising of the effect—the *sphoṭa*—is established as proof that such [obstructors] are not the cause. Nor should it be argued that because this absence of an obstructor is the cause, the non-arising of the effect is possible even when other distinct absences exist; for if this particular absence were the cause...

Because there is an absence of valid evidence [for its existence] and because there is the presence of contrary evidence. To explain: the object under dispute (the state of being a cause) does not produce a *sphoṭa*, because it is an absence of an obstructer (*pratibandhaka*), just like the absence of something other than that [obstructer]. Likewise, even when this [specific] obstructer has ceased and its absence is present, if another obstructer exists, the effect—the *sphoṭa*—does not arise; therefore, this [absence of a specific obstructer] is not the cause.

Success! Nor is the absence of all obstructors the cause [of an effect], because if that were so, it would follow that a sprout would arise from a seed even when the removal of the light above—which was the obstructor to the production of the sprout—has ceased. If you argue that it is not the destruction of the removal of light that is the cause, but rather the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that [removal] which is the cause, and that such [prior non-existence] does not exist here because the light has been led away from there, we say: not so.

Because it would follow that a sprout could arise even when there is the existence of another prior absence of the removal of the lamp above; nor can it be said that this [specific absence] alone is the cause, for since the prior absence of the removal of this lamp exists in those seeds and sprouts where the lamp has already been removed,
it would follow that a sprout would arise from those seeds as well.
Therefore, from the disappearance of the illuminating light, it is understood that some supersensible cause has been destroyed;
for in a state where there is no obstruction to its absence, the non-arising of the effect occurs because of the absence of the non-existence of the obstructer. Now, if one asks:

"In the case of the destruction of power (*śakti*), due to the absence of a cause, when an obstructer is perceived, there is the absence of the effect, such as a flash of fire, and likewise in the case of the paralysis of movement," [the answer follows].

If it is argued that the absence of movement in a snake and the like would follow because its power has been destroyed by a mantra, this is not so. For when a flame whose power is destroyed is extinguished, a new flame arises; since there is no destruction of power in that new flame, the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* is possible.
In the case of the snake, however, the absence of movement is due to the force of meditation (*dhyāna*), not due to the destruction of power; thus, its movement again is possible.
Therefore, the existence of power (*śakti*) is established by the fact that the effect would otherwise be inexplicable. As it has been said by Bhaṭṭapāda:
"The powers of all entities fall within the scope of the presumption (*arthāpatti*) based on their effects.
This very supreme power is non-different from the Supreme Lord; its modifications are [the products] of the Will (*icchā*).
"The powers are non-different from that [Lord]. This has been stated in the *Mātaṅga*:
"The supreme, subtle power of the Lord is capable of illuminating the waking state;
by means of her, the Lord, whose self is awakened and who is independent, is Sadāśiva" (*Vidyāpāda* 5.20).
The pervasion of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) by this Śakti-tattva is as follows:

"To Ananta" and so forth; that which was previously the fourfold group of words is the power (śakti) of the principle (tattva), transcending the kalās, and it is distinguished from what precedes it. (7)
The commentary: Having thus established the Śiva-tattva, he describes the Śakti-tattva, which is its effect, with the words "cid" (consciousness), etc.
For Śiva, desiring to bestow grace—that is, liberation—upon conscious beings (cit), acts for the sake of ripening their impurities (mala).

Having performed the creation and other acts for the sake of the experience of karma, He effects the grace toward the bonds (*pāśas*) by generating the capacity for their own function. Here, since the goal to be accomplished is the grace toward the bonds, it is stated that *bindu* is the means because it is the primary material cause (*upādāna*). Therefore, this is the final meaning: for the Supreme Lord who desires to create, regarding the objects of consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*), [the process proceeds].

That grace which is the first unfolding (*unmeṣa*), the initial transformation of this *bindu*—which consists of the means for that [grace] and whose nature comprises the worlds beginning with Śānti and is essentially *nāda*—is called the *śaktitattva*. Now, is this *śaktitattva* partless like the *bindu* and so forth, or is it possessed of parts? To this he says: "attained to non-differentiation" (*avibhāgāpanna*). By these [parts], things are differentiated.

The "divisions" (*vibhāga*) are the parts (*avayava*), because objects are differentiated from one another. That which has attained non-division is the partless essential nature; for this very supreme cause—whether it be the *bindu* or *māyā* in the form of power—is the ultimate cause. However, the principles (*tattva*) such as *śānti* and the rest are of the nature of effects, because they exist as manifest entities and serve as the substrata for the worlds (*bhuvana*) and so forth.
[The worlds] indeed possess parts. But is it not the case that even within the Śiva-tattva, worlds are heard of in scripture? True; however, they do not exist directly [within it].
Rather, they are situated at the very summit of the Śānti-kalā, just as the worlds of Māyā are situated at the summit of Kalā; thus there is no contradiction. || 27 ||
The wise call that expansion which occurs through the absence of decrease or increase in the two powers known as knowledge and action the reality called Sadāśiva. (28)
The *Tātparyadīpikā*: Now, in order to define the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*) beginning with Sadāśiva, he says: "Jñāna... (Knowledge...).

The intended meaning is as follows: during the state of expansion of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*), will (*icchā*), and action (*kriyā*), which are transformations of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*).

When there is an equilibrium between the two powers consisting of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), if an intensification of will (*icchā*) is intended to be expressed, then that is the *śivatattva* designated as *sadāśiva*. As it is stated in the *Siddhāntahṛdaya*:
"When the two powers called knowledge and action are equally latent, one attains the intensification of will."
"When it is called Sadāśiva, then it is termed Śiva.
That reality (tattva) resembles crystal. As it is said in the *Candrajñāna*:
"That which is named Sadāśiva is stainless and resembles pure crystal."
The pervasion of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) within this Sadāśiva-tattva is as follows:
here, the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) consists of the letter *ka* and the triad beginning with Śāśvatā;
the path of words (padādhvan) is itself the principle (tattva), the world (bhuvana), and Peace (śānti). (8)
Commentary: Now he describes the Sadāśiva-tattva with the words "jñāna" and so forth.
This is because Paramaśiva, who was previously described as desiring to emit [the universe], presides over the equilibrium of his powers of knowledge (jñāna) and action (kriyā).

That which is the second expansion or transformation of that very *bonds* (bondage), described as its material cause (*upādāna*), which arises through the intervention of the *Śakti-tattva*, is called the *Sadāśiva-tattva*. || 28 ||

Where power (śakti) becomes subordinate and the [power] called knowledge (jñāna) attains predominance in action, that is here declared to be the Īśvara-tattva, which is always the agent of all things. (29)
The *Tātparyadīpikā*, for the purpose of defining the principle of Īśvara, says: "Nyag... etc.

When there is an equilibrium between the two powers consisting of knowledge (*jñāna*) and will (*icchā*) which have become subordinate (*nyagbhūta*), and when there is an intensification (*udreka*) of the power of action (*kriyā*), then—

The Śiva-principle is designated as Īśvara. It possesses the nature of being the agent of all sentient beings due to the predominance of activity (*kriyā*). It has the luster of fire. As it has been said—(this verse would belong to the *Candrajñāna*): "Above that, there is another great covering, that of Īśvara."

"The Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) are situated there, possessing a radiance like that of a blazing fire. Now, one might object: since the state of being subordinate to knowledge and will, having manifested its own object, consists in a state of silence, it lacks the nature of non-existence. As it is said in the *Siddhāntahṛdaya*:
"When knowledge and will are equal, and power attains a preponderance of action, then that Supreme Lord receives the name 'Īśvara'.

The pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) for this [mantra] is as follows: the letter *kha* is the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*). The three words beginning with "dhyānāhārāya" constitute the path of words (*padādhvan*).
The two mantras are "naṃ" for the head of Īśāna and "namaḥ śivāya. The path of principles (tattvādhvan) is itself [the Self].
The worlds (bhuvanāni) extend from Ananta to Śikhaṇḍin. The path of arts (kalādhvan) is Vidyā. || 9 ||
In the third flow, however, it is "downward" (nyak);
that is, where there is an abundance of activity from the power of action through the presiding influence of infinite agents such as the Creator of the world.

They say that the expansion situated below the principle called Sadākhya is the Īśvara-tattva. Its nature as the agent of all objects follows from its being presided over by the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and because it will be explained later that Ananta and all other agents are included within this very principle.
That reality where the power of the agent becomes subordinate and attains the predominance known as cognition is called Vidyā; it is illuminating because its nature is knowledge.
The *Tātparyadīpikā* describes the *vidyātattva*: "Nyag... etc.
When there is an equilibrium of the downward-turned powers of will (*icchā*) and action (*kriyā*), and an intensification of knowledge (*jñāna*) occurs, then that is the *śivatattva*.
It becomes known as *vidyā*. As it has been said:
"When the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) surges upward while the powers of action and will (*kriyecchā*) are suppressed, then Śiva, the treasury of all knowledge, is designated as *śuddhavidyā*."
He states the purpose: "It is the illuminator. He provides the reason for this: "Because it has the nature of knowledge.
It possesses a color equal to that of a ruby. As it has been said:
"On its exterior, there would be Śuddhavidyā [consisting of] ten million [petals]" (this verse would belong to the *Candrajñāna*).
"Consisting of a hundred lakhs, well-illuminated, stainless, subtle, and possessing a luster equal to a ruby.
Regarding this [mantra], its pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) is as follows: the letter *ga* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). The words beginning with "to Śiva" (*śivāya*)...

There are three words: the two mantras "maṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya" and "namaḥ śivāya"; the principle (tattva) is Śuddhavidyā; the nine worlds (bhuvanas) are Vāmā and the others; and the kalā is Pratiṣṭhā. || 10 ||
The commentary is as follows: "Likewise,

'downward' refers to that which [exists] below the principle of Īśvara, in the principle consisting of the transformation of the *bindu*, by means of the presiding presence of the seventy million great mantras."

The intensification of the power of knowledge occurs; because those who dwell in that reality consist of the nature of knowledge and because it is the cause for the manifestation of omniscience, that illuminating principle is called the *vidyā-tattva*. || 30 ||
Nāda and Bindu are said to be dependent upon the two principles (tattva) of Sakala and Sādākhya;
furthermore, the Mantras are in the principle of Īśa, while the Vidyās are in the principle called Vidyā.
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states:

"Now, in another scripture (*śāstrāntara*), Nāda and Bindu are mentioned among the principles (*tattva*). Therefore, one must explain either an increase in the number of principles or their inclusion within [the existing ones]. For instance:"
Above that is the Bindu-tattva, stainless and facing in all directions;
it is the supreme among all principles, an infinite and imperishable light.
And so forth. Likewise, some maintain that the Vidyeśvaras, Vidyās, and Mantras have their function (*vṛtti*) within Sadāśiva.
Therefore, in order to refute that view and to establish their inclusion within those two [Nāda and Bindu], he says: "Nāda.
The intention is as follows: Nāda and Bindu, by virtue of possessing *kalās*, are "with parts" (*sakala*) at all times—that is, always—within that which is called Śiva.
The meaning is that they are said to be based upon that [tattva] and non-different from it. Some say they are based upon the *sadāśiva-tattva*.
The Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*), Ananta, and others reside in the *īśvara-tattva*. As it is stated in the Siddhāntāgama:
"Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivatama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra," and so forth.
Śrīkaṇṭha is before Trimūrti, and Śikhaṇḍin is the eighth after him.
"These eight Vidyeśvaras are proclaimed as belonging to Īśvara.
Thus, the mantras and the vidyās exist by depending upon the Vidyātattva, which serves as their illuminator.
As it has been said:
For mantras and vidyās indeed become the seeds within the Vidyā. || 11 ||
The commentary (*vṛtti*), having thus described the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*), states that other entities are included within those very same principles: "Nāda, Bindu," and so forth.
In this context, since the supreme *bindu* constitutes the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), its effect—the subtle *nāda*—is included within the principle of Śakti (*śaktitattva*).

Because it has been stated [that they are included], the *sakala* (*bindu*) consists of both the *akṣara-bindu* and *nāda*, which is the form of gross sound. These two should be understood as being included within the *sadāśiva-tattva*. The inclusion of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*), such as Ananta and others, occurs within the *īśvara-tattva*.
[This applies to] the seven crores of mantras and the vocal sounds such as *vyomavyāpin* and so forth.
And the twenty-eight tantras, beginning with the Kāmika, which belong to the [category of] Vidyās, are included within the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattva). || 31 ||
Indeed, there is no sequential order among these five here, because they are devoid of temporal succession;
rather, their arrangement in the treatise is established solely by virtue of their functional activity.

In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the objection—"Since these [elements] are eternal and all-pervasive, a sequence is impossible; how then can their existence as such be established?"—it says: "Of the five... and so forth.

This is the intended meaning: although a sequence consisting of "first" and "last" produced by space and time is impossible, the existence of these principles is nevertheless maintained on the basis of a distinction inferred from the difference between their powers (śakti) and their operations (vyāpāra). || 12 ||

The reading "vṛttiḥ pañca" found in certain manuscripts is incorrect; for it is said: "In this manner, the dissolution of both paths, which proceed through successive emanation, occurs in reverse order, extending as far as the two principles of Śakti. (Mṛgendrāgama-vṛtti 13.179).

Because of the contradiction with such statements— which establish the sequence of creation and dissolution, describe the specific locations of the inhabitants of those respective worlds, and inform us of the existence of pure time even within the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan)— this [passage] must be disregarded as an interpolation by those ignorant of the scripture. || 32 ||
In reality, the ultimate principle (tattva) is one, designated as Śiva, and is inlaid with hundreds of diverse powers;
these various distinctions are merely conceptualized due to the different operations of His powers. || 33 ||

In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, one might ask: "For what purpose are these divisions of the reality of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-tattva*) not accepted as being inherent (*svataḥ*), such that one must resort to divisions produced by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the operation of His power (*śakti-vyāpāra*)? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The reality... (*tattvam iti*).

Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), no differentiation within the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is possible, these five divisions are produced solely by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the operation of its powers (*śakti*). Furthermore, the impossibility of such differentiation arises either because the postulation of multiple Lords (*īśvara*) is impossible, or because the very nature of differentiation is impossible. And that [nature] is impossible due to the impossibility of a substratum (*āśraya*). To explain: what is this substratum of differentiation?

Is it distinct or non-distinct? If difference resides in a non-distinct entity, then there follows the consequence of the non-existence of any single object, because of the co-inherence of difference. If difference resides in a distinct entity, then what is the purpose of difference, since by its very nature it is already distinct? Let it be that difference resides in that which possesses difference. In that case, if [it resides] by means of another difference...
If it were distinct [from the locus], then the admission of its subsistence therein would lead to an infinite regress, because another distinction would likewise have to subsist in a distinct entity.

Nor can it be said that it subsists in itself as something distinct from itself, for that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Therefore, one must admit that the subsistence of difference occurs only in a non-distinct reality; and in that case, its lack of ultimate reality (*aparamārthatva*) follows from its subsisting in what is non-distinct, just like the "difference" in the case of the moon. Not so.

Furthermore, difference cannot be the very nature [of the thing itself], because that would entail the absence of any appearance of difference that is dependent [on another], such as "this is non-different from that.

Nor should it be argued that when one says "a jar," there is also the manifestation of the exclusion of non-jars; for if the exclusion of non-existence and so forth were manifested through the manifestation of existence and so forth in objects, it would result in the absurdity of momentariness and other such [unwanted] consequences. In reality, this is the truth.

In the ultimate sense, it is one, undivided, and non-dual. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Named Śiva," meaning designated as Śiva; for according to scripture, "The single Śiva, eternally one, shines forth in manifold ways as both the knower and the known universe. It is "inlaid with hundreds of variegated powers," meaning it is sealed with thousands of powers of diverse forms. As it is said in the *Adhvasiddhi*:
"The Śiva-principle, enriched with thousands of diverse powers, transcends all and is one; yet it is divided fivefold through the differentiation of the manifestation of its powers.
Therefore, these distinctions such as Sadāśiva and the others belong to that Great Lord solely due to the different operations of his power. || 13 ||

The function (vṛtti) of Śiva is also heard of in the scriptures as being divided into Sadāśiva and so forth; to the question of whether this exists in ultimate reality or not, he says: "the principle" (tattvam).

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is only one principle (*tattva*) known as Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*), whose nature is that of the presiding subject (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). This is because his agency is never dissociated from consciousness (*caitanya*), and consciousness is devoid of modification (*vikāritva*), as has been stated. Furthermore, that [principle] is inlaid with hundreds of diverse powers (*śakti*);

the meaning is that it is inherent with a power that is divided into infinite distinctions based on limiting conditions (*aupādhika*), due to the infinity of objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and effects (*kārya*).

Therefore, due to the differentiation of the operations of his powers (*śakti*), the distinctions such as Sadāśiva and so forth are merely conceptual and figurative, and not in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). However, it has been stated that the differentiation of states for the *bindu*—which is the object of his presiding—is indeed real.
As it is heard:
"But as for this division of the Lord, it arises from the division of power (*śakti*) in the scripture;
that division is produced by the difference in the locus of its manifestation, through the metaphorical designation of the difference in functions," and so forth. (Mṛgendravṛtti 13.164–165)

"The division into *laya* and so forth previously described, which belongs to Śiva by way of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), should be understood as the *bindu*; she herself is considered to be *kuṇḍalinī*.
For this very reason, even the conceptualization of forms such as Sadāśiva and others is solely for the purpose of meditation, and not in an ultimate sense."
Thus it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"The form of that [deity] has been described for the sake of the practitioner's goal.
And in the venerable Mṛgendra as well:
"Because no [fixed] body exists, whatever action he performs, in each instance his body is made to conform to the body of that agent. (33)

Having assumed these forms for the sake of bestowing grace upon both the conscious and the unconscious, that Lord effects the grace of consciousness for those whose powers are obstructed by beginningless impurities. (Kriyākālaguṇottara 3.41)
In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the doubt— "For what purpose does the Blessed One assume these forms?"— he says "cid" (consciousness), etc.:
[He acts] for the sake of the bound souls (*paśus*), whose nature as Śiva is obscured by beginningless impurity, and for the sake of the fetters (*pāśas*), which are insentient.
The meaning is that the Blessed One assumes these forms in order to bestow grace. As it has been said:
"This entire universe is of the nature of Śiva; Śiva is the foundational cause.
His power is the transformer, and Sadāśiva is the controller."
"The Lord is the agent and the causal factor, and Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) is the illuminator;
through these established distinctions, the Lord bestows grace upon all that is moving and unmoving. (14)
The commentary says this very thing: "Consciousness" (cid).
For Śiva indeed assumes these forms solely for the purpose of bestowing grace through consciousness.

The meaning is that [the Lord] presides over the forms beginning with Sadāśiva. Having thus presided over them, He bestows grace upon those very selves who have been accumulated through the grace of consciousness (*cid-anugraha*), because it has been stated that even His [presiding] is for the purpose of gracing both the conscious and the unconscious.
The phrase "of those whose powers are obstructed by beginningless impurity" serves as the reason, expressed by way of a qualification, for the requirement of such grace. || 34 ||
Śambhu, the benefactor of all, bestows enjoyment and liberation upon individual souls and imparts the capacity for their respective functions to the insentient category. 35.
Anticipating the question of what kind of grace the Lord bestows upon both the conscious and the unconscious, the author says: "Enjoyment" (bhukti).
Enjoyment consists of the experience of pleasure and pain, while liberation (mukti) is characterized by the experience of eternal bliss.

He bestows the capacity for their own respective functions upon the atoms—that is, upon the transmigrating souls—and upon the insentient category, the category of bonds; because he is the benefactor of all, for that reason he is Śambhu. Now, one might ask: how can the granting of the experience of pleasure and pain be considered a form of grace, given that [the soul] possesses eternal and unsurpassed bliss?
If it is argued that because the bestowing of even a slight trace of pleasure— such as poisoned food or drink— is impossible to regard as a form of grace,
and because the bestowing of the experience of suffering is universally agreed upon by all to be a non-gracious act, we reply: even such an experience of pleasure [is not necessarily so].

Its nature as a benefactor consists in its being a cause of liberation by way of generating an attachment to eternal bliss; likewise, even the experience of suffering is of the nature of a benefactor because it is a cause of liberation by way of producing world-weariness and agitation.

Thus, the one who bestows these [experiences] possesses the quality of being a benefactor. Now, one might object: even so, this [Lord] is not a benefactor of all, as seen in the case of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and similar instances.

Because of the scriptural accounts of his subduing Dakṣa and others, his status as a treasury of compassion (*ghṛṇānidhitva*) is contradicted by that very fact; for one possessed of compassion is never seen to harm living beings. Furthermore, his possession of passion and other such afflictions is inferred by that same [evidence]; for one devoid of passion and the like is never seen to harm living beings. This is not so, because that subduing was for the purpose of removing faults and was beneficial to the whole world.
And because it is of the nature of grace. As it has been said in the venerable Vāyavīya:
"Whatever acts of restraint have been demonstrated in the world toward Brahmā and the others, even those were performed for the sake of the welfare of the world by the form of Śrīkaṇṭha."

"The gods and others, though possessed of faults, were subdued in a fitting manner; therefore, they too became free from sin, and the subjects were freed from their feverish distress. (Śivapurāṇa, Vāyavīyasaṃhitā 1.31.23, 25)

In this context, the censure of Īśvara constitutes the fault of Dakṣa and others. That this is a fault is understood from such scriptural passages as, "He who hates Him becomes even more sinful," and so forth; the word "eva" (even) serves as an emphatic restriction. Furthermore, the fruitlessness [of merit] is likewise [the case].
[The faults are: the censure of Śiva, the censure of the Guru, and the disparagement of the knowledge of Śiva.
The misappropriation of the property of the gods and the destruction of the property of the guru.
And those who, being utterly deluded, steal a manuscript of the Śiva-jñāna—
it is said that these six constitute great sins of infinite consequence.

Thus, from the *Śivadharmottara* scripture, this is understood. Therefore, considering that the fruit of the sin of reviling Śiva— which yields infinite results— cannot be destroyed except by experiencing its consequences through the punishment of Yama, the Lord, whose heart is overflowing with compassion, brought Dakṣa and the others under His own control by means of restraint, and [performed] that which consists of prostration to Himself.

He caused [the offender] to perform an expiation for his self-reproach. For it is not possible to remove the fault of reviling Maheśvara—who is like the night-time darkness—by means of other expiations that are like fireflies; because those [other expiations], having limited scope, cannot possibly remove the unlimited reproach directed toward the unlimited Maheśvara. Just as:

Just as the destruction of even infinite nocturnal darkness occurs through the powerful rising of an infinite sun, so too does the rejection of infinite censures against Him occur through infinite prostrations to Maheśvara. As it is said in the venerable Vāyavīya [Purāṇa]:
"Even punishment, by its very nature, is not to be despised by the wise."
For this very reason, the infliction of punishment upon those deserving of it brings glory to kings.
Every form of restraint in the world is not preceded by hatred;
for a father does not hate his son, even when he restrains him for the sake of instruction.

"For a physician who knows the cause of the disease, when inflicting harm upon the patient, there is not even the slightest cruelty; rather, it is compassion itself that is the motive here. (Śiśupālavadha 1.31.26, 34, 38)
Therefore, it is established that [the teaching] is beneficial to all. || 15 ||
The commentary shows that very same grace directed toward the objects consisting of both consciousness and unconsciousness: "Enjoyment," etc. (Verse 35).
This liberation, which indeed consists in attaining equality with Śiva, is said to be the grace of consciousness;
yet, because karma is beginningless, it does not reach fulfillment here without [the exhaustion of] experience.

In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the objection—“In that case, [the Lord] should bestow upon [the soul] the supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), which is the most primary of the two favors of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), rather than the subordinate enjoyment consisting of worldly experience”—he says: "The consciousness... (*cid iti*).

It is true that the primary grace consists solely in bestowing liberation (*apavarga*), which is characterized by the cessation of *saṃsāra*, and not in bestowing worldly enjoyment; nevertheless, because it is impossible for those karmas— which have existed from time immemorial and yield the fruits of birth, lifespan, and enjoyment— to be destroyed without the experience of those fruits, and because the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) cannot be attained without their destruction, [the Lord acts] for that very purpose.
The bestowal of enjoyment (bhoga) is that which must be resorted to. Anticipating the doubt as to whether liberation (mokṣa) consists of action, he says: "having the nature of equality with Śiva.

That whose form—its essential nature—is equality with Śiva, meaning non-differentiation and discernment, is "that which has the nature of equality with Śiva"; that is to say, it is characterized by union (sāyujya). || 36 ||

Commentary: Now, let it be granted that liberation (*mokṣa*) is a favor (*anugraha*), because it is the cause for the cessation of suffering. But experience (*bhoga*), which consists of the perception of pleasure and pain—how can that be called a favor? To this, he says:

Truly, by the removal of bonds and through the manifestation of Śiva-hood—which consists of the vision and action regarding all objects—liberation alone, whose nature is identity with Śiva, constitutes grace; as for worldly enjoyment, however, [it must be experienced] until it is exhausted (*nābhuktam*). (This half-verse is seen following line 2200 in the supplement to the thirteenth Anuśāsana-parvan in the Bhandarkar edition of the Mahābhārata.)

There is no contradiction [in this], because it is stated as being "for the sake of favor" (anugraha) in the sense that it is an indirect cause for favor by way of being a cause for the exhaustion of karma, according to the principle: "Karma is exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons. || 36 ||
Therefore, for the sake of that [individual soul's] experience, the Lord brings about the production of bodies, instruments, and worlds;
for without an agent, there can be no effect, nor can there be one without the material cause and the instruments.

The *Tātparyadīpikā* raises the objection: "In that case, then, only the enjoyment of the fruits of karma should be ordained, not the creation of the universe. Anticipating this, it says: "By that," etc.
Since karma is not destroyed without enjoyment, the Lord [acts] for the sake of its experience.
It effects the production of the body (*tanu*), the instruments (*karaṇa*), and the worlds (*bhuvana*). The body is the physical frame; it is of two kinds: subtle (*sūkṣma*) and gross (*sthūla*).

The instruments are also twofold: external and internal. Among these, the external is tenfold, consisting of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) and the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*). The internal instrument (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is threefold: mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*). By the word "worlds" (*bhuvana*),...
Two hundred and twenty-four worlds are spoken of. It is said that the Blessed Lord Maheśvara creates these for the sake of enjoyment.

Now, why is it said that Maheśvara created those worlds? [The opponent might argue: "Let it be that their production occurs without a Supreme Lord. To this he says: "There is no effect without a maker, nor likewise without the material cause and the instruments. For:

In the absence of an agent, the production of an effect is impossible; therefore, it is said that Maheśvara created the body, the instruments, and the worlds. Likewise, in the absence of a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), an effect could not arise; thus, some material cause must also be resorted to in that case. Similarly, in the absence of instruments (*karaṇa*), the production of an effect is impossible; and here, the instrument is—

"Something must necessarily be accepted. For instance, in the production of a jar and the like, it is observed that the potter and so forth are the agent (*kartṛ*), the hands, feet, and so forth are the instruments (*karaṇa*), the clay and so forth are the material cause (*upādāna*), and the wheel and so forth are the auxiliary tools (*upakaraṇa*); because if even one of these were absent, the production of the effect, such as the jar, would be impossible. Therefore, in this case as well, those [factors] must necessarily be resorted to; otherwise, regarding the world-nature...

"Because the production of an effect is impossible [otherwise]. Now, what is the proof for the existence of a creator of the world? We reply: for people like us, it is inference and scripture; for yogis who are distinct from us, it is perception. To explain: the collection of effects, from time down to the earth, has an intelligent cause, because it is an effect—whatever is such...

Every effect is observed to have an intelligent cause, as for example a jar; likewise, this world, from time down to the earth, is an effect; therefore, it has an intelligent cause. Nor should it be argued that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) because its presence in the subject (*pakṣa*) is uncertain due to the non-perception of the "effectness" of the earth and so forth, for [this is not the case] by means of inference and scripture.
Because its status as an effect is established. To explain: the earth and so forth are effects, because they are insentient while being distinct from their ultimate material cause (*mūlopādāna*).
Whatever is insentient and distinct from its ultimate material cause is an effect, just like a jar; and this [earth, etc. is likewise; therefore, it is so.
Nor is [the reason] unestablished for us, since we accept that the earth and so forth, having attained the state of atoms (*paramāṇu*), constitute the ultimate material cause.
It should be stated that the qualification "being something other than the root material cause" is intended, because the negation of the atom's status as a root will be explained later.

Likewise, earth and the other elements are effects, because they are dependent, because they consist of the three *guṇas*, and because they are non-substantial entities having the Self as their root, like a jar and so forth. Similarly, from the Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire.
From such scriptural authority as, "From fire comes water; from water, earth" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), the fact that earth and the other elements are effects is understood.
Likewise, it is established that everything other than the Self has *māyā* as its root. Thus, it is said in the *Īśvaragītā*:
"The twenty-four principles consist of *māyā*, karma, and the [three] qualities."

"These are the bonds of Paśupati, and the afflictions are the shackles that bind the individual souls (paśu). ... Māyā is said to be the cause of these very bonds" (7.21, 30). Thus, it is not the case that the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) with respect to the earth and other elements.

If it is argued that the world under dispute is real because it appears, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—since this inference determines the non-existence of the earth and other elements—or alternatively, that this [inference] suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), as in "a hare’s horn is sharp because it is a horn, like a cow’s horn," we reply: not so; for in the case of erroneous cognition, the object is the mother-of-pearl.

This is because it is untenable for it to have as its object silver that is unreal and distinct from that [perceived thing]; furthermore, since an unreal silver is impossible, this [inference] lacks validity due to having a subject-less example (*asiddha-dṛṣṭānta*). Moreover, like the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), this too suffers from the same fault of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*). Finally, it lacks validity because it contradicts perception, as the existence of the earth and so forth is understood through direct perception. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that there is a "partial unestablishedness" (*āśrayaikadeśāsiddhi*) because factors such as necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the qualities (*guṇa*), and the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) are unproven;

for it has already been stated that these are established through scripture and other means. Nor should it be argued that the reason is "partially unestablished" (*bhāgāsiddha*) because time, space, and so forth lack the property of being an effect due to their eternity; for their status as effects has been proven by both inference and scripture.
Is this inference not invalid due to the presence of the fallacy of *asiddha* (unestablished), characterized by proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*)?

For instance, you have sought to prove that the earth and other things possess an intelligent cause; yet this is already established for us as well, since even intelligent beings such as ourselves possess agency toward the collection of principles like time and so forth by means of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit).

Nor should it be argued that the agency involved in producing a different effect consisting of merit and demerit cannot be the same as the agency involved in producing the world; for this is logically consistent due to its being the cause of the cause. Just as a weaver, who is the agent merely of the conjunction of threads that are the cause of a cloth, is nonetheless the agent of the cloth, or as one who hurls an arrow and so forth [is the agent of the flight].

[Objection: Since the agency of harming enemies is [established], it follows that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because for us and others, the status of being the creator of the world is logically possible only for one who is the agent of the karma that is the cause of the world. [Reply:

This is not so, because [the world] possesses a cause that is an intelligent being (*buddhimat*) characterized by direct perception regarding the material cause (*upādāna*), the instruments (*upakaraṇa*), the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the object (*viṣaya*).

Because [the subject] is intended by the term "having an intelligent cause," there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) for people like us, since we lack direct knowledge regarding those four objects.

[Objection: Even so, there is the consequence of *siddhasādhyatā* with respect to a certain portion, namely, that which is the material cause of effects produced from triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth.

The triads and so forth, as well as the primal elements (*bhūta*) and the like which serve as the material causes (*upādāna*) for effects produced by them, are perceptible to persons such as ourselves. Furthermore, the agency (*kartṛtva*) of persons such as ourselves through the medium of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) is established. Among the instruments (*upakaraṇa*), time and other factors are in some cases perceptible. Those who constitute the recipients (*saṃpradāna*), such as Devadatta and others, are established through perception. And as for the purpose (*prayojana*)...

If it is argued that since standing, sitting, and so forth are perceptible, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in that respect, it is not so; for we are proving the possession of such an agent only for the earth and other objects which are themselves subjects of dispute (*vimata*). In those cases where the material causes, such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and triads (*tryaṇuka*), or time and so forth, are not perceptible, [the proof applies].
Thus, because we establish the existence of such an agent, there is no room for the aforementioned defect.

But surely, "being capable of being produced" (*śakyakriyatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*), since it possesses the defining characteristics of a limiting condition. For its definition is as follows: a limiting condition is that which does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*) but is co-extensive with the probandum (*sādhya*). Now, this [condition] exists in the case of jars and the like.

Because it is present in all cases and because it is not a probandum (*asādhya*) in terms of being an effect (*kāryatva*) due to its being the fundamental reason, the argument "it exists" is rendered irrelevant by having a limiting condition (*sopādhitva*); thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" is unestablished (*asiddha*). This is not so, because "being capable of being produced" (*śakyakriyatva*) lacks the characteristics of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and therefore this [argument] is not subject to such a condition; for that [condition] would necessarily pervade the probans (*sādhana*). To explain: the earth and so forth must be capable of being produced by someone.

Because it can be established by the fundamental proof, "because it is an effect, like a jar," [the probans] is pervaded by the probandum. Nor should it be argued that the argument, "the earth and so forth cannot be produced by anyone because they are effects, like a jar," is irrelevant due to the presence of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of "having an agent," for whatever— be it "capable of being produced" or "having an agent"— is posited as such a condition...

This is being established by you; however, since all of that is to be proven by a single application [of the reason], it is impossible for it to be an upādhi (limiting condition) because it pervades the probans (*sādhana*). Furthermore, this is the same in all inferences. For instance, even in the case [of the inference]:
"The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen," there is the upādhi of "possessing recently produced ash."

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even the inference of smoke [from fire] would be non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*). If it is argued that in that case, since the possession of ashes—which arises precisely through the possession of smoke—is itself the probandum (*sādhya*), it cannot be a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and thus the inference is not non-conclusive; we say no.
For even there, because the possession of fire remains a present limiting condition, that [possession of ashes] cannot be established as the probandum. Now, if...

If it is argued that there is no such fault here because every possible condition (*upādhi*)—such as possessing smoke, possessing ash currently being produced, or possessing fire—is not actually a condition, since it is itself the probandum (*sādhya*) and thus pervades the probans (*sādhana*), then [we reply]: in this case as well, by the very fact of being an effect (*kāryatva*), every suspected condition is itself the probandum; therefore, since it is impossible for there to be a condition, there is no room for the aforementioned fault.

Furthermore, if your position is that "the state of having a possible action" (*śakyakriyatva*) refers to that which possesses an action characterized by motion, then even in your view, since the state of having a possible action exists for both atoms and the mind— which are eternal—
this [property] lacks the necessary co-extension with the probandum (*sādhyasamavyāpti*), and thus it cannot function as a limiting condition (*upādhi*). If [you mean] "possible" in the sense of...

The acceptance that "the state of being capable of action" (*śakyakriyatva*) belongs to that whose action is characterized by origination (*utpatti-lakṣaṇā*) results in the fallacy of a redundant qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*), which is another name for an excessive qualification (*adhikaviśeṣaṇatva*). This is because the word "capable" (*śakya*) is redundant, since origination alone is the necessary condition for possessing an agent. Furthermore, this would apply even to sprouts and the like, given the existence of their origination.
It might be argued that the inclusion of the term "capable" (*śakya*) is for the purpose of excluding those [things] that lack an agent;

however, this must be rejected because it is impossible to exclude them—since they too are capable of being produced—and furthermore, because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Only if the fact that the earth and so forth lack an agent were already established would the qualifying attribute "capable" serve its purpose as an exclusionary qualifier, given the existence of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) provided by that qualification.
Once it is established that "being an effect" is not a probative reason (*aprayojaka*), the proof of its being devoid of an agent (*kartṛśūnyatā*) follows. As it has been said:
"When its lack of an agent is ascertained, [the reason] would here possess a limiting condition (*sopādhitva*).
When the inference possesses a limiting condition, there is the ascertainment of the absence of an agent."

Furthermore, "being impelled by hands, feet, and so forth" cannot be an *upādhi* (limiting condition), because it is absent in cases such as the manifestation of grace (*prasāda*), and because it lacks co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other such things. Likewise, in the argument "the earth and so forth must be impelled by the hands, feet, etc., of someone, because they are effects, like a jar," this [proposed *upādhi*] cannot be an *upādhi* because it pervades the probans (*sādhana*). Thus, it is not [an *upādhi*].

Furthermore, "being produced by hands and so forth" (*karādijanyatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because it is a superfluous qualification. Nor can "the earth and so forth" (*kṣityādi*) be the object to be excluded [from the pervasion], as this would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), as has already been stated; and because, in cases such as the drawing of a snake or the movement of one's own body—which possess an agent—there is an absence of "being produced by hands," the co-pervasion (*samavyāpti*) with the probandum is lacking. Moreover, there is no pervasion of a specific kind of effect by an agent.
This must be stated, because no such distinction is perceived.

[Objection: One who perceives a certain effect develops the cognition that it has an agent, whereas one who perceives another kind of effect does not; since this would otherwise be inexplicable, a specific distinction among effects must be admitted. And that distinction exists in things such as jars and the like.
Indeed, being permeated through all things possessing an agent and excluded from those lacking an agent, such as grass and the like, it is itself indescribable, like a particular taste.
As it has been said:
"It is that which is permeated through all things possessing an agent and is indeed excluded from others."
A particular task must be undertaken by others according to their differing opinions.
"The dispute as to what its nature is is resolved by the example of the direct perception of the various degrees of sweetness found in sugarcane, milk, molasses, and so forth.

Therefore, it is that [specific quality] alone which is pervaded by the agent, not the general category of the effect. This is not so, because in the case of effects such as filling a pit and so on...
Because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the absence of such a cognition in cases that do have an agent. As it has been said:
"When a long period of time has elapsed since the completion of a work, such as the filling of a pit, the state of being understood through the cognition of having an agent is simply not perceived."

This same objection applies equally to well-known inference (*prasiddhānumāna*). For instance, even for someone who perceives smoke on a mountain and so forth, the presence of fire may not be understood due to an obstruction such as a lack of conviction (*asaṃbhāvanā*). It is precisely for this reason that one employs inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), which depends upon the instruction of another, in such forms as "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke. Therefore, in that case as well—

Because fire is the pervader of that very [mountain] through a specific conceptualization, it follows that the inference from smoke would be rendered ineffective (*aprayojaka*). If it is argued that inference proceeds there by the force of grasping a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) such as "wherever there is smoke, there is fire," then in this case as well, one must rely on the operation of inference by the force of grasping a general pervasion, namely, "an effect is preceded by an agent."

"Because there is no distinction. Furthermore, "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) is not the determinant for having an agent, because if it were, it would follow that for another thing—such as a cloth—which lacks pot-ness, there would be an absence of an agent. Nor is "cloth-ness" (paṭatva) the determinant, because if it were, it would follow that for a pot and so forth—which lack cloth-ness—there would be an absence of an agent.
Nor should it be said that all [properties] such as pot-ness, cloth-ness, and wall-ness are determinants for an agent, for that would result in the fallacy of having too many determinants.

And that is not tenable, because it would entail that only individual instances are the causes of the potter’s activity, which in turn would entail that other pots lack a maker; for the impossibility of grasping a pervasion with a maker due to [the pot's] infinity is equal in both cases. Likewise, it would follow that properties such as "being in a kitchen" or "being in a workshop" would be the causes [of the potter's activity].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the property of possessing smoke would be irrelevant [as a reason]. As it has been said:
"The pervasion of individual instances such as jars with a creator is not apprehended;
just as there is infinity [of instances], so too let the [pervasion] of jar-ness and the like be understood by the knower."
[Objection: "In that case, one must resort to a wider pervasion (*vyāpti*) based on 'knowability' (*prameyatva*) alone rather than 'being an effect' (*kāryatva*). [Reply:

No, because it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatvāt*). For you accept that objects possess both knowability and existence even in the absence of a creator, by virtue of mere knowledge whose object is themselves. In our view as well, this applies to Māyā, Puruṣa, and Śiva.

It is accepted that even things devoid of an agent possess the status of being objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and existence (*sattva*); therefore, it is impossible for [properties] such as being an object of knowledge to be pervaded by an agent. However, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is not possible in the absence of a specific cause—an agent who is the primary factor in bringing about other causes. For indeed, even when clay, a staff, a wheel, and so forth are present, [the production of the jar does not occur] without one who employs them.

In the absence of a potter, the production of a jar is not possible; however, when a potter is present, the arising of the effect is established through the accomplishment of other causal factors. Thus, because it is an effect, the existence of an agent is proven. Furthermore, the "effectness" of objects consists in their production, and that production depends upon the activity of a cause. Moreover, such activity does not occur without human effort; and that [effort]—
It would not exist without effort; and that [effort] does not occur without desire; and desire would not exist without the knowledge of a means to achieve what is desired.

Thus, the state of being an effect (kāryatva) does not occur in the absence of an intelligent cause (buddhimatkāraṇa). Therefore, because this [reason] is the necessary condition for that [effect], it is not unestablished (asiddha).

Nor is this reason contradictory (viruddha), for it has been stated that a reason is "contradictory" only if it exists in both the subject (pakṣa) and the counter-example (vipakṣa). This is contrary to that definition.

Because there is an absence of the characteristic of contradiction (*viruddha*). To explain: since "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as a jar, and since it is absent in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), such as the root cause Śiva who is not an agent, it is impossible for this [reason] to exist in both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances; therefore, there is no contradiction.

But is it not the case that the earth and so forth are being proven to have an omniscient creator, and not merely some other creator, since it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to be the creator of the manifold universe? For instance, agency is being established only for one who possesses direct perceptual knowledge regarding the sequence of the employment of the fourfold requirements— the material cause and so forth— of the world.

Consequently, he [the opponent] would possess omniscience. Furthermore, since there is no other accepted instance created by an omniscient being that could serve as a similar case (sapakṣa), there is an absence of existence in the sapakṣa. Therefore, because the property of "being an effect" (kāryatva)—which resides in the subject (pakṣa) ranging from the earth to time—is devoid of the probandum (sādhya), namely "being created by an omniscient being," and because it also resides in jars and so forth which constitute the dissimilar cases (vipakṣa), [the reason exists] only in the subject and the dissimilar cases.

[Objection: "It is contradictory because it exists [only] in the present. Likewise, since the state of having a bodied agent is absent in things such as sprouts, the state of having a bodiless agent is also what is being proved here. And in that case, because there is no similar instance (sapakṣa), the property of being an effect—which is absent from the similar instance—exists only in the subject (pakṣa) and the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa); therefore, it is contradictory. [Reply: This is not so, because here what is to be proved (sādhya) is not "having an omniscient, bodiless agent. For instance:

In this context, because the statement of the probandum (sādhya) is given in accordance with the specific point of contention (vipratipatti): when the dispute is whether the earth and so forth have an agent or are without an agent, then the statement of the probandum is "the earth and so forth have an agent. When the dispute is whether they are preceded by an intelligent being or not, then the statement of the probandum is "the earth and so forth are preceded by an intelligent being. When...

Whether [the world] is produced by one who possesses direct perception of its material cause, instruments, and so forth, or not—if it is then stated that "it is produced by one who possesses direct perception of the material cause and so forth," there is no contradiction, because the probandum and the probans both exist in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), such as a jar.

Furthermore, the formulation of the probandum is not "earth and so forth are at any time produced by a creator who possesses a body and is omniscient," because there is no disagreement regarding such a claim. (Sa...)

[And] because you do not accept that the earth and so forth have a creator who possesses a non-omniscient body. Now, if it is argued that even when the probandum (*sādhya*) is stated in that way, since such a creator is intended, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), we say no; for this would apply equally to all inferences. To illustrate: he who proves that a mountain possesses fire [is subject to the same objection].

For him as well, "fire-possessingness" (agnimattva) is not intended by means of a fire that is currently perceived and already established through inference at a different place and time; rather, it is intended by means of a fire produced by the friction of trees preceded by a person who is not currently perceived and is subject to doubt, located on a mountain and distinct from the fire found in places such as a kitchen. Of that [fire]...

Otherwise, even the inference of smoke [from fire] would become contradictory, because [smoke] is absent in the kitchen and similar places. If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the property to be proven (sādhya) is not explicitly mentioned by the word, and because the mountain's possession of fire is established by the fire residing within itself, then in the present case as well, the fact that the earth and so forth have an omniscient and bodiless creator is not explicitly mentioned by the word.
Furthermore, because we establish that [the world] possesses an agent capable of producing its own material cause (*upādāna*), there is no room for the aforementioned defect.

Nor should it be argued that "because [the property of being an effect] is pervaded by having a non-omniscient embodied agent, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) also excludes an omniscient embodied agent";
for the state of being an effect is not pervaded by an embodied agent. And this [pervasion] does not exist even in the case of grass and the like, despite the absence of such an agent.
This is understood from the perception of its being an effect. As it has been said:
"Even the opponent does not, in reality, desire a pervasion of the body [by the self];
for, due to the contradiction of direct perception, the embodied self is not admitted here in the case of a sprout."

Nor does the absence of a bodied creator imply the non-existence of a creator in general, because that [creator-in-general] is not a suitable subject for such an inference. As it has been said: "The state of being a bodiless creator is not to be refuted, for when the body is refuted, the supreme self lacks the suitability [for action], just as a body [lacks it when it is absent]."

[Objection: But surely, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) does not negate a bodiless agent because it is contradictory with a bodied agent who is its own pervader; rather, we say it negates it because it is contradictory with the general property of agency (*kartṛtvasāmānya*), which is its own pervader. For where there is agency, as in the case of a potter and the like, there is no bodilessness; and where there is bodilessness, as in the case of a liberated soul (*mukta*), there is no agency. Thus, there is a co-incompatibility (*sahānavasthāna*) between agency and bodilessness.

Because of the existence of a contradiction between its own characteristic and its locus, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) itself rejects a bodiless creator, since it is contradictory to its own pervader, the creator. If you argue that this is like how the presence of smoke—pervaded by a fire that is neither cold nor dark—rejects a fire that is cold, dark, and smoky, we say: not so;
for if *kāryatva* were not pervaded by the general category of "creator," its rejection would be impossible. And thus, if *kāryatva*...

If pervasion [of the effect] were by way of a common agent (*kartṛsāmānya*), then the agent would not be a pervader of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*). Consequently, even if [bodilessness] were contradictory with that [common agent], it would not exclude bodilessness, because the latter is not contradictory with its own non-pervader. If "being an effect" were pervaded by a common agent, then there would be no exclusion [of bodilessness], because a specific [agent] is obtained through the non-termination of the common agent. As in the case of a mountain.
Just as, having inferred the general property of fire from the smoke currently being perceived,

one postulates a specific fire not yet seen in the kitchen and so forth because that generality does not terminate there, in the same way, the state of being an effect observed in the phenomenal world, being untenable without an agent, establishes the general property of an agent.

Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the relationship [of the probans] by means of a qualification, one must indeed set aside the qualification of the embodied being (*śarīrin*)—because it is impossible—and establish instead the qualification of the omniscient embodied being as its opposite; otherwise, it would be impossible to establish the general category of an agent (*kartṛ*) which pervades [the specific instance]. And that is not tenable, because [the probans] exists where the pervaded (*vyāpya*) exists.

Because the non-existence of the pervader is untenable; for indeed, the absence of fire when smoke is present is not possible. Nor should it be argued that there is a rejection [of the probans] merely by perceiving a pervasion even when there is no actual pervasion, because such [perception] lacks validity. For one cannot, on the basis of a pervasion established by an unauthoritative statement uttered by someone—such as "the property of being produced (kṛtakatva) is pervaded by eternality (nityatā)"—[invalidate the probans] by means of the property of being produced.

Thus, the rejection of impermanence, which is contrary to that [eternity], is established. Furthermore, agency does not entail the rejection of bodilessness; for agency, once proven by the nature of being an effect, cannot be rejected unless there is a specific absence of a bodiless agent, since it would otherwise be untenable. Nor does the implication of a specific embodied agent result in the rejection of a specific bodiless agent, because such a [bodiless] agent is excluded by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*), making its implication impossible.

Furthermore, it is impossible for the agency already established [in the case of a creator] to be devoid of these two specific attributes; thus, there must be the acceptance of a bodiless agent. Nor does the absence of a body in sprouts and the like preclude [the existence of] an unestablished agency, because there is no contradiction.
Likewise, even in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), despite the absence of a body, sense organs, and so forth, the qualities of the self—
The venerable Bhaṭṭapāda maintains that there arises a continuous stream of cognitions regarding eternal objects of pleasure;

therefore, there is no contradiction between [the world's] being bodiless and its having an intelligent cause, because it is accepted that the self, as qualified by a preceding cognition, is the cause for the production of a subsequent cognition. Furthermore, if the inference of a creator of the world were thus...
If you are pointing out a contradiction [in my position], then a contradiction would also follow for the inference of atoms (paramāṇu) which you yourself have accepted. To explain:

the inference of atoms is as follows—"The first effect has multiple inherent causes that are smaller than itself, because it is a causal substance, like a jar and so forth. By this, atoms are established as the causes of the first effect.

By implication, [the opponent's position] entails that [atoms] possess such qualities as eternality, partlessness, being an effect, and unsurpassed minuteness; yet even there, this fault is quite evident. For in your view, where there is eternality—as in the case of space (ākāśa) and so forth—there is no corporeality (mūrtatva), which is defined as the dimension of a non-pervasive substance. Conversely, where there is corporeality—as in the case of a jar and so forth—there [is no eternality].

Because there exists a contradiction characterized by the impossibility of coexistence between corporeality and eternity, the inference of atoms (paramāṇu) would likewise result in a contradiction; the same applies to the inference of another self (parātman). To illustrate: the inference of another self is as follows—"The movement of another's body is preceded by a self, because it is the movement of a living body, like the movement of our own body. In that case as well, where there is "selfhood" (ātmatva)...
In that case, there is no "otherness" (paratva) in the self; and where there is otherness, as in a jar and so forth, there is no "selfhood" (ātmatva).

Since otherness and selfhood are mutually exclusive, the inference of a supreme self is impossible. Now, even if the eternality of a corporeal substance—which serves as the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of an effect—is not observed elsewhere, its eternality must nevertheless be accepted on the grounds of its being the cause of the first effect.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, its eternity is understood by implication. There is no contradiction here, because the proof establishes only that the first effect has a substantial cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) that is smaller than itself; likewise, in the inference of another's self, it establishes only that the movement occurring in another's body is preceded by a self, [not] regarding one's own activity therein.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because "otherness" (paratva) is understood through implication (*arthāt*)—since it has been excluded by the non-perception of what is otherwise possible—and not from the word itself, then, in the same way, regarding the inference of a creator of the world: when all things have perished, if one were to establish a mere intelligent being as the cause of the present effect, its impermanence would entail the consequence of an infinite regress due to the postulation of further creators and causes; therefore, its permanence must be understood through implication.

"It is understood through implication (*arthāt*), not from the word itself. Likewise, when proving merely that there is an agent, there is no contradiction because an embodied agent is excluded by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible, while an unembodied agent is understood by implication; thus, the path is the same.

Now, [one might object]: "If there is a contradiction between two specific properties obtained through the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) and the means of knowledge that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*)," [then...]
No objective would be established. For instance: by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), one understands the agent to be embodied, non-omniscient, non-lordly, and subject to saṃsāra;

yet, by the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), one understands the agent of the effect to be capable of producing it, omniscient, bodiless, eternal, eternally liberated, and the Lord of all. If there were a contradiction between these two [conclusions] which are mutually dependent, nothing at all would be established. But this is not so.

Because this is common to all inferences. To explain: in the case of an inference from smoke, for instance, the specific fire—which serves as the example—is qualified by properties such as being produced by a person, by sandalwood fuel, and so forth, as perceived on the ground of the example-site, yet not [previously] inferred with respect to the mountain that is the object of inference.

It is apprehended by the means of valid cognition that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*). However, by way of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), it is apprehended as qualified by properties such as the fact of having invisible sandalwood fuel produced by contact with trees on the mountain—which are the objects of inference—yet even in that case, nothing would be established. Now, if it is argued that the grasping of pervasion occurs in a general form, namely, "that which possesses smoke possesses fire," [the response follows].
If it is argued that the operation of inference is resorted to here not in a specific manner, then in the present case as well,

the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) in the form "an effect has an intelligent cause" occurs only in a general sense and not in a specific one; since such a creator is not observed in the case of sprouts and the like, the operation of inference must proceed without distinction.

If it is asked, "In that case, why should one not rely on what is observed in the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) regarding the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika)? we reply: there is no contradiction. Nor should it be said that the cessation of agency follows from the cessation of the body and its instruments; for agency is established even through the existence of other instruments consisting of volition, as seen in the case of impelling and drawing toward oneself one's own body. And it is not...

In the case of the impelling of one's own body, it is possible for the body being impelled to function as the instrument (*karaṇa*), because it is impossible for an object (*karman*) to function as an instrument. For indeed, it is not possible for the tip of a finger to touch its own tip. Nor should it be argued that in that case another body serves as the instrument, for that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor can it be argued that, in the case under consideration, the connection with a body is the instrument everywhere without exception.

Because the connection with the body is not required by the agent for the movement of the fingers and other limbs of the hand. To explain: when the self performs the raising or lowering of the hand, it requires only the connection with that [hand], and not the connection with the body; for even while that [bodily connection] exists, if the connection with the hand is destroyed and the hand becomes like a piece of wood—
Because no agency in the performance of manual actions is observed [in the Lord], therefore, by means of pure negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireka*),

it is precisely the fitness to be the substratum of an action that directly conforms to His will which is the operative cause here. That [fitness] is established by inference for the Blessed One in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

For instance: "The subject of dispute, such as the primal cause (mūlakāraṇa) and so forth, is capable of being the substratum of an action that directly conforms to [His] will, because it is insentient, like a body. By this very argument, the contradiction regarding the eightfold forms (aṣṭamūrti) mentioned in the Purāṇas—even though [the Lord] is bodiless—is resolved, since the entire collection of principles from the primal cause down to the earth possesses the definition of a "body" insofar as they are the substrata of actions that directly conform to His will.

This is because the possession of a physical form is established by virtue of [the Lord] having the body of Maheśvara. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how is the statement regarding his being 'without a body' (adehita) to be understood? It is explained as follows: Just as a body distinct from the material cause, such as the clay-substance, is observed in the case of a potter or a weaver, so too there is no body here belonging to the Blessed One that is distinct from the root cause and its effects; thus, the state of being "without a body" is logically established.

Nor is there the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), for that is defined as occurring in all three positions (the subject, the similar instance, and the dissimilar instance), and such a definition is absent here. To explain:

even if the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) were to occur in the subjects—such as the earth and so forth, which are under dispute because their probandum is doubted—and likewise in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as jars and so forth, where the probandum is certain; nevertheless, [it remains valid] because of the absence of the probandum in the certain dissimilar instances.

Because the reason "being an effect" does not occur in those things that constitute the counter-example—such as illusions or inanimate objects—the reason does not occur in all three categories [of the thesis, the similar instance, and the counter-example].

If it is argued: "But since 'being an effect' is observed in sprouts and the like which are devoid of an agent, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its occurrence in all three categories," we say no; for sprouts and the like are themselves the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), and thus they cannot be considered counter-examples (*vipakṣa*). If it is further asked: "But..."

The sprout and so forth do not constitute the subject (*pakṣa*) because they lack a doubtful agency. For it is the definition of a subject that its probandum (*sādhya*) is doubtful. That [definition] does not apply to the sprout and so forth, because they are counter-examples (*vipakṣa*) due to having a certain absence of the probandum. If this is argued, it is not so;
for since the probandum—an intelligent agent—is incapable of being perceived, there is no certainty of its non-existence with respect to the sprout and so forth.

This is because the state of having a doubtful probandum is possible. Furthermore, one should not suspect that "being an effect" (kāryatva) is a doubtful inconclusive reason (sandigdhānaikāntika), because a subverting argument (bādhakatarka) against the contrary has been stated. As it has been said:
"If there were no director of all the causal factors..."

"Then there would be futility for those [reasons], even though they exist, as if they did not. Nor is it "unascertained" (*anadhyavasita*), because that definition applies only to a reason that resides exclusively in the subject (*pakṣa*) while failing to prove the probandum; for the property of being an effect does not reside exclusively in the subject, as in the case of the argument: "The earth is eternal, because it possesses odor."

And because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as a jar and the like. Nor is this [reason] "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), for a reason is called "mistimed" when it occurs while the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has been sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and since that definition is absent here, it is not like [the fallacious argument]: "Fire is not hot, because it is produced, like water."
There is the fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadi�ṣṭa*) because it contradicts perception; for an intelligent cause other than the Self is incapable of being perceived.
If one were to admit the non-existence of something merely because it is not perceived despite being beyond the reach of perception, it would follow that all inference would be abolished.
Likewise, even in the case of a jar and the like, the potter as its maker is not apprehended through perception, since only the body—which serves as an instrument—is perceived.
Because [the agent] is perceptible. However, the body does not possess agency because it is insentient, like an axe;

thus, when the agency of the bodies of potters and others is negated, what remains is that the self possesses agency and the body possesses instrumentality. Therefore, since an agent is never capable of being perceived, its non-existence cannot be established by its non-perception—so say some. Others, however, [hold that] even if the agent possesses a body...

They argue that because non-perception can occur due to factors such as subtlety, distance, or location, the non-perception of [the agent] at the place of the effect does not follow from his non-existence.
As it has been said:
"Since the existence of an effect is never found without an agent..."

"Therefore, this [Lord], though situated in another place, creates the world by His mere will. In this context, there are two kinds of effects: those produced by physical activity and those produced by mere will. Among these, that which is produced by physical activity—such as a jar and the like—requires the proximity of a body. That which is produced by mere will...

[The power of] attraction and so forth does not depend upon the proximity of that body, because those situated at a distance perform the attraction of snakes and other objects even when separated by hundreds of *yojanas*. Others, however, maintain that the non-perception [of the body] through direct perception is due to its unsuitability for such perception, and not due to its non-existence. As it has been said:
"Alternatively, let the body itself be visible, like the eyes and other sense organs;
it is established by both Śruti and Smṛti, whereas the horn of a hare is not such.
Now, it was argued that if the body were impermanent, its own self-creation would be an act of extreme audacity.

"Does it not follow that there would be an infinity of Īśvaras due to the production of other agents? True; however, some maintain that there is no contradiction because the body is beginningless, like the seed and the sprout. As it has been said:
"By means of a previously established body, one acts as the creator of another body."

"And that [creation] was by means of the previous body; thus, beginninglessness is accepted here. Since another cosmic egg exists when all effects within a single cosmic egg and its inhabitants are destroyed, he remains there and performs his work; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. The plurality of cosmic eggs is established by Śruti and Smṛti, as for example:

Just as fruits are spread upon the vine of the *khalva* gourd, so too, according to the Śruti, thousands of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) exist within the power (*śakti*) of Maheśvara; indeed, it should be understood that there are millions of such eggs by the thousands.
