In each of those places, there are four-faced Brahmās, Haris (Viṣṇus), and Bhavas (Śivas).
And from such traditional authority (*smṛti*), that [body] is understood. Others hold that Maheśvara’s body is eternal, because it is beginningless;

for one must accept that the body of Maheśvara—the agent of the beginningless creation and so forth—is itself beginningless. They say that this body is *māyā*. Still others consider the Lord to have the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) as his body. Now...

This inference is sublated by a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*). For instance, since there is the inference that "the earth and so forth are not created by an omniscient being, because they are effects," the inference of an omniscient creator possesses a counter-probans (*sapratisādhana*). That is incorrect, because the conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) are untenable. Is it intended merely to negate an omniscient creator, or rather [to establish] that there is a creator who is someone-someone-knowing (*kiñcijjña*)?
Or is it the absence of an agent? Not the first position, because that would entail the acceptance of a non-omniscient creator;
for a specific negation, like the statement "he does not see with his left eye," has as its object the permission of the remainder.
If it is argued that the opponent intends [the world] to have an omniscient creator and thus only a negation of that is being made here, this is not so.

Since the negation of an omniscient creator is established simply by the negation of an agent in general, that [agent] alone is the object of negation, not its specific attributes. Furthermore, since even objects such as jars must be admitted to have been preceded by an omniscient creator of the world through the mediation of the impelling force of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), the example would be deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). Nor is it the case that...

In that case, there is no other agent, because there is a lack of evidence for a plurality of agents. Nor should it be said that a plurality of agents must be postulated because of the magnitude of the effect;

for in an effect produced by mere will, plurality is of no utility. However, in the case of an effect produced by physical exertion, the postulation of plurality applies only where, due to the procurement of materials and so forth, one person alone would not be able to accomplish it through any other means. Alternatively:

Since there is agency for only one individual in all tasks, there is no assumption of plurality anywhere; this is because they follow a single teacher, or because even if there were many, the others would lack agency— just like the tools such as the axe— and because if there were multiple teachers,
agency belongs to only one on account of his superior knowledge, and when that is equal, it is determined by the difference in the task or the difference in the portion.

The proof for a single creator [is established], because otherwise there would be the consequence of its [the creator's] uselessness. Likewise, since the magnitude of the effect can be accounted for by the magnitude of the creator alone, there is no possibility of postulating a plurality [of creators], as that would entail the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating additional substrata (*dharmin*). Furthermore, if they were of identical intention, [the plurality] would be useless; if they were of conflicting intentions, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of a failure in the production of the effect. Thus, it is not the case in any way [that there are multiple creators].

The assumption of a plurality of agents is thus untenable. Furthermore, the unseen operation (adṛṣṭavyāpāra) of a jar and so forth is produced by a creator of the earth, because it is an unseen operation, just like the unseen operation of the earth and so forth; once a single creator is established in this way, his omniscience, omnipotence, and other attributes are proven.

If it is argued that what is intended is "having a creator who possesses some limited knowledge," we say no, because that would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). For the Mīmāṃsakas and others do not accept that the world has a creator; therefore, the notion of being created by one who possesses only limited knowledge is utterly discarded. Furthermore, since possessing "some" [limited] knowledge is useless for the production of an effect, it is redundant. Likewise, [this applies] to one who is not omniscient.

Because it is impossible for [the Lord] to be the creator of all, there would be the consequence of contradicting one's own thesis (pratijñāvirodha), just as in the statement, "My mother is barren. If the agency of even a limited knower were to be established, then that would be proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā), since it is accepted that individual souls (kṣetrajña) are also causes of the world by means of unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa). Nor does the establishment of agency for the individual souls imply the non-agency of the Supreme Lord.

This must be stated, because [the existence of] a creator who possesses knowledge of the material cause and so forth has been established by means of an inference characterized by five features (*pañcarūpavat*). Nor is it the case that [the argument applies to] individual souls (*jīva*) as creators, since what is intended is merely their status as a cause. If it is argued that "non-agency" is what is intended, this is not so; for in that case, the example of a jar and the like would lack the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), since jars and such do possess an agent. Furthermore, if the root cause (*mūlakāraṇa*) were taken as the example, the instance would lack the probans (*sādhanavikala*).

In that case, because of the absence of a reason (*hetu*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to jars and the like when one puts forward proofs such as "being an existent" (*sattva*) or "being knowable" (*prameyatva*); furthermore, if jars and the like were included within the subject (*pakṣa*), this would contradict perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*). This same fault applies even to the inference of smoke (*dhūmānumāna*), for it could be stated as follows: "The mountain is the locus (*dharmin*);
it possesses fire not present on other mountains, which is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*); because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen."

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with inference—namely, that Maheśvara cannot be the creator of the earth and so forth because he is bodiless, or because he is a person (*puruṣa*), or because he is a liberated soul (*muktātman*), like ourselves and others—we say: not so; for in that case, since your own proof of Maheśvara’s status as the creator of the world would fail, your argument would suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*). If, on the other hand, you claim that in your own position the creator of the world is unestablished, then [the objection does not apply].

If it is argued that this is a "fallacy of proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*), it is not so; for if the opponent’s proof is rooted in a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇamūla*), then it is sublated by that very same means of cognition which apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhaka*). Nor should it be said that the latter does not sublate the former because the contrary inference (*viparītānumāna*) does not arise, since the latter cannot possibly be a sublater of the former precisely because it is rooted in it. Nevertheless, if one were to admit such sublation, then:

Since Maheśvara is not established [for the opponent], there arises the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for this [reason]. If it is argued that "the establishment of another's position does not require a basis in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," we say no; for in that case, one would have to present a contrary inference. This is because, due to the very absence of valid cognition, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) remains unestablished, which results in the fallacy of the unestablished locus.

If it is argued that even for that which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the status of being a subject (*pakṣatva*) is tenable because, precisely due to its being established, the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) does not occur—this is not so. For otherwise, in the case of the argument "The sky-flower is fragrant because it is a flower, like a [commonly] accepted flower," there would follow the absurd consequence that the fault of the unestablished locus is absent, since the term "sky-flower" itself is established. And yet, this is not the case.
It should be stated that the Puruṣa is not the creator of earth and so forth, because he is a Puruṣa, like ourselves and others;

for otherwise, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Even if one takes a specific Puruṣa as the subject (*pakṣa*), if he is qualified by the attribute of being a creator other than the creator of the world, there is still the fallacy of proving what is already established.

If one were to take as the subject (pakṣa) a person characterized by being the creator of the world, there would indeed be the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), or else a sublation by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*).

Nor should it be argued that "not all persons are the creators of the earth and so forth, because they possess humanity, like a potter and others," for this would result in three defects: partial proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), the fallacy of the unestablished locus, and sublation by the means of knowledge apprehending the subject.
"And because there is an absence of examples.

Now, one might argue: "The subject under dispute (the person) is not the creator of the earth and so forth, because he is a person"—in this proof, there is no room for the three defects. First, there is no lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because the self, as a person, is already established. Nor...

If it is argued that there is no disagreement regarding a proven probandum because [the subject] is distinguished from other persons, and that there is no sublation by the means of knowledge that apprehends the locus (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*) because that [person] is established by not being accepted as the creator of the world—this is not so; for there is no disagreement regarding a person in general. The disagreement concerns the effects such as the earth and so forth, not the person. Or, even if there were disagreement regarding the person, nevertheless...

If [the subject] is "a person" in general, that is not accepted because such a person is not admitted to be the creator of the world. If it is a "qualified" person, by what qualification? If it is qualified by being "limited in knowledge" (kiñcijjña) and so forth, there is no dispute regarding that. If it is qualified by attributes such as "omniscience" (sarvajña), there is likewise no dispute, because such a [subject] is unestablished prior to the operation of the inference for a creator of the world; for an inference cannot proceed when the locus (dharmin) is not apprehended.

Misconception is logically rooted in [the acceptance of] dharma; furthermore, there is no misconception following the engagement in the inference of a creator of the world, because such a creator is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, misconception does not function as a differentiator. Likewise, arguments such as "God possesses a body and so forth, because he is an agent" are to be refuted, as they are subject to the same logical principles already stated.

If it is argued that the earth and so forth are devoid of an agent because they lack a body, which is the pervader [of agency]— since whatever lacks its pervader also lacks its pervaded, just as water, lacking fire (the pervader of smoke), also lacks smoke— this is not so. For this inference is invalid due to the non-establishment of its qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*), because there is no necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*) between having a body and being an agent.

Because the absence of a body that pervades [the soul] is unestablished by virtue of [the soul] being all-pervasive; furthermore, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), wherein the invalidity of our inference would depend on the avoidance of the non-establishment of your inference, and the invalidity of your inference would depend on the sublation of our inference. Moreover, [our inference remains valid] even without the invalidity of your inference.
The validity of both [the opponent's and your own] arguments is independent of the arising of the fivefold form [of the probans].

Even though there is an equality between the two contradictory positions regarding that which is to be sublated and that which sublates, your inference is not a sublater because it suffers from another defect, namely, the unestablished nature of its qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*). Now, [if you argue]: "The earth and so forth are devoid of an agent, because they are devoid of a body."

If it is argued that the presentation of this reason (*hetu*) would avoid the fallacy of unestablishedness (*asiddhi*), we say no, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) found in jars and the like. For jars and such things are indeed devoid of a body, yet they are likewise devoid of an agent. If it is then claimed that what is intended is "not being produced by a body," we say no, because the qualification "by a body" would be redundant; for the state of not being produced (*ajanyatva*) alone is already pervaded by the absence of an agent. Nor can that very same [qualification] be the reason itself.

It must be stated that [this argument] would result in the fallacy of the unestablished nature of its own essence (*svarūpāsiddhatā*). Likewise, the argument— "The killing of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma has dharma as its fruit,

because it is an act of killing, like the killing of a Brahmin"— does not suffer from the fallacy of being contradicted by scripture (*āgamaviruddha*) or being mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), since no scripture is found that establishes the absence of an agent [for such a sacrifice].

Nor does this contradict such scriptural passages as, "He is not an agent, untainted, eternal, and indifferent toward all actions," for that [scripture] merely negates agency involving active operation (*savyāpāra-kartṛtva*). And this is confirmed by other scriptural texts such as, "You do not know him who produced these" (*Ṛgveda* 10.82.7; *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 4.6.2.2), and "May he who is the progenitor of the earth not harm us" (*Ṛgveda* 10.12.9).

It is understood from the demonstration of the Supreme Lord’s status as the creator of the world that His agency is like that of a magnet—devoid of actual activity; thus, this is established. Furthermore, this [reason] is not a *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized) fallacy, because the definition of such a reason has been stated as "a reason that is threefold in form for the establishment of both one's own and the opponent's position," and that definition is absent here. To illustrate: just as...

In this formal argument—"The earth and so forth are preceded by an intelligent agent because they are effects, like a pot"—this property of being an effect possesses the three required characteristics consisting of presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), and absence from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*); it is not the case, however, that [the same applies to] the counter-argument: "The earth and so forth are not preceded by an intelligent agent because they are effects, like an illusion."

In the proof of the opponent’s position, this [reason] possesses the three required characteristics: because the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is absent in *māyā* and so forth, it lacks existence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*); and because the property of being an effect exists in jars and so forth, which are dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), there is no exclusion from the dissimilar instances.
Therefore, due to the presence of these five characteristics, this inference [serves] for the existence of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) as the creator of the world.
Thus, it is established that [scripture] is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, scriptural texts such as "He who has eyes on all sides" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 3.3) reveal the existence of the Supreme Lord as the creator of the world. Nor should it be argued that these texts lack authority regarding their own subject matter because they are merely supplementary to injunctions (*vidhi-śeṣatva*).

"Because it is a Vedic statement, like an injunctive sentence. Nor is it figurative, as in the case of "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*Āitareya Brāhmaṇa* 5.27), because there is no sublation of its literal meaning; for likewise, in the *Brāhmaṇas* and other texts, it is stated by the seer that "thus [it was] said by the Ṛṣi," thereby establishing the authority of the mantras with respect to their own literal sense. Therefore, through inference and scripture, Maheśvara is established even for people such as ourselves.

Thus [it is said]. For yogins, however, who perceive everything as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand, [the existence of the Lord] is established even through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To explain:

the Supreme Lord is accessible to the direct perception of some, because He is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand; by this inference, the fact that Maheśvara is accessible to direct perception is established. Furthermore, the existence of yogins is not directly perceived by people such as ourselves.

The fundamental causes, such as dharma and adharma, are directly perceived by the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa, because they are objects of knowledge (prameya), like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand; this is established through inference. In that context, the "Pradhāna and Puruṣa" refers to Maheśvara, while the "non-pradhāna puruṣas" refers to the yogins; thus is their establishment. || 17 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, the Determination of the Pure Category, in the *Tattvaprakāśatātparyadīpikā*.

The function [of the Lord] is thus that even the favoring of the *pāśas* (fetters) is solely for the sake of favoring the *paśus* (bound souls) by means of providing them with experience; therefore, he says "by that.
In this context, by the term "body and organs" (*tanu-karaṇa*), the uncommon creation of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) is expressed. By the term "production of worlds" (*bhuvana-niṣpatti*),...

Creation is said to consist of both the common, which is the nature of the worlds (*bhuvana*), and the uncommon, which is the nature of the bodies born within those worlds. It has been stated that He effects this through Ananta and the other [deities]. Here, an objection is raised: "Without an agent. Just as the production of an effect is never seen to occur without an agent, so too it would not occur without the material cause and the instruments; this applies to Śiva as well.

The prima facie view is as follows: what is the material cause (*upādāna*) and what is the instrumental cause (*karaṇa*) for the production of the body, the senses, and so forth, within the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*)?
In this regard, his powers (*śakti*) are held to be the instrument (*karaṇa*), while subtle Māyā is accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*).
She is one, eternal, pervasive, without beginning or end, and attached to Śiva. (38)
The Tātparyadīpikā: Now begins the third chapter.
Next, in order to define the nature of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and the material cause (*upādāna*), he says: "The powers... (*śaktayaḥ*).

This is the intended meaning: the powers such as will (*icchā*) and the rest, which are transformations of the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), serve as the instruments (*karaṇa*) of the Supreme Lord, corresponding to the hands and other limbs. The existence of these powers as instruments is established by the Śruti text: "His supreme power is indeed declared to be manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are innate" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8). As for *māyā*, it is the material cause (*upādāna*), corresponding to clay, thread, and so forth. Thus, regarding *māyā*...

From the Śruti text, "But one should know [the Self] as the material cause" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10), its status as the material cause is established. If it is asked, "In that case, why is that Māyā not perceived like a jar?", he says: "Subtle. The meaning is that the non-perception of Māyā is due to its subtlety, not because of its non-existence. For instance, [objects are not perceived] due to excessive distance, excessive proximity, impairment of the sense organs, instability of the mind, or subtlety—...
In the world, obscuration, overpowering, similarity, and non-manifestation are seen to be the causes for the non-perception of an object that actually exists.
For example, a bird flying in the sky, though present, is not perceived through direct perception due to its extreme distance.

Due to extreme proximity, collyrium applied to the eye, though present, is not perceived by direct observation. Due to the instability of the mind, one whose consciousness is overwhelmed by desire and the like does not see the assembly and so forth. Due to the impairment of the sense organs, such as blindness or deafness, there occurs a non-perception of objects like jars, forms, or sounds. Due to subtlety, [objects such as] atoms and the like [are not perceived].
Even one whose mind is directed toward it does not perceive [an object], due to obstruction; for example, a jar situated inside [a house] is not perceived.

Because they are overwhelmed by the light of the sun, stars are not perceived during the day. Because of being mixed with similar things, the streams of water released from clouds are not perceived in a reservoir. Because of non-manifestation, curds and so forth are not perceived in the state of milk and the like.
Thus, for these reasons, because one observes the non-perception of an object that actually exists, the certainty of non-existence cannot be established by mere non-perception alone.

The non-perception of the seventh taste is due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not due to these aforementioned reasons. Furthermore, there is the non-perception of an existing illusion (*māyā*) due to its subtlety, and [the non-perception of the self] due to its being the cause for the production of the world, which is its effect.
"Because its existence is established. This has been stated by the Sāṃkhya teachers:
"Due to excessive distance, proximity, impairment of the senses, instability of the mind, subtlety, obstruction, being overwhelmed, and merging with what is similar."
"Its non-perception is due to subtlety, not due to non-existence, because it is perceived through its effects" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 7–8).
The collection of principles beginning with time and ending with earth possesses a material cause that is extremely similar to itself, because it is an effect.

Whatever is an effect is observed to possess a material cause that is absolutely similar to itself; for example, jars, bowls, and the like, being made of clay, are produced from a material cause of clay that is absolutely similar to them. Likewise, this collection of principles is an effect; therefore, it must possess a material cause that is absolutely similar to itself. And since all the insentient principles are insentient by nature...
The accomplishment of that [unmanifest] is as follows: its material cause (*upādāna*) is similar [to it], and that reality is called *māyā*. As it has been said:
"Because the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the unmanifest is also established" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 8).
Likewise, the principles beginning with Time and ending with Earth have a single, unlimited material cause, because they are limited;

for whatever is limited is seen to have a single, unlimited material cause, just as limited objects such as jars and bowls have a single, unlimited clay as their material cause; and since Time and the others are limited, they therefore have a single, unlimited material cause.

That which is the single, immeasurable material cause (*upādāna*) of these [effects] is *māyā*. Likewise, time and the other factors possess as their cause an unmanifest state, because they are manifest, like the limbs of a tortoise being extended from it; thus, *māyā* is established.
It is one, because there is no evidence for its multiplicity. If it is argued that multiplicity follows from the lack of evidence for unity, this is not so.

For oneness is established by its mere existence, whereas manifoldness has its existence established only through dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, that [oneness] is eternal, because it is not an effect due to the absence of any other material cause (*upādāna*); and if such a cause were absent, there would follow the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Māyā is said to be the cause of these very bonds; and because she is designated as the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) and the unmanifest (avyakta), her status as the root-nature is established. Furthermore, she is all-pervasive within her own effects.

Because it pervades all things. "Without beginning or end" means devoid of arising and destruction. "Auspicious" (śivā) means pure, because it is free from the bondage of the *guṇas*. Thus she is described by those who know the reality (*tattva*).

Alternatively, by the word "one" (*eka*), [the text] refutes the view accepted by the proponents of *ārambhavāda* (the theory of new production), which holds that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is produced from multiple material causes.

He refutes this as follows: For instance, the dissolution (*saṃhāra*) of earth, water, fire, air, and their constituent parts occurs through the division of those parts, ending in the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*). However, the destruction of an ultimate atom is not possible, because the division of its parts is impossible;
that [division] is impossible due to the absence of further parts, and that [absence of parts] is due to its being an ultimate atom. Consequently, at the time of creation...

From the conjunction of two atoms, the first effect, the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), arises. In that process, the two atoms are the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), because they serve as the substratum for the effect. Their conjunction is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), because it initiates the effect in its own substrata. The remaining factors, such as the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), are the instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). Then, from three dyads, the triad (*tryaṇuka*) [arises].
Of what is there production? In that case, three dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); their conjunction is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*);
and the remainder is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). This is to be understood in this manner until the production of the ultimate composite (*antyāvayavin*).

Such is the view of the proponents of the theory of origination (*ārambhavādinaḥ*), such as the Vaiśeṣikas, Naiyāyikas, Bhāṭṭas, Prābhākaras, and others, because in the case of cloth and so forth, one observes that they have multiple constituent causes (*upādāna*) each smaller than themselves.

They assert that even for the manifold world (*prapañca*), there is a single, uniform material cause (*upādāna*) consisting of its own constituent parts. He refutes that [view] with the word "one" (*eka*):

from a single lump of clay as material cause arise many things such as jars, bowls, pots, and drums; or from a single lump of gold arise earrings, svastikas, rings, and so forth; or from a tree arise boxes, planks, and the like. This is because they are seen to be produced by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) itself.

Since [these effects] are perceived, when postulating a material cause for the world on the basis of its being an effect, one must postulate its unity in order to avoid the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); thus, the primal material cause is not manifold. This was stated by the venerable Vedavyāsa—(this statement is found in the edition of the Mahābhārata prepared by Bhāṇḍārkar, in the Udyogaparvan, within the Viduranīti, verse number 169).

It is found in the reading marked by Tārā: "From one tree [O King—this is the reading there] sacrificial vessels are fashioned; from the *takṣya* tree, the *sruk* and the *droṇī* and the *boḍanī*, and so forth. She is eternal (*nityā*), meaning devoid of destruction. She is pervasive (*vyāpinī*), like clay in jars, bowls, pots, and the like; she is woven through her own effects—from time down to the earth—in their insentience.

"Without beginning or end, devoid of increase and decrease. Increase (*vṛddhi*) is the accumulation of parts; decrease (*vyaya*) is their diminution. The meaning is that she is free from both of these. This is because she is one, eternal, and all-pervading. Some read "attached to Śiva" (*śivāsaktā*); in that case, it means she is constantly connected to Śiva, existing as the very form (*vigraha*) of Śiva. (1)
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: "The powers" (*śaktayaḥ*).

As previously stated, it is the power itself, differentiated by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for Him even in this impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*); it is the material cause (*upādāna*).

But it is *māyā*. And she is subtle and formless, because, as the supreme cause, she exists in the form of power (*śakti*). And she is one. Since multiplicity implies impermanence when there is insentience, the sense is that she is "one. She is eternal because she is devoid of beginning and end; for the continuous process of creation and dissolution persists eternally, and that [process] likewise lacks beginning and end. Therefore, she is all-pervasive (*vyāpinī*) with respect to everything.

And because it is devoid of the arising and destruction of its own effects, such as the *kalās*, it is beginningless and endless; moreover, it is unattached and non-inherent in Śiva, because, like the *bindu*, it possesses the power of grasping by way of being the material cause (*upādāna*). || 38 ||
She is common to all men and is the cause of all worlds; inscribed by the karma of every living being, she produces delusion by her very nature. (39)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states its nature as "common" (*sādhāraṇī*).
This is the intended meaning: it is common to, or equal for, all living beings (*sakalajīva*), because it pertains to everyone—

Māyā, transforming itself into the form of living beings, bodies, sense organs, and objects, is the object of enjoyment for all puruṣas; therefore, it is common to all puruṣas. Anticipating the objection that if it were common to all puruṣas, there would be the undesirable consequence of even a liberated puruṣa being subject to the production of a body and so forth, he says: "inlaid with the karma of all people. This refers to the merit and... [of all unliberated beings].
"Sealed by merit. The sense is that because there is an absence of karma for those who are liberated, there is consequently an absence of the commencement of a body and so forth caused by it.

Alternatively, one must state where the activity of karmas resides during the state of dissolution (*pralaya*). It cannot reside in the Self (*ātman*), because, being of the nature of pure consciousness and stainless, it is impossible for it to be the locus of such activity. As it has been said:
"Just as space, being all-pervading, is not defiled because of its subtlety,
so the Self, though dwelling everywhere in the body, is not defiled" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.32). For just as space does not become soiled by contact with smoke...
"Likewise, the Self is not tainted by the states born of the internal organ" (Īśvaragītā 2.24).
Nor should it be said that at that time karma residing in the subtle body [remains], for at that time it has dissolved back into primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Because [the world] is non-existent due to being dissolved; nor should it be argued that at that time, because actions (*karman*) are non-existent, their status as a substratum cannot be determined—for if actions were non-existent, there would be no efficient cause (*nimitta*), resulting in the undesirable consequence that creation could not occur again. Therefore, having raised the doubt as to where the activity of actions resides at that time, he says: "inlaid with the actions of all living beings" and "by its very nature generating delusion. By its own...
By concealing the Self through the state of insentience (*jaḍatva*) and causing the notion of "Self" to arise within itself, it deludes the bound souls (*paśu*).
As it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Māyā is declared to be the deluder, due to the enjoyment of the relish of sense objects."
"Wherever he may be situated, it is due to the cause of the impurity of his own karma. (Vijñānabhairava 2.16–17).
Now, one might object: "The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the material cause of all effects; therefore, one should not postulate a *māyā* distinct from that."

This is not so; for since it consists of the three *guṇas* and is therefore an effect, one must necessarily postulate another eternal material cause that serves as its cause. To explain: the proof of its being an effect is established by the argument that "the *pradhāna* is an effect because it consists of the three *guṇas*, like a jar and other such things. Nor is [this argument] invalid for the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

It should not be said that its nature as consisting of the three *guṇas* is unestablished; for its nature as consisting of the three *guṇas* is established by its being of the nature of the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Likewise, its establishment follows from such scriptural texts as: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 4.5). Now, [an objection may be raised]:

If it is argued that this is incorrect because it contradicts such scriptural authorities as, "O best of beings, both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as well as Time, are eternal," we say: not so; for [the scripture] states, "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices indeed becomes inexhaustible" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.5.4.1).

This is because what is intended to be expressed is a connection with a period of time longer than that of the *mahat* and other cosmic principles, just as the indestructibility (*akṣayatva*) of merit is understood from the verbal statement itself.

Now, one might object: in that case, since the impermanence of the fruit of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice is established by another means of knowledge—namely, through inference such as "the fruit of the Cāturmāsya is impermanent because it is an effect, like the fruit of other ritual acts"—it would be appropriate to assume that the word "indestructible" (*akṣaya*) refers to a connection with a long duration of time.

If it is argued that this is not so, we say no; for here too, an inference has been stated which makes known the unmanifest and its impermanence, and because there is the existence of scripture as well.
Thus: "From the Unmanifest arose Time, the Pradhāna, and the Supreme Puruṣa;
from these all this was born" (3.1).

Thus, because the *Īśvaragītā* establishes the production of *pradhāna*, its impermanence is proven; and likewise, because the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa* establishes the production of *pradhāna*, *puruṣa*, and *kāla*. For it is said therein:
"Those two [puruṣa and kāla] indeed proceed from beyond the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Viṣṇu."
"O Brahmin, in form (rūpa) there is both the primary matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa).
When that very [form] is held by another and separated, O twice-born one, that which remains is what is designated as 'time' (kāla). Thus it is said.
Furthermore, its existence is established by the teaching that Māyā is the fundamental material cause, as stated in: "One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10).
Therefore, it is established that Māyā is the fundamental material cause of the universe. That Māyā resembles yellow orpiment.
As it has been said:
"Outside of that, however, there would be Māyā, resembling the color of yellow orpiment"— this statement [would belong] to the *Candrajñāna*.

The pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) for this [mantra] is as follows: the letter *gha* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). The three words beginning with "to Aghora-hṛdaya" (*aghora-hṛdayāya*) are the words (*pada*). "Śim" and "Aghora-hṛdayāya" are the two mantras (*mantra*) consisting of five syllables each. *Māyā* is the principle (*tattva*). The seven worlds (*bhuvana*) beginning with Mahātejas. *Nivṛtti* is the level (*kalā*). || 2 ||
The function (*vṛtti*) is common to all selves and is the cause of all worlds; this is an elliptical expression that includes the body and so forth as well.

Furthermore, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), since even the intellect (*buddhi*) dissolves into that very [self], it is endowed with all the fruits of the actions of the self in the form of the qualities of the intellect. For action is...

Like agriculture and similar activities, because it consists of the refinement of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it is accepted as a quality of the intellect (*buddhi*) alone, and not as a quality of the self (*ātman*), for that would entail the consequence of the self being subject to modification. Furthermore, this [ignorance] is delusive, because it is the cause of perceiving the eternal, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is actually impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self. (39)
Having observed the karmas and having agitated Māyā with his own powers, Śambhu [creates] bodies for each individual for the sake of experience.
And it assumes the instruments of action. || 40 ||
In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the doubt—namely, how the Lord creates the world, by what instruments, and for what purpose—it says: "The actions... and so forth.

In accordance with the karma of each individual, Śambhu—having agitated Māyā through His own powers (śaktis) and wills, thereby producing various disturbances and transformations—manifests bodies, sense organs, and objects such as sound for the sake of experience.

For material causes such as the *apādāna* (the point of departure) are not sufficient to produce an effect unless impelled by an agent; thus, the necessity of agitation (*kṣobha*) is established. || 3 ||
And from that [the] commentary says: "The karmas.
Even Śiva, having recognized at the time of dissolution (pralaya) the karmas of the selves as ripened, [acts] for the sake of their experience.

He agitates *māyā*—that is, he makes it ready for procreation—by means of infinite powers presided over by his own capacity. As it is stated in the venerable *Raurava*: "Endowed with the powers beginning with Vāmā, impelled by the will and ordinance of Śiva, the Lord of the Sovereign Kings of Knowledge, the King of Mantras, having agitated *māyā*, brought forth *kalā*" (1.6–7). Having agitated it, [he does so] precisely through that presiding [of his own power].

He creates for each individual distinct gross bodies (vapaṃṣi), as well as subtle bodies characterized by their instruments (karaṇa)—the word "and" (ca) implying that he also creates common things such as the worlds and so forth. || 40 ||
Consisting of various powers, she first generates the very principle of Time (kālatattva);
therefore, this Time impels the world, which consists of the future, the present, and the past. || 41 ||
The *Tātparyadīpikā*:

Now, he defines the principle of Time (*kālatattva*), which was mentioned first among them because it is the cause of all effects—beginning with the word "diverse" (*nānā*): impelled by various powers such as Will (*icchā*) and the rest, Māyā produces the principle known as Time; "in the beginning" means first.

Because it is impossible for other principles (*tattva*) produced by time to arise if time itself is not produced; therefore, those other principles are produced by it. Just as a potter first produces the wheel and other such instruments which serve as the causes for the production of a jar—since the production of the jar is impossible if they are not produced—so too Māyā first creates Time (*kāla*). Of that [Time]...

"Because it is the cause of everything other than itself. As for time (*kāla*), since there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if time were required for its own production by depending on another time—which would necessitate the postulation of yet another time—it does not depend on time for its production.
Thus, time is produced by the fourfold set consisting of Śiva, Śakti, Karma, and Māyā. He states its definition: "That which has the form of the future, the present, and the past."

"Because it impels the world, it is called *kāla* (time). That principle which, by virtue of its true nature, causes the manifestation of objects in their future, present, and past forms is the principle known as *kāla*. Alternatively, that principle which impels—that is, binds—the world in its future, present, and past forms, or which measures it in the form of moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), and so forth, is the principle known as *kāla*. Likewise:

The Vaiśeṣikas and others have also stated: "Time is the cause of the cognitions of priority, posteriority, slowness, quickness, and so forth. When there is an appearance of posteriority in a youth who is the locus of spatial priority, and an appearance of priority in an old man who is the locus of natural posteriority, that is the "confusion of priority and posteriority" (*parāparavyatikara*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the confusion] of the usage of "slow" and the usage of "quick," as well as "simultaneous," is included. He acts [upon this].

Furthermore, that which is the cause of the conventional usage [of terms] such as "he acts successively" and so forth is time (*kāla*). By this very definition, the proof for the reality of time is also presented. To explain: a cognition qualified by [attributes] such as "having occurred in the past" must be preceded by its qualifier, because it is a cognition of a qualificandum; whatever is a cognition of a qualificandum is preceded by its qualifier, just as [the cognitions] "one with a staff" or "one with earrings."

The cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*), such as "an umbrella-bearer" and so forth, is preceded by the cognition of its qualifier (*viśeṇa*), such as a staff; and this [cognition of the Self] is likewise a cognition of a qualified object; therefore, it is preceded by a qualifier. That which is the qualifier here—distinct from the principles beginning with Niyati and ending with Earth—is the principle of Time (*kālatattva*); thus is its establishment. Its color is variegated. As it has been said:
Then: (This verse belongs to the *Candrajñāna*: "The *sampuṭa* called Kālaniyati pervades and envelops [all];
it is black, dark, ruddy, white, and in some places mixed.
Its pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is as follows: the letter *ṅa* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). "Oṃ namo namaḥ" and so forth are two [mantras].
In the *pada*, for Vāmadeva’s secret, there are two five-syllable mantras; they are the sole heroes who bestow happiness in the world, and the *kalā* is Śāntyatītā. || 4 ||

The commentary here states that in order to demonstrate how the thirty principles from Time (Kāla) down to Earth (Pṛthivī) serve the subtle body, the sequence of their creation is described, beginning with the word "Nāna."

By accepting the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), since effects exist there during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) in the form of potentiality (*śakti*), Māyā— which consists of a collection of such potencies— produces the principle of Time (*kālatattva*) when it is infinitely agitated.
And this transformation of the Bindu occurs not in its entirety, according to the analogy of milk turning into curd, but rather according to the analogy of a worm [transforming] into ghee.
It should be understood that [this occurs] "in part. Now, one might object:
in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures, its operation is heard of as occurring immediately after time (*kāla*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and passion (*rāga*). True;

however, there the sequence of activity is shown for those factors starting from time onwards, whereas here it is the sequence of creation [that is intended], so there is no contradiction. Now, this...

Time is accepted as eternal by the Naiyāyikas and others; therefore, he says "bhāvī" (future). The meaning is that since it exists in three forms—past, present, and future—and since it is insentient, its impermanence is established by virtue of its multiplicity. He asks by what effect this [time] is established, and answers: "kalayati" (it measures). This means that it measures—that is, it determines—by means of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of such notions as "long" and "quick."
As they say: "Time is divided by the intellect. (41)
Niyati is of the nature of regulation; it arises immediately after Māyā. Because it regulates everything, it is called Niyati. (42)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* now states the definition of *niyati*: "Niyaṭi... etc.
From the *māyā*-principle alone, the *niyati*-principle arises immediately after the *kāla*-principle; for even in the production of *kāla*, [the cause is] *niyati*.

Because it is the cause. He states its definition preceded by an etymological explanation: "it restricts" (*niyamayati*). Because it restricts—that is, establishes—everything, it is designated by the name *niyati*. By this very statement, its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is also stated. For instance, in the world, oil is found in sesame seeds, not in sand; rice-grains are found in paddy, not...

In the case of mung beans and the like, as well as milk in the udder and not in other parts, such a restriction is not possible without a restricting agent; therefore, some such restricting agent must be admitted, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of that restriction. That which serves as the restrictor in this case is the principle of Niyati (the principle of necessity); thus, its existence is established. As it is said in the *Pārameśvara*:
Now, O tiger among sages, the power that restrains the person of immeasurable splendor has been imparted by you,
who possess great being.
By means of a restrictive nature, which is the cause for the persistence of restriction,
the atom is constrained and turned back within the continuum of experience;
there exists no other [cause] that effects such a determination within the continuum of reality.
The two poles, consisting of dharma and adharma, are immeasurable for the bound soul (paśu).
For that purpose, the body of all embodied beings manifests;
having thoroughly ascertained the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) as being effortless amidst the ripening of those [karmas].
Because it indeed causes [beings] to be led, it is called *niyati* (destiny);
and whatever suffering or happiness is greater for those two [is determined by it].
"It does not give; it maintains [the fruit] through its own power alone, and not otherwise," and so forth. (*Mālinīvijayottara*, 13.1–2, 5–8).
And the color of *niyati* is like that of *kāla*. Its pervasion across the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is as follows: the letter *ca* is the color. To the Protector (*goptre*).

The two words "nidhanāya" [constitute] the mantra for Sadyojātamūrti; it consists of five syllables. The principle (tattva) is that called Niyati. The two worlds (bhuvana) are Saṃvarta and Jyotis. The kalā is Śānti. || 5 ||
Furthermore, regarding the term "niyati" (destiny):
this is the intended meaning— that in the absence of destiny, others might experience the fruits of karmas acquired by someone else.

In the absence of a royal authority, [the senses] would be like bandits seizing the fruits of agriculture and other labors; therefore, this [power] is established as their regulator. Nor can karma be the regulator, because its purpose is fulfilled solely in the production of results, and there is no evidence for its being the cause of another effect, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of postulating numerous underlying principles (*tattva*). If it is argued that the power of Śiva is the regulator, that is not so.

Because that [power] performs its function regarding objects of experience only through the mediation of other principles (*tattva*), and otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of all principles. || 42 ||
Subsequently, from Māyā, Kalā takes up the impurity (mala) of men as one [portion] and manifests the power of agency; therefore, it is called "Kalā" here. (43)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* now defines the principle of *kalā*: "From Māyā.
Immediately after the principles of Time (*kāla*) and Necessity (*niyati*), the principle of *kalā* arises from Māyā itself; by means of which the *āṇava* [impurity] of bound souls...

By contracting impurity (*mala*) into a single locus, their power of agency (*kartṛśakti*) is manifested; that is the principle of *kalā*. Since the power of agency is manifested by this [principle], its existence is thereby established. As it has been said: "Thereafter, Māyā [manifests] *kalā*; she, having localized impurity on one side..."
For that which manifests agency cannot arise from an insentient cause without an agent.
And as stated in the Mātaṅga: "Just as a clay vessel heated by fire is capable of withstanding contact with lac,
so too can enjoyment perfume the individual soul (aṇu) that has been pierced by a portion [of the power]."
The *kalā* should be known as the nourisher of enjoyments, and the *pudgala* is its substratum;
indeed, there is no other support for enjoyments apart from the *kalā*.
"Consequently, this manifest cycle of existence is fixed and exceedingly difficult to transcend," and so forth.
(Viṣṇu Purāṇa 9.28, 31, 33).
Therefore, the principle known as *kalā* must be accepted. || 6 ||

The commentary states: "Following that, from Māyā, Kalā comes into being"—this is the connection with what precedes. Because the souls are unable to experience [objects] due to being veiled by impurity (mala), for their sake, [Kalā] manifests the power of agency by fragmenting—that is, casting away—the impurity in one part of these [souls].

Because power is one, it manifests the power of knowledge and action to some extent; therefore, the meaning is that through that effect, the accomplishment of the *kalā* occurs. (43) Constantly accompanied by Time and Necessity as its subordinates, this [power] indeed performs its own activity as far as the earth extends. (44)
He states in the *Tātparyadīpikā* that the triad of principles (*tattvatraya*) is applicable everywhere: "By Time," etc.
By means of this [triad], accompanied by Time and Necessity (*niyati*), He brings about and performs the entire range of effects, from the state of mere Māyā down to the earth.

This is *kalā*. Its color consists of a mixture of white, yellow, reddish-brown, and black. As it has been said—(this verse would belong to the *Candrajñāna*): "The *tattva* of *kalā* is more excellent than that *vidyā-tattva*."
"White, yellow, reddish, black, and likewise mixed colors.
The pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) for this [mantra] is as follows: the letter *e* is the phoneme (*varṇa*).
"To her who has attained all unions," and so forth, are two words (*pada*). *Yaṃ* and *astrāya* are two mantras of five letters each. The principle (*tattva*) is that which is called *kalā*.
The five [elements] and the two—Antaka and Sūkara—are in the world; Vidyā and Kalā [are also there]. || 7 ||
And from that, the commentary says: "by time.
For *kalā* is primary because it is internal, serving as an aid to the nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), whereas *kalā* and the other [categories] are not.
The sense is that it is secondary because it is external. || 44 ||
For the person whose power as an agent has been awakened, the *vidyā*-tattva—which is of the nature of light—is produced for the purpose of manifesting objects; this indeed is *kalā*. 45.
The *Tātparyadīpikā* now states the nature of impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*): "Having been awakened," etc.
For the sake of the individual soul’s experience of objects, once its power of agency has been manifested by *kalā*, *kalā* generates the principle of *vidyā*.

Because it is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), it is possible for it to serve as the cause for the manifestation of objects. Others, however, maintain that *vidyā* arises from *māyā* itself. As it is stated in the *Śaivarahasya*:
"That which is the manifestor of the intellect (*buddhi*)—which consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and is the object of experience—"
From Māyā itself, Vidyā, whose nature is light, arises. Thus [ends the eighth verse].
And the commentary says: "Thus, awakened," etc.
As it is stated in the venerable *Raurava*: "From the principle of *kalā*, the two—*rāga* and *vidyā*—and *avyakta* were born within *sattva*."
(Vi. 2.15) Thus [it is said]. || 45 ||
Having pierced through the veil of its own karma, this instrument reveals the multitude of objects belonging to the power known as knowledge; it is the supreme [instrument] of the Self. (46)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states the manner in which it demonstrates its subject matter: "The veil," etc.
This *vidyā*, by its own power alone, having pierced through the concealment of the individual's (*pudgala*) capacity for knowledge, [manifests itself].
Because it displays the collection of sense objects, this Vidyā is the most excellent instrument for the self, who is like a beast, on the path of saṃsāra.
The commentary clarifies that the very nature of the *vṛtti* (mental modification) is to serve as the cause for the manifestation of the object—this is what is meant by "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*).

Now, it might be argued that through the removal of impurity (*mala*) by means of the *kalā*, the capacity for knowledge (*jñatva*) has also been demonstrated. True; however, even though its true nature is manifest [in that regard],...

Without that instrument, it is incapable of grasping an object; therefore, this *vidyā*, by its own operation, removes the obscuration—which is characterized by the incapacity of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) to grasp objects—and manifests the object. [Objection: But there are instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*) for the grasping of objects. [Reply: True. Just as...

The cognition of a jar and the like is not possible without the eyes and other sense organs; likewise, the apprehension of objects such as pleasure is dependent upon an instrument (*karaṇa*). For this very reason, this [internal organ] is the supreme internal instrument (*antaraṅga-karaṇa*) of the self, because those [other senses] are external instruments (*bahiraṅga*).
This is what is meant: even though the result here is accomplished by multiple instruments, it is like the expression "he goes by horse, on the road, with a lamp," and so forth.
Thus, this indeed is the supreme instrument. || 46 ||
When the intellect (buddhi) is of the nature of objects of experience such as pleasure and so forth, then it becomes the instrument (karaṇa);
likewise, when it is pure knowledge (vidyā), it would be the instrument, whereas in the apprehension of objects, it is the intellect (buddhi).

In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the objection—"Is it not the case that cognition (*buddhi*) is the determination of objects such as sound? Therefore, since the presentation of objects is accomplished by that [cognition] alone, for what purpose is the postulation of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*)?"—the author says: "Cognition... [and so forth].

When the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, undergoes transformation into the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and thus becomes an object of experience for the experiencing self (*ātman*), then this [intellect] would be the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, it might be argued that in the apprehension of objects, the intellect alone will be the instrument, such that the person (*puruṣa*) perceives the object as determined by the intellect. That is incorrect, because of the [nature of the] person...

Because it consists of the activity of citing [objects] and because its activity is contrary [to that of the Self], it follows that the Puruṣa experiences what has been determined by the intellect (buddhi) through impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā). This is logical because impure knowledge is distinct from the Puruṣa, is an effect of Māyā, and is subject to transformation and other such changes. Furthermore, the intellect is not self-luminous, because it is an effect and possesses qualities (saguṇatva).

By the argument "like a jar and so forth," it is established that cognition is illuminated by something distinct from itself; for in that case, cognition is an object of illumination because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), and it is insentient because it is an effect, like a jar and so forth. Nor can cognition be grasped by another cognition, because such a second cognition does not exist. Nor is there its apprehension through another mental modification (*vṛtti*), because two modifications cannot occur simultaneously in a single cognition. Furthermore, impure [cognition] is not pure knowledge (*vidyā*).
"Because it causes one to experience. When that which causes the experience of the impure is supreme, it is established as the principle (tattva) called Impure Knowledge (aśuddhavidyā).
As it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "The enjoyments that have arrived through [karmic] realization, whose objects are sequentially arrayed..."
"One who enjoys worldly pleasures declares, by means of the knowledge seated within the self:

'When the manifestation is intent upon discerning the categories belonging to primordial matter (pradhāna), then let it be thoroughly examined by means of the knowledge residing in the self. Thus [it is said].
(Avadhūta Gītā 10.13–14,
18–19) It is called *aśuddhavidyā* because it causes one to experience the impure principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), or because it is both impure and a form of knowledge (*vidyā*),

or because it is the knowledge belonging to the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) which is rendered impure by impurity (*mala*) and other factors. Its establishment [is known] through pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
According to the Śaiva Siddhānta, Śuddhavidyā is the supreme power (paramaśakti) which is non-different from Śiva and is self-luminous;
this Vidyā bestows impure objects upon all sentient beings.
There is another knowledge, skilled in the true nature of Śiva, which has the pure as its domain.
Because it has been stated thus: "Its color is like that of the indragopa insect. As it is said:
"The Vidyātattva is supreme, yet impure due to passion, and it deludes bound souls (*paśu*). (This statement is understood to be from the *Candrajñāna*).
"Resembling a red insect (idragopaka) in some places, and possessing the luster of gold elsewhere.

The pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) for this [mantra] is as follows: the letter *ja* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). "To her who has the form of light" (*jyotīrūpāyai*) and so forth constitute two words.

*Vāṃ* and "to the three eyes" (*netratrayāya*) are the two mantras consisting of five syllables each. The category (*tattva*) is that called Impure Knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*). Caṇḍa and Krodha [are the deities].
In Bhuvana is the *kalā* Pratiṣṭhā. || 10 ||

The commentary demonstrates that very point: "The intellect (buddhi)," etc. The intellect determines the object presented by the sense organs under the direction of the mind; it is that determined object which [the ego-sense conceives as its own].
The person (*puruṣa*) perceives. As they say—(see *Mañjuṣā-pāda-vṛtti*, p.

314, note 21, cited on page 35 of the *Syādvādaratnākara*): "The person cognizes the object determined by the intellect" (*buddhi*). And in that act of perception, the intellect is not capable of making itself known as the instrument (*karaṇa*) while the self has already become the object of perception (*grāhya*). Therefore, in the perception of that [intellect], there is knowledge (*vidyā*).

"Karaṇa" refers to the accomplishment of knowledge (*vidyā-siddhi*). As it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "Even if [the self] were great and of the nature of light like the sun, nevertheless, because it is an object [of action]... (verse 14), and so forth. || 47 ||

Attachment (rāga), whose nature is clinging, is common to all and is the cause of human activity even without the destruction of sense objects; it is distinct from the attributes of the intellect (buddhi). 48.

The *Tātparyadīpikā* now defines the principle of attachment (*rāgatattva*)—beginning with the word "attachment. Attachment, which consists of intense longing, is the general cause for the activity of the person toward an object, even in the absence of that specific object. Some [teachers]...

They maintain that passion (*rāga*) is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*). He refutes this by stating: "It is distinct from the properties of the intellect. Passion is a property of the intellect that serves as the cause for the activity of the *puruṣa* by means of presenting objects. Its distinction from the properties of the intellect is established because it cannot serve as a cause for the activity of the *puruṣa* without the manifestation of its object. This is especially true for one seeking liberation who is free from craving for sense-objects.

In establishing that [agency], activity is observed even without the manifestation of an object; therefore, the *rāga-tattva* (the principle of attachment), which is the cause of such activity, must be admitted. As it is said in the *Mataṅgapārameśvara*:
"Now, for this individual soul (*aṇu*) who has been projected forth with speed, pierced by *kalā*..."
[This occurs] for one who has entered [the path] through longing and whose consciousness has been opened by knowledge...
by which he is quickly colored, becoming an enjoyer of pleasures and intent upon enjoyment...
there is another passion, supreme and subtle, which is distinct from this [passion] consisting of intoxication.
"By which [means] there arises in men an inclination toward the supreme good (naiḥśreyasa);
and it is observed that among dispassionate men there is a longing for the search of a teacher and for the attainment of Śiva with reverence," and so forth.
And in the *Kiraṇa*:

"The individual soul (*paśu*) is bound because its conscious nature is colored by passion and it is conjoined with the three qualities (*guṇas*), due to its connection with the host of instruments such as limited knowledge (*vidyā*). (Vi. 1.17) and so forth.

Therefore, the existence of the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*) is established. Its color is like saffron. As it has been said: "Outside of that [is] the principle of passion, resembling the interior of saffron" (this statement would belong to the *Candrajñāna*).

The pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) for this [mantra] is as follows: the syllable *jhakāra* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). "O Supreme Self" (*paramātman*) and so forth constitute two words (*pada*).

"Śiṃ" and "to the armor" (*kavacāya*) are two mantras of five syllables each (*pañcārṇa*). The principle (*tattva*) is that called Passion (*rāga*). The worlds (*bhuvana*) are the five beginning with Pracaṇḍa. The energy (*kalā*) is Nivṛtti. || 11 ||
The commentary states the establishment of the principle of *rāga* (attachment):
"Rāga" means that whose nature is attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) or longing (*abhilāṣa*) as its effect; it is *rāga* by virtue of its effect, which consists in longing.

The meaning is that this is the establishment of the reality of passion (*rāga-tattva*). Now, one might object: let the excellence of the object itself be the cause of a person’s desire, or rather, let it be a quality of the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by a lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*); what is the need for another [cause]? To this he says: "the cutting off of objects.
If the mere delimitation by an object were the sole cause of desire, it would follow that there could be no one free from passion (*vītarāga*), since even they [would still possess objects].
Because the delimitation of objects is possible, passion (*rāga*) is established here as the cause for the activity of the *puruṣa* even in its absence [as a distinct entity].

Furthermore, since non-detachment (*avairāgya*) is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*) and exists in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it cannot directly benefit the *puruṣa*; otherwise, due to the intellect's connection with infinite latent impressions, the *puruṣa* would [be affected].

It has been stated by us in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* that this would result in the calamity of simultaneous and contradictory infinite cognitions; therefore, this should be understood from that very source. For this reason as well, this passion (*rāga*) is distinct [from ordinary desire] and is indeed the cause of the longing for all objects.

When the bound soul (paśu), conditioned by these principles (tattvas), is brought to the state of being an enjoyer, it then attains the designation "puruṣa" and its reckoning among the principles. (49)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* now states the essential nature of the principle of the Puruṣa: "By the principles," etc.
When this Lord, through connection with these five principles known as Time (*kāla*), Necessity (*niyati*), Limited Agency (*kalā*), Ignorance (*avidyā*), and Attachment (*rāga*), [becomes bound]...

Having attained the state of a bound soul (*paśubhāva*), he reaches the condition of being an enjoyer; then, because he dwells within the "city" (*puri*) composed of the twenty-four principles beginning with the Manifest (*vyakta*), he receives the designation *puruṣa* (Person), and is also counted among the principles (*tattva*) excluding the principle of Śiva. His color is naturally pure, yet it appears as manifold colors due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Its pervasion across the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is as follows: the letter *ña* is its phoneme (*varṇa*).
The two words beginning with "vyomin" [are the first two]. "Maṃ" and "śikhāyai" are two five-syllabled mantras. The principle (tattva) is called Puruṣa.
The six worlds are Vāma and the others. The kalā is Śāntyatītā. 12.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Determination of the Pure and the Impure, in the Tattvaprakāśatātparyadīpikā.
Commentary: Now, since the Puruṣa is non-inert (ajaḍa), unlike Śiva, it is not possible to count him as a "principle" (tattva) among the principles which are inert in nature.

Furthermore, because he is all-pervasive throughout the principles, his mention in the scriptures immediately after the principle of Attachment (rāga-tattva) is also inappropriate; therefore, he says: "by the principles" (tattvaiḥ).

The individual soul (*aṇu*), augmented by the five principles beginning with *kalā*, attains the designation of the *puruṣatattva* by virtue of being the enjoyer. However, in the ultimate sense, neither its status as a principle nor its status as the support of the worlds exists for it. For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures that the location of its worlds resides within the *rāgatattva* alone. And regarding that [soul], in the context of initiation (*dīkṣā*), immediately after the purification of the *prakṛtitattva*, right here—
In some cases, there is no fault in the recitation being for the purpose of purifying the impurity of masculinity. 49.
For it is indeed for the sake of the Spirit's experience that Nature (Kalā) brings forth the Unmanifest;
because its qualities are unmanifest, that Unmanifest is indefinable. 50.
The Tātparyadīpikā: Now begins the fourth chapter.
Next, in order to define the nature of the unmanifest (avyakta), he says: "Of the Puruṣa... and so forth.

For the sake of the Puruṣa’s experience of pleasure and so forth, the Unmanifest (avyakta) arises from the principle of Māyā. He states the ground for applying the term "Unmanifest" to this: because it possesses the qualities (guṇas) of sattva and the others in an unmanifest state, this principle is called "unmanifest. [This Sāṃkhya Sūtra is explained in the Sāṃkhyapravacana-bhāṣya (1.61) as follows: "Because of the non-manifestation of sattva, rajas, and tamas..."

[This] should be observed: the teachers of Sāṃkhya state that *prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium; therefore, its nature as having unmanifest qualities (*anabhivyakta-guṇatva*) is possible. This is because the elements (*bhūta*), subtle elements (*tanmātra*), sense organs (*indriya*), mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—which are the effects of the Unmanifest—are composed of the three qualities (*triguṇātmaka*), since they serve as the causes of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Thus, it is established that their cause, the Unmanifest, is also composed of the three qualities.
Its essential nature is beyond logical reasoning.
As it has been said—(this statement may belong to the *Candrajñāna*): "But outside of that, there is another supreme reality, unmanifest, beyond reasoning, unknowable, and abiding like nirvāṇa. Thus.
The pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) for this [mantra] is as follows: the letter *ṭa* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). "O formless one" (*arūpin*) and so forth are two words (*pada*).

"Naṃ" and "to the head" (*śirase*) are two mantras of five syllables each (*pañcārṇa*). The category (*tattva*) is called *guṇaprakṛti*. The worlds (*bhuvana*) are the eight beginning with *kṛta* and *akṛta*.
The digit (*kalā*) is *śānti*. (1)

The commentary [continues]: Thus, for the person who has attained the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), there are the "objects of enjoyment" (*bhoga*)—namely, the principles (*tattva*) such as the *guṇas* and so forth—by means of which things are enjoyed for the sake of experience. For the sake of establishing those [objects], there is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), acting as their cause. Therefore...

Immediately after the state of passion (*rāga*) mentioned previously, *kalā* arises. Now, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the *guṇas* alone are the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the cause of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest; however, this is incorrect, as the author states with the words "unmanifest" (*anabhivyakta*). Since the *guṇas*, being insentient and manifold, must be preceded by a cause, it is for this very reason—namely, because its effect consists of the unmanifested *guṇas*—that it is called "unmanifest."

If this were so, one might argue that this [consciousness] must be eternal, just like the *prakṛti* accepted by the Sāṃkhyas; but that is not correct. For *prakṛti*, being distinct for each individual and being insentient, its multiplicity establishes its status as an effect. || 50 ||
From the Unmanifest (avyakta) arises the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva), which consists here of manifestation, activity, and restriction;
namely, sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as pleasure, pain, and delusion.
The *Tātparyadīpikā* defines the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*) as follows: "From the unmanifest" (*avyaktāt*).
From the unmanifest, whose nature is the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇasāmya*), the principle of the qualities arises, characterized by disequilibrium (*vaiṣamya*).

That [guṇa-reality] consists of the forms of manifestation, activity, and restriction, and has them as its functions (*vṛtti*). Manifestation (*prakhyā*) is luminosity, which is knowledge; it is the function of the quality *sattva*, because of its clarity. Activity (*vyāpāra*) is motion, which is the function of *rajas*, because of its mobility. Restriction (*niyama*) is constraint, which is the function of *tamas*, because of its heaviness. Thus, the reality of the qualities (*guṇatattva*), named *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, has pleasure, pain, and delusion as its essential nature. As it has been said:
By the Sāṃkhyas: "Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping. Their functioning occurs for a purpose, like a lamp. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 13)
The color of this principle of *guṇa* consists of white, red, and black. As it has been said:
"Outside of that (this verse would belong to the *Candrajñāna*), there shall be another [enclosure] known as the *guṇāvaraṇa*, resembling a great sapphire gem and pure crystal. (2)
And from that, the commentary says: "From the unmanifest.
This is established by the three effects known as illumination, activity, and restraint. Furthermore, those qualities are sattva and the others.

Because they produce pleasure and so forth, they are called "pleasure, pain," and so on, respectively. The detailed proof for all these principles (*tattvas*) is to be seen in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other works (specifically in the *Vidyāpāda* of the *Mātaṅgapārameśvara*, chapters 3–23, where the expansion of the *tattvas* is found). It has not been written here for fear of prolixity. 51.
In this world, the intellect (dhī), which consists of the determination of objects, arises from the three qualities (guṇas);
that too is said to be of three kinds according to the qualities and in accordance with one's karma.
Now, the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) is defined in the *Tātparyadīpikā*: "It comes into being," and so forth.
From the triad of the qualities (*guṇa*)—namely, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—the intellect (*buddhi*) arises. Of that...

He states the definition: "and having the form of determination regarding objects. That whose nature (rūpa) or function (vṛtti) is determination (adhyavasāya)—that is, certainty—regarding objects such as sound and so forth, is described as such. By the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that the intellect possesses eightfold functions in the form of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, power, vice, ignorance, passion, and lack of power. As it has been said:
"Ascertainment is intellect; virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—this is its sāttvika form; the tāmasa is the opposite of this. (Sāṅkhyakārikā 23).
Among these, that which is the cause of worldly prosperity and the supreme good is virtue (*dharma*). In that regard:
Dharma produced by the performance of sacrifices and other rites preceded by desire is the cause of *abhyudaya*, that is, happiness such as heaven and the like.
Dharma produced by the performance of sacrifices and the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) devoid of such desire is the cause of *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good).
We shall explain the definition of yoga later on. Knowledge is right knowledge; it is of two kinds: valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and...

And memory (*smṛti*). Memory is the non-loss of an experienced object. For example, the cognition "This is my mother," "This is my father," or "That is my house" arises solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by previous experience. Correct experience is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it has been said:
"Experience is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); that which is other than it is recollection (*smṛti*).
Knowledge arising solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience is called recollection.
By the word "correct" (*samyak*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), error (*viparyaya*), and so forth are excluded here. By the word "experience" (*anubhava*), recollection is [excluded].

It is excluded. That [means of knowledge] is of two kinds: that which reveals reality (*tattvāvedaka*) and that which does not reveal reality (*atattvāvedaka*). Among these, the knowledge consisting of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self is that which reveals reality. As it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"In this insentient transformation, beginning with the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) and ending with the specific elements (*viśeṣa*),"
"Knowledge is said to be the consciousness that distinguishes between the sentient and the insentient.
Thus, valid knowledge whose object is the non-self (*anātman*) does not reveal reality (*atattvāvedaka*). As it has been said:
"In this regard, two kinds of knowledge (*vidyā*) are to be known: the higher (*parā*) and likewise the lower (*aparā*)."
"For the lower knowledge consists of ritual action and so forth, while the higher knowledge is contained within the Upaniṣads.
Regarding this, the Cārvākas maintain that it is exclusively perception (*pratyakṣa*). The Ārhats (Jainas) hold that it is twofold, consisting of the manifest and the non-manifest.
The elder Buddhists and the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that there are two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), consisting of perception and inference (*anumāna*).
In this regard, the Buddhists postulate a twofold division because they consider scripture (*āgama*) to be invalid.

Others assert a twofold division because they maintain that verbal testimony (*śabda*) and the rest are included within inference (*anumāna*). The followers of Sāṃkhya, the Neo-Vaiśeṣikas, and the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa* hold that this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) includes verbal testimony (*śābda*). The older Naiyāyikas, including comparison (*upamāna*), maintain that there are three.

The teacher Prabhākara states that those four [means of knowledge] together with presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) constitute five; the venerable Bhaṭṭa and his followers state that those five together with non-existence (*abhāva*) constitute six. The historians and purāṇic scholars state that those six, together with tradition (*aitihya*), probability (*sambhava*), and negative concomitance (*virodha*), constitute nine. As it has been said:

The Cārvāka accepts perception alone; the Sugata (Buddhist) and Kaṇabhuj (Vaiśeṣika) accept that [perception] along with inference; the Pāramarṣa (Mīmāṃsaka) accepts those two along with verbal testimony;
Akṣapāda (Nyāya) accepts those three together with comparison;
Prabhākara declares them all together with presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); and the Bhāṭṭa accepts those five along with non-existence (*abhāva*).
"In the case of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is both clarity and lack of clarity at the time of the Lord of Days.

Based on the statement, "The teaching of Śiva, like the Sāṃkhya, relies upon the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*)," for us [the Śaivas], that [means of valid cognition] is indeed threefold: perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*). Others, however, say:

That [knowledge] is of three kinds: sensory (aindriyaka), inferential (laiṅgika), and verbal (śābda).
