Perception (pratyakṣa) is the cognition that arises from the contact of an object with a sense-organ regarding an object that is currently in contact. When it is stated that "perception is cognition," there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of conceptual construction (vikalpa); to exclude that, the word "object" (artha) is used. When it is stated that "cognition is [the perception] of an object," there is a deviation in the case of error (viparyaya); to exclude that, the word "in contact" (saṃprayukta) is used.

The phrase "from the contact of the object and the sense organ" (*arthendriya-saṃprayogāt*) is for the purpose of excluding inference and other means of knowledge. That [perception] is of two kinds: non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Among these, non-conceptual perception is a perceptual cognition devoid of the mention of name and genus, such as the consciousness produced by the initial contact with the sense organ, which manifests the mere thing-in-itself. As it has been said:
For there exists a primary non-conceptualizing cognition of mere observation,
which arises from the pure object itself and resembles the cognition of infants, the mute, and others.

(Ślokavārttika, Pratyakṣa 112). Conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is perceptual knowledge that reflects the connection with names and so forth. For example: "Devadatta" is a conceptualization of a name; "the staff-bearer," "the earring-wearer," and so forth, are conceptualizations of substances (*dravya*); "white," "black," "large," and so forth, are [conceptualizations of qualities].

Conceptualizations of qualities; conceptualizations of actions, such as going, coming, falling, and so forth; and conceptualizations of genus, such as human, animal, jar, and so forth—thus conceptual cognition is fivefold. Furthermore, that [perception] is of two kinds:
the perception of yogis and the perception of non-yogis. It is direct knowledge whose object is things remote in space, time, or nature.
Yogic perception; its opposite is non-yogic perception. For example: spatially remote objects such as Mount Meru and the like;

temporally remote objects such as Rāvaṇa and the like; and by nature remote objects such as the primordial cause, the sense faculties, and so forth. That direct cognition which yogis possess regarding these is yogic perception. An example of the other [non-yogic perception] has already been stated.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) arising from the mark (*liṅga*). The mark is that which is related to the probandum (*sādhya*) without any limiting condition (*upādhi*).
It is of three kinds: *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*. Inference by means of a cause for the sake of [knowing] an effect is *pūrvavat*;
for example, the cognition that "there will be rain" based on the rising of specific clouds. As it has been stated by those who know the Nyāya:
The rising of clouds, accompanied by lightning and producing a tumultuous roar in the sky,
has never been observed to fail in its result of rain.
These clouds, whose lofty forms are turned tawny by contact with streaks of lightning flashing across their skins, never fail to bring rain; such is the nature of these water-bearers.
Likewise:
"The earth is proclaimed as 'the rainy season' by the mountains, thick with clouds, which display the grandeur of fierce *tāṇḍava* dances commenced by circles of peacocks. Thus.

Inference based on an effect [to deduce] a cause is "the remainder" (*śeṣavat*). For example: inferring rain upstream from the swelling of a river. That which is other than this is "inference from common observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). For example: [inferring] the cognition of a visible object from its taste. Others hold that "inference like the previously seen" (*pūrvavat*) has as its object a generality whose specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been perceived. For example:

The cognition that arises regarding fire—which is perceptible—upon seeing a mark such as smoke, while the fire itself is not currently being perceived, is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general correlation). It has as its object a generality whose specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) has not been perceived. For example: "The apprehension of color and so forth is produced by an instrument, because it is an action, like the action of cutting"—this is an inference establishing the existence of the sense organs. [This is so] because the nature of being a sense organ is the object of this inference.

Since its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) was not previously established, it does not possess the nature of being "prior" (*pūrvavat*). Because these two [types of inference] proceed by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), they are *vīta*. That which proceeds by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and functions as a negation is *avīta*;
that itself is the *śeṣavat* inference. It is called *śeṣa* because it remains (*śiṣyate*); and since that [remainder] exists as the object of this inference, it is called *śeṣavat*.
As it has been said: "When that which is applicable [to all] is negated, because it does not apply elsewhere, there is a cognition directed toward what remains" (Nyāya-bhāṣya 1.1.5).

This is inference based on remainder (*śeṣavat*). For example: "Every effect is produced by an omniscient being, because it is occasional; for whatever is not produced by an omniscient being is not occasional, such as a magical illusion (*māyā*) and the like; and this [world] is not..."

Likewise, this [cognition] is not occasional; therefore, it is not even a creation of an omniscient being. Furthermore, that [cognition] is of two kinds: for one's own sake and for the sake of others. As it has been said:
"That which does not depend on the instruction of another is for one's own sake and leads to the inference of [the object] for oneself."
"That which depends upon the instruction of another is called for the sake of others.
Here, "instruction by another" refers to a five-membered syllogism.
Logicians maintain that the five members are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that there are three [members of a syllogism], namely: the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*udāharaṇa*). The Buddhists hold that there are two, namely: the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*).
Among these, the statement of the subject (*pakṣa*) with the desire to communicate [the probandum] is the proposition (*pratijñā*), such as "the mountain possesses fire.
The statement of the mark (*liṅga*) which makes known its status as a means of proof is the reason (*hetu*), such as "because it possesses smoke. That [reason] is of three kinds:

[The three types of inference are] the positive-negative (*anvayavyatirekī*), the purely positive (*kevalānvayī*), and the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekī*). Among these, the positive-negative [inference] possesses five characteristics (*rūpa*). These characteristics are: presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), existence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ*), having a non-sublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatvam*), and having no counter-balancing argument (*asatpratipakṣatvam*).

In this context, the subject (*pakṣa*) is the locus qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). The reason’s (*hetu*) presence in the subject consists in its being pervasively present therein.

The subject (*dharmin*) which possesses the property common to the probandum (*sādhya*) is the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). The presence of the reason (*hetu*) in all or part of that [similar instance] is its existence in the similar instance (*sapakṣe sattvam*). The subject which possesses a property from which the probandum is excluded is the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). The non-occurrence of the reason in that [dissimilar instance] is its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ*). The occurrence of the reason in the object of the thesis (*pratijñātārtha*) without contradicting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the state of having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatvam*).

The three-fold character for the establishment of one's own position and the refutation of the opponent's position consists in having no counter-argument. For example: "The earth and so forth are preceded by an intelligent agent, because they are effects, like a jar," and so on. A purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason is that which exists in the subject and the similar instances (sapakṣa) but has no dissimilar instances (vipakṣa). For example:
"The subject of dispute, such as the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth, is perceptible to someone, because it is an object of cognition (prameya), like the palm of the hand."

A *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative) reason is that which resides in the subject (*pakṣavṛtti*), lacks a similar instance (*avidyamānasapakṣa*), and is excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttaḥ*).

An example of this is *avīta* inference. For instance: "The disputed [principles], such as *kalā* and the rest, do not differ from *māyā*, because they are effects of *māyā*; for whatever differs [from *māyā*] is not an effect of *māyā*, like Puruṣa and Śiva; but these are not so."

The effects of *māyā* are *kalā* and the rest; therefore, they do not differ from *māyā*. Thus, by stating the definition of a valid reason (*hetu*), fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are excluded. These consist of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), and the counter-balanced (*prakaraṇasama*). They arise because they lack the essential characteristics such as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). Among these, the unestablished is that which does not reside in the subject with certainty. For example: "Sound..."

"Permanent, because it is visible," and so forth. A contradictory (*viruddha*) reason is one that exists only in the subject (*pakṣa*) and the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). For example: "Sound is a specific quality of space, because it is knowable"—this lacks a similar instance (*sapakṣa*). "Earth and so forth, up to time, are permanent, because they are effects"—this possesses a similar instance. An inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason is one that occurs in all three positions [subject, similar instance, and counter-example]. For example: "Sound is permanent..."

"Because it is an object of cognition" (*prameyatvāt*) is a reason that does not prove the probandum (*sādhyāsādhaka*). That which exists only in the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is the "unascertained" (*anadhyavasita*). For example: "The earth is eternal because it possesses odor" is one where a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) exists; "Everything is momentary because it exists" is one where a similar instance does not exist. A reason that applies to a thesis-meaning (*pratijñātārtha*) that is sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). [Example: "Pure..."

"A human skull is [pure] because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell," is contrary to scripture (*āgama*). "An owl sees form during the day because it possesses eyes" is contrary to inference (*anumāna*), because the absence of activity—which is invariably concomitant with the perception of form—allows for the inference of the absence of visual perception. "Fire is not hot because it is produced by friction, like butter" is contrary to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

A reason that is equally capable of establishing one's own position or the opponent's position is the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) reason. For example: "Sound is impermanent, because it is one of the two—either the subject or the similar instance—just like a jar," versus "Sound is permanent, because it is one of the two—either the subject or the similar instance—just like an illusion. In both cases, the three required characteristics (*trairūpya*) of a valid reason are present. A "citation" (*udāharaṇa*) is the statement of a correct example.

The locus for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For instance: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just as a kitchen" is an example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), because it is stated by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). On the other hand, "That which does not possess fire does not possess smoke either, just as water" is an example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), because it is stated by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Because this is a statement of examples, various fallacious examples (*udāharaṇābhāsa*) are excluded. For instance: "The mind is eternal because it is corporeal; whatever is corporeal is eternal, like a jar"—this is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). "Like the self"—this is deficient in the probans (*sādhanavikala*). "Like karma"—this is deficient in both. "Like a sky-flower"—this is devoid of a locus (*āśrayahīna*). That which is eternal is not...

"Like the Self" is an example where the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is not excluded; "like a jar" is an example where the probans (*sādhana*) is not excluded; and "like Māyā" is an example where neither is excluded. Māyā possesses form (*mūrtatva*) because it is inferior to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). Pervasion (*vyāpti*), however, is stated precisely as being pervaded by its own effects. "Like a sky-flower" is an example that lacks a locus (*āśrayahīna*).

"He will exercise great sovereignty because he is born of the Lunar dynasty, like a future prince"—this is an example of a reason with a doubtful substratum (*sandigdhāśraya*), and so forth. The application (*upanaya*) is the statement that establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of the comparison with the example, for a reason whose pervasion is well-known in the example. "And this [subject] is likewise possessed of smoke" is an application based on similarity (*sādharmyopanaya*). And it is not "not likewise."

"This mountain possesses smoke" is the application by dissimilarity (*vaidharmyopanaya*). Following the application, the statement of the proposition accompanied by its reason is the conclusion (*nigamana*): "Therefore, it possesses fire indeed. This was stated by the Blessed Vedavyāsa: "Of that which is endowed with five members... (*Mahābhārata*, Bhāṇḍārkar edition, Sabhāparvan).
In the first appendix (*pariśiṣṭa*), this statement is seen: "One who knows the merits and defects of speech,
and who speaks with ever-increasing eloquence even when Bṛhaspati himself is speaking" (Mahābhārata 2.1.7–8).

Others, however, maintain that a reason which possesses the three forms—namely, presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), and exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*)—is a non-concomitant negative-only (*anvayavyatirekin*). Furthermore, the definitions of the subject and so forth are as follows: the subject (*pakṣa*) is that in which the probandum (*sādhya*) is doubtful; doubt arises from conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti*). A similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is that in which the probandum is ascertained. A dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is that in which the absence of the probandum is ascertained. Therefore, in the case of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) as a proof for the non-heat of fire:

Because it lacks the form of exclusion from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) and thus fails to be a prover, sublation of the object (*bādhitaviṣayatva*) is included within [the category of] non-exclusion from the heterologue.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for a single [reason] to possess the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) simultaneously for the establishment of both one's own and the opponent's position, there is an absence of the form of being "unopposed" (*asatpratipakṣatva*);
this is because it is impossible for a single entity to be either the subject (*pakṣa*) or the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). As it has been said:
That which is related to the object of inference, which is well-known to exist in what possesses that [property],
and which is absolutely absent when that is absent— that alone is a valid mark (liṅga) that brings about inference.
Kāśyapa stated that whatever is contrary to this— whether by one or two [of these criteria]— is a non-reason (*aliṅga*), being respectively contradictory, unestablished, or doubtful.

Thus, they maintain that the purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) [reason] possesses two forms, because it lacks the form of exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*); and the purely negative (*vyatirekin*) likewise [possesses two forms], because it lacks the form of presence in the similar example (*sapakṣa*) due to the absence of a similar example. Correct knowledge produced by words is *āgama*. It is of two kinds: that produced by human sentences and that produced by non-human (Vedic) sentences. Among these:
The statements of the Tantras, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Manu, and so forth are of human origin; the statements of the Vedas, however, are not of human origin.

If it is argued that the non-human origin of the Vedic statements is established by the inference: "Vedic statements are of human origin because they are sentences, like the sentences of the Mahābhārata and similar works," this is not so, because of [the Vedic mantra]: "To him, for the sake of the shining one, with speech that is manifold and eternal" (Ṛgveda 8.75.6).

Thus, because the eternity of the Veda is established by scripture (*āgama*), this [argument] lacks validity due to being *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (vitiated by the lapse of time). For it is said: "When the dissolution has arrived and all moving and stationary beings have perished, O Goddess, I alone remain; there is no second anywhere."
In that five-syllabled mantra, the Vedas and the Śāstras are established;
they have not met with destruction at all, for they are protected by my power.

Thus, [the eternity of the Veda is established] because it would otherwise contradict the *Laiṅgāgama*. Nor should it be argued that its eternity is untenable because one perceives the production and destruction of the Veda at every utterance; for since utterance is merely a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*), neither of those two [production or destruction] actually occurs. And this [recognition of identity] is like saying, "This is that very same Veda," or "This is that very same pillar."
It is understood from the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*) that the Veda exists now just as it did previously;

and it should not be argued that because there is an absence of persons capable of preserving the Veda during the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), the Veda would perish, and thus, being composed by the Supreme Lord at the beginning of a new creation, it would be non-eternal.

Even in the absence of the twice-born who uphold the Vedas, the Supreme Lord, who is the upholder of the Vedas, exists; for instance, the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain the non-eternality of the Vedas admit that the Veda produced at the beginning of creation persists until the dissolution of the universe (*pralaya*). Therefore, there is no dispute regarding that point. However, as for the time of dissolution (*pralaya*):
The existence [of the creator] is established. For instance: "The time of dissolution is accompanied by persons who know the Vedas, because it is a period of time, like any other period of time.
Nor should it be argued that there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because the existence of the earth, mountains, and so forth could also be inferred by that same logic;
for the time devoid of the earth, mountains, and so forth is what constitutes dissolution, and to prove that such a time possesses those [beings] would be like saying, "My mother is barren."

Because it would entail a contradiction with one's own thesis; and because even upon the destruction of all Vedic persons existing within a single cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), the eternity of the Veda is maintained due to the continued existence of infinite Vedic persons residing in other cosmic eggs. Furthermore, other cosmic eggs also possess this same Veda, because they are cosmic eggs, just like the one currently accepted [by us]; thus, there is a unity of the Veda everywhere.

In the view that the Vedas are non-eternal, there would result the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) due to the postulation of the generation and destruction of infinite Vedas spread across infinite branches, as well as the postulation of their causes. However, if they are eternal, there is no such defect, because there is the parsimony (*lāghava*) of merely postulating the eternity of the already established Veda. Furthermore, the Vedas cannot be of human origin because an author of the Vedas is impossible. To explain: it is not the Lord (*īśvara*).

The Veda has an author, because there is no reason to abandon the notion of a prior Veda. Nor should it be argued that the Veda did not exist in a previous *kalpa*, for the existence of the Veda in a previous *kalpa* is established by inference. For instance: every previous *kalpa* was endowed with the Veda and its auxiliary sciences, because it is a *kalpa*, just like the present *kalpa*. It is not as if [the present *kalpa*] were alone in this regard.
It should not be argued that there is an over-extension of the argument because one can infer the existence of beings in other kalpas based on the existence of beings today;
for what is intended is the existence of beings that is not contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As it was said by the Blessed Manu:
"Just as the various signs of the seasons appear in their succession during the seasons..."
"Those very same [words] are seen likewise among Brahmā, Hara, and others.

Therefore, it is established that the collection of the Vedas is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). The Vedas are authoritative (*pramāṇa*), because they are words not produced by an unreliable person (*anāpta*), like that which is commonly accepted. The study of the Vedas under dispute is preceded by the study of those same Vedas, because it is the study of the Vedas.
"Like the study of the Vedas at the present time.

This is the comparison (*upamā*). If the sentence "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow," or the cognition produced by it, were the means of knowledge (*upamāna*), then it would be nothing other than scripture (*āgama*), not a separate means of knowledge. As for this word "gavaya" [applied] to that which is similar to a cow...
The cognition regarding the relationship between a name and the named object, namely that "this is the denoter," is indeed inference. For instance:

this word *gavaya* is the denoter of this object which resembles a cow, because it is employed by elders (*vṛddha*) in that regard; for whatever word is employed by elders in reference to a certain thing, that word is its denoter provided there is no other mode of application (such as indication), just as the word *go* is employed in reference to cowness.

The word is the designator; furthermore, since this word "gavaya" is employed for that which resembles a cow, the cognition that it is its designator does not differ from inference. And as for the cognition of similarity to a cow regarding a gavaya perceived through the senses, because it is born from the contact of the sense organ, it is included within perception. In the same way, [the cognition] regarding a cow being remembered is likewise nothing but perception.

The cognition of similarity to a gavaya [is not non-perceptual], because there is no contradiction in its being accessible through perception due to its unity. To explain: the conjunction of many common features of parts, residing in one species while existing in another species, is called "similarity. Since that [similarity] is a single entity, there is no contradiction in its being perceived in the gavaya and subsequently being perceived in the cow immediately after the recollection of the cow.

Since the similarity of a gavaya to a cow is either perceived non-conceptually as before or is being remembered, there is nothing whatsoever to be known through comparison (*upamāna*); thus, it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Likewise, [the existence] outside of the living Devadatta is [known] by seeing his absence from the house.

Presumption (*arthāpatti*), which consists of the postulation of something not known through other means of valid cognition, is also not a separate means of valid cognition, because it is in fact inference (*anumāna*). For that which exists but is absent in one place must exist elsewhere; likewise, that which exists but is non-pervasive and absent in one place must exist elsewhere. Thus, the apprehension of the invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*) is possible within its own very nature.

And thus, Devadatta is connected with the outside, because, while being existent, he is not found in the house, like a tree standing outside; therefore, the knowledge of his existence outside, produced by the mark (liṅga) of his absence from the house, is indeed inference (anumāna). Nor is there any contradiction between the two means of valid cognition—the astronomical science (jyotiḥśāstra) which makes known his mere existence, and perception (pratyakṣa) which makes known his absence from the house.

It must be stated that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arises from the resolution of a contradiction between two [statements] regarding a single locus; however, this is impossible because there is no contradiction between "existence" (unrestricted) and "non-existence in the house" (restricted), as they do not conflict. Indeed, a contradiction with "non-existence in the house" is not possible for "existence anywhere whatsoever," because their loci are different. Nor is the absence from the house certain.
The existence of the house is rejected because it is only occasional and doubtful, since non-existence is more powerful.

Furthermore, the absence of the house, by rejecting its occasional existence in that particular location, is neither able to reject mere existence nor to render it doubtful, because it remains indifferent to existence in general.

Since there is no contradiction between the existence of a mere entity and the non-existence [of another], the removal of that contradiction is not effected through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); therefore, it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, non-existence (*abhāva*) is not something other than a positive entity (*bhāva*), such that a means of valid cognition called "non-existence" would have to be resorted to for its establishment.
Indeed, there is no such thing as the "absence of a jar" other than a specific transformation of the ground at the moment of its isolation.

For all entities, except for the supreme Lord who is the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), undergo transformation at every moment; thus, this particular transformation is established by the senses. Alternatively, even if non-existence were distinct from another positive entity, nevertheless...
Since it is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), no further means of valid cognition need be accepted for its establishment. To illustrate:

because the cognition "there is no jar on this ground" conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the opening of the eyes, it is sensory in nature (*aindriyaka*). Likewise, the absence of jars and other objects in the house is [known] through their being located outside.
[The existence of others] is inferred on the basis of one's own body. Likewise, the non-existence of the people of Bhārata is understood through the scripture concerning Bhārata;

therefore, there is no separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence" (abhāva). As for "possibility" (sambhava), it is the understanding of a droṇa, an āḍhaka, or a prastha within a khārī; and that is inference (anumāna), because [the presence of] the state of being a khārī [implies the presence of its parts].
Because [the existence of] Droṇa and others is pervaded by that [scripture], he infers them from it.

Furthermore, that which has no specified speaker and consists of mere report, such as "The elders say thus" or "There dwells a yakṣa here in this banyan tree," is tradition (*aitihya*). This is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is characterized by doubt due to the lack of certainty regarding the words of a reliable person (*āpta*).
When there is certainty regarding a trustworthy speaker, however, it is simply scripture (*āgama*) and not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, gesture (*ceṣṭā*) is a form of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*); and since it brings about the experience of something imperceptible through the force of convention (*samaya*), it is simply scripture and not a separate means of valid cognition.

The same applies to contradiction (*virodha*). The cognition of the absence of fire in the middle of a lake is indeed an inference, because water and fire, being mutually contradictory, cannot coexist in one place and are thus pervaded by their mutual non-existence. Therefore, there are only three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As it has been said:
Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony—these three types of valid cognition are accepted because all objects of knowledge are established through these means of valid cognition.
For the establishment of the objects of knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition.
Perception is the ascertainment of each respective object; inference is declared to be threefold:
that preceded by the mark (liṅga) and the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), as well as authoritative revelation and the word of a reliable person.
Furthermore, the establishment of supersensuous things proceeds from inference based on what is perceived in a general way.
"Therefore, even that which is unestablished and beyond the senses is established through authoritative scripture" (Sāṅkhyakārikā 4–6).

Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the consciousness of mastery (*vaśīkārasaṃjñā*) in one who is free from thirst for objects pertaining to this world and the next; it is not merely the absence of attachment.
It arises from perceiving defects such as impermanence and comparability in objects pertaining to this world and the next.
Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consists in the power of non-obstruction; it is eightfold:
*aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *laghimā*, and likewise *garimā*;
Mastery, control, attainment, and indeed the power of irresistible will;

In that context, *aṇimā* is minuteness, being situated like an atom. *Mahimā* is greatness, becoming gross according to one's desire. *Laghimā* is lightness, by which one travels to the world of the sun by taking hold of the sun’s rays. *Garimā* is heaviness, remaining in a state such that one cannot be moved by others. *Īśitva* is lordship, the state of being a master over the primary elements and their derivatives.
The state of being the cause of manifestation and so forth; sovereignty (*vaśitva*) is the state of mastery, the power to bring everything under one's own will;

attainment (*prāpti*) is reaching [anything], by which one touches the moon with the tip of a finger; irresistible will (*prākāmya*) is the non-obstruction of desire, such that one sinks into and emerges from the earth as if it were water; others say it is "truthful resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatā*), whereby whatever his resolve becomes, exactly so does it come to pass.
"Beings come into existence"—such are the determinations of people like us, which correspond to the objects themselves; for yogins, however, the objects conform to their determinations.

This tetrad, in brief, is of the nature of *sattva*; it is a form produced from *sattva*. And the four that are of the nature of *tamas* are the opposites, designated as non-dharma, ignorance, non-detachment, and lack of mastery.

Those characterized by *tamas* are born from *tamas*. Unrighteousness (*adharma*) is the cause of the absence of prosperity and the absence of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the opposite of knowledge; that is to say, it is incorrect knowledge. It is threefold: error (*viparyaya*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and sleep (*nidrā*). Error is false knowledge established in the form of that [object], such as the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl and the like. It follows upon verbal cognition...

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is empty of a real object (*vastuśūnya*). For example, it is like the cognition whose object is the meaning [of a word] that arises immediately after hearing words such as "the horn of a hare.
Sleep (*nidrā*) is that modification of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*) which arises by relying on the intensity of *tamas*, which is the cause for the absence of waking and dreaming cognitions.
This was stated by the venerable Patañjali in the aphorism: "Sleep has the cognition of non-existence as its support" (*Yogasūtra* 1.10).

Lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*) is the attachment to objects seen or heard of; lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*) is the quality of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*) that opposes the manifestation of powers such as *aṇimā*. Others, however, state that knowledge which reveals the principle of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-tattva*) is [true] knowledge, while that which is other than it is ignorance (*ajñāna*).
This has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas:
Through righteousness there is ascent; through unrighteousness, descent occurs.
Through knowledge comes liberation, while from its opposite, bondage is held to arise.
"From dispassion comes dissolution into nature; from passion, characterized by attachment, comes worldly existence;
from envy comes lack of success; and from its opposite, the reverse [of that].
(Sāṅkhyakārikā 44–45)
By the phrase "having the form of the determination of objects," the existence of the intellect (*buddhi*) is established.

For instance, since the activity (*vṛtti*) consisting of the determination of objects and so forth is observed, one must admit the existence of the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), which is the substratum of that activity; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of activity. As it is said in the *Pārameśvara*:
Now, that expansion of the intellect which is inferred by its own nature as having previously arisen from the agitated *guṇas* toward the sphere of the elements;

"The auspicious intellect (*buddhi*), endowed with eight qualities, is described as the mother of all entities through its function of determination (*adhyavasāya*); it is analyzed in due order. And so forth.
(Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.2.1–2)

He states its division: "That too is threefold. That intellect (*buddhi*) is of three types. Why? To this he says: "According to the *guṇas*, in accordance with previous karma. This means that due to the distinction of the *guṇas* following the karma consisting of merit and demerit performed by the person (*puruṣa*) in a prior birth. As it has been said: "The intellect follows karma. For instance, through one kind of merit, it is *sāttvika*.

The intellect (*buddhi*) is *tāmasī* through demerit (*apuṇya*), and *rājasī* through mixed [merit and demerit]. Likewise, the intellect is threefold according to the distinction of the *guṇas* and in accordance with one's karma, by way of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. For instance: the *sāttvikī* intellect, impelled by gross karma, remains in the waking state; under the influence of subtle karma, the *rājasī* intellect enters the dream state.
The intellect (buddhi) enters the state of deep sleep by relying upon a preponderance of darkness (tamas), which is the cause for the cessation of the functions of waking and dreaming.

For the sake of the Self’s rest—though that Self is eternally of one nature, all-pervading, pure consciousness, and the witness of the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—the triad of states such as waking exists only for the intellect, which possesses modifications; it does not exist for the Self, which is devoid of these three states.

Its color is like the rising sun. As it has been said—(this verse may belong to the *Candrajñāna*): "Even externally, the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) is established as being like the rising sun, as if awakening everything."

Its pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) is as follows: the letter *ṭha* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). The two words "tejas," "tejas," and so forth, constitute the word-path (*pada*). The five-syllable mantra of the Heart of Tāra is the mantra-path (*mantra*). The principle called intellect (*buddhi*) is the category-path (*tattva*). The eight worlds beginning with Paiśāca are the world-path (*bhuvana*). The power of knowledge (*vidyākalā*) is the level-path (*kalā*). || 3 ||
The function [of cognition] is established as *buddhi* by its effect, namely the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) such as "this is a jar.

That [cognition], too, arises for the person in forms such as *sāttvika* and so forth, due to the predominance of the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the rest, according to the force of its effects; for the qualities are present everywhere.

This is because its activity is observed. Furthermore, that this intellect possesses eight qualities such as dharma, as well as the distinctions among its cognitive states such as attainment (*siddhi*), should be noted in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures. || 52 ||
This egoity (ahaṅkāra) is threefold, consisting of the forms of vital impulse, exertion, and pride;
through its differentiation, the object of experience attains the state of being communicable in linguistic usage.
The *Tātparyadīpikā* now defines the principle of egoity (*ahaṅkāratattva*), beginning with the word "syāt" (it may be).
From the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), the principle consisting of egoity arises. Egoity (*ahaṅkṛti*) is *ahaṅkāra*.

The meaning is that it possesses an activity of the form "I am. He states its divisions: "it is threefold. Anticipating the question "In what form?", he says: "this consists of the forms of vitalization, impulsion, and pride. These are the ego-sense of vitalization (*jīvanāhaṅkāra*), the ego-sense of impulsion (*saṃrambhāhaṅkāra*), and the ego-sense of pride (*garvāhaṅkāra*). Among these, the ego-sense of vitalization has the form "I live"; the ego-sense of impulsion is "I act"; [and the ego-sense of pride is] "I am powerful."

"Possessing form" (*rūpavān*) and so forth refers to the prideful ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). One who has these forms is described as such. He states the proof: "Because of the fusion," and so forth. Through connection with the ego-sense, the objects such as sound attain the state of being communicable and the fitness for experience. For instance, the self (*ātman*) is indeed devoid of qualities, inactive, pure consciousness, and indifferent by nature; therefore, it is not [the agent].

This egoism consists in [the thought] "I hear," "I do not see," and "I do not act," whereby one attributes to the witnessing Self (sākṣin) the hearing and so forth performed by the ear and other organs, the speaking and so forth performed by speech and other organs, the determination and so forth performed by the intellect (buddhi), and the doubt and so forth performed by the mind (citta), through such mental modifications (vṛtti) as "I hear," "I speak," and "I determine."
It establishes a connection. Therefore, the principle (tattva) called *ahaṅkāra* must be accepted;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that hearing and other functions performed by the ear and so forth could not be connected to the self, just as an action performed by Devadatta cannot belong to Yajñadatta. This has been stated in the *Śaivarahasya*:

"The appearance of a connection between the knower and the known, as well as [the appearance of connection] through space and time, is easily obtained; this operation is called 'I-conceit' (abhimāna), belonging to this ego-function (ahaṅkṛti). Thus [ends the verse]. 4.
And its function (vṛtti) is as follows: it would be [the state of] "it might be.
For the impetuous impulse (saṃrambha), consisting of effort, is indeed derived from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). As it has been said: "Impetuous impulse is the function of the ego-sense."
(Bhāskara’s Kārikā 33). Furthermore, even life itself is caused by that [the *ahaṃkāra*], since it is the cause for the activity of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other winds.

As it has been said: "The five bodily winds exert themselves through the impulsion (*saṃrambha*) of that [which is the *ahaṃkāra*]" (Mṛgendra-vṛtti 11.20). Likewise, pride (*garva*) is also [caused by it].

Since the determination of the object (*grāhya-adhyavasāya*) is the effect of the intellect (*buddhi*), the determination of the subject as "I" (*grāhaka-adhyavasāya*) is likewise its effect. Therefore...

Through these three, the establishment of the *ahaṅkāra* occurs; and from that very connection, there arises the conventional usage, "I know the jar. Thus he says: "from the blending" (*saṃbhedāt*). And that [blending] is produced from the intellect (*buddhi*). As it has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas as well: "From the Great One (*mahat*) comes the *ahaṅkāra*" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 23). || 53 ||
Through the divisions of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*, it is born again as threefold; and it breathes forth by the names of *vaikārika*, *taijasa*, and *bhūtādika*. (54)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states that there is another way in which that very [ahaṃkāra] is threefold, beginning with the words "sāttvika":
due to being a modification of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, the *ahaṃkāra* becomes threefold, distinguished as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*. It is that...

Furthermore, egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) is threefold by name: Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Bhūtādi. That which is characterized by an excess of *sattva* is the *sāttvika*, called Vaikārika; that which is characterized by an excess of *rajas* is the *taijasa*. Some maintain the opposite order, stating that the textual reading is "Taijasa, Vaikārika, and Bhūtādi. That which is characterized by an excess of *tamas* is the *tāmasa*; it is named Bhūtādi both according to its qualities (*guṇa*) and its designation.
Thus, the threefold nature of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) comes to be. || 5 ||

Furthermore, regarding the commentary [on the term] "sāttvika" and so forth: the meaning is that the names *taijasa* and the others belong respectively to the *ahaṅkāra*-skandhas beginning with the *sāttvika*. || 54 ||

From the Taijasa [ego] there arises the mind, and from the Vaikārika [ego] the sense organs; from the Bhūtādi [ego] the subtle elements (tanmātras) arise. This is the sequence of their creation from this [unmanifest source].
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states the effect [of this]: "From the taijasa...
From this very threefold *ahaṅkāra*, there arises this [group] of the organs of cognition, the organs of action, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the mind.

The sixteenth chapter: On the creation of the sixteen [evolutes]. Anticipating the questions—of what nature is the origin of the mind (*manas*), from what form do the sense organs (*indriya*) arise, and from what kind of source do the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) emerge—the author describes their production through a detailed classification, beginning with the words "from the *taijasa*," and so forth.
From the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) known as *taijasa*, which is of the *rajas* quality, the mind—which is mobile by nature—is produced; and from the *vaikārika*, which is of the *sattva* quality...

The ten sense organs are endowed with luminosity (*prakāśa*) and lightness (*laghu*). From the *bhūtādi*—which is *tāmasa* and abounds in darkness—the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise. Others hold that from the *taijasa*, which is *sāttvika*, the clear and light mind (*manas*) is produced.
From the *vaikārika*, which is *rājasa* and assisted by the *sāttvika*, the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) arise, because they are the instruments of knowledge.

Regarding the statement "from the *vaikārika* [ahaṃkāra] assisted by *tamas*, the organs of action [arise]," the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the eleven organs arise from the *sāttvika* ego, while the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) arise from the *tāmasa* [ego].
This is because *sattva* and *tamas*, being devoid of activity, lack the capacity for self-production; rather, they are impelled by *rajas*, which is mobile by nature.

They maintain that both [the elevenfold group and the five gross elements], while being causes, arise with *rajas* as their instrumental cause (*nimitta*), but it does not have the status of a material cause (*upādāna*);
rather, that belongs only to *sattva* and *tamas*. For it is said: "The elevenfold [group] of the nature of *sattva* proceeds from the *vaikṛta* ego."
"From the *bhūtādi* comes the subtle element (*tanmātra*), which is *tāmasa*; from the *taijasa*, both [the subtle element and the sense organ]. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 25).
This sequence of creation—namely, that "from this [the *ahaṃkāra*] come these"—is redundant with respect to the five [subtle elements] derived from the five gross elements (*pañcabhūta*).

He refutes the view favored by the logicians (*tārkika*) and others regarding the origin of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*). For instance, there is the *Nyāya-sūtra*: "The sense organs—smell, taste, sight, touch, and hearing—arise from the elements" (1.1.12). The common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of the elements (earth and so forth) is their possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are perceptible by each respective external sense organ and their serving as the material cause (*prakṛti*) of those organs.

"Even for the five [elements], there is the state of being an element, the nature of being a sense-organ faculty, and the possession of specific qualities that are external and perceptible by each individual sense-organ"—
this is the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* from the section on common and uncommon properties. Thus,

both the *Praśastapādīya-vaiśeṣikabhāṣya* and [the other texts] establish the relationship between the elements such as earth and so forth, the sense-faculties such as the olfactory organ and so forth, and the [objects] such as sound and so forth.
[The author] explains its origin: "And the mind is eternal," so say the logicians and Mīmāṃsakas.
This is untenable because it contradicts the scriptures. For instance, in the *Pārameśvara*:
"O observer of good vows, the quality of *sattva* belonging to the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is threefold."
It is threefold: Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Bhūtādi.
Pride arising from sattva with preeminent vigor is known as vaikārika;
that which is joined with abundant rajas is proclaimed as taijasa.
Among those, Bhūtādi is predominant in tamas; I shall describe its functions.
Vaikārika is said to be the cause and the source of the host of the senses.
From the *garva* (I-principle) arises the mind (*manas*), which possesses the nature of both;
from that very *vaikārika-garva*, the organs of action (*karmendriyāṇi*) also arise.
"They manifest from the agitation of the causal self who desires to create;
indeed, from the *ahaṅkāra* of *bhūtādi*, the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) arise," and so forth. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.2.43–45, 46, 50, 68–69, 98)
And in the Śivadharmottara: "From Pradhāna, by the will of Śiva, arose the intellect (buddhi), which is the cause of the world;
and from the agitation of the intellect, the ego (ahaṅkāra) became threefold."
"And from the *ahaṅkāra* [arise] the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) and the sense organs.
This is also established through inference. For instance: "The sense organs under dispute are not elemental (composed of the gross elements), because they are sense organs, like the mind (*manas*).
The mind is non-eternal, because it is a sense organ, like the eye and so forth. All sense organs are produced.

Because they are entities distinct from their own material causes, because they possess insentience arising from something other than their material cause, because they possess qualities, or because they are corporeal—just like a jar and so forth—through such inferences, the non-material and produced nature of the sense organs is established.
When there is a requirement for a cause of these sense organs, the causality of the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-principle) is accepted on the strength of scripture (*āgama*). For this very reason:

The inference that "the sense organs are not derived from the *ahaṅkāra*, because they are sense organs, like the mind" is invalid due to being *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (contradicted by perception) and because of the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). Likewise, [the arguments] that "earth, water, fire, and air are not the material causes (*upādāna*) of smell, taste, form, and touch, because they are elements (*bhūta*), like space," and "space is not the material cause of sound, because it is an element, like earth," [are similarly invalid].

Sound and the other [sensory objects] possess material causes because they are effects; and these effects, being insentient, are distinct from their primal cause, just like a jar and similar objects. From this inference, the existence of the *ahaṃkāra* as their material cause, which is distinct from the gross elements (*bhūta*), is established.
Its color is like that of fire. As it has been said:
Outside of that, however, there should be the imperishable reality called Ahaṅkāra, resembling a blazing fire, of terrifying form, and difficult to approach. Thus [it is said].
Its pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is as follows: the letter *dh* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). The two words beginning with *arūpa* are the two words (*pada*).
The two mantras are the five-syllabled Īśāna and [the other]. The principle (tattva) is that called Ahaṅkāra. The two worlds are Chagalaṇḍa and Dviraṇḍa.
The digit (kalā) is Pratiṣṭhā. 6.

The commentary on this is as follows: from among those [three types of *ahaṃkāra*], the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the sense organs (*indriya*) are born from the *taijasa-ahaṃkāra*;

the organs of action (*karmendriya*) from the *vaikārika*; and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) from the *bhūtādi*—this is the meaning. Furthermore, it is not the case that the mind alone arises from the *taijasa*.

It should be explained that from the *vaikārika* [sattva] arise the sense organs of both types, because this would contradict the original statement and because it would contradict reason. It is logical that *sattva*, being of the nature of illumination, is the cause of cognition, while *rajas* is the cause of activity. And it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose, together with the mind..."
Because it possesses the quality of luminosity, it is *sāttvika*; and because it is *taijasa* (fiery), it is also *sāttvika*.
Speech, hands, the generative organ, the anus, and the feet—these are born of rajas;
for in this group, which is of the nature of transformation (vaikārika), rajas predominates due to its connection with action. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 12.3–4) 55.
For the mind, whose form is desire, has volition as its function;
the organs of perception are the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose. (56)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* now states the essential nature of the senses preceded by the mind: "Desire," etc.
The mind is of the nature of desire, that is, of the nature of longing. Its activity is its function (*vṛtti*). This refers to that mind.
*Saṅkalpa* is that which has not yet determined a specific form; that is to say, it is of the nature of doubt. By this, its definition is stated.

Furthermore, its existence is inferred from the possessor of the function (*vṛttimat*) through the function (*vṛtti*) consisting of doubt. Likewise, because knowledge does not arise simultaneously regarding multiple objects of desire when they are in contact with the instruments such as the eyes.

It is understood that there exists another instrument distinct from the eye and the other [senses]. If that did not exist, the cognition of color-form (*rūpa*) and other objects would arise simultaneously. Therefore, since there is another instrument, it is established that this is the mind (*manas*). Furthermore, its atomic nature is understood precisely because cognitions do not occur simultaneously; thus, the inference of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) as stated by the followers of Kumārila is refuted.
"It is not a valid means of knowledge because it contradicts the means of knowledge that apprehends its own substratum. The sense organs are the instruments for the functioning of the intellect.
To the question "Which are they?", he says: "The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose. (7)
The commentary states that the mind is established through will:
"will," etc. Resolve, attentiveness, and one-pointedness—by means of such activity, the mind, whose nature is will, becomes established; this is the meaning.

This is the intended meaning here: even when there is contact between the self and the objects of the senses, that which is the presiding factor—without which the external sense organs do not function, even for one whose attention is directed elsewhere—is the mind (manas). He states the sense organs of cognition (buddhīndriyas) as "the cognitive faculties" (buddhyakṣāṇi). || 56 ||
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are to be grasped by them;
thus, these five objects correspond respectively to the five [senses]. (57)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states their object: "They are to be grasped.
Since these five—sound and the rest—are the objects of the five sense organs, such as the ears and so forth.
They are to be grasped; therefore, they are the objects. He shows them in order: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. (8)
Commentary: Now, he states their objects of apprehension with the words "the objects of apprehension.
The function of these [senses] is proclaimed as the grasping of sound and the other [objects], respectively.
The organs of action (karmendriya) are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ. || 58 ||
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states the nature of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) as follows: "śabdādi... etc.
Those of which sound is the first are "sound and the rest" (*śabdādayaḥ*). Their "grasping" (*grahaṇa*) is the assuming of their respective forms.

The function of these sense organs has been stated by the knowers of reality; that is to say, it is impossible for one [organ] to apprehend another [object] out of sequence. By this, the definition of each of the organs, beginning with the ear, has been stated. Furthermore, this statement is intended for further investigation. For instance: the apprehension of sound is produced by an instrument (karaṇa), because it is an action (kriyā), like the act of cutting; thus, the existence of the ear is established.

In this manner, the existence of the sense organs, such as the skin and others, is to be understood through their function as the instruments for perceiving touch, form, taste, and smell. To explain: the perception of sound, which is of two kinds—articulated and inarticulate—is not possible without the instrument of the auditory organ, since it is observed that one who is deaf does not perceive it. Likewise, the perception of touches such as cold, hot, soft, hard, liquid, and sharp is accomplished by the tactile organ.
It could not exist without it, because it is not perceived by one whose sense of touch is impaired by skin disease.

For instance, the perception of forms— distinguished by differences such as white, red, black, yellow, green, smoky-grey, dark, short, long, and so forth— is not possible without the eye as its instrument.

For it is impossible for one who is blind to see that; likewise, the apprehension of the sixfold tastes—sweet, sour, bitter, salty, pungent, and astringent—would not occur without the instrument of the tongue which initiates that perception, since such apprehension is not possible for one whose sense of taste is impaired by dullness (*jāḍya*). Similarly, [this applies] to the perception of fragrant and non-fragrant odors.

Furthermore, the perception of the two kinds of odor is not possible without the instrument of the nose as its organ, because that [odor] is not perceived by one whose sense organ is impaired by the absence of a sniffer. || 9 ||
The commentary [states]: "Therefore, their existence is established solely by the fact that the perception of sound and so forth would otherwise be impossible"—thus he says, "Sound and so forth.
Nor is it logical that these [organs] are composed of the elements (*bhautika*) simply because they have restricted objects, for other elements and their qualities [are also perceived].

Because it is observed that the eyes and other senses perceive due to the commonality of their karma, it was said by the Siddhaguru: "If there were a restriction based on being composed of elements (bhautikatva) regarding both [the senses] and the commonality of karma, then cognitions would not arise for embodied beings from the deities through their inherence. Thus it is stated.

(bhā0 kā0 40) In this context, they are called "deities" (*deva*) because of their shining or illuminating; thus, the sense organs (*indriya*) are referred to. He speaks of the organs of action: "Speech, feet... (58).
And their functions are speaking, grasping, moving, excretion, and sexual pleasure.
The internal organ is threefold: intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and mind (cetas). || 59 ||

The *Tātparyadīpikā* states that the organs of action (*karmendriya*) are five: speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ. Regarding their functions and the classification of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he speaks in the following verse beginning with "vacana":

Because these serve as the instruments for action, they are the organs of action (*karmendriya*); their respective actions are speech and so forth. This statement is intended for the purpose of investigation; for instance, the existence of the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*) as the instrument for that [action] is understood through the impossibility of the utterance of sound otherwise. Nor should it be said that the organ of speech is merely its physical locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

"Because it would follow that even a mute person would have the capacity for vocal utterance. This should be understood to apply to the other sense organs as well; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that one possessing a sense organ characterized by deafness, lameness, constipation, or impotence would still possess the capacity for grasping and so forth. As it has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas:
"Deafness... [this statement appears in the *Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī* as verse 49, concerning the "afflictions of the eleven organs"].
It is found cited in the *Kārikāvyākhyā*: "Leprosy, blindness, dullness, loss of smell,
as well as muteness, deformity, lameness, impotence, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), and dullness."

Therefore, the existence of those which are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), distinct from their respective substrates (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and denoted by the term "organ" (*indriya*) as marks of the Lord (*indra*)—that is, the Self—is established. Furthermore, their status as being beyond the senses is proven by the following inference: "The organs under dispute are beyond the senses, because they are organs, like the mind. The internal instrument is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

It is threefold; in what form? To this he says: "Intellect (buddhi), ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and mind (cetas). That is, intellect, ego-sense, and mind. Alternatively, each internal organ is threefold due to the distinction between past, future, and present objects. As it is said in the Mātaṅga:
That which is called the internal organ has as its object the three periods of time.
"From which it is determined: therefore, that which has been accumulated over a long period—whether present, past, or yet to come—is known through inference. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 18.86–87, 88)
Likewise, by the Sāṃkhyas: "The external organ pertains to the present time; the internal organ pertains to the three times. (10)
(Śāṅkhya Kārikā 33) Commentary: Now, by which activities is their accomplishment achieved? To this, he says: "By speech," and so forth.

Moving (*viharaṇa*) means going; evacuation (*utsarga*) means the removal of waste. The rest is easy to understand. For this very reason, those who do not accept the existence of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) have been refuted. Since activity (*kṛti*) is observed to be the cause for the application of names [to these organs]. [Objection: If that is so, then because actions such as the raising of eyebrows and the like are also activities, the organs of action would be infinite. [Reply: That is not so, because they are like the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*).
Because these [organs] are accepted as pervading the entire body, there is no fault in saying that the movement of the eyebrows and so forth is the function of the hands and other [limbs] alone.
Regarding those [organs], he states the distinction between the internal and external organs: "The internal organ... (verse 59).
Furthermore, the external [evolutes] are tenfold, distinguished by the sense organs of cognition and the organs of action.
From the subtle elements (tanmātras) arise the five gross elements: ether, air, fire, water, and earth. (60)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* states the division of the external organs and their functions as being limited to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), beginning with the word "intellect" (*buddhi*).
The external organs are of ten kinds: the five sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) and the five organs of action (*karmendriya*). Alternatively, [it continues:]

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consists of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*). The external [organ] consists of the organs of action and the organs of cognition; thus, due to the distinction in their functions, it is also threefold. The function of the internal organ is characterized by the maintenance of the body through its modifications such as *prāṇa* and so forth;
that of the organs of cognition is illumination; and that of the organs of action is grasping. As it has been said:
"The instrument is of thirteen kinds; it performs the functions of grasping, retaining, and manifesting" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 32).
The pervasion of the six paths for the sense organs, preceded by the mind, is stated in sequence: the letter *ukāra* is the phoneme.
*Ādhūma*, etc., consists of two words; they are two five-syllabled mantras of the *tatpuruṣa* [form]. The principle (*tattva*) is *manas*;

the world (*bhuvana*) is named Mākoṭa; the power (*kalā*) is *nivṛtti*; the phoneme (*varṇa*) is the letter *na*. *Śarva* and *Maheśvara* are the two words; they are two five-syllabled mantras of the *kavaca* [form]. The principle is that called *śrotra* (the sense of hearing); the world is Maṇḍaleśvara; the power is *śāntyatītā*; [the phoneme is] the letter *pa*.

The phoneme is *va*. "Mahādeva" and so forth are two words. The two mantras consist of five syllables each. The principle (*tattva*) is that which consists of the skin. The world-sphere (*bhuvana*) is Kālañjara. The digit (*kalā*) is Peace (*śānti*). The phoneme is the letter *ḍha*. "Mahātejas" and so forth are two words. The two mantras consist of five syllables each. The principle is that called the eye. The world-sphere is Śaṅkukarṇa. The digit is Knowledge (*vidyā*).
The letter *ba* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). "Release, release," and so forth, are two words (*pada*). The two mantras consist of five syllables each and have the heart as their essence.
The reality (*tattva*) is that which consists of speech. The world (*bhuvana*) is Maṇḍaleśvara. The power (*kalā*) is Śāntyatītā. The letter *ya* is the phoneme.
"Causing the presence of all," and so forth.
Two words; two mantras consisting of five syllables each, [namely] Aghora. The principle (tattva) is that of the hands. The world (bhuvana) is Kālañjara.

The digit (kalā) is Śānti. The phoneme (varṇa) is *ra*. Two words beginning with "anarcita"; two mantras consisting of five syllables each, [namely] Vāmadeva. The principle is that of the feet. The world is Śaṅkukarṇa. The digit is Vidyā. The phoneme is *la*.

The two words beginning with *pūrvasthita* [are the first pair]. The two five-syllable mantras are those of Sadyojāta. The principle (*tattva*) is that consisting of the anus. The world (*bhuvana*) is Sthūleśa. The digit (*kalā*) is Pratiṣṭhā. The phoneme (*varṇa*) is the letter *va*. The two words beginning with *turu turu* [are the second pair].
The two five-syllable mantras are those of Astra. The principle is that consisting of the generative organ (*upastha*). The world is Sthaleśvara. The digit is Nivṛtti.

Commentary: Now, he states that the subtle elements (tanmātras) are established precisely as the causes of the gross elements, beginning with "From the subtle elements" (tanmātrebhyaḥ). "Space, air, and fire" refers to *kha*, *pavana*, and *tejas*. The remainder is easy to understand. || 60 ||
The five subtle elements (tanmātras), beginning with sound, are proclaimed to be "without distinction" (aviśeṣa).
From them arise the five gross elements (bhūtas), which possess an increasing number of qualities by one at each stage.
Regarding the phrase "from the tanmātras" in the *Tātparyadīpikā*, [the author] asks: what are the tanmātras, and how is the production of the elements from them? To this, he says:
"The tanmātras..."

The five subtle elements, such as sound and the rest, which are devoid of specific qualities, are called *tanmātras*. By the word *mātra*, the conjunction with the gross elements (*bhūta*) or their transformation into the state of gross elements is excluded. The meaning is that they are merely sound and the other [objects] existing in a subtle state. From those five *tanmātras*, the five gross elements arise.
They arise through the increase of each successive quality. For instance: from the *tanmātra* of sound, space (*ākāśa*) arises, possessing the single quality of sound;

from the *tanmātra* of touch accompanied by the *tanmātra* of sound, air (*vāyu*) arises, possessing the qualities of sound and touch; from the *tanmātra* of form accompanied by those two aforementioned *tanmātras*, fire (*tejas*) arises, possessing the qualities of sound, touch, and form; and from the *tanmātra* of taste accompanied by the aforementioned *tanmātras*, [water arises], possessing four qualities.

From water— which is the material cause consisting of the subtle element of smell accompanied by the subtle elements of sound, touch, form, and taste— the earth, characterized by the five qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, is produced. Others say that the gross elements arise from the subtle elements alone, while still others [hold a different view].

From the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), space and the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*) arise; from the subtle element of touch, air and the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*); from the subtle element of form, fire and the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*); from the subtle element of taste, water and the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*); and from the subtle element of smell, earth alone arises. Thus it has been said:

From *tamas* [and the other *guṇas*], according to the statement of the *Śaivarahasya*, the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) arises from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) consisting of *bhūta-ādi*.
From that subtle element as well, space (*ākāśa*) and the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*) arise.
"Form, taste, and smell alone arise in successive order together with air and the other elements;

from the preceding subtle element (tanmātra) alone, and from smell alone, earth arises. Thus, from the supreme sound-tanmātra comes space (ākāśa), and from the touch-tanmātra accompanied by those two [sound and touch] comes air (vāyu).

They say that from the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra) accompanied by those three [subtle elements], fire arises; from the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra) accompanied by those four, water arises; and from the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra) accompanied by those five, earth arises. Others say that from the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) comes space (ākāśa), from that the subtle element of touch (sparśatanmātra), and from that wind (vāyu).

From that [comes] the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*); from that, fire; from that, the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*); from that, water; from those two [subtle elements], the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*); and from that, earth—so they say. The pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) of the subtle elements is as follows: the letter *ṇa* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). The two words beginning with "anāda" are the two mantras consisting of five syllables each, namely Aghora. The principle (*tattva*) is the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*).
The world is Maṇḍaleśvara; the power (kalā) is Śāntyatītā; the phoneme is the letter *ta*; the two words begin with *dhūtra*;

the two mantras consist of five syllables each, beginning with Vāmadeva; the principle (tattva) is the subtle element of touch (sparśatanmātra); the world is Kālañjara; the power is Śāntyatītā; the phoneme is the letter *tha*; the two words begin with *oṃ bhuvaḥ*; the two mantras consist of five syllables each, beginning with Sadyojāta.

The *tattva* is *rūpatanmātra*; the *bhuvana* is Śaṅkukarṇa; the *kalā* is Vidyā; the *varṇa* is the letter *da*; the two words are *anidhana* and *adhi*; the two mantras consist of five syllables each, beginning with the weapon (*astra*). The *tattva* is *rasatanmātra*; the *bhuvana* is Sthūleśa; the *kalā* is Pratiṣṭhā; the *varṇa* is the letter *dha*; the word is *nidhanodbhava*; [the two mantras] consist of five syllables each, beginning with the eye (*netra*).
The two mantras; the principle (tattva) of smell-potentiality (gandhatanmātra); the world-sphere (bhuvana) of Sthaleśvara; and the kalā of Nivṛtti. || 12 ||

As for the function [of the tanmātras], what indeed are these tanmātras? To this he says: "the tanmātras. They are the unmanifested particulars—subtle forms—in which the five [qualities] beginning with sound and touch have not yet manifested their specific distinctions.
They are called the five *tanmātras*, as it has been said: "The *tanmātras* are not distinguished by the [gross] qualities; they are designated by the term *tanmātra*" (*Mṛgendratantra-vṛtti* 12.5).
And from those subtle causes, the five elements (*bhūtas*) arise as gross, because their qualities are perceptible by the external senses of beings such as ourselves; thus he says: "the elements."

Furthermore, those elements beginning with space possess qualities that increase by one in each successive case. Space has the single quality of sound; air has the qualities of sound and touch; fire has the qualities of sound, touch, and form; water has the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste;

and earth possesses the five qualities beginning with sound and ending with smell. As it is heard: "Space and the others have functions [of providing room, etc. and possess qualities that increase by one, beginning with sound."

(Mṛgendra-vṛtti 12.20), and so forth. Now, an objection may be raised: "The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that sound is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of space (*ākāśa*). This is not so, because [sound] is perceived elsewhere than its substratum. As it has been said: "Because this reason (*hetu*) is contradicted by perception and scripture, it is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed/invalidated by lapse of time). For instance, first, an echo is heard in space; [the rustling of] leaves and the like is heard in the wind;...
The sound of fire begins with *dhamadhamā* and so forth; that of water with *calacala* and so forth; and that of earth with *kaṭakaṭa* and so forth. And it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Thus, this [sound] exists in the five [elements], while touch exists in the four elements."
The earth and wind possess neither cold nor heat; water and fire possess cold and heat respectively;
the sun and fire possess light; water possesses whiteness; and the earth possesses whiteness and many other qualities.
"Form resides in three [elements], taste in water, and in earth there are six kinds of taste;
fragrance in earth is considered by the wise to be both non-fragrant and fragrant. (61)
Providing space, arranging, maturing, gathering, and supporting— these, respectively,
are declared to be the functions of the elements, beginning with space (ether). (VI.12.27–29)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* now states the function of the five elements, beginning with "avakāśa" (space).
Providing space—that is, granting room—is the function of space (*vyoman*), because it is the cause of differentiation. *Vyūhana*...
The function of air is the carrying of various things or its accumulation; the function of fire is digestion, which is the act of ripening;
the function of water is cohesion or moistening; and the function of earth is support or sustenance.
Regarding "activity" (*vyāpāra*): it has been said—
[this may be a statement from the *Śaivarahasya*]— "The giving of space by ether, the fanning of fire by air, the cooking by the consumer of oblations [fire],
the holding together of waters, the supporting of the earth, and the functioning through the nature of all things."

Space is the supreme element here; it has sound as its quality because it is produced from the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). Just as a jar produced from clay possesses the quality of clay, and a thread produced from cotton possesses the quality of cotton, so too space, being produced from sound, possesses the quality of sound. This element must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, for a material object—
Because it would follow that all activities—such as going and coming, growth, healing, and physical exertion—would be impossible. As it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
"Space arises from the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), characterized by the quality of providing room."
"O Brahmin! It is manifest and makes manifest for the sake of establishing distinct configurations. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.2.6–7).
That one [Principle], though partless (*amūrta*), is divided into manifold distinctions through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of material forms such as jars, pots, huts, wells, and so forth.
Its color is indescribable, resembling pure crystal. Others say the mandala has the shape of the lunar disc.
As it is said—this verse from the *Candrajñāna* is understood to follow after that: "But outside of that, there should be space within the element of earth."
"It is well-established, inconceivable, and unknowable, like another station of liberation.
Its pervasion through the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is as follows: the letter is *śa*; [the mantra] begins with *piṅga-piṅga*, and so forth.

Two words; two mantras consisting of five syllables each; the principle (*tattva*) whose nature is space (*ākāśa*); the eight worlds beginning with Vastrāpada; the *kalā* known as Śāntyatītā; wind (*vāyu*), which possesses formlessness and touch; it has the qualities of sound and touch. By the authority of the scripture stating "From space, wind arises" (*Tai. U. 2.1*), the production [of wind] from an atom is refuted. It is of three kinds: body, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and...

And as for the object [of the wind element]: the fact that the body of the hell-beings (yātanā) and so forth is composed of air is due to its predominance there, not because it consists of that alone. Prāṇa, residing in the body, is of the nature of a common function of the three internal organs. As it has been said: "The specific function of each of the three is distinct; this is their uncommon [activity]."
"The common function of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 29).
The other is the objective air. This is stated in the Mātaṅga:
"Pervaded by which the entire world vibrates and attains growth,
wherein eighty million celestial chariots are bound and revolve like a wheel— this is that wind, the best among those who sustain life. Thus it is said.
(vi0 20|3,4) Its color resembles collyrium, its shape is circular, and it has a mandala of six dots. As it has been said—
[this verse from the *Candrajñāna* would follow here]— outside of that is the wind element (*vāyutattva*).
"Having a luster like split collyrium, resonant with a gurgling roar, and crowded with people of great strength. Thus [it is said].
Its pervasion through the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvavyāpti*) is as follows: the letter *ṣa*; the two words beginning with "sound of sound" (*śabdaśabda*), etc.

The two mantras are the Kavaca and the Pañcārṇa. The principle (tattva) is that of air (vāyu). The eight worlds begin with Gaya. The digit (kalā) is Peace (śānti). Radiance (tejas) is of a luminous form; it is of two kinds: internal and external.
That which is the means for digesting the food consumed within the body is internal; the other is external. And that [external radiance] is of two kinds: the body...
Regarding the term "object": the bodies of the celestial sages (*devarṣis*) are composed of fire (*taijasa*);
for those of wondrous deeds, their bodies are fiery. (The reading found there is: "they become [bodies] here, as they are reborn [in that state]").

This is because of the statement [in the *Mālinīvijayottara-tantra* (Ma0 bhā0 3.261.13): "The other [elements] are the sun, moon, fire, lightning, and so forth; its color is like lightning. As it has been said:
"But the *tejas*-tattva outside of that [the *prakṛti*-tattva] has a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning. (This verse may belong to the *Candrajñāna*).
"Resounding with the thunder of clouds, having the form of splendor, and crowded with people.
Thus [is described] the triangular mandala marked with the svastika. Its pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is as follows:
the word "Śiva-Śarva"; the two mantras consisting of five syllables for the *śikhā*; the principle (*tattva*) of fire; and the eight worlds beginning with Śrīśaila.
The *vidyā-kalā* consists of water, which is naturally fluid and possesses the qualities (*guṇa*) of sound, touch, form, and taste. Among these, its own specific quality is taste;
the other three are produced through mixture. As it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
"In this context, taste should be understood as its own [quality], while the other three arise from mixture."

(Vi. 22.2) That is twofold: the body and the object. The body is the abode in the world of Varuṇa; the other is the object, because it is that which is to be enjoyed. And this is crystal-colored. As it is said in the *Candrajñāna*:
"Having pervaded the earth-tattva, water extends tenfold outward;
