it is the support of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and resembles pure crystal.

Thus [it is said]. Its pervasion of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) is as follows: the letter *ha* is the phoneme (*varṇa*). The two words beginning with *sarva* are the word-path (*pada*). The five syllables beginning with *śiras* are the mantra-path (*mantra*).
The two mantras; the principle (tattva) consisting of water; the eight worlds beginning with Amareśa; the *kalā* of *Pratiṣṭhā*;

and the earth, which possesses fragrance and five qualities. As it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "From the agitated subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*), [the earth] arises, endowed with the five qualities."
"Her own natural odor is said to be [one], while the other four are produced as secondary adjuncts.
The essence, indeed, is the supreme limit; [so too are] the types consisting of nails, teeth, and bones," and so forth. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 23.1–2, 5)

And this [matter] is twofold: the body and the object. The body is also twofold, consisting of the immobile and the mobile. The immobile extends from grass up to trees. The mobile is fourfold: viviparous, oviparous, sweat-born, and non-womb-born. Among these, humans, domestic animals, and wild beasts are viviparous; birds and reptiles are oviparous.

The sweat-born [beings] consist of lice, bedbugs, moths, and so forth; and the non-womb-born (ayonija) consists of the lords of the worlds, the gods, and the ṛṣis. The objects established by hundreds of Purāṇas and Itihāsas—the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), the seven continents within it, the netherworlds (pātāla), the twenty-eight crores of hells, and an equal number of celestial chariots (vimāna) and so on—are [included here] because they are objects of experience. Thus, the earth-element (kṣititattva) is of the nature of the cosmic egg.

It is one hundred crore yojanas in extent. As it is stated in the *Śaivarahasya*: "The final principle, the earthly element, which consists of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and is indeed indivisible, is said to be one hundred crore yojanas in both breadth and length."
And in the Mataṅgapārameśvara it is said:
"In this system, the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) is thus complete as one hundred crores;
water is ten times this [amount], fire is greater than water, and air is greater than that."
From wind comes space; from space, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); and beyond that, the Great One (mahat).
Beyond the Great One, O Sage, the triad of qualities (guṇas) is to be known.

From the three qualities (guṇas) arises the principle called Pradhāna, which is ten times greater; from Rāga onwards, up to Māyā, each subsequent principle possesses a hundred times the quality of its predecessor.
The power known as *vidyā* increases a thousandfold; thereafter, the power of *aiśa* increases a hundred-thousandfold (*lakṣa*);
and that which has further increased ten-millionfold (*koṭi*) is proclaimed as the *śivatattva*.
"Immediately following, it would be infinite, immeasurable, and eternal. (Viṣṇudharmottara 24.41–45).
This is the *kṣiti-tattva* (earth-principle), which resembles gold. This has been stated in the *Candrajñāna*:
"The earth-element is golden, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is proclaimed to be like the egg of a hen. Thus [it is said].
The lunar mandala is square and marked with a vajra.
The deities beginning with Brahmā are to be known as belonging to the five [elements] starting with earth, respectively,
throughout all the categories (tattvas) from Śiva down to earth.
There are twenty-four worlds, making two hundred and twenty-four in total.
Its pervasion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is as follows: the phoneme is *kṣa*; the word is "Obeisance, obeisance to Śiva" (*śivāya oṃ namo namaḥ*);

the mantras are the five-syllabled *Hṛdaya* [mantras]; the principle (*tattva*) is the earthly (*pārthiva*); and there are one hundred and eight [deities] beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Bhadrakālī.
The worlds; withdrawal is the *kalā*. || 13 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Determination of the Impure Category, in the *Tattvaprakāśatātparyadīpikā*, the commentary.
Now he states their respective functions: "Providing space," etc.

Providing space is the function of ether (*ākāśa*); arranging—that is, the joining of parts—is the function of air (*vāyu*); cooking is the function of fire (*agni*); supporting—that is, holding together—is the function of water (*ap*); and sustaining is the function of earth (*bhūmi*). In this regard:

Furthermore, the distinctness of space from mere vacuity and its impermanence have been demonstrated in detail by us in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*; therefore, this should be understood from that work. || 62 ||
This tenfold effect is produced by the instruments having entered into it;
for the instruments, being incapable [of acting independently], exert their activity by depending upon the effect.
The Tātparyadīpikā: Now begins the fifth chapter.
Thus, the twenty-three principles have arisen from the Pradhāna, which consists of the equilibrium of the guṇas.

They are of two kinds by way of being the effect (*kārya*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). Among these, the tenfold effect consists of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the five gross elements (*bhūta*). The thirteenfold instrument is divided into the external and the internal. He demonstrates their respective functions with the words "the effect" (*kāryam*).
This is the intended meaning: that which is the tenfold effect (*kārya*) is brought about by the instruments (*karaṇa*), accepted, or—in other words—grasped.

The effect is the body, which is tenfold in its subtle and gross aspects. Having entered and resorted to them, [the self acts], because it is impossible for them to function without a substratum; this is the sense. Alternatively, "effect" (*kārya*) refers to the object (*viṣaya*).
This [object] is of ten kinds; it is made an object by the instruments [of cognition]. Having entered into it, one becomes connected with it. || 1 ||

Commentary: Now, he states that these ten possess the nature of being effects (*kārya*) and serve as the substrata for the sense organs (*indriya*): "The effect," etc. This group of ten principles, consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*bhūta*), having entered into the instruments (*karaṇa*), [performs] activity.
It is brought about. And because they are not all-pervading (*avibhu*), those [faculties] exert themselves only by presiding over the effect; as it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
"This effect is brought about through exertion by the instruments having entered into it in ten ways;
but because they are not all-pervading, the instruments exert themselves by presiding over the effect."

(Tattvasaṃgraha 4) Now, it might be argued: "Let the gross elements themselves, which are established by both disputants, serve as the supports for the sense organs; what is the use of the five *tanmātras*, which are like internal goiters and purposeless? This is incorrect, because those [elements] exist as the supports for the sense organs in both their gross and subtle forms.

It is heard [in scripture]. This statement is seen in the venerable *Mataṅgapārameśvara* (*Viṣamapada*, 19.21)—it is not in the *Mṛgendra*—where it says: "In this world, the subtle elements are like a jar, and the gross elements are like a coating" (*mataṅga-pārameśvara*, *viṣamapada* 19.21). || 63 ||
In the Śaiva tradition, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the first five [categories] is stated to be by way of their having consciousness as their nature,
whereas for the other seven, beginning with *māyā*, it is proclaimed to be twofold.

In this context, there is a pervasive connection (anvaya) of all things, beginning with the unmanifest (avyakta), by way of the qualities (guṇas) whose nature is pleasure, pain, and delusion; however, at the end of this group of ten, there is this specific distinction.

The *Tātparyadīpikā*: Thus, having described the nature of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), [the author] now states the cause for establishing their purity, impurity, and mixed state— terms which were previously indicated by the words "pure" and so forth— in order to demonstrate purity, impurity, and the state of being both pure and impure.
Regarding the phrase "of the five":
this is the intended meaning—*anvaya* (concomitance) is the inclusion within a single genus, which is to say, identity of form, that is, oneness of self (*aikātmya*).

In that regard, there is a concomitance among the first five—the *tattvas* of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā—by virtue of their having consciousness as their essential nature (*cidrūpatā*). By means of that...
Their purity is due to this cause: because that which is of the nature of knowledge cannot be connected with the impurity of ignorance (*ajñāna*).
The seven principles—*māyā*, *kāla*, *niyati*, *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, and *puruṣa*—are associated in two ways, by virtue of having both conscious and unconscious natures.

Since *māyā* and the others, excluding *puruṣa*, consist of unconscious matter permeated by consciousness, they are associated in two ways; whereas *puruṣa* [is associated solely as pure consciousness].

Because that which is of the nature of consciousness (*citsvabhāva*) appears as non-consciousness (*acidrūpa*) due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Just as a crystal, though pure by its own nature, appears red through proximity to a hibiscus flower (*japā*), so too the Person (*puruṣa*) appears as non-consciousness through the superimposition of the attributes of the adjuncts. Consequently, the seven principles beginning with *māyā* possess both purity and impurity. This is because the principles beginning with the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) are external and devoid of connection with consciousness.
They are associated with the *guṇas* by virtue of having the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion; therefore, they are exclusively impure. (2–3)

The commentary: Having thus stated the definition of the principles (*tattva*), [the author] says "of the five" to address the question of in which [principles] there is the inclusion (*anvaya*) of which [categories], and in what manner.
Inclusion is the cause of the recurring cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*), such as "this is a cow, this is a cow. And that [inclusion] exists in this Śaiva scripture.

Even if one does not accept a universal (*jāti*) distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), it is nonetheless spoken of by way of some degree of similarity alone. Consequently, because the first five pure principles (*tattva*) are the causes for the manifestation of omniscience and omnipotence, they possess a commonality (*anvaya*) by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) and being beneficial to consciousness; however, it is not logical to admit that they themselves possess sentience (*caitanya*), as their insentience has already been established.

Because it has already been established; and because for others—namely the impure principles beginning with *māyā* and ending with *puruṣatva*—there is a twofold connection between consciousness (*cit*) and the non-conscious (*acit*), due to their being instrumental causes that support limited knowledge and so forth, due to their being helpful to consciousness by means of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), and due to their generating pleasure, pain, and delusion through their connection with the *guṇas*. || 64 ||

Regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*): there is a pervasive connection (*anvaya*) with the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion due to the association with the *guṇas* of all principles from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) down to earth. For it is said that [these qualities] end within the group of ten. || 65 ||
In this context, the connection should be understood as being based on equality when there is a similarity of qualities such as sound and so forth;
however, for some, a distinction arises from the relationship of subordinate and principal elements.

In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, at the end of the tenth chapter, regarding the question of what the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*) is that will be described as consisting of the elements and their subtle potentials (*tanmātra*),
he says: "Of sound and so forth."
Although sound and the other [objects] are equal in their possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*), their relationship should be understood as being unequal.

This refers to the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) and the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); by means of these, the specific distinction known as the "creation of states" (*bhāvasarga*)—which pertains to certain effects ranging from Time (*kāla*) down to the Earth (*avani*)—is to be understood. [This applies] to effects...
The manifestation of existence (*bhāvasarga*) occurs within its own specific causes. As it is stated in the *Śaivarahasya*:

"In the system of the theory of pre-existent effects (*satkāryavāda*), 'existence' (*bhāva*) is the persistence of the subtle effect, which consists of each respective principle (*tattva*), within its own individual causes."

This very creation of entities is understood through the relationship of cause and effect. For instance, the relation of cause and effect is not possible if the effect—which is one of the relata—does not exist; this is because non-existent things, such as a donkey’s horn, are never observed [to enter into such a relation]. The objects under dispute (the effects) must already exist within their causes, because they possess the quality of being produced. Whatever...

That which does not exist within its causes cannot possess origination, just as a donkey's horn; yet these [causes] do not lack such origination, therefore they must indeed exist within their causes. Furthermore, this is because of the acceptance of the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). If oil were not present in sesame seeds, then those seeking oil would not seek it from sesame seeds any more than they would from sand.

There would be no acceptance [of the effect], for it does not exist; thus, the existence of oil in sesame seeds is established. For this very reason, and because everything exists [in the cause], the effect is indeed existent. If an effect that is non-existent were to arise from causes, then there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of all possible effects arising from those same causes, since non-existence is indistinguishable everywhere. And yet, such is not the case.

It arises as something already existent (*sadeva*). This is because an effect is produced from a capable cause, and because it is generated by that which possesses the capacity for that specific effect. If an effect were to arise that does not exist within its causes, then it would follow that it could also arise from what is incapable; for if it were non-existent, the postulation of a "capacity" would be futile. Furthermore, the effect is existent because capacity consists in the subtle state of the effect. Likewise, if the effect were non-existent, it would be impossible [to produce].

Then the effect would be produced, because the cause possesses efficacy (*śakti*). Nor can it be said that the efficacy resides only in that [cause] when the effect is non-existent, for there is no distinction [between causes and non-causes] due to their common state of non-existence. Furthermore, the effect is existent because of its causality. If the effect were not present in the cause, then the cause itself would lack causality, as it would be indistinguishable from other things. Since this is observed, the effect is therefore existent. As it has been said:
"Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause, because not everything is possible from everything,
because the efficient cause produces only that for which it has the capacity, and because of the nature of the cause, the effect exists [in the cause]. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 9)

Nor should it be argued that in the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the cause would be rendered useless; for causes serve the purpose of manifestation. Just as rice, milk, and oil are produced through threshing, milking, and pressing, so too do the principles beginning with *kāla* and ending with *prthivī*, as well as their transformations such as jars and the like, come into being. And as for destruction...

For them, it is merely a matter of concealment (*tirobhāva*), not non-existence. Nor should it be argued that if one accepts the manifestation of a manifestation, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); for the same applies to production (*utpatti*). Thus, the production of a cloth—whether defined as its inherence in its own causes or its inherence in its own existence—is not itself produced; nevertheless, causal factors (*kāraka*) are employed for its sake. In this way, even though the jar and so forth already exist, they [manifest] by themselves.
Thus, it is logical that for the manifestation [of an effect], there is a dependence upon causes. As it was said by the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu:
"The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.16).
And in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:

"The best of sages have declared this entire universe to be imperishable and eternal, yet it possesses the conceptual distinctions of manifestation and disappearance, and of birth and destruction. (1.22.60)
Alternatively, the "distinction" (viśeṣa) established by the relationship of part and whole is a conceptual construct;

for the properties of having causes, impermanence, non-pervasiveness, activity, multiplicity, dependence, being a mark (liṅgatva), possessing parts, and dependence on others exist in the manifest entities (vyakta) ranging from time (kāla) down to earth (avani).

The properties of being composed of the three *guṇas*, non-discriminative, objective, general, insentient, and productive belong to the *avyakta* (the unmanifest), which is the *māyā*-principle. However, these—such as having a cause and so forth, as well as being composed of the three *guṇas*—do not belong to Śiva, who is pure consciousness, nor to the *puruṣa*.

This is because those [properties] are established by the relationship of cause and effect, and such a causal relationship is impossible in the *puruṣa*, who is devoid of being either cause or effect.

"This dharma belongs to some [only]. As it has been said: "The manifest is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composed of parts, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite."

"The manifest and the Pradhāna are composed of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive; the Puruṣa is the opposite of these and likewise [in certain respects]. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 10–11)
Alternatively, a limb is insentient because it exists for the sake of consciousness; its possessor (the whole) is sentient because it is the principal.

The state of these two is their relationship. The "distinction" that is the reverse of that is the mutual superimposition, which is the distinction established by the relationship of limb and possessor.
As it has been said:

"Therefore, through conjunction with that [Purusha], the insentient linga appears as if it were sentient; and while the gunas are the agents, the indifferent [Purusha] likewise appears as if he were the agent. (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 20)

Alternatively, the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (aṅgāṅgibhāva) is the relationship between the primary and the secondary (pradhānāpradhānabhāva). Intellect (buddhi) is the primary [factor], because it is most closely proximate to the Puruṣa; therefore, it possesses the status of being the principal. The external senses are the subordinates and are secondary, because they are accomplished by means of that [intellect]. Thus, there exists a distinction based on their respective natures among certain causes. As it has been said:
These specific qualities, which are like lamps and mutually distinct,
having illuminated the entire purpose of the Puruṣa, present it to the intellect.

"Since the intellect accomplishes every object of experience for the Puruṣa, it is that very same intellect which again distinguishes the subtle difference between Pradhāna and Puruṣa. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 36–37)
Therefore, the production of the principles [occurs] from that very [source]. || 4 ||
Regarding the question "What is this function?", he says: "Sound and so forth.
This is because the groups of *tanmātras* and *bhūtas* are identical in that they possess the qualities (*guṇas*) such as sound, and are equally denotable by the term "effect" (*kārya*).

The sequential order (anvaya) is to be understood as twofold. Among all these principles (tattvas), there is a distinction for some—such as Bindu, Māyā, and the rest—in that they function as the primary members (aṅgin) by virtue of being causes, while others—such as Śakti and the rest—function as subordinate members (aṅga) by virtue of being effects.
Thus he says: "The relationship of member and principal" (aṅgāṅgī). || 66 ||
This stability of all the principles has been described according to the order of emanation;
through reverse transformation, they dissolve back into Māyā.
The *Tātparyadīpikā*, having thus described the sequence of the creation and the persistence of the principles (*tattva*s), states the sequence of their dissolution: "Of the principles," etc.
The creation of these principles in the manner previously described, as well as their persistence within their respective causes, has been explained.
By reversing the process of transformation, those [elements] dissolve into their respective causes within Māyā; thus they are said to "dissolve" (līyante). || 5 ||
Commentary: Now he concludes the definition of the principles (*tattva*) with the words "of the principles" (*tattvānām*).

He states the process of dissolution with the word "in reverse order" (*pratilomam*). This refers to the group of principles beginning with earth, [dissolving] into *māyā* by way of their absorption into their own respective causes.
The conclusion. || 67 ||
Beyond Māyā lies the pure path; the entire [universe] dissolves into Śakti.
She too, having attained non-differentiation, abides within Śiva, the Supreme Self. (68)
In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the doubt as to where those principles (*tattva*) that lie beyond *māyā* dissolve, it says: "Of *māyā*.
That path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) called "Pure" (*śuddha*), which lies beyond *māyā*, all of it dissolves into the principle of Power (*śaktitattva*).

That power remains merged and dissolved upon attaining oneness with Śiva; for this is understood from the Vedic scripture: "In the beginning, that One breathed by its own nature, without air" (Ṛgveda 10.129.2). || 6 ||

The function [of the withdrawal] is that of *māyā*. However, for *śuddhavidyā* and the rest, it is into the power known as *mahāmāyā*. The entire pure path (*adhvan*), augmented by time (*kāla*), is dissolved therein. As has been stated by us:
Earth is in smell, water in taste, fire in form, wind in touch, and space in sound; furthermore, these subtle elements (tanmātras) belong to the quality of darkness (tamas).
The organs of action, along with the mind, intellect, and senses, belong to the quality of passion (rajas), while those belonging to the quality of goodness (sattva) are the cognitive faculties.
That [intellect] dissolves into the qualities (guṇas), and that multitude of qualities goes to dissolution in the unmanifest (avyakta).
That [Māyā], along with rāga and avidyā, attains the state of kalā; and Kāla, Niyati, and Kalā attain the state of the individual soul (puṃstva).
This [Māyā] reaches the level of Vidyeśvara within the Māyās, together with Sadāśiva.
"She is Śakti; he is Śiva; this is the Bindu.

In that context, by the word "Śiva," the world of Śāntyatīta (Beyond Peace), situated at the summit of the Śāntikalā (the Power of Peace), is denoted. And at that time, [the phrase] "in the Supreme Self" refers to that Mahāmāyā; by the word "also" (api), it is meant that she resides in the consciousness of the self enveloped by impurity (mala). And Māyā resides in Śiva.

It should be explained that while the presiding Lord exists as the efficient cause (*nimittabhūta*), the effect remains solely within the Self alone, undivided and existing in the very nature of the cause; it does not, however, attain inherence (*samavāya*) by becoming non-different from Śiva, for that would entail defects such as the Self undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) through inherence with consciousness. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
Even while in sleep, he remains awakening those fit for awakening,
restraining those fit for restraint, ripening the karma of those under the influence of karma, and manifesting the powers of *māyā* that are ready for manifestation.
"Seeing all the various classes of entities exactly as they are" (Vi.
And that [consciousness], relying upon the Self, remains for the sake of rest.
"Because he is devoted to the welfare of all beings, for those living creatures who are weary of cyclic existence. || 68 ||
Māyā, Puruṣa, and Śiva—this triad remains during the withdrawal of the Great Purpose; then, once again, it proceeds as before in the process of emanation. (69)

In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the objection that at the time of dissolution (*saṃhāradaśā*) the total destruction of everything makes a subsequent re-emergence impossible, he says: "Māyā... and so forth.
In the dissolution of the principles from Kāla down to Avani among those of great significance, as well as the pure Vidyeśvaras and Sadāśivas,
because Māyā, Puruṣa, and Śiva— the causes of the world— still exist, the production of the world occurs once again just as before. || 7 ||

And from that follows the definition: "Māyā. This is the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya), because of the existence of the dissolution of the end of the three worlds and the middle, which is the end of the qualities (guṇas).
There is a complete dissolution [of all things], because even the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) attain liberation therein. Only a triad beginning with Māyā remains.
In that context, by the term "Māyā," as expressed in the Tantras, two types of material causes (upādāna)—namely Māyā and Mahāmāyā—are denoted.
By the word "Puruṣa," used in the singular to denote a class, all bound souls (baddhātman) endowed with impurity (mala) are meant; and by the word "Śiva,"...

Śiva, as well as the liberated souls, are endowed with conjoined powers. Furthermore, at the end of the dissolution, He proceeds as previously described for the sake of creating those entities beginning with Śiva. (69)
Out of compassion, the Lord brings about the withdrawal of all these great objects for the sake of the rest of all living beings who are weary in saṃsāra. (70)
In the *Tātparyadīpikā*, having raised the objection, "Well then, what is the purpose of dissolution?", he says: "The cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
[This refers to] that which arises from the incessant contact with bodies, senses, and objects as they are produced.

The Lord, whose heart is overflowing with compassion, effects the withdrawal of the Great Purpose for the sake of providing rest to living beings who have become exhausted by the activity of experiencing pleasure and pain. As it has been said: "Just as night serves as a time of rest for those whose minds are preoccupied with their duties,"
Out of compassion, Śiva effects the withdrawal [of the world] for those weary of worldly existence. Thus [it is said]. (8)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Discussion on Universals, in the *Tattvaprakāśatātparyadīpikā*.
Commentary: Now he states the purpose of this great dissolution: "In saṃsāra... (verse 70).
For the sake of ripening their karma, out of compassion for those bound in animal existence, the Supreme Lord again creates them here and brings the karma of those embodied beings to fruition.
The Tātparyadīpikā: Now begins the sixth chapter.
Now, one might object that it is improper for him to engage in creation once again, since rest alone constitutes the goal of the Puruṣa; anticipating this doubt, he says:

Regarding the term "action" (*karman*): this is the intended meaning. Observing those bound by action—beings who, being like cattle, are devoid of liberation (which consists of the cessation of all suffering and the attainment of eternal, unsurpassed bliss) and have not realized the goal of human existence, and who are thus objects of compassion—the Blessed Lord ordains the creation of the body, the senses, and their objects as the means for the removal of the bondage of action through experience. And the removal of their bondage of action [is achieved]...
"For the sake of liberation" means that creation for the purpose of liberation is logically established. || 1 ||

"Vṛttiḥ karma" means: for the sake of the rest of all souls and for the ripening of their karmas; and because this [power] is an indicative mark, it also serves for Māyā, whose power has not been diminished by the incessant production of infinite bodies and so forth.

The meaning is that withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is for the purpose of generating capacity. He states that even emission (*sṛṣṭi*) is for the sake of liberation by saying "out of compassion for bound souls" (*paśudayayā*). It "ripens karma," meaning it ripens it specifically; that is to say, it brings previously accumulated karmas forward as objects of experience in the sequence of their maturation for the sake of [experiencing] karma. || 71 ||

Having brought about the ripening of karma through experience, Śambhu—the eternal treasure-house of compassion—always liberates all bound souls (paśus) by means of the power known as initiation (dīkṣā). 72.
The *Tātparyadīpikā* asks: "By what, then, is the ripening of karma brought about, and how is liberation possible? To this, it says: "By experience (*bhogena*).
The underlying intention is as follows: the Lord Time brings about the ripening—that is, the destruction—of karma through experience.

While waiting for the equilibrium of karma to occur, Śambhu—being supremely compassionate—matures the power that grants liberation, becomes a teacher (*ācārya*), and having performed the initiation (*dīkṣā*), liberates all those bound souls (*paśu*) who are worthy of final release at all times.
Now, one might object: "There is no such human goal as liberation, nor even one called heaven, because there is a lack of valid evidence for the existence of either."

Nor should it be said that the existence of those two [the self and the external world] is established through inference and scripture, because inference and scripture lack validity. Among these, inference lacks validity because it depends upon the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is impossible in this case;
for the probandum and the probans are not perceptible due to being situated in different places and times.

Because it is impossible to apprehend through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) that constitutes the rule of literary [logical] connection; nor can it be said that the apprehension of that invariable concomitance occurs through inference (*anumāna*), for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): namely, that the operation of inference occurs once the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been apprehended, and the apprehension of pervasion occurs once the operation of inference has taken place. Nor [can it be apprehended] by another inference...

The apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible, because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor can the apprehension of pervasion be derived from scripture (*āgama*), because that [scripture] is itself doubtful and because such [pervasion] is not perceived therein. Furthermore, it should not be said that the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*) arises from a means of proof (*sādhana*) where the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) has not been grasped, for that would result in an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, perception alone is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And since that does not bring about the understanding of heaven (*svarga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), [it follows that... *Note: The sentence fragment ending in "kāma" appears to be incomplete.*
Thus, pleasure (*prīti*) is the primary human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and wealth (*artha*) is [also a goal] because it is a means to that. As it has been said:

"The human goal is pleasure accomplished through the functioning [of the senses]; that is desire alone and nothing else, such as liberation (*mokṣa*) and so forth, because that would entail the abandonment of what is perceived and the postulation of what is unperceived.
Likewise, earth, water, fire, and air alone are the principles (*tattva*).

The Cārvāka maintains that because the body, the sense organs, and their objects are merely aggregates, there is no distinct reality (*tattvāntara*) apart from them; nor is cognition a distinct reality, for—like the redness produced by contact with lac-dye—it is determined to be an attribute of the elements (*bhūta*) since it arises from their inherence (*samavāya*). This is incorrect, because [the existence of such a self] remains doubtful given the lack of authority in inference and scripture.
Otherwise, it would follow that it is impossible for a speaker to employ words toward an object of instruction that is already perverted.
For instance, having inferred through signs such as the words of the person to be instructed that "ignorance, doubt, or error exists in this person," one thinks:
"By means of the words uttered by me, this person will achieve a correct understanding; [therefore] those words shall remove his ignorance and so forth."
For the employment of words by a speaker toward a person to be instructed is preceded by inference, such as [the inference] "he will dispel [my doubt]" and so forth.

If it were not preceded by that, there would be the undesirable consequence of the speaker being treated with indifference like a madman; furthermore, ignorance, doubt, and error residing in another cannot be apprehended through direct perception. Therefore, even one who does not wish [to employ words] must [accept this].

The Cārvāka must accept the validity of inference and scripture, because if words were incapable of producing valid cognition, the employment of [logical] arguments would become impossible. Nor is inference invalid due to the impossibility of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*), for that is possible through the mediation of universals (*sāmānya*), just as the relation [of concomitance] is grasped across all individual instances. To explain:

At the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), by setting aside specific qualities such as smallness and so forth, one grasps that "whatever belongs to the class of smoke does not deviate from whatever belongs to the class of fire. By virtue of this inclusion of universals (*sāmānya-upagrāhaka-vaśāt*), all individual instances—those yet to be born, those already passed, and those presently existing—are grasped as such through their respective class-memberships. Since the pervasion is thus grasped, there is no impossibility of grasping the pervasion; therefore, the grasping of pervasion occurs between two universals alone.
The argument that "the specific [nature] is established by the logic of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established incidentally)" is refuted by the following:
"Because there is no concomitance (*anugama*) with respect to the specific, and because proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) applies to the general,
and because that which possesses those [qualities] is untenable, whence can there be any talk of inference?"

For it has already been stated that the occurrence of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth is possible; likewise, the occurrence of all activities such as eating is possible, because they are preceded by inference. Furthermore, for a person who has understood the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), the cognition of fire is observed upon seeing smoke. What kind of form, then, should this [cognition] be accepted as? It cannot, first of all, be of the nature of an error (*viparyaya*).

It is not [mere] absence, because there is no sublation and because direct perception is possible. Nor is it of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it lacks the defining characteristic stated in the *Yogasūtra* (1.9): "Conceptual construction is that which follows upon verbal knowledge and is devoid of a real object. Nor is it sleep, because deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is absent.
Nor is it of the nature of memory, because it is not produced solely by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising from smoke and the like, and because it appears as "this-ness" (*idantayā*).

And because there is an absence of such a prior experience, it is not of the nature of doubt either; for the definition of doubt has been stated as "knowledge that is non-determinative," and that definition is absent here. Therefore, this cognition is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor is it perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is not produced by the contact of the sense organ with the object. Furthermore, there is no contact of the object, fire, with the eye or other senses.

Because it is obstructed, visual consciousness is for the purpose of producing the cognition of smoke—which is the cause for the cognition of fire—just as the operation of the auditory faculty is for the purpose of the cognition of sound, which is the cause for the cognition of heaven and so forth. Furthermore, since there is no dependence on the eyes and other senses in cases such as inference based on what has already been inferred (*anumitānumāna*), it is established that inference is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, inference is proven.
The authority of scripture (*āgama*) has already been described, so let us refrain from further elaboration.

For instance: the aggregate of body, senses, and their functions exists for the sake of another, because it is a means to experience; and it is a means to experience because it is insentient (*jaḍa*), and it is insentient because it is an effect, like a house, a field, or similar objects. Thus, the Supreme Self (*ātman*), distinct from the material elements, is established. Of that [Self]...

Eternality [of the self] exists because it does not perish even upon the destruction of the body; and that [eternality] is understood through such means as the recollection of past births. Furthermore, its liberation [is possible] because it is bound; therefore, since liberation occurs only occasionally, it depends upon a cause.
And the cause is [the performance of] dharma and adharma characterized by non-violence and violence, respectively.
"The Digambaras say that liberation arises from the non-injury of the body and so forth.
For instance: attachment to permanence and aversion toward impermanence—both of these are to be abandoned through the cultivation of non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
To illustrate: a jar and the like are permanent in their nature as clay and so forth, because they are perceived in all their various states.

An object such as a jar is impermanent by virtue of its form as a jar, because that [form] eventually perishes. Likewise, the existence of objects consists in their being supported by their own place, time, and cause; their non-existence consists in their not being present in other places and so forth; their agency consists in their producing their own effects and their non-agency in producing other effects; their denotability consists in their being expressible by their own name and their non-denotability by other names. In this way, the manifold nature (anekāntatva) of objects is to be inferred.
The Digambaras [assert this].

However, this is untenable, because the meditation on non-absolutism (*anekānta-bhāvanā*), being false in nature, cannot be a means to liberation (*apavarga*). This is because it is perceived as having a determinate form, such as existence and so forth, restricted to its own locus and other attributes. Likewise...

Furthermore, because an effect such as a jar is eternal and its cause, such as clay, is invariably eternal, it cannot possess a dual nature. Likewise, since it is expressible by its own name and also expressible by other names, there is no inconclusiveness [regarding its nature]. As for this aforementioned duality of form, therein lies the dispute.

For we also accept [non-existence] by way of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). Furthermore, if things were non-existent even in their own locations and so forth, then there would be the manifold nature (*anekāntatā*) of objects; but that is not the case. Therefore, since objects do not possess a manifold nature, the knowledge of manifoldness—being false—is not the cause of liberation. Nor does [liberation arise] by virtue of the cultivation of manifoldness...

There is no proof for the attainment of an imperishable body and so forth in a specific location. Nor is their scripture (āgama) a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks a foundation in a valid means of knowledge. Furthermore, it has been stated that the authority of words in non-eternal scriptures—which lack a foundation in perception, inference, or eternal scripture—is not possible. Nor [is there proof] regarding the body, the sense organs, and their objects...

The permanence of effects is impossible, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, that which has been asserted by certain followers of the Ārhata school—namely, that the ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) consists in the soul, which is limited in size to the body, remaining like a star after the destruction of the body—that too is not tenable; for if the soul were limited in size to the body, it would follow that it is material (*mūrta*) and therefore impermanent, just like the body. Likewise, [this would apply] to one who has occupied the body of an elephant...

Upon entering the body of a mosquito, there would follow the consequence of [the self] being subject to transformation (pariṇāmitva), by resorting to contraction and expansion— just as the light of a lamp covered by a drum contracts like the lid of a jar.
Therefore, among the six categories consisting of form, taste, smell, touch, sound, and consciousness, that which...

The fourfold categories known as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—meditation upon these as being momentary and so forth is the cause of liberation (*apavarga*). According to the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists), liberation is the arising of a pure continuum of consciousness. Suffering consists of the five aggregates (*skandha*), beginning with form (*rūpa*); namely, the aggregate of form, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā*), and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā*).

The aggregate of formations and the aggregate of consciousness—these constitute the five aggregates. Among them, the aggregate of form is fourfold, consisting of color, odor, taste, and tangibility. The aggregate of feeling is threefold: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neutral feeling. [The aggregate of perception consists of] the perception of the eye, the perception of the tongue, the perception of the ear, and the perception of the nose.

The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is of six types: the perception of touch and the perception of mind. The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is of two types, distinguished as wholesome and unwholesome. Among these, the unwholesome is of ten kinds, categorized by way of mind, speech, and body. Therein, the mental [unwholesome] consists of the three: false view, desire, and hatred. The vocal [unwholesome]...

There are four types of unwholesome verbal actions: false speech, slanderous speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech. There are three types of unwholesome physical actions: violence, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. Thus, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) consists of twenty types. Furthermore, there are ten wholesome [actions] which are the opposites of these; likewise, the aggregate of formations is of twenty kinds. [The five consciousnesses are: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, [tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness].

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is of six kinds: visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness. Thus, because it is a cause of suffering and is mixed with suffering, even pleasure is suffering. Its cause is the origin (*samudaya*). Their cessation is destruction (*nirodha*). The means for that is the path (*mārga*). Through the very state of being momentary and so forth, by the power of meditation, one realizes that [everything] is momentary.

The cessation of passion and the like occurs because of the absence of the relationship "this is mine. Likewise, the cessation of passion and the like results from the cultivation of selflessness (*nirātmaka-bhāvanā*), due to the absence of a connection between self and other. Similarly, the cessation of passion and the like arises from the cultivation that "all is empty," because of non-existence;
for indeed, passion and the like cannot possibly arise with respect to things such as a sky-flower or the son of a barren woman.

The Vaibhāṣikas, Sautrāntikas, and the Buddhist proponents of non-dual knowledge maintain that liberation is the arising of a pure continuum of consciousness (*cittasantati*). The proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) maintain that even the destruction of the pure continuum of consciousness constitutes liberation.
This, however, is untenable, because meditations on momentariness and the like are of a false nature.

This is because [the practice] cannot be a means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Nor should it be argued that the cultivation of momentariness is not false, since the momentariness of objects—namely, their form, taste, smell, touch, and cognitions—is established by the inference: "All entities are momentary because they exist, like consciousness. For that [inference] is like the argument for the non-hot nature of fire based on its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which lacks valid evidence (*māna*).

This is because [the claim that the pot is momentary] is invalid due to being sublated by such direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) as "this is that very same pot. Nor should it be argued that this [perception] lacks validity—just like the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "this is that very same nail" or "these are those very same hairs"—because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) for this [perception].
Furthermore, it should not be argued that this [recognition] is sublated by the inference itself, since inference is rooted in perception.
Because it is impossible for [the inference] to subvert its own basis; nor is the perception grasping heat subverted by that which establishes non-heat.

Likewise, since consciousness—by virtue of persisting for three moments—lacks momentariness, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). Now, one might object: since existence characterized by causal efficiency is impossible for a non-momentary entity, the observed existence...

One should establish the momentariness of earth and the other elements. For instance: if that which is momentary were to produce everything it brings about all at once, then it would not do so even in subsequent moments; for in that case, everything would be known at that very time, since its cause would already exist. Indeed, it is not possible for an effect not to arise when its cause is present. Nor can it act sequentially, because in the first moment...

For this reason, since there is no possibility of delay due to the existence of this [entity] which serves as the cause for effects arising in subsequent moments, it cannot be argued that the production of the effect occurs in accordance with the attainment of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). This is because, if the excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by the auxiliary factor—or the destruction of the cause—were distinct from the cause itself, it would be as irrelevant as everything else other than that cause. Thus, in the absence of such an excellence...

If [the cause] were the cause of producing an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the cessation [of the effect], then since it would be distinct from a cause that depends on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its producing that [effect] even when those [auxiliaries] are absent. Furthermore, if it neither produced an excellence nor removed the lack of excellence, then there would be the undesirable consequence that the auxiliaries would be as disregarded as everything else other than it.
Therefore, because they lack existence characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), non-momentary things are non-existent. Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): whatever...
"That which does not produce an effect either successively or simultaneously does not exist, just like a donkey's horn;

and non-momentary things do not produce effects either successively or simultaneously. Therefore, since existence—though perceived in the subjects such as earth—is impossible in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) even in the absence of a similar instance (sapakṣa), it proves momentariness. This is not so.

Even for non-momentary things, it is logically possible for them to produce an effect in that same manner through successive or simultaneous acquisition of auxiliary conditions. Now, an objection was raised: the alternatives presented—whether the auxiliaries impart an excellence (*atiśaya*) to the cause or remove its lack of excellence—are untenable because [the cause] already exists; for this very [existence] is itself the excellence. That which, upon its presence, causes an effect to be produced, is the excellence of that [cause]; thus, the causal factors such as clay and so forth [are themselves the excellence].

Since it is observed that [the potter's wheel and other factors] produce an effect such as a jar when they are present together as auxiliary causes, that [wheel, etc. is a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) of that [clay]. || 2 ||
And from that, when the ripening of impurity occurs gradually— by means of experience (*bhoga*).
When the impurity has ripened, because the karmas have ripened simultaneously, [the teacher acts] by his own power known as initiation (*dīkṣā*).

The meaning is that, either through the manifestation of the teacher’s activity alone or by itself, having brought about the destruction of karma—which consists in the simultaneous enjoyment of manifold experiences—he liberates the bound souls (*paśu*) from impurity (*mala*) and the other [obstacles]. As it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"Karma pertaining to many births is like a burnt seed for the individual souls (*aṇu*)."
"For that by which even the future [karma] is restrained is indeed the bestower of enjoyment" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.1.19).

For this very reason, it is established that in the initiation for immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), there is the destruction of even that karma whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*)—the karma that initiated the present body. Furthermore, there are divisions of initiation, such as the final (*naiṣṭhikī*) and others.
This should be understood from the venerable Mataṅga and other such scriptures. || 72 ||
That which remains until the dissolution of the universe, providing enjoyment for all beings, is declared to be the Reality (tattva); therefore, the body, a jar, and so forth, are not the Reality.
In the *Tātparyadīpikā*,
having raised the objection that it cannot be said there are only thirty-six principles because the body, a jar, and so forth also exist, he says: "Until the dissolution" (*ā pralayam*).

This is the intended meaning: because the body, a jar, and so forth lack the defining characteristic of a *tattva* (principle), there is no increase in the number of *tattvas* by virtue of their existence. To explain: the definition of a *tattva* is that which persists until the state of dissolution (*pralaya*) and serves as the cause of experience for all beings; this definition does not apply to the body, a jar, and so forth, because they do not pervade those respective places and times. Thus, regarding the body, a jar, and so forth...

Furthermore, because they consist of the functioning of the principles (tattva) such as earth and so forth—just like the determination (*adhyavasāya*) and other functions of the intellect (*buddhi*)—it is impossible for them to be distinct principles; thus, there is no excess of principles. As it was said by the venerable teacher, the Guru-devācārya:
"The wise know them as *tattvas* because of their being that (*tata*) and because of their continuity (*santata*)."
Continuity is pervasion in terms of space, and persistence is [pervasion] in terms of time.
"The reality (tattva) pervading hundreds of thousands of yojanas and so forth remains until the dissolution of the world;
otherwise, even pillars, jars, and the like would result in being [considered] reality. (3)

If this is so, why is the body and so forth not included among the categories of reality? To this he says: "until dissolution. Therefore, that which bestows experience either directly or indirectly and persists until the state of dissolution— [The remainder of the sentence follows: —that alone is [to be enumerated]. Thus, the body and so forth are excluded from the list of categories because they are merely instruments for the sake of another. However, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and the *puruṣa* (spirit) are included because they are the ultimate causes of experience. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* are eternal; therefore, they are not mentioned as being "until dissolution," for there is no such thing as their dissolution. On the other hand, the body and so forth are impermanent; hence, they are mentioned as lasting "until dissolution. Thus, it is established that the body and so forth are not enumerated as categories of reality. This is the conclusion. Now, one might ask: if the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* are eternal, then how can there be liberation (*mokṣa*)? To this he says: "the cessation of the conjunction of the two. The conjunction of the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* is the cause of bondage. When that conjunction ceases, liberation occurs. How does that cessation come about? It is said: "through the discernment of the difference between the two. Through the discernment of the distinction between the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*, the conjunction ceases. Why? Because the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. Once its purpose has been fulfilled, it no longer acts. And since the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, it is indifferent (*udāsīna*). Thus, when the conjunction ceases, the *puruṣa* abides in its own nature, free from all qualities (*guṇa*), and this is called liberation. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it perceive objects? To this he says: "it perceives through the intellect. The *puruṣa* perceives objects by means of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is its instrument. Just as a king sees through his minister, so the *puruṣa* sees through the intellect. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* perceives through the intellect, then is it not subject to change? To this he says: "it is immutable. The *puruṣa* is unchanging; it does not undergo modification. How then does it perceive? It is said: "it reflects the image of the intellect. The intellect, being transparent, reflects its own form onto the *puruṣa*. The *puruṣa*, though itself unchanging, appears as if changed due to the reflection of the intellect. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then what is the purpose of the *pradhāna*? To this he says: "for the sake of the experience and liberation of the *puruṣa*. The *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the experience and liberation of the *puruṣa*. Experience consists of the perception of sound and the other sense objects. Liberation is the cessation of the conjunction. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*, then why does it not act for all *puruṣas* simultaneously? To this he says: "it acts according to the specific capacity of each. The *pradhāna* acts according to the specific capacity of each individual *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*, then is it not subject to the fault of being insentient? To this he says: "it is insentient. The *pradhāna* is indeed insentient, yet it acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to have experience? To this he says: "experience is the apprehension of the intellect's form. Experience is the apprehension of the form of the intellect by the *puruṣa*. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be liberated? To this he says: "liberation is the cessation of the conjunction. When the conjunction ceases, the *puruṣa* is liberated. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be bound? To this he says: "bondage is the conjunction with the intellect. Bondage is the conjunction of the *puruṣa* with the intellect. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be an enjoyer? To this he says: "it is the enjoyer. The *puruṣa* is the enjoyer. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be a witness? To this he says: "it is the witness. The *puruṣa* is the witness. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be isolated? To this he says: "it is isolated. The *puruṣa* is isolated. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be neutral? To this he says: "it is neutral. The *puruṣa* is neutral. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be inactive? To this he says: "it is inactive. The *puruṣa* is inactive. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be eternal? To this he says: "it is eternal. The *puruṣa* is eternal. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be omnipresent? To this he says: "it is omnipresent. The *puruṣa* is omnipresent. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be partless? To this he says: "it is partless. The *puruṣa* is partless. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be unchanging? To this he says: "it is unchanging. The *puruṣa* is unchanging. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be non-material? To this he says: "it is non-material. The *puruṣa* is non-material. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be devoid of qualities? To this he says: "it is devoid of qualities. The *puruṣa* is devoid of qualities. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be beyond the reach of the senses? To this he says: "it is beyond the reach of the senses. The *puruṣa* is beyond the reach of the senses. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be unmanifest? To this he says: "it is unmanifest. The *puruṣa* is unmanifest. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the *puruṣa* is pure consciousness, then how can it be said to be non-dual? To this he says: "it is non-dual. The *puruṣa* is non-dual. This is
Thus, "the reality" (tattva) has been stated. For this very reason, we have presented the principles (tattvas) according to the order of dissolution (saṃhārakrama), as follows:
earth, water, fire, air, ether, smell, taste, form, touch, sound;
the generative organ, anus, feet, hands, mouth, nose, tongue, eyes, skin, ears, and the mind.

"I praise Śiva—the pride, the quality of intellect, here [the principle of] Rāga, the Puruṣas, Vidyā, Niyati, Kalā, Kāla, and the power (śakti) residing in the Lord who is both delusion and awakening.
In this verse, by the inversion of the order in the phrase "rāgapuruṣān," it is shown that the Puruṣa does not constitute a path (adhvan). || 73 ||
That from which a reality arises, that which is its cause and its fulfiller—that is declared to be the established order of all realities whatsoever. (74)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* concludes the subject matter proposed [at the outset] with the words "tattvam" (the reality).
The meaning is as follows: the systematic arrangement of all the principles (*tattvas*), beginning from Śiva down to the earth, has been explained.

Likewise, the form known as Śiva—partless (niṣkala), transcending the paths, and the constant fulfiller (āpūraka) of all principles (tattvas)—has been described; for it is said in the scripture: "Therefore, by this Puruṣa, all this is filled" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9).
Whatever principle exists, whatever cause, and whatever fulfiller or instrument there may be—that too has been described. Thus ends the fourth [verse].

Function consists of the performance of what has not been done and the further development of what has been done; this is a property of the intellect (buddhi). Now, he concludes the section: "The established order has been explained. (74)
He by whom even the reality of all realities was explained with ease—that King Śrī Bhojadeva composed this *Tattvaprakāśa*. (75)
The *Tātparyadīpikā* illuminates its own author for the purpose of accepting the treatise: "Of the principles...
By whom [the truth] of even the principles—their very nature—was previously grasped in its entirety, as a whole, with ease and without exertion.

It has been stated that he himself composed the *Tattvaprakāśa*, having arranged it in its various divisions. Now, one might object: the acceptance of a scripture does not arise merely from the knowledge that it was composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*), because the acceptance of a scripture must be preceded by the knowledge that it is logically consistent (*yuktiyukta*). As the venerable Bhaṭṭācārya has said:
"One may, if one wishes, eat grains or consume buffalo curds."
"If a composition is endowed with reasoning, it should indeed be accepted by the wise.

This is not so, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). For there would be an understanding of its being endowed with reasoning for one who is engaged in hearing [the scripture], and engagement in hearing would occur only when there is an understanding of its being endowed with reasoning. Therefore, at the outset of hearing, there must be an understanding that it was composed by a reliable authority (*āpta*).

The cause of engagement (*pravṛttihetu*). For it is logical that the author is mentioned because engagement [with the text] occurs due to great respect for the author, such as [thinking], "This was composed by Manu" or "This was composed by Vyāsa. Here, cessation (*nivṛtti*) is the path of the *kalās* (*kalādhvā*). The path of the *tattvas* (*tattvādhvā*) is the earth (*pṛthivī*).

The path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvā*) consists of one hundred and eight worlds, beginning with Bhadrakālī and ending with Kālāgni. The letter *kṣa* is the path of the phonemes (*varṇādhvā*), or else the letter *la*.

The path of words (*padādhvan*) consists of twenty-eight words. The path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) consists of the two mantras known as Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya. The extraction of the words is stated as follows: "O best of sages, that which is the word of Mahādeva is taught to consist of four syllables; however, the one designated as Sadbhāveśvara consists of five syllables."
The word "mahātejaḥ" is declared to consist of four syllables;
the word known as "yogādhipati" is specified as having five syllables.
Release, release! The four-syllable and six-syllable [mantras] are of the nature of the first;
here, the four-syllable [mantra] "Śarva-śarva-pada" is to be understood.
Likewise, there is a pair of *bhava* syllables, and again the word *bhavodbhava*;
then another eight-syllable word that bestows happiness upon all beings.
Preceded by the presence of all, ending with the hand, consisting of seven syllables,
it is the eight-syllabled mantra, the supreme beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
A word consisting of eight syllables that is unaccented and repeated twice is called an *asaṃskṛta-pada* (unrefined word); likewise, it is also a *pūrvasthita-pada* (previously situated word).
In the *sākṣin* meter, there are likewise four syllables in each quarter due to the doubling;
in the *ṣaṭpataṅga* meter, there are four syllables in the *piṅga* name.
In the same way, the state of knowledge (jñānapada) consists of four syllables known as *śabda* and *sūkṣma*;
likewise, the state of Śiva (*śivapada*) and the state of the All-pervasive Lord Śarva (*śarvapada*) consist of two syllables each.
The three-syllabled mantra that bestows all things begins with the *praṇava* and is "namo namaḥ.
The five-syllabled mantra "śivāya" is declared to be three-syllabled [when combined with the *praṇava*].
"The pair of bows, five-colored, with the star, is the supreme word.
Now, from what and how does the arising of the *kalās* occur? We reply: by the will of Śiva, from the *bindu*. This has been stated in the *Gurudevapaddhati*:
From that Bindu, which is of the nature of Nāda, the five Kalās beginning with Nivṛtti have been set in motion by the will of Śiva; in these the entire universe is established.
In this world, the mantras are pervaded on all sides by words and syllables;
the syllables are pervaded by the worlds, and those worlds are pervaded by the principles (tattvas).
These principles (tattvas) here are pervaded by the kalās in succession;
the principle of Śakti is established from Sadāśiva down to the level of Bhūmi.
Thus, beginning with Sadāśiva, [the hierarchy] remains pervading its own effects;
it has the four ages as its great feet and the earth-principle as its root-cavity.
That [lotus] has its stalk from the principle of time (kālatattva), possesses fifty stamens representing the states of existence (bhāva),
a great knot of the principle of illusion (māyātattva), and is adorned with the lotus of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā).

"The pedestal (pīṭha) should be fashioned in this manner: covered by the petals of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara), joined with the filaments of Power (śakti), and originating from the seed-syllables of the Mātṛkās. Thus [it is said].
It is complete with the limbs described for the path of time (kālādhvan), and it bears the hair-pores described for the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan).
Endowed with the stated nature of the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), it is accompanied by the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) and blood.
It resides in the feet, the pathways, the head, the vessels, the flesh, the semen, the marrow, the bones, and the skin.
Sadāśiva is the essence of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan); his vital breath is known as Śiva.
Mahādeva, both transcendent and immanent, assumes a manifest form during meditation.
In the absence of that [manifest form], however, it is partless; yet it consists of thirty-eight kalās.
This triad—the seat, the form, and that which is to be invoked—is present throughout the path.
"Having understood [the relationship] through the state of the pervaded and the pervader, one should begin the sacrifice.
The seat extends up to Śuddhavidyā; the form (mūrti) has its range up to Śakti;
that which is to be invoked is the Śiva-tattva—this is the instruction of the Śaivas. Thus [ends verse 5].
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Nivṛtti," in the Tattvaprakāśatātparyadīpikā.

The commentary asks, "By whom was this treatise [composed]? and answers: "Of the principles" (*tattvānām*). The meaning is: by whom the illumination—that is, the knowledge—of the principles, the very nature of the principles, was told or made known. || 75 ||
That King Śrī Bhojadeva, in whose mind the entire collection of principles shines forth like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand,
[composed this work] for the sake of the meaning of the Śiva-āgamas.
He composed this incomparable illumination of reality. || 76 ||
The *Tātparyadīpikā* [is that work] in whose consciousness the entire collection of principles shines forth like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.
That King Śrī Bhojadeva composed this incomparable Tattvaprakāśa for the sake of the meaning of the Śiva-āgamas.
Salutations to that Blessed One, Bhoja, whose actions are effortless;
to Śiva, the devotee of Śiva, whose mind is solely intent upon Śiva.
Homage to Śiva, the sole cause of the birth, maintenance, and destruction of the entire world;
who possesses a single, eternal nature, and who bestows auspiciousness.
Whatever has been composed here by me with a mind overflowing with devotion, yet without having fully mastered the *Tattvaprakāśa*, the wise ought to forgive it.
Thus was it composed by the illustrious Śrīkumāra, the ornament of the Bhāradvāja lineage, son of Śaṅkara,
who was gratified by the ritual tasting of the essence of Soma juice, and whose mind acted like a bee clinging to the two lotus-feet of Śiva.
The *Tattvaprakāśa-tātparyadīpikā* is complete.
He elaborates on that very point [regarding] the "vṛtis" with the words "yasya" (of whom):
he who has attained the status of the supreme commentator upon the scriptures proclaimed by Śiva.

The wise Aghoraśiva, who is preeminent in the study of grammar and phonetics regarding general linguistic categories such as words and so forth, being earnestly requested by the ornaments of the Śaiva tradition, has clearly explained the *Tattvaprakāśa* in brief, he who is the most excellent of gurus.
Thus ends the *Tattvaprakāśikā* commentary, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand [verses].
